News.title: Manhunt for gunman as CCTV released of masked man in ‘distinctive’ bright orange hi-vis outfit & carrying backpack
News.content:
SHOOTING RIDDLE Manhunt for gunman as CCTV released of masked man in ‘distinctive’ bright orange hi-vis outfit & carrying backpack







Next

A MANHUNT has been launched after shots were fired in a cul-de-sac – with cops releasing CCTV of a masked man.

The footage was released after gunshots were reportedly fired in Toxteth, Liverpool, around 1.20pm on September 23.

Police revealed pictures showing a man wearing a hi- vis outfit and carrying a backpack.

The man was also wearing a balaclava and black gloves.





No damage or injuries were reported in the alleged shooting.

Merseyside Police said they are currently undergoing an extensive enquiry, including CCTV analysis, house-to-house enquiries and forensic examinations.

Police have also asked anyone who was in the area at the time or may have any information to get in contact.

Det Insp Chris Clark from the Firearms Investigation Team said: “Although the image does not show the person’s face, we think the distinctive clothing and bag may jog someone’s memory.



“You may have seen them in the area or be familiar with them from their clothing and build. Please come forward as soon as possible if so.

“Likewise, we are still looking for any other information to assist our ongoing investigation.

“If you live locally or were passing on the day of the incident, please check CCTV, dashcam or doorbell devices if you have not already.

“We will follow all leads to find those responsible and bring them to justice.”

News.title: Tributes paid to stepdad & son, 46 & 21, killed in horror crash with lorry as ‘driver’ arrested over ‘drink or drugs’
News.content:
CRASH TRAGEDY Tributes paid to stepdad & son, 46 & 21, killed in horror crash with lorry as ‘driver’ arrested over ‘drink or drugs’







Next

A STEPDAD and son who were killed in a horror crash have been pictured after a man was arrested on suspicion of driving while unfit.

Finley Munro, 21, and Paul Elliot, 46, died after their Vauxhall Astra collided with a Citroën C3 Picasso and a DAF lorry on the A49 just after 4pm on October 13.

Both men were declared dead at the scene and their families have paid tribute.

A 65-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of causing death by careless driving whilst unfit through drink or drugs and he has since been released on bail.





In a tribute Finley’s family said: “A much-loved son of Ellie Munro and his step-father Paul Elliott, who also sadly lost his life in this incident, much-loved partner of Jenna-May, much-loved brother to Martha and Ollie and a much-loved grandson.

“He will be deeply missed by all who knew him.”

In a second tribute Paul’s loved ones said: “He will be deeply missed by all who knew him.

“We would like to thank all emergency services for their incredible efforts and support.”



Detective Constable Joshua Wildig said: “Our thoughts remain firmly with family and loved ones at this incredibly difficult time.

“This is a deeply tragic incident, and we are committed to establishing exactly what happened in the moments leading up to the collision.

“We continue to carry out a thorough investigation and would urge anyone who may have witnessed the collision, or who was travelling in the area at the time and may have dashcam footage, to come forward and assist us.

“Even the smallest piece of information could prove vital in helping us provide answers for his family.”

News.title: Woman, 36, killed by car being chased by police in hit-and-run as manhunt launched after abandoned car found
News.content:
CHASE HORROR Woman, 36, killed by car being chased by police in hit-and-run as manhunt launched after abandoned car found







Next

A WOMAN has been killed after she was hit by a car involved in a police chase in a “hit and run”.

The 36-year-old pedestrian was rushed to hospital with serious injuries where she later died after the crash in Leeds just before 10am yesterday.

The black Vauxhall Corsa had failed to stop for officers just minutes before on Harehills Road.

It was later found abandoned on Nipper Lane and the occupants had fled the scene.





West Yorkshire Police have seized the car for forensic examination and launched a manhunt for the occupants.

A spokesperson for the force said: “At 9.50am this morning (29 October) a black Vauxhall Corsa failed to stop for officers on Harehills Road, Leeds.

“A pursuit was authorised and at 9.52am the Corsa was involved in a collision with a pedestrian on Beckett Street, the driver failed to stop at the scene.

“Emergency medical attention was given by officers at the scene. The 36-year-old woman was taken to hospital with serious injuries. Sadly, the woman died in hospital.

“The Corsa was then found abandoned on Nippet Lane, at least two people in the vehicle left the scene. The vehicle has been seized pending forensic examination.

“Enquiries are ongoing to locate the people in the vehicle.

“The Homicide and Major Enquiry Team have launched an investigation and are appealing for witnesses or anyone with dash-cam to come forward.

“Due to prior police contact a mandatory IOPC referral has been made.”

News.title: Brit student pilot among 3 killed as two helicopters crash into each other mid-air near airport in Oregon
News.content:
CHOPPER TRAGEDY Brit student pilot among 3 killed as two helicopters crash into each other mid-air near airport in Oregon







Next

A BRIT student pilot is among three dead after two helicopters crashed mid-air near an Oregon airport.

Texan flight instructor Maddie Aasbo, 22, who was flying with the unidentified Brit, and Tyler Delane Sturdevant, 38, were also killed.



The helicopters crashed in a field described as a “privately owned farm” after colliding near McMinnville Municipal Airport at 2.10pm local time.

It was not immediately clear what caused the collision.



The aircraft involved were a 1995 Robinson R22 Beta helicopter and an 2018 Airbus AS350B2 helicopter, according to the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB).

Police said the occupants of the Robinson R22 were identified as Maddie Aasbo and a student pilot from the UK, whose identity is being withheld pending next of kin notification.

Tyler, of Newberg, Oregon, was named as the Airbus pilot.

Yamhill County Sheriff Sam Elliott said the scene had been turned over the Federal Aviation Authority (FAA) and the NTSB, who sent to investigators to the crash site.

“After the wreckage is documented, it will be recovered and moved to a secure facility for further examination,” the NTSB said in a statement.

Jerry Trimble Helicopters said one of its helicopters was involved in the crash.



The company said in a statement: “Our hearts and thoughts are with the individuals involved, their families, and everyone affected by this event.

“We are immensely grateful for the rapid response and the dedication of local emergency services and first responders.”

It added that it was “fully cooperating” with local emergency, services, police, the FAA and the NTSB to determine the cause of the collision.

The crash closed Oregon Route 233, a highway bordering the field, for about one mile near McMinnville Airport.

It comes as four people were killed after a military helicopter plunged from the skies in Bosnia-Herzegovina.



The aircraft had been carrying personnel from the European Union‘s peacekeeping force when it suddenly plummeted into a field.

Horrifying photos show the massive Italian CH-47 Chinook helicopter lying destroyed on a lawn in the small village of Gorice near Brčko.

The chopper had been flying over Bosnia-Herzegovina as part of Operation Althea – established to keep peace over the region since the 1995 Dayton agreement spelled the end of the bloody Bosnian War.

Some 1,200 EUFOR soldiers took over from NATO back in 2004 to help maintain security.

The EUFOR military mission previously said “a number” of its crew had been killed and others injured.

“As a result of this crash, a number of EUFOR personnel tragically lost their lives, and others were seriously injured”, they said in a statement.

What caused the helicopter to crash is still unclear.

News.title: Mushroom killer Erin Patterson set to die in prison after appeal spectacularly backfires and increases her sentence
News.content:
Next

MUSHROOM killer Erin Patterson is set to die in prison after her appeal spectacularly backfired and increased her sentence instead.

The triple murderer was jailed for life with a non-parole period of 33 years for serving her estranged husbands relatives poisoned beef Wellingtons laced with death cap mushrooms.



But an Australian appeals court on Friday ordered Erin Patterson to never be released from prison after agreeing with prosecutors that her parole period was inadequate.

The three judges of the Victoria state Court of Appeal also dismissed Pattersons challenge to her convictions that stemmed from a family meal she hosted at her rural home in Leongatha in July 2023.



Patterson, 51, insisted she added death cap mushrooms to the meals accidentally.

Her mum-in-law Gail Patterson, dad-in-law Donald Patterson and Gail’s sister Heather Wilkinson died in hospital within six days of the fatal lunch in July 2023.

Patterson was also convicted for the attempted murder of Heather’s husband, Ian Wilkinson, a small-town local pastor who was the sole survivor of the poisoning.

She was sentenced last year to three life sentences for murder and 25 years for attempted murder with eligibility for parole after 33 years.



Patterson appealed the verdict and the Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP) appealed the sentence, arguing her non-parole period was “manifestly inadequate”.

Central to Patterson’s bid to overturn her conviction was the “catastrophic” decision to place members of the jury in the same hotel as a police witness, journalists and members of the prosecution.

Barrister Richard Edney argued that the move “fatally undermined the integrity of the verdicts” and means the verdicts should be quashed and a retrial should take place “so that justice can be done”.

But Justice Stephen McLeish today dismissed the arguments and denied the appeal.

Instead, the judge sided with the DPP’s appeal, meaning Patterson will spend the remainder of her years behind bars, reports 7News.



McLeish blasted Patterson’s crimes as “extraordinarily cold and calculated” and a “cruel breach of trust”.

Patterson will still be able to challenge the decision at Australia‘s High Court.

During the appeal, the court heard that, despite Edney’s complaints, there was no evidence that the jury came into contact with anyone at trial.



While the defence acknowledged that there was no evidence that the jury spoke with the witness or prosecution, they highlighted that the crossover occurred during jury deliberation week.

Another contentious point concerned the prosecution’s use of evidence about Patterson’s activity on the foraging website iNaturalist and mobile phone tower data.

At the trial, the prosecution argued that Patterson found two sightings of death cap mushrooms reported online near her home.

The court heard how her phone connected to cell towers in both areas, with the prosecution indicating she’d visited both spots.

Hours after visiting one of the locations, Patterson bought a food dehydrator to prepare the mushrooms for the fateful beef Wellingtons.



CCTV captured Patterson travelling to a local dump and disposing of the dehydrator, which was later found to have traces of the deadly mushrooms.

'MUSHROOM' MURDER TIMELINE All the twists & turns that led to Erin Patterson being jailed for life 2021-22 – A 48-year-old man, believed to Patterson’s ex-husband Simon, falls ill after three separate meails. July 29, 2023 – The deadly mushroom lunch takes place July 30 – Gail and Don Patterson & Heather and Ian Wilkinson are rushed to hospital – all die but Ian. August 5-7 – Patterson’s home is searched, she is questions and becomes an official suspect. November 2 – Police arrest and charge Patterson with three counts of murder and five of attempted murder. May 7, 2024 – Patterson pleads not guilty to the eight charges. April 29, 2025 – Her trial begins. The prosecuction drop three charges related to the attempted murder of Simon. July 7, 2025 – The jury finds Patterson guilty. September 8, 2025 – She is sentenced to life imprisonment with a non-parole period of 33 years.

When sentencing Patterson, the judge said that it didn’t necessarily matter where she sourced the mushrooms from as it was abundantly clear that she had.

Patterson has maintained she unknowingly used foraged death cap mushrooms in the meal.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

There were also complaints that prosecutors had been “unfair” in the court proceedings, as they made 35 complaints throughout.

Police have also alleged Patterson may have attempted to poison her ex-husband, Simon Patterson, on three separate occasions between 2021 and 2022.

News.title: Train driver, 36, dead in horror Spain smash that killed 69 is pictured as TV presenter, composer among missing
News.content:
Next

THE train driver behind the wheel in the horror railway crash in Spain has been pictured as heartbreaking details of his “hero” final moments emerge.

Antonio Acedo, 36, was in the cockpit of the Renfe train when it slammed into the back of a Iryo train at 124mph on Wednesday.



At least 69 people were killed in the devastating collision – with rescuers still combing the site for bodies and missing loved ones.

A headmaster, a composer, a TV presenter and a food bank volunteer are among those still missing.



More than 100 people were also injured – some of them critically – when multiple carriages derailed and flipped over down an embankment.

Both Antonio and his fellow trainee train driver sat beside him in the cockpit were killed.

The family of the deceased train driver have described him as a “hero” after revealing that Antonio activated the emergency brake – saving the lives of hundreds of passengers.

But the fate of him and Daniel Muñoz Cob, 31, sat beside him was sealed with a single haunting conversation.



Chilling audio recordings of communications between Madrid’s control room and Antonio reveal the exact moment the deadly mistake was made.

The command centre told him: “Resume [driving] at normal speed.”

“At normal speed?” Antonio asked.



“Yeah” the control worker replied.

The train driver was never informed of the fact that there was another train ahead of him unable to move – despite the fact that the control room knew of the “equipment problems” on the stranded Iryo train.

In a further tragic twist, Antonio had been an active member of the Izquierda Española political party and had warned of the crumbling infrastructure and chronic underfunding of the train system.

His friend, journalist Paula Fraga, said: “Antonio was one of the frontline workers who sounded the alarm over deteriorating rail infrastructure—one of those ignored and dismissed workers who died because officials refused to listen.”

Party leader Guillermo del Valle remembered him as “a good man” and a “cautious, kind and exemplary colleague”.



Previously on social media Antonio had reflected on death, writing: “I imagine that when we reach the end, if we look back and find happiness, we aren’t saddened to leave.”

A former politician died in the tragedy, confirmed by the Spanish Confederation of Business Organizations.

Fátima Báñez served as minister for employment and social security while in government between 2011 and 2018.

A classical music composer is also missing following the disaster.

Friends of María Luisa Manchado have issued appeals to find her after the train operator confirmed she had scanned her ticket for the ride.



A young athlete, 24, and a policeman, 36, also lost their lives in the crash.

Julieta Gallego, a runner for AD Sprint, had her life “unjustly extinguished”, said Raúl Chapado, president of the Royal Spanish Athletics Federation.

Cop José Manuel Chacón was travelling back to his hometown of Seville when he was killed in the horror collision.

He married just four months earlier.

Still among the missing is die-hard Atletico Madrid fan David Martinez Mendez who his family describe as “cheerful and devoted to his loved ones”.



In another heartbreaking case, the family of engineer David Reina Reguera are still searching for their son.

The 22-year-old called his family at 8.30 – less than half an hour before the fatal crash.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Another missing person – architect Alexandra García Bartolomé – also spoke to her family approximately 20 minutes before the collision.

She had been heading to Seville on business when the tragedy unfolded.

News.title: Labourer dies after ‘being hit by HGV’ on Sir Winston Churchill’s family estate
News.content:
'LORRY DEATH' Labourer dies after ‘being hit by HGV’ on Sir Winston Churchill’s family estate







Next

A LABOURER has died after being hit by an HGV on Sir Winston Churchill’s family estate, The Sun understands.

The 50-year-old labourer died on the scene of the lunchtime accident on grand Blenheim Palace in Woodstock, Oxfordshire.

The 12,000-acre estate is the ancestral seat of aristocrat James Spencer-Churchill, 12th Duke of Marlborough.

It hosted US President Donald Trump on his 2018 presidential visit to the UK for a lavish, black-tie diplomatic dinner with ex-PM Theresa May.





The Sun understands the labourer was working on a pathway for construction on the estate.

It is thought the worker, who has not been named, was struck by a heavy goods vehicle and died almost immediately on October 14.

Bosses from the Health and Safety Executive have since launched a probe.

A Thames Valley Police spokesperson told The Sun: “We are working with the Health and Safety Executive to investigate a fatal industrial incident at Blenheim Palace on 14 October.



“We were called at around 1pm that day following an incident involving a heavy goods vehicle in the palace grounds.

“A 50-year-old man sadly died at the scene. A specially trained police officer is supporting his family at this difficult time.”

Blenheim Palace was the birthplace of war hero Churchill and features a dedicated Churchill Exhibition.

The estate features over 2,000 acres of landscaped parkland and formal gardens plus water terraces, a Walled Garden, and a butterfly house.



The Duke of Marlborough has been tied to the estate for over 300 years, and James Spencer-Churchill, 70, is thought to still have a residence there.

Visitors can tour the opulent State Rooms, the Long Library, housing over 10,000 books, and a permanent exhibition dedicated to Sir Winston Churchill.

The palace recently underwent a massive £12million restoration “Glow Up” project to repair the palace’s roof which concluded in October.

DBR Limited, the contractor for the restoration project, said the accident was not on their site but involved another project.

There are other restoration works at the palace as part of a ten-year £40million conservation project which started in 2017.



They include work on the estate’s “Queen Pool” and its 300-year-old chapel.

Dominic Hare, Chief Executive of Blenheim Palace, said: “We are deeply saddened by the death of a man who was working for a contractor on a construction site on the wider Blenheim Estate on Wednesday 14 October.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“Our heartfelt condolences are with his family, friends and colleagues at this extremely difficult time.

“We are supporting Thames Valley Police and the Health and Safety Executive with their investigation, and it would not be appropriate to comment further while that continues.”

News.title: John Healey seemed adamant about cutting welfare bill… but Labour’s position has descended into chaos
News.content:
Next

LABOUR’S position on cutting the benefits bill has descended into chaos.

Chancellor John Healey appeared to be adamant on the BBC yesterday morning at 6am that the benefits bill would be cut before the next election.



But a couple of hours later, Treasury sources disputed the story saying his words had been incorrectly interpreted.

The fuss all kicked off after the Chancellor was asked whether there would be a cut in the bill before the next polling day.



He replied: “There will be, there will be a reduction in the benefits bill, we’ll do that in a Labour way.”

Bear in mind that the Budget watchdog said on Wednesday that the bill would hit an eye-watering £430billion by the start of the next decade.

Then shortly before 1pm, Number 10 told journalists that they had never set a target date.

Andy Burnham popped up in the afternoon saying the government was working “flat out” and the bill would come down “as soon as possible”.

Fast forward to 4pm and the Chancellor tells Channel 4 that Labour will not bring down the welfare bill in this Parliament – scheduled at the moment to end in 2029.

An about-turn in just a matter of hours.



Two big reviews on the welfare system – from Alan Milburn and Sir Stephen Timms – will help frame the debate.

But after Labour shied away from benefits cuts last year it seems Andy Burnham doesn’t want to have the fight.

Mr Healey said cutting the welfare bill will be done in the Labour way – and it could take years.

Labour insiders are happy with how the Budget has gone this week. After all, the bond markets and the Parliamentary Labour Party are on side.

The trouble is how much patience do taxpayers have to keep paying for Benefits Street?

News.title: Sir Ian McKellen leads tributes to 'beloved actor' Sir Patrick Stewart after his death at 86
News.content:
Sir Ian McKellen has led tributes to Sir Patrick Stewart following his death at the age of 86, calling him "the most respected and beloved actor of his generation".

Tributes to the renowned British actor have poured in since his death at his Los Angeles home after "a brief and poignant journey" with Alzheimer's disease and Lewy Body Dementia was announced on Thursday.

"He wore his heart on his sleeve, which made him a man to rely on, to admire and, in my case, love," Sir Ian, Sir Patrick's X-Men co-star, said.

Famous for his role as Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek, Sir Patrick was a versatile actor who won multiple awards, balancing Hollywood roles and a career in classical theatre.

William Shatner, who also helmed the SS Enterprise in Star Trek, said Sir Patrick brought "intelligence, grace and a deep sense of humanity to everything he did".

"Captain Picard stood for the best of us and so did the man who played him. I was filled with affection and admiration for him and his work," Shatner added.

Stewart depicted Picard in more than 170 episodes of the hit sci-fi TV series between 1987 and 1994, as well as in four feature films. He returned to the role for Star Trek: Picard in 2020.

News.title: Democrats have an identity crisis - it won't be an easy fix
News.content:
James Stevens calls himself a democratic socialist. The 24-year-old film student is the type of Democrat who recalls watching the provocative left-wing internet commentator Hasan Piker six years ago, "before he became relevant in politics". Last year, James flew up from his home in Georgia to New York City to canvass for Zohran Mamdani's mayoral campaign.

His mother, Tamara, 56, is a loyal Democrat too. But of a different ilk. She grew up Republican then switched to the Democratic Party after seeing Barack Obama on Oprah. These days, she's a loyal party woman, championing reproductive rights, attending campaign rallies and donating to local candidates.

Both mother and son want Democrats to win control of Congress at next Tuesday's midterm elections, but they don't entirely agree on what they want their Democratic Party to be.

"I'm very sick of how compromising Democrats are to Republican policies that don't benefit a large group of people," James told me, as his mother looked on. "There needs to be a bold vision for the Democrats," he says, arguing that the party should adopt policies affiliated with the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), a left-wing splinter group. In his view, that means anti-Zionism, getting corporate money out of politics, and government-run free healthcare.

The conventional wisdom in Washington is that Democrats are well-positioned to take control of the House, and possibly even the Senate, after the vote next week.

Underlying conditions are in Democrats' favour â Republican US President Donald Trump's approval rating is at a record low for a president heading into a midterm, comparable to George W Bush in his final term in 2006; the Iran war still isn't over and it's proving unpopular with American voters; and this has led to higher gas prices, which are frustrating an electorate that is already worried about the cost of living. Traditionally, the midterms are a referendum on a sitting president. In 18 of the last 20 US midterm elections, the party in power has lost seats in the House.

News.title: China made Mbappé apologise - but many don't know exactly what he said
News.content:
On Monday night, as Kylian MbappÃ© was attending the Ballon d'Or ceremony in London, he was also becoming the centre of a huge controversy on Chinese social media.

Football fans had stumbled upon a clip of him joking about the meme that makes him "laugh the most" - where his face is superimposed on a "Chinese dictator" resembling Mao Zedong, who oversaw one of the bloodiest chapters in the country's past.

The controversy spread like wildfire as Chinese brands cut him off one by one and China Media Group, the parent group of state broadcaster CCTV, suspended broadcasts of La Liga matches. A foreign ministry spokesperson said: "Words and actions that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people will naturally be met with joint opposition from all sectors of Chinese society."

But on the Chinese internet, few were explicitly spelling out those words and actions, or even using the name of Mao - who remains a near-sacred figure in the country.

News.title: Bombshell confession in The Traitors as faithfuls finally turn the screw
News.content:
As ever, James B was as far off the pace as me in the year 11 cross-country race.

When Leigh-Anne Pinnock, probably the most astute faithful of the series, brought up James A being a potential traitor over breakfast, James B sarcastically replied: "I think that's a good theory to start banishing the most innocent."

Sharon - aka Poundland Poirot - failed to appear in the dining room, having been chosen for the chopping block so soon after escaping banishment, throwing all the faithfuls into more confusion. She was getting a bit stressed, so it was probably for the best.

Michael had a warning for the traitors though, giving his most rousing oratory since his motivational speech for the Welsh football team ahead of the 2022 World Cup.

"Traitors... today is going to be a living hell for you, I am going to push and push and push and you are going to suffer today. This is the apocalypse.

"Vengeful daddy is in the house today."

Theories were soon flying left right and centre, with Bash throwing the spotlight on "the head of the round table" Michael, Kenny putting suspicion on James B, while Romesh pointed the finger at actual traitor Maya, shock, horror.

And the obsession with the peacock perfume wasn't going anywhere.

Finally Michael 'Vengeful Daddy' Sheen seemed to be on to something, telling a shell-shocked Maya in the kitchen: "I think you could be a brilliant traitor, and if you and Kenny paired up, amazing."

She was probably relieved when the jeeps turned up for another day trip, and Romesh was all of us with his hilarious reaction to news of yet another insane mission.

On being told by host Claudia Winkleman that they had to find the severed heads of some of the murdered celebrities and reunite them with the head of the buried body, he got the giggles: "It's just so ridiculous. I love it though!"

James B tried to get one group in the Frankenstein-style lab to sing his hit Beautiful - which had Leigh-Ann and Michael bopping along but by the puzzled look on Kenny's face, he had clearly never heard it. Awks.

This mission was a bit of a rehash of the wailing in the well challenge from the first Celebrity Traitors series, with Claudia going full headteacher and cheering - or should we say, shouting - the teams on.

Digital versions of the dead celebs in bell jars had to be matched to the correct gravestone in the castle gardens.

"Seeing Ross's face when he was alive was enough to give a man pause, let alone when his dismembered head is looking out at you from a pickle jar," quipped Michael.

Back at the castle, it seemed that Michael wasn't the only one starting to turn up the heat on Maya.

Romesh and Bash decided she had gone under the radar long enough: "One of the greatest gliders in the game. Maybe Olympic level gliding," mused Bash. And King Kenny was also in their sights.

And so to the penultimate round table. (A shout out to Claudia's sequin-tastic midnight blue trouser suit).

Michael was under the spotlight first due to his presence, intelligence and status as "the father of the table."

In turn, he first went back to his previous suspicion of Leigh-Anne on the night of the murder in plain sight, accusing her again of using her Big Mix dance with Miranda as a distraction.

Romesh put heat on James B due to his vocal accusations, which were often wrong.

The quiet ones - traitors James A and Maya - were then questioned by Michael and James B, who soon honed in on the murder in plain sight, working out that Maya, Kenny and James A were in the library at the end of the night when Ross was killed.

Vengeful Daddy was indeed in the house, and James B was on the money for once. Credit where it's due.

Then the bombshell of the series - something that has never happened before in the history of the show.

James A, who failed dismally to defend himself against Michael's accusations, clearly couldn't take any more and confessed he was a traitor at the table.

"I was made a traitor without wanting to be," he revealed, as the others gasped.

"I've had a unique experience on this that no-one has had before, I wanted to be a faithful and that's all I wanted to be. But I couldn't just say 'guys, vote for me.'"

At least no-one had to explain their decision when they all wrote his name down on the boards.

And as Michael and Maya stood round the firepit before heading to bed - or the turret in Maya's case - she looked like a dead woman walking. And DI Sheen is on her case.

News.title: Hazardous driving conditions for Friday as fog warning issued by Met Office
News.content:
Thick fog has formed on Friday morning across parts of the United Kingdom which could lead to hazardous driving conditions.

The Met Office has issued a yellow severe weather warning for fog from Lincolnshire, the East Midlands, the Home Counties into parts of Greater London.

Fog will be dense in places with visibility below 100 metres at times and it will be most extensive and disruptive during the morning rush hour.

It will slowly begin to thin, lift and clear later this morning but in some rural spots in eastern England it may not clear until this afternoon.

News.title: Yorkshire Water boss resigns after firm downgraded
News.content:
Yorkshire Water's chief executive has announced she is to step down, just 24 hours after the company was given the lowest possible environmental rating by the Environment Agency

Nicola Shaw, who has led the firm since 2022, will leave the role on 1 January to be replaced by Nicola Medalova, a chartered environmental health officer who previously worked for the National Grid.

In a statement on Friday, Shaw said it had been a "privilege" to lead the company but that it was "the right time" to leave her post.

Shaw has faced criticism in recent years, including for for taking Â£1.3m in undisclosed payments between 2023 and 2025, while the company has come under scrutiny for its performance.

On Thursday, the Environment Agency gave the firm one star out of four - its lowest possible rating - meaning Yorkshire Water was classed as a "poorly performing company".

The EA said Yorkshire Water was responsible for 260 pollution incidents in 2025, which was its highest total since 2011.

In 2024, Ofwat announced it was fining the company Â£47m for historic sewage leaks.

News.title: 'I run a spotless kitchen', says Michelin-star restaurant chef in wake of food hygiene debacle
News.content:
Ynyshir was previously ordered to stop serving raw lobster after Ceredigion council found "significant hazards" were not properly identified.

The restaurant received its first Michelin star in 2014 and its second in 2022, becoming the first and only restaurant in Wales to hold two.

It missed out on a third star at the ceremony this year.

The 16-seat restaurant serves Japanese-inspired raw dishes as part of its nearly Â£500 a head 30-course tasting menu, and accused inspectors of not understanding its specialised procedures.

By August, the council had reinstated its five-star hygiene rating after it found the "business had addressed all matters identified during the original inspection".

But, for Ynyshir, the scrutiny was a major setback, and Ward shared his frustration in the documentary.

"I'm very proud of my whole team and my business, and what we've achieved," he said.

"It's obviously massive in the media, which anyone instantly jumps on and thinks it's about cleanliness," he said. "I run a spotless kitchen.

"When something like this happens you're a bit blown away."

Ward said the restaurant served a lot of raw food and did a lot of things "that aren't normal".

"We have done some things wrong, but we don't deserve everything [we were accused of]," he said.

"It's just, we dare to be different."

He said the inspection left him feeling the weight of responsibility, with more than 30 members of staff and the business potentially at risk.

Management of food safety at Ynyshir was categorised by inspectors as needing major improvement, as was cleanliness and condition of facilities, while "hygienic food handling" was rated "generally satisfactory".

A dirty floor, inadequate hand-washing facilities in some areas and broken equipment posing a potential contamination risk were also identified in the inspectors' report.

Ynyshir responded at the time, saying the inspection "identified a small number of minor issues typical of a busy professional kitchen situated in the countryside of rural Wales" which had been "rectified immediately and in full".

It said biological testing, at "significant cost" to the restaurant, had "conclusively confirmed that our techniques are safe, compliant and appropriate".

It said at the time it was prepared to work constructively with the council but expected "an informed, consistent and fair assessment process that recognises the realities of modern, non-conventional restaurants".

When Ynyshir was reinspected, Ceredigion council said the "business had addressed all matters identified during the original inspection".

News.title: Heart attack patient, 83, had to drive four hours for hospital appointment
News.content:
An 83-year-old recovering cancer patient who has suffered two heart attacks was forced to drive himself on a four-hour round trip for medical tests.

Charles Swift was referred to Withybush Hospital in Haverfordwest, Pembrokeshire, for tests on his heart in August - he lives in Borth, Ceredigion - which is 70 miles away.

He made inquiries about getting non-emergency transport but was refused by a call handler from the Welsh Ambulance Services Trust (WAST) when he told them he owned a car.

"I can't understand why pensioners have to run about in their own car," he said.

WAST said it was not always able to meet the increasing demand for transport, and changes were underway to improve the service.

Swift, who has been treated for three types of cancer and has had two heart attacks, said when he rang hospital taxis, he was asked if he could walk, climb stairs and owned a car.

When he replied yes to all three, he said he was told: "You'll have to use that then.

"I don't understand. What's the difference if you've got a car or not? I'm 83. It's not a good journey to do. It was tiring."

On another occasion, Swift was told on a Friday afternoon that his hospital transport for an appointment in Haverfordwest on the Monday had been cancelled, leading him to cancel the appointment.

When he got hospital transport for a subsequent appointment, he said it was "very pleasant, no problem at all".

Hywel Dda University Health Board's website says patients travelling to and from hospital are normally expected to organise their own transport.

When that is not possible, some patients could be eligible for non-emergency patient transport provided by the Welsh Ambulance Service, but must meet eligibility criteria.

This includes receiving regular dialysis or cancer treatment, needing a stretcher or oxygen or needing to travel in their own wheelchair.

Public transport is not a realistic option as trains from Borth to Haverfordwest take a minimum of three-and-a-half hours in each direction.

News.title: Biggest fibre boost could be scraps in your bin, experts say
News.content:
KCL has been experimenting in its canteen, external, offering staff and students root-to-tip meals, such as banana skin curry.

At home, people might want to try leaving skins on kiwi fruit, using broccoli stalks in stir-fries or adding bell pepper seeds to dishes, the researchers suggest.

While cooking can change the fibre content, it doesn't usually destroy it all.

Steaming, microwaving or quick sautÃ©ing tends to preserve nutrients best.

Gibson said: "This isn't about perfection and this isn't about forcing people to eat unpalatable food â it's about recognising the nutritional value in components we've been conditioned to discard."

She acknowledges some may be hesitant to try it.

Some diners raised concerns during the canteen trial.

Over the nine-week period, "root-to-tip" dishes made up a third of total daily hot menu sales at the university.

Those choosing the new dishes were less likely to finish their meals than diners eating from the conventional menu.

Kirsten Jackson, a dietitian with the British Dietetic Association who specialises in irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), says the food hacks are useful as long as produce is washed thoroughly.

She suggests blending pineapple cores into smoothies, but says the tough skins are not something she would recommend.

Some stalks may need to be cooked or finely chopped to make them more palatable, she adds.

"Just because a broccoli stalk doesn't fit into tonight's meal doesn't mean it needs to go in the bin. Chop it up, freeze it and add it to a soup or stir-fry another day," she said.

She advises increasing fibre intake gradually to avoid bloating, noting that people who have IBS may find it harder to tolerate.

And there are some things to avoid entirely, said the British Nutrition Foundation.

Green potatoes and rhubarb leaves contain toxic compounds, while tough stalks and seeds may not be suitable for young children.

News.title: Traders' tools stolen every 20 minutes in UK
News.content:
Traders' tools worth thousands of pounds were stolen somewhere in the UK every 20 minutes last year, figures show.

At least 26,164 tool thefts were recorded in 2025, based on responses from 30 police forces who shared data. The true figure is likely to be higher as a further 15 forces could not respond.

Gangs and "chancers" are behind the crimes, according to Labour MP Amanda Martin, who is calling for her government to do more to help.

The Home Office said it was "working with the police to tackle and prevent tool theft to protect more hardworking tradespeople", including increasing neighbourhood policing, investing in police and working with industry and AI to tackle the sale of stolen goods.

Lulzim Pjetri owns Alliance Refrigeration Group, a commercial refrigeration business in Aston, Birmingham, from which tools were stolen six times in a year.

On one occasion, thieves broke into a parked van while two staff sat in its cab eating their lunch.

Those responsible were not wearing masks, held up crowbars and told the workers it was not worth them trying to stop it, Pjetri said.

Pjetri said: "Unless they choke the second-hand tool market, this problem will always be there."

News.title: Burnham says he wants to cut welfare bill 'as soon as we possibly can'
News.content:
The prime minister faced questions about his approach after the Treasury disputed that Chancellor John Healey had suggested to the BBC that the benefits bill will be cut before the next election, which must be held by August 2029.

When Healey was asked by the Today Programme on Radio 4 whether there would be a cut in the bill before polling day, he said: "There will be, there will be a reduction in the benefits bill, we'll do that in a Labour way."

But several Treasury sources took issue with this being interpreted as a promise to do so by the next election. Downing Street later said it was "not setting an arbitrary target or timetable".

The prime minister's official spokesman would not say whether the government's ambition to cut welfare spending meant reducing it below its current level, or ensuring that future spending rises at a slower rate than is currently projected.

Further details about the government's proposals are expected after two major reports are published in November.

These include a review of disability benefits co-chaired by Labour minister Sir Stephen Timms and one on young people not in education, employment or training (Neet) led by former minister Alan Milburn.

The two reviews were announced by former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer after his attempt to make significant changes to the welfare system, including restricting eligibility for some health-related benefits, resulted in a mass revolt of Labour MPs and an embarrassing climbdown in June 2025.

Speaking during a visit to Derby, Burnham said the "big next priority in front of us" is the publication of the Milburn report.

He said: "We just want to get stuck into supporting people to help people off benefits and into work. There's no delay there. We want that to happen as quickly as possible."

Pressed again for a timeline on his plans, the prime minister said: "We're working hard to cut the welfare bill as soon as we possibly can. But we're doing it in a way that supports people into work.

"If we just went and made crude cuts, in the end, that leaves people in crisis, and you spend more public money somewhere else, so it's about getting people into sustainable employment."

News.title: Scottish police to target online gangs forcing children to self-harm
News.content:
Detectives in Scotland have joined international law enforcement in targeting online gangs which groom and coerce children into acts of self-harm.

Officers are hunting members of loose online networks of sadists known as "The Com", which mainly targets girls on gaming platforms and social media.

The groups, mostly comprised of teenage and young adult males, have risen in prominence in recent years after cases involving sextortion and hacking, as well as self-harm encouragement.

So far, there has been one arrest in Scotland, while there have been a handful of convictions in England.

The Molly Rose Foundation - a suicide prevention charity helping young people and families victimised by the network - said the groups "represent the gravest risk to children online".

News.title: DUP blocks Michelle O'Neill's engagements over Drumcree
News.content:
A meeting of the party's ruling officer committee was held earlier on Thursday.

DUP leader Gavin Robinson said the first minister's "arrogance will have consequences", but O'Neill accused the party of being "reckless and irresponsible".

"Her complaints today that she's frustrated from engaging with the British Prime Minister within the sovereign United Kingdom will so be it because her law breaking must have consequences," Robinson said.

O'Neill said the DUP leader's comments were "arrogant and supremacist" adding that the DUP "is consumed with their own internal leadership troubles and divisions".

She said she would be at the Assembly on Monday with her party colleagues to "keep showing up every day for people".

Earlier she described the move to block the meeting with the prime minister as "reckless and irresponsible" and meant people in Northern Ireland "will not be represented".

"This is a reactive stunt, driven by the DUP's own internal pressures and electoral problems," she said in a statement posted online.

The prime minister revived the National Economic Council over the summer to encourage greater collaboration between the nations and regions.

Earlier Little-Pengelly said the concerns arising from O'Neill's conduct and the "anger and hurt felt by many people across Northern Ireland, cannot simply be ignored or minimised".

She said the decision comes after stopping a separate planned engagement with the President of Ireland, Catherine Connolly.

"I have requested a separate meeting with the Prime Minister to ensure Northern Ireland's interests, including the urgent budgetary and funding challenges facing the Executive, continue to be represented directly," she added.

The Secretary of State Sir Chris Bryant said it was "deeply frustrating" that the Northern Ireland executive would not be represented at the National Economic Council.

"I understand feelings are running high but it must be in the interests of the people of Northern Ireland that everyone gets round the table."

News.title: Wicker review – Olivia Colman fornicates with a sentient basket in this sweet, bawdy comedy
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Riding the crest of a thousand memes about ending up in A&E with splinters in unutterable places, Wicker is a bawdy new comedy that fulfills all expectations. For one, we do indeed discover what fornicating with a sentient wicker basket might look like. But Wicker also complicates the gag with a touching portrait of how patriarchal expectation has robbed romance of the use of its tongue – in all meanings of the phrase.

At its centre is a gender-swapped Pygmalion fairytale, set in some vague configuration of Ye Olde England, in which the unmarried Fisherwoman (Olivia Colman) – lonely, yes, but also sick of everyone’s snide comments – commissions the Basket Weaver (Peter Dinklage, unmatched in delivering the character’s florid soliloquies) to make her a husband.

He emerges in wicker Alexander Skarsgård form, via some astounding practical prosthetics, who is kindly in soul and mighty in downstairs package; he says things like, “you are the reason I live and breathe”, which is literally true – though the film takes care to consider his autonomy in all of this. Wicker Husband will break the marital bed that night and fix it the next day.

Directors Alex Huston Fischer and Eleanor Wilson have a refreshingly unfussy but sexy way of shooting their romance scenes. There are no candles. No mewl of the violin. A cow moos outside. Both bed and husband sound out a seesaw creak. Yet the film trusts that Colman’s performance can communicate every unexpected wave of pleasure that hits her character.

open image in gallery Olivia Colman and Alexander Skarsgård in ‘Wicker’ ( Black Bear )

Skarsgård’s a dream get for the role. There are very few actors who, recognising their own heartthrob status, have embraced it in such playful and unexpected ways, from last year’s BDSM romance Pillion to the feral viking cry of The Northman (2022). A lot of the actor’s appeal is that he can exude deep sincerity from a place of ironic detachment, a contradiction in theory that helps guide the film’s more unexpected turns.

Wicker, when we’ve all had our kinky kick, expands beyond the confines of the Fisherwoman and Wicker Husband’s bed chambers to the repressed and dissatisfied villagers next door. Men are known only by their job titles and women only by their relation to said men. Marriage rituals involve a collar around the neck and a goat chomping on a carrot penis.

It’s a strange and amusing world conjured by Tóth András Dániel and Godena-Juhász Attila’s costumes and Renátó Cseh’s sets, then given a touch of the Yorgos Lanthimos thanks to cinematographer Lol Crowley’s cold but beautiful images and Anna Meredith’s jaunty score.

The arrival of the Wicker Husband has made the men of the village look bad. They’re jealous, then angry, then sad, because they’re incapable of expressing their genuine love for their wives. Most affronted of them all, however, is the Tailor’s Wife (Elizabeth Debicki). She’s beautiful, immaculately dressed, and entirely subservient to her husband (Nabhaan Rizwan); seeing the Fisherwoman’s rejection of traditional femininity – she stinks of fish and earns her own keep – rewarded with a handsome, doting husband in her eyes tips the scales entirely the wrong way.

open image in gallery Olivia Colman and Alexander Skarsgård in ‘Wicker’ ( Black Bear )

Debicki is wonderfully exacting in the role, a counter to Colman’s bold vulnerability (Richard E Grant also crops up as a mad doctor at one point, delightful here as on The Celebrity Traitors). Wicker ridicules the patriarchy but shows great empathy for all those afflicted by it. Even the Fisherwoman must learn how easy it is to succumb to the paranoia and distrust woven deep into the fabric of love. It’s a lesson as hard as a wicker erection.

Dir: Alex Huston Fischer and Eleanor Wilson. Starring: Olivia Colman, Alexander Skarsgård, Elizabeth Debicki, Marli Siu, Nabhaan Rizwan, Richard E. Grant, Peter Dinklage, Ben Ashenden. 15, 105 mins.

‘Wicker’ is in cinemas from 30 October

News.title: Gold medal-winning para-athlete who was serving four-year doping ban found dead aged 42
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A gold medal-winning Indian para-athlete who was serving a four-year suspension for doping has been found dead in Delhi aged 42.

Neeraj Yadav, a three-time Asian Para Games gold medallist from the northern Indian state of Uttar Pradesh, was found beside his SUV near Maujpur metro station in northeast Delhi on Monday night.

Yadav was serving a four-year ban after he was suspended over doping charges in 2023.

Delhi Police said they received information from Guru Teg Bahadur (GTB) Hospital shortly after midnight on Tuesday that a man had been brought to its emergency department and declared dead.

A team reached the hospital, “and the body had already been shifted to GTB Hospital’s mortuary”, a police officer was quoted as saying by The Times of India.

Yadav ran the Anshneer Sports Academy in Sonipat, in the neighbouring state of Haryana, and is survived by his wife and three-year-old daughter.

Police said they were investigating the death and that a post-mortem was expected to reveal more information. Proceedings have been started under Section 194 of criminal code, which governs inquiries into suspected suicides.

The Independent has reached out to the Paralympic Committee of India for comment.

S Satyanarayana, head coach of India’s para-athletics team, said Yadav “would have been looking forward to competing” in the recent Asian Para Games in Japan.

“Medals at the Asian Para Games can bring substantial government cash awards. But his suspension had not ended, and he could not compete. It is possible this affected him deeply,” he said.

Earlier this year, it was reported that Indian athletes will now face stricter anti-doping requirements after the country’s athletics federation was moved to the highest-risk category by World Athletics.

India has ranked among the top two countries globally for anti-doping violations in athletics for each year between 2022 and 2025.

In response, the Athletics Integrity Unit (AIU) board reclassified the Athletics Federation of India (AFI) from Category B to Category A, placing it alongside the likes of Russia, Belarus and Nigeria and subjecting it to more stringent anti-doping measures.

Yadav was diagnosed with post-polio residual paralysis at the age of seven. He began his sporting career in wheelchair tennis, competing between 2005 and 2012, before switching to para-athletics.

His breakthrough came at the 2015 Delhi State Athletics Meet, where he won gold medals in the shot put, javelin and discus.

He gained international recognition at the 2018 Asian Para Games in Jakarta, winning the men’s F55 javelin throw with an Asian record of 29.84 metres. He went on to win two more gold medals at the 2023 Asian Para Games in Hangzhou, in the javelin and discus events.

However, his career was later derailed by the 2023 doping case. India’s National Anti-Doping Agency provisionally suspended Yadav after an out-of-competition sample collected in Bengaluru tested positive for stanozolol, an anabolic steroid.

He sought DNA testing of the sample during the disciplinary proceedings but was eventually handed a four-year ban.

The suspension prevented him from competing at the 2026 Asian Para Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan. According to reports, his two gold medals from the 2023 Hangzhou Games were also revoked following the anti-doping proceedings, and he did not receive the associated government cash awards.

“It is very unfortunate that such a thing has happened,” Satyanarayana told The Hindu.

If you are experiencing feelings of distress, or are struggling to cope, you can speak to the Samaritans, in confidence, on 116 123 (UK and ROI) or visit the Samaritans website to find details of your nearest branch.

If you are based in the USA, and you or someone you know needs mental health assistance right now, call or text 988, or visit 988lifeline.org to access online chat from the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline. This is a free, confidential crisis hotline that is available to everyone 24 hours a day, seven days a week.

If you are in another country, you can go to www.befrienders.org to find a helpline near you.

News.title: Jennifer Lawrence ‘came down hard’ after extra crew members were on set for nude scene
News.content:

Jennifer Lawrence has described the time she took a firm stance after unauthorised crew members appeared on set during a nude scene.

The 36-year-old actor emphasised that being "malleable" is "part of the job", citing her dramatic hair transformation for 2025’s psychological drama Die My Love, but noted there are moments to put her foot down to protect herself and others across the film industry.

She told the Call Her Daddy podcast: "There was an instance on set where crew members who were not approved when I was doing nudity were on set.

"I came down hard on it, purely because if we are not setting that principle, then what on earth is going to happen to an 18-year-old unknown when she shows up and there’s people on set who are not approved [to be there]?

"She’s going to be in a position of: ‘Do I say something and get a reputation for being difficult, or do I let these people that I’m not comfortable seeing me naked see me naked?’

"It was important to me to explain that to the people why that was not okay."

Lawrence previously mentioned wanting to grant director Lynne Ramsay, 56, "total freedom artistically" for Die My Love.

Speaking to Vulture, she said: "I don't care about nudity. I'm not sensitive about it. I wanted Lynne to have total freedom artistically."

Jennifer Lawrence in ‘Die My Love’ ( Mubi )

She noted that "being pregnant" with her second child while filming took much of her "vanity anxiety away".

She added: "What was I gonna do? Like, not eat? I was working 15 hours a day. I was just tired.

"I remember them sending over a close-up of, like, cellulite being like, 'Do you want us to touch this up?' And I was like, "No. That's an ass.'"

Meanwhile, Lawrence disclosed her beauty goals in a cover interview with The Cut.

Regarding her personal beauty targets, Lawrence admitted: "I want to be a sexy mom."

She added: "At drop-off, I want to look like a woman that has her s*** together even when I’ve just woken up and don’t have my s*** together."

The mother of two has previously opened up about cosmetic procedures and physical changes following motherhood.

These remarks follow a conversation with The New Yorker last October, where she admitted considering breast surgery following her second child's arrival.

She said: "Everything bounced back, pretty much, after the first one. Second one, nothing bounced back."

She has since confirmed having a breast lift and considering a future facelift, having previously discussed using subtle amounts of Botox, which she termed "baby Botox" in Vogue.

News.title: Tadhg Furlong cleared of grabbing opponent’s groin by disciplinary panel
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The Leinster and Ireland prop Tadhg Furlong has been cleared by a disciplinary committee after an allegation that he grabbed the groin of Munster’s Gavin Coombes during a United Rugby Championship (URC) game.

Coombes alleged during Munster’s 24-18 defeat at the Aviva Stadium that he had been grabbed at a ruck, but the television match official (TMO) Colin Stanley could not find conclusive video evidence after a referral from referee Andrew Brace.

Furlong was subsequently cited, though, under Law 9.27, which states "a player must not do anything that is against the spirit of good sportsmanship including but not limited to grabbing, twisting or squeezing the genitals".

On Thursday, however, the 33-year-old was cleared of sanction at a hearing, leaving him free to feature in Ireland’s Nations Championship games in November.

“Having reviewed all of the evidence and considered the submissions in this case, the Independent Disciplinary Committee unanimously concluded that the citing complaint against the Player should be dismissed, on the basis that he did not commit an act of foul play contrary to Law 9.27,” a URC statement said.

“Notwithstanding the dismissal of the complaint, the Independent Disciplinary Committee found that Munster No 8, Mr Gavin Coombes, had given an honest account of his recollection of events surrounding the incident, and that the Citing Complaint was properly brought before the Independent Disciplinary Committee for determination.”

News.title: Sir Patrick Stewart: Shakespearean actor who brought gravitas to every role
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

If Patrick Stewart’s efforts had been successful, he might never have developed the look that made him an icon of stage and screen. He was just 17, still a young man finding his way in West Yorkshire, when he first began to lose his hair. As he recalled in his 2023 memoir Making It So, Stewart found work as a bricklayer and poured all of his earnings into treatment at a clinic in Bristol that involved having electrodes attached to his head. “But it was hopeless,” wrote Stewart. “By the age of 19, I was as bald on top as I am now.”

If Stewart — who has died at the age of 86 — feared his alopecia would harm his chances at building an acting career, he need not have worried. An interviewer once described him as having “the most famous cranium in the world.” His striking appearance helped him secure a string of signature roles, notably Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek: The Next Generation and Professor Charles Xavier in the X-Men film series, but there was always more to Stewart than his looks.

He was a deeply gifted and classically trained actor who could take fanciful material and ground it. While he will be fondly remembered for his blockbuster film roles, his first love always remained his long association with the Royal Shakespeare Company.

Born in Mirfield, West Riding on July 13, 1940, Stewart was the youngest of three sons born to a textile worker mother and a father who had served as a regimental sergeant major in the British Army during World War II. Later in life, Stewart opened up about the domestic violence he and his family had suffered at his father’s hands.

“He was a very charming, charismatic man, and a great storyteller,” Stewart told The Independent in 2009 about his father. “But I have only recently come to understand that after I left home, the abuse continued for a long time, and I wasn't aware of it. One carries a certain amount of guilt and remorse for that, for not knowing, and not having done something about it at the time.”

open image in gallery Patrick Stewart as Launce, with his dog Crab, during rehearsals for a Royal Shakespeare Company production of 'Two Gentlemen Of Verona' in 1970 ( Getty )

From a young age, Stewart felt the pull of acting. He later credited Cecil Dormand, his English teacher at Crowlees Junior and Infant School, for putting a copy of a Shakespeare play in his hand and encouraging him to act. He made his professional debut at the age of 18, appearing in a 1959 production of Cyrano de Bergerac at the Theatre Royal in Bristol.

In 1966, he joined the Royal Shakespeare Company and remained with them until 1982, appearing in a string of productions while making a handful of minor television appearances. However, it wasn’t until he was cast in Star Trek: The Next Generation in 1987 that he received mainstream attention. A casting announcement in the Los Angeles Times referred to him at the time as an “unknown British Shakespearean actor.” To land the part, he had to win over Star Trek creator Gene Roddenberry, who initially doubted he would be a fit for the series.

open image in gallery Patrick Stewart returning to the role of Captain Picard in 1998's 'Star Trek: Insurrection' ( Paramount )

In the end, Stewart’s Picard became one of the franchise’s defining figures. He played the character in four spin-off films, as well as the standalone series Star Trek: Picard that ran from 2020 to 2023. If anything, the character became so successful that it hampered Stewart’s hopes of building a varied film career. “I had come to the point when I realized it was unlikely that my film career was going to move beyond a certain level of role,” he told The Independent. “And I was – because I had graphic instances of it – handicapped by the success of Star Trek. A director would say, ‘I don't want Jean-Luc Picard in my movie’ – and this was compounded by X-Men as well.”

In 2000, Stewart found his next signature role in the form of the telepathic Professor Charles Xavier. He went on to play the character in seven X-Men movies, during which he forged a lifelong friendship with Ian McKellen, who played the supervillain Magneto.

open image in gallery Patrick Stewart as Professor Charles Xavier in 2003’s ‘X2’ ( Fox )

Even as his Hollywood roles made him wealthy and famous around the world, Stewart continued to dream of England, and specifically the countryside near Shakespeare’s home in Stratford-upon-Avon. “My fantasy had always been that I would end up with a nice little house somewhere in the Cotswolds,” he confessed to The Independent. “And I would literally put myself to sleep at night in Los Angeles, by creating a virtual imagined home. Where would I live? What part of the Cotswolds? What sort of house would it be? And added to that, I would drive from my house to Stratford every day where I'd have some nice parts to play.”

In his later years, Stewart used the attention that his global fame had brought him to shine a spotlight on the plays he loved the most. On Broadway, he performed in about a dozen productions, making his debut in a 1971 revival of A Midsummer Night's Dream. In 2007, he starred in a production of Macbeth that was later filmed for television. In 2013, he and McKellen performed Samuel Beckett’s Waiting For Godot in repertory with Harold Pinter’s No Man’s Land. Those would turn out to be Stewart’s final Broadway bows.

open image in gallery Patrick Stewart and his longtime friend Ian McKellen go in for a kiss at the premiere of ‘Star Trek: Picard’ in 2020 ( David Parry/PA )

He was married three times, to Sheila Falconer from 1966 to 1990, to Wendy Neuss from 2000 to 2003, and to Sunny Ozell from 2013 until his death. He had two children, Daniel and Sophie, with Falconer, and later expressed regret for not spending more time with them. “I could've done better as a parent, when my kids were little,” he said. “I was just obsessed with my work and everything else took second place. I’m trying to correct that now wherever possible with my grandchildren. And my own children seem to have forgiven me.”

He also poured himself into charitable work, notably becoming a patron of the women’s Refuge, a British charity for abused women, in memory of his mother. “There are women just like my mother who can now take an initiative to protect themselves or to remove themselves from these situations, which my mother couldn’t,” he said. “And that makes it worthwhile.”

Until the very end of his life, he was illuminated by a passion for sharing Shakespeare with the world. His final appearance on camera came in a video posted to social media in which he recited the Bard’s Sonnet 116. “I hope it has brought pleasure and curiosity,” said Stewart. “But more than anything else, I want it to have communicated all the multiple features that love might have.”

News.title: Netflix’s Pride and Prejudice hands Jane Austen’s iconic line to one of its characters for the first time
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

It’s a truth universally acknowledged that everyone knows the opening line of Pride and Prejudice – but it’s never actually been uttered on screen.

A starry Netflix adaptation of Jane Austen’s beloved novel is set to change all of that, with Dolly Alderton’s script finally featuring the words: “It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune must be in want of a wife.”

While in the book the line comes from the narrator, Alderton has gifted the line to one of the characters: family matriarch Mrs Bennet, played by Oscar-winning actor Olivia Colman.

In a new trailer, Colman’s Mrs Bennet can be seen saying the iconic phrase. Speaking about finally using the landmark line on screen, the show creator Dolly Alderton said it made sense because Mrs Bennet is a mother consumed with the marital status of her daughters.

“It’s the central drama of her story,” said Alderton. “It’s all she’s thinking about, it’s a preoccupation that any time a single man comes into her orbit she’s thinking this might be safety for all of my daughters this might be salvation not just for one of them but for all of us so the fact that this is so in her mind all the time felt that it had to be her line.”

“It was most natural for her to take it because it’s all she thinks about,” said Alderton, who admitted that she was initially hesitant about adapting Austen’s classic because it is “too much responsibility”.

She added: “Since then, I’ve just thought about the honour and the privilege of being entrusted with this story.”

open image in gallery The Bennet Sisters ( Netflix )

The new trailer follows on from a sneak peek that was unveiled back in February, and gives fans a closer look at Corrin’s protagonist, last played by Keira Knightley in a 2005 film adaptation. Here, Corrin appears to channel that same spirited defiance as their predecessor, at one point saying: “One day Jane, I shall either be a governess or a spinster… or a wife and a mother. And then finally we may talk about something else!”

Viewers also got a closer look at Jack Lowden’s enigmatic Mr Darcy. Every bit as intense and awkwardly romantic as Matthew MacFadyen and Colin Firth who played the part before him, Lowden looks set to bring his own brooding intensity to Austen’s famously reserved love interest.

open image in gallery Jack Lowden as Mr Darcy ( Netflix )

It’s a hugely significant role for Lowden at a time when he is being heavily tipped for another, with the James Bond rumour mill running high after reports that the final screen tests happened last weekend.

The trailer also offers a glimpse at Jamie Demetriou in the role of Mr Collins, the pompous potential suitor to Elizabeth Bennet, and one of the most memorable characters in the book. “Mrs Bennet, if there is one thing I am not in need of, it’s counsel on how to charm a young lady,” he says, before raising to his feet and knocking over a table of glasses.

While there have been several adaptations of the work, including the BBC series in 1995 starring Laurence Olivier, this is the first major screen adaptation of Austen’s novel since Joe Wright’s 2005 film, which was released to critical acclaim and received four Oscar nominations.

open image in gallery Jamie Demetriou as Mr Collins ( Netflix )

“Pride and Prejudice is such a timeless story because of the emotions in the book; they are as pertinent now as they were in 1812,” said Alderton.

“Embarrassment of your family, fear that you’re going to get left behind, fear that the world is not going to be a safe place for your children as it was for you, mortification that you judged someone incorrectly or that you had been misjudged. We go to that book to see our hearts reflected in it.”

Pride and Prejudice, the series, will debut on Netflix on 3 December.

News.title: Everton give Burnham something to shout about by booking quarter-final spot
News.content:
David Moyes took a glug of water and glanced up at the big screen away to his right, almost as if he wanted confirmation that what he was seeing was true.

Had he looked behind him, Moyes would have seen Andy Burnham and his wife, Marie-France, in raptures, along with thousands of others. It was true, all right. Everton had scored their third goal and were bounding into the Carabao Cup quarter-finals, seemingly without a care in the world.

What a happy change of direction. Moyes has spent months spinning plates, dealing with owners who do not care about a proud club and want to sell up and a squad that was left criminally short in the transfer window. Then, before Newcastle’s visit, came more disruption.

Jack Grealish’s selfish and reckless decision to go Awol from training on Monday could have been a catalyst for more misery and invited Newcastle to deliver a hammer blow to Everton’s season, but again, Moyes fostered a siege mentality. He was rewarded in the most emphatic fashion.

True, Newcastle collapsed like a deckchair without hinges and this performance – which encouraged many of their 8,000 followers to head for the exits early – would not have done anything to convince those who view Matthias Jaissle, the head coach, with ambivalence to change their minds.

News.title: Trump administration loses grip on bird flu, experts warn
News.content:
The Trump administration has been criticised for losing control of a bird flu outbreak that has spread among mink and cattle farms across the United States.

The H5N1 virus has infected around 1,000 people since it was first detected in the late 1990s, killing roughly half of them. While it currently does not spread among humans, scientists have long worried that it could trigger a pandemic, and that each human infection raises the risk of the virus mutating.

A new variant emerged in 2020 and has since spread to millions of birds and hundreds of animal species across the globe, leading to devastating losses in both wildlife and farmed livestock and poultry.

While some countries have introduced tough measures to curb its spread, including mandatory culls of infected animals, “flockdowns” (where birds are kept indoors) and vaccination of farm workers who handle at-risk livestock, experts say the US is allowing the virus to run rampant.

For more than two months, an outbreak has raged unchecked on a Utah farm that raises thousands of mink for fur, news outlet ProPublica reported last week.

Mink in captivity have previously been described as pandemic “time bombs”. The size and density of the farms give invading viruses a perfect environment in which to mutate.

Mink have very similar respiratory systems to humans, increasing the risk that a virus can spread between the animals and people, and undergo a process known as “reassortment”, when two or more viruses mix together to make a new, more dangerous strain.

News.title: Britain faces unprecedented squeeze on incomes, IFS says
News.content:
Thanks for joining me. John Healey has ruled out making “crude cuts” to welfare after he failed to tackle the rising benefits bill in Wednesday’s Budget.

The Chancellor acknowledged last night that the current benefits system is “unsustainable” but said he will only look to make cuts “in a Labour way”.

Speaking to the BBC in the wake of Wednesday’s Budget, Mr Healey promised that “there will be a reduction in the benefits bill” before the next election.

However, he said this will not include “crude cuts” to payments.

He said: “We will do that in a Labour way, and we will do that because it is simply not good for Britain, or progressive, to have a bigger and bigger benefits bills.

“This system is unsustainable. I’ve been clear about that. The Prime Minister’s been clear about that. It’s what you do about it.”

He added: “We have to bring the benefits bill down. You don’t do that by crude cuts, especially when people are feeling the cost of living pressures.”

His comments on welfare come after Tory leader Kemi Badenoch accused Labour of presiding over a Government that had left Britain “overspent, overborrowed, overtaxed and drowning in an out-of-control welfare system”.

She said: “Next year, under Labour, the tax burden will be the highest in our country’s history and our benefits bill is going up by tens of billions of pounds because this Government has put welfare first.”

The latest figures from the Office for Budget Responsibility released on Wednesday revealed that benefits spending is expected to jump by almost 30pc to £431bn by 2032.

Almost half the total is pensions and disability benefits for pensioners, despite the planned abolition of the triple lock. Here is what you need to know.
