Sports.title: Fans “pay a bit less attention” to Formula 1 as calendar gets longer – Sainz | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Carlos Sainz Jnr suspects the growing size of the Formula 1 calendar may not be helping to make the sport more popular.

F1 has increased the number of rounds to 24, though only 23 are scheduled to happen this year due to the cancellation of the Saudi Arabian Grand Prix. The number could fall further if either of the final two rounds are cancelled.

If the final rounds go ahead as planned, F1 will hold nine events in just eleven weeks. Sainz says he would have enjoyed more regular races when he was younger but suspects it may have become a turn-off for some fans.

“I think if I were a fan, I would love it because the more F1 I can watch on TV, the better,” he said. “I remember when I was a kid and there were only 16 races in the calendar, or 18. I used to miss Formula 1 [because it was not on] for a lot of weekends.

“But we also need to consider as a sport if that’s something that maybe is also counterproductive. Sometimes you need to miss the sport to get people engaged. When you get so many races in a row, people or the sport can maybe feel a bit like a league, like the Premier League rather than the Champions League. So maybe you pay a bit less attention to the matches or to the races in this case.

“So, it’s more a philosophy for the sport to consider whether you want to keep having so many races in a row.”

However Sainz, a director of the Grand Prix Drivers’ Association, is also concerned about the effect F1’s long calendar has on the teams’ staff.

“More important than that, I think as the GPDA, we’ve been told more or less that 24 races, 25 races is the limit of the championship that they’re willing to go for. I don’t know if that will be the case, the more offers there are to keep increasing venues. But I think that is the limit.

“I think it’s more about the members of the team that are going to spend only three or four days at home, or five days at home every month. And it’s the people in the teams that get the tougher end rather than the drivers. I think we are in a more privileged position in that sense.

“So, let’s see. I have the motivation to do however many races we need to do. I have the will to race. I love racing. But it is true that this end of the triple header, with three triple headers in a row, is going to be tough for the body, tough for the people, tough for the mind.”

Sports.title: F1 newcomers Tsolov, Mini and Slater among nine drivers to run in practice on Friday | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Nine teams will give practice outings to inexperienced drivers at this weekend’s Mexican Grand Prix.

Three of them – Red Bull junior driver Nikola Tsolov, Alpine’s Gabriele Mini and Audi’s Freddie Slater – will make their debuts in an official F1 test session. Tsolov will drive for Red Bull’s second F1 team, Racing Bulls.

Teams must give four opportunities to inexperienced drivers – two in each of their cars – in first practice sessions over the course of the year.

Among the others driving this weekend is Luke Browning. Williams has entered him for a fifth session this year after he completed no laps when he appeared for them at the Circuit de Catalunya. Colton Herta will also appear in a session for the fifth time this year at Cadillac.

Also in action this weekend are Leonardo Fornaroli and Jak Crawford, making their fourth appearances for McLaren and Aston Martin respectively. McLaren recently confirmed Fornaroli, the 2025 Formula 2 champion, will drive for its new WEC Hypercar team.

Ayumu Iwasa will also make his fourth appearance this year, and third for Red Bull. He has also previously driven for Racing Bulls. Ryo Hirakawa will appear for the third time in a Haas this season.

More than half the teams will have completed their obligation to run drivers on four occasions after next week’s Brazilian Grand Prix. Unlike in previous years, none of the remaining rounds are sprint events, meaning they theoretically have more opportunities to run their junior drivers. But with doubt continuing to hang over whether the final races in the Middle East will go ahead, teams appear to be ensuring they do not fail to fulfil their practice quotas should they be cancelled.

Sports.title: Ben Davison: Help Or Hindrance To His Heavyweights?
Sports.content:
It is rare for a trainer to attract as much publicity as his fighters. However, that is precisely what Ben Davison has succeeded in doing this year. For the uninitiated, Briton Davison is the trainer of heavyweights Moses Itauma, Fabio Wardley and Anthony Joshua.

Ben Davison’s profile as a trainer of heavyweights, though, really skyrocketed when he trained Tyson Fury from 2017 – 2019. During this time, many credited Davison for being responsible for The Gypsy King’s successful return to the ring after an absence of two and a half years, which Fury spent battling his demons and putting on weight.

Indeed, Davison was Fury’s trainer for his world title fight against Deontay Wilder in Los Angeles on 01 December 2018, resulting in a draw, and Wilder retaining his WBC title as the defending Champion. Fury performed well in this fight, proving that he is a talented boxer.

However, he felt there was something missing, and adjustments needed to be made. This fight demonstrated Fury’s skills as a boxer. The Gypsy King was, though, astute enough to know that just being a good boxer was not going to win him any rematch with The Bronze Bomber, famous for his legendary right hand.

Fury therefore changed trainer, enlisting the help of SugarHill Steward, the nephew of the famous Emanuel Steward, who had trained former World Heavyweight Champions Lennox Lewis and Wladimir Klitschko. The Brit did this in the hope that he would be not just a skillful boxer, but also become a ferocious puncher to combat the threat Deontay Wilder posed.

This plan worked. When Fury fought Wilder in their rematch on 22 February 2020 in Las Vegas, Fury beat Wilder by TKO in the 7th Round to win the WBC world title and the vacant The Ring heavyweight title.

Then, again with SugarHill Steward as his trainer, Fury successfully defended his WBC world title and The Ring heavyweight title against Deontay Wilder. This time, Fury went one better and beat Wilder by knockout in the 11th Round of their world title fight on 09 October 2021, also in Las Vegas.

Up to Fury’s last two fights against Wilder, The Gypsy King was not known to have the punch power to become a knockout artist. Under Steward’s tutelage, this situation changed, and Fury’s decision to leave Ben Davison was vindicated.

After Tyson Fury, Davison became the trainer of former World Champion Anthony Joshua. This is where things become interesting, as Davison was in AJ’s corner for his challenge for the IBF world title against then-champion Daniel Dubois. This all-British clash took place on 21 September 2024 at Wembley Stadium in London, England.

Joshua was having trouble in this fight, suffering knockdowns in the 1st, 3rd and 4th Rounds. In the break between the 4th and 5th Rounds, Davison seemed to advise Joshua to take a chance, coming out with the now-infamous “roll the dice” comment to his fighter.

When Davison was questioned about what he meant by this comment in a recent interview with the boxing commentator Spencer Oliver, Davison informed Oliver that the intention was for Joshua to throw a double jab and then a right uppercut at Dubois. Doing this, however, would leave Joshua’s chin exposed.

As the insightful YouTube channel Chris Talks Boxing explains, it would have been better for Davison to have advised AJ at that stage to stay out of trouble for a couple of Rounds, and rely on the jab, giving both trainer and fighter a chance to review tactics at the end of the 5th Round. In this way, Joshua would have conserved energy for the later Rounds, which was necessary, given that he had been in the wars up to that point.

As we know, however, Joshua tried to throw a right uppercut early in the 5th Round, but was caught on the chin by Dubois, forcing the former two-time World Champion to the canvas, and unable to beat the count in the same Round. It would therefore appear that Ben Davison’s tactics in this fight were at best clumsy, and at worst reckless.

Turning now to Moses Itauma, Davison has been his trainer since 2023, and was in Itauma’s corner for his fight for the vacant IBF world title against Filip Hrgović on 29 August at The O2 Arena in London, England. Up to this fight, Itauma had not been past the 6th Round in any professional fight.

Further, Itauma admitted publicly that he had not sparred 12 continuous Rounds, which is bizarre to say the least. On fight night, Itauma ran out of gas and lost to Hrgović by TKO in the 9th Round. In his recent interview with Spencer Oliver, Ben Davison mentioned that Moses Itauma is inexperienced, inferring that this is a possible reason for his loss to the Croatian.

As Chris Talks Boxing again rightly states, however, Itauma may be inexperienced, but it is his trainer Ben Davison’s responsibility to “manage” this lack of experience to get the best out of his fighter. Inexperience on the part of Itauma is therefore no excuse for Davison not preparing the young man adequately for a 12 Round fight.

Finishing with Fabio Wardley, Ben Davison was his trainer for both Wardley’s world title fights against Daniel Dubois this year. Both fights ended in TKO losses for the Ipswich man. Wardley lost his WBO world title to Dubois by TKO in the 11th Round on 09 May at Co-op Live in Manchester, England.

It was a respectable performance by Wardley. However, the rematch on 17 October at The 02 Arena in London, England was a much more one-sided affair, with Dubois winning by TKO in the 2nd Round. This last fight prompted former three-weight World Champion Duke McKenzie to go on the record saying that Ben Davison should seek help from “someone more technically minded” in training Wardley – hardly a ringing endorsement of Davison as a trainer.

Taking Davison’s record with all these heavyweights into account, it is clear that a pattern is emerging. The pattern is that Ben Davison seems unable to step up to the plate when it comes to training heavyweights for world title fights. Boxing is a results-driven sport, or at least it should be. In this regard, Davison has been found wanting, with one draw and four losses in all the Heavyweight world title fights he has been a trainer in.

This represents a 80% loss ratio with not one win. It is, of course, easy to criticize. In his last two Heavyweight world title fights, however, Ben Davison has thrown in the towel to save his fighters from further punishment. You don’t need to be a rocket scientist to come to the conclusion that there is definitely room for improvement.

Ultimately, though, it is for Davison’s heavyweights to decide whether he stays or goes!

Romer Cherubim

Freelance journalist

UK

Sports.title: Eddie Hearn Must Get Ben Whittaker’s Next Move Right
Sports.content:
Eddie Hearn needs to find Ben Whittaker a fight that prepares him for a world title shot, and Conor Wallace remains the obvious choice. At 29, Whittaker needs meaningful rounds against opponents who can expose his weaknesses, followed by evidence that he can correct them.

Anthony Yarde is among the opponents Hearn has mentioned for Whittaker, although the meeting does not establish that a fight between them is being negotiated.

Plotting what’s next 🌎 https://t.co/AWWFNVJk3p — Eddie Hearn (@EddieHearn) October 29, 2026

Whittaker earned his IBF mandatory position by beating Wallace on October 3, but the closing rounds weakened the case for sending him straight into a title fight. He controlled much of the contest before fading and getting hurt late, leaving a very different impression from the one he had built earlier.

“For me, no, he needs another fight,” Hearn said after the bout, naming Yarde, Wallace and the Joshua Buatsi–Willy Hutchinson winner as possibilities.

That leaves Hearn with a decision about what Whittaker actually needs. Another quick stoppage against an overmatched opponent would offer little preparation for championship opposition. Wallace forced him to work over the distance and exposed weaknesses that a better fighter could punish earlier.

A rematch would give Whittaker the chance to show he can finish strongly against someone who already knows how to hurt him. Wallace would have reason to attack sooner, having allowed Whittaker to collect too many of the early rounds before making his strongest effort.

Trainer Andy Lee cited COVID during the buildup to their first fight. If illness contributed to Whittaker’s late decline, facing Wallace again would provide an opportunity to demonstrate the difference a healthier preparation makes. It would also address the controversy surrounding a chaotic final round in which Whittaker went to the canvas three times without a knockdown being scored.

Yarde would bring a bigger domestic name and a heavier punching threat. That makes him an interesting option, but potentially a dangerous choice for someone who just struggled when Wallace increased the pressure. Whittaker would need to retain his concentration and defensive discipline when tired.

The Buatsi–Hutchinson winner would provide another demanding route. However, Hearn should be careful about treating any of these opponents as a convenient bridge to a title shot. Whittaker’s last performance showed why he needs the work.

Moving away from Wallace could also carry a cost with fans. Hearn has mentioned the rematch, but choosing someone else would leave the impression that his unbeaten fighter is leaving unfinished business behind.

Whittaker has time to improve at 29. His next fight needs to show that improvement, and beating Wallace more decisively would give Hearn something firmer to sell when the world title opportunity arrives.

At Whittaker’s age, a fighter does not develop an engine or an iron will out of nowhere. Those traits are either built into the foundation during the amateur days, or they simply do not exist. Whittaker entered the professional ranks with massive fanfare, an Olympic pedigree, and a style built entirely around showboating, reflexes, and athletic arrogance.

That works beautifully against overmatched opposition or journeymen who stand frozen in front of him. The moment a fighter stops watching the dancing, plants their feet, and marches forward with hard physical pressure, the entire facade begins to crack.

Liam Cameron proved it first. Cameron is a gritty, durable operator who made Whittaker uncomfortable by simply refusing to respect the theatrics, dragging him into physical trench work until that bizarre spill out of the ring brought a premature end. Instead of treating that as a warning light on the dashboard, Matchroom went right back to soft touches.

The Popeye Rivera matchup in Brooklyn was prime evidence of Hearn trying to protect the investment with harmless opposition rather than preparing him for genuine world caliber operators.

Conor Wallace brought that reality back to the surface in vicious fashion. It was not just a case of getting tired. Whittaker looked completely depleted, mentally rattled, and physically incapable of handling heavy incoming fire once the fight entered the championship rounds. Spending the twelfth round touching the canvas multiple times without the referee counting knockdowns was embarrassing for a guy calling out the division elite.

Whittaker does not possess the luxury of two or three developmental years to rebuild his gas tank and learn how to fight inside a phone booth. If he steps into the ring with a puncher like Anthony Yarde, or goes anywhere near the division monsters like Artur Beterbiev or Dmitry Bivol, the outcome is predictable. Those men do not wait around for nine rounds before turning on the pressure. They hunt you down from the opening bell.

If Hearn sends him into a rematch with Wallace and Whittaker runs out of gas again, the entire promotional work pops for good. What we saw down the stretch on October 3 might simply be Whittaker’s absolute ceiling under real pressure.

Sports.title: Jaime Munguia Gets Showcase Treatment Against Nikita Zon
Sports.content:
Jaime Munguia against Nikita Zon looks thin for a pay-per-view co-feature. Munguia supplies the name recognition, but Thursday’s press conference offered little proof that his challenger can keep the second biggest bout on Saturday’s Riyadh card competitive.

Richard Schaefer confirmed Munguia against Zon will take place immediately before Canelo Alvarez faces Christian Mbilli. That gives the WBA super middleweight title bout a prime broadcast position, yet the promotional pitch leaned on Zon entering with twelve victories and ten knockouts.

“I watched some of his fights. He’s strong, incredible power, as obviously 10 knockouts show,” Schaefer said during the media session. “I call him actually the new Siberian Rocky.”

Schaefer praised Zon’s power and stoppage record without naming a single credible opponent who proves he belongs in the ring with Munguia. Buyers heard he possesses danger, yet received zero evidence to evaluate that claim.

From a competitive standpoint, it is a gross mismatch. Munguia has logged 48 professional bouts, headlined major cards, and shared the ring with elite competition. Zon has exactly 13 fights, spent his entire career on regional Russian cards, and has never faced anyone remotely close to world class.

Slapping the moniker “the Siberian Rocky” on a completely untested fighter does not make him a threat. It is a fabricated sales gimmick designed to distract from the reality that Zon has done nothing to earn a shot at a belt on a massive international stage. Munguia should blow right through him inside five rounds, and anything less would actually look bad for Munguia.

“I came here to win and I’m leaving with nothing less than a victory. I will become the new world champion,” Zon said through a translator.

That served as his loudest quote, delivering standard bravado expected during fight week. He provided zero tactical detail on what vulnerabilities he intends to target against Munguia.

Munguia kept his comments just as brief. Asked if taking on a challenger with twelve bouts invites complacency, he pointed to his work with trainer Eddy Reynoso.

“I can just say that I’m ready. I had a great camp along Eddie. We prepared strongly,” Munguia stated through a translator. “It will be a great fight. You will see the best version of Jaime Munguia.”

The fighters offered little interest for the event. Schaefer tried filling that void by selling Zon as a raw puncher receiving a life-changing shot against an established Mexican name.

For viewers spending money on the broadcast, that pitch sounds empty. Munguia scoring a routine knockout over an untested opponent helps his record, but a premium slot requires legitimate drama. Watching an established contender cruise through a soft assignment leaves little intrigue.

As for why this fight is happening, it comes down to this. It is about keeping Munguia winning while minimizing any real risk. After picking up the WBA title against Armando Resendiz in May, his team wants him active and collecting paydays without putting him anywhere near dangerous 168-pound contenders like Osleys Iglesias, Diego Pacheco, or Hamzah Sheeraz.

Zon represents the path of least resistance for Munguia: an opponent with zero profile who will stand in front of him and provide highlight-reel footage. Boxing fans are completely exhausted by this specific brand of cynical matchmaking, which is exactly why the fight has generated virtually zero pulse online or in ticket sales.

Promoters seem to operate under the delusion that casual fans will see a gaudy knockout record, hear a goofy nickname like the “Siberian Rocky,” and instantly buy in. Today’s boxing public is far too savvy for that trick. Everyone recognizes an artificially manufactured record compiled in remote regional shows when they see one.

Sports.title: Tim Bradley Gives Shakur Stevenson A Muratalla Escape Route
Sports.content:
Tim Bradley just offered Shakur Stevenson a convenient exit, one that spares him from a dangerous matchup with minimal reward. Raymond Muratalla brings serious heat without anywhere near the $15 million purse Bradley claims Stevenson wants. Stevenson could get caught, maybe even stopped, or grind out a safety-first decision that leaves fans booing anyway.

Heading back down to lightweight might not double his money, but it gives him cover. It lets him chase a different target under the banner of championship glory. Bradley basically handed him the script: drop back to 135 pounds, then unify the division.

“Now if he says, ‘I’m not going to fight him, and I’m going to go down, and I’m going to fight Zepeda for a belt,’ I’m cool with that. I’m cool with that. Stay at 135 and clean up the division. That’s what you should do,” Bradley said on his channel.

That backing carries weight while critics blast Stevenson over whether he will actually take the WBO mandate against Muratalla. Bradley opened by claiming there is “no hiding,” only to lay out the exact road map for Stevenson to walk away with his blessing.

Muratalla creates a tactical nightmare where even a victory might fail to win over frustrated fans. If Stevenson chooses to stand his ground, he gives a heavy hitter chances to connect. If he gets on his bicycle to protect the zero on his record, he only fuels the talk about being boring.

A knockout loss is a real danger here. Bradley insists he expects Stevenson to win, but picking him to prevail does not remove the physical threat, nor does it guarantee the performance builds any future buzz.

The money also looks shaky according to Bradley.

“He’s going to have to take a little bit less. It ain’t going to be $15 million. It’s going to be a lot less,” Bradley said.

From a business standpoint, retreating to lightweight makes plenty of sense. Stevenson does not even need a massive raise to justify the switch. Taking similar cash against someone his camp feels better about beats stepping into Muratalla’s crosshairs.

Dropping to 135 guarantees nothing simple, of course. Bradley’s plan means hunting down titleholders, specifically giving the green light to a tilt with William Zepeda. The real value comes down to the matchup details rather than just stepping on the scale at a lighter weight.

When a fan noted that Bradley pushed for a 135-pound return before the sanctioning body stepped in, the analyst stood firm. Stevenson can leave junior welterweight behind, but he has to plant his feet at lightweight instead of bouncing right back up after ducking Muratalla.

That bargain works for Bradley, but skeptical fight fans who want to see Muratalla get his shot will be a much tougher crowd.

Bradley supplied the public excuse by urging a chase for undisputed glory at lightweight. The real payoff is ducking a punishing clash for a paycheck that falls flat. Both realities can coexist, yet picking up another strap somewhere else will not silence the whispers about Muratalla.

Shakur’s silence is deafening, especially coming from someone who usually treats social media like a live microphone. When a fighter makes noise 24/7 about nobody wanting to get in the ring with them, going completely dark the second an actual mandatory gets called creates an awful look. It looks like battlefield freeze.

Usually, the moment a sanctioning body steps in, guys start chest-thumping about easy work, post-training clips, or talk about who is getting exposed. Instead, crickets. In combat sports, sudden radio silence often signals hesitation rather than quiet confidence. Stevenson knows Muratalla is not an aging name brought in to pad a highlight reel or a blown-up featherweight looking for a payday.

Muratalla is big, physically imposing, applies relentless forward pressure, and throws with spite. He does not care about fancy footwork or playing a game of tag to lose a decision.

Taking on a heavy-handed, high-volume puncher with everything to gain and nothing to lose requires digging into the trenches. When the reality sets in that there is no massive eight-figure check waiting on the other side to justify that kind of physical punishment, battle nerves kick in fast.

Right now, his camp is likely running the numbers and looking for every possible exit route. Dropping back down to 135 to claim an undisputed crown sounds a lot more heroic in a press release than admitting you want no part of an absolute buzzsaw at 140.

Sports.title: Richard Schaefer Oversells Canelo Alvarez’s Christian Mbilli Choice
Sports.content:
Canelo Alvarez looks to have picked the softer option in Christian Mbilli, though nobody expects an easy night at the office. Mbilli gives Canelo clear lanes to time counters, letting him steal rounds on the scorecards even if he gets outworked. Osleys Iglesias, on the other hand, represents a far more unforgiving matchup.

Promoter Richard Schaefer repeatedly praised Canelo at Thursday’s final press conference for picking Mbilli to give fans the best fight possible. That narrative ignored how slim the pool really was. With WBA titlist Jaime Munguia practically off the table due to gym loyalty, plus a vacant WBO belt, Canelo really only had Mbilli or IBF champion Iglesias to consider.

“Because I do not believe in shortcuts. I have been a champion for many years. I just want to fight the best,” Canelo said when asked about the decision.

Even if Mbilli throws a hundred punches a round, Canelo knows how judges score fights. A crisp, explosive counter shot that snaps an opponent’s head back often wins rounds over flurry work that lands to the body, head, or gloves. Against Mbilli, Canelo has a clear path to win rounds on the cards.

Iglesias is an entirely different problem, and arguably a far more punishing one. The Cuban is a rangy, hard-hitting southpaw who controls real estate with a stiff jab and detonates with a lead right hook. Canelo struggling against disciplined boxers with length and movement is well established.

Following Iglesias around the ring while absorbing straight lefts, right hooks, and jabs would be grueling, with very few clean openings to fire back. Iglesias brings real knockout danger without needing to smother himself on the inside to get it. Iglesias brings the bigger punch, but he also possesses the technical skill to dominate without hunting for a knockout.

Canelo risks trailing, missing, and soaking up damage without landing enough in return to keep pace. Reaching the final bell would still leave him battered. That is a projection, yet the Cuban’s length, precision, and power make it a very real danger.

Mbilli brings heat of his own. His swarm could pin Canelo against the ropes for long stretches. The difference is that Mbilli’s relentless forward motion keeps him squarely in range for Canelo’s signature counter rights and body hooks.

That gives Canelo a realistic path to victory. Mbilli can throw and land three as many punches, but judges often reward Canelo’s cleaner, harder single shots. Activity does not guarantee points, and Mbilli will offer plenty of targets for flashier work.

Canelo would get far fewer looks against Iglesias. He would need to evade the jab, close the gap, and connect before Iglesias moves away or fires back with something harder.

“I just need to be myself, and that is how I am going to win this fight,” Mbilli stated.

He could be right. Mbilli’s furious engine could easily overwhelm the veteran if Canelo cannot punch with enough authority to slow him down. Calling him the better option is far from guaranteeing a Canelo win.

Canelo never admitted to dodging Iglesias over stylistic concerns, and this remains a personal breakdown of the matchup. Still, Schaefer’s spin invites a reality check. Between the two champions on the table, Canelo selected the opponent who gives him room to land and a much clearer route to a victory on the cards.

It still could be controversial if Canelo wins a decision against Mbilli, but at least he would see the final bell, and his face wouldn’t be as beat up as it would be against Iglesias.

Sports.title: Tim Bradley’s Canelo Massacre Pick Ignores Reality
Sports.content:
Tim Bradley expects Canelo Alvarez to completely destroy Christian Mbilli, but that forecast fits the fighter Canelo used to be, not the one we see in the ring today. While his counterpunching remains lethal, blowing out an energetic pressure fighter requires relentless, high-gear output that recent outings just do not support.

Bradley argues that veteran savvy and sharp timing will punish Mbilli’s defensive flaws. That prediction hinges on Canelo avoiding the ropes and dictating action in the center of the ring.

“Canelo by massacre. Canelo by massacre. That’s what I got. He might even stop him,” Bradley said on Into the Storm. “Canelo is not gonna throw more punches than Mbilli, but his punches gonna be way more accurate, way more sound, way more placed than Mbilli.”

Bradley points to a glaring habit in Mbilli’s approach. When Mbilli bites on feints, he tends to dip his head and stare at the canvas, opening himself up to clean hooks and uppercuts. The expectation is that Canelo will time those flaws, threading counters through the incoming storm to force a late stoppage.

Still, even peak Canelo rarely battered elite competition into submission the way Bradley imagines. Older versions of Shane Mosley and Miguel Cotto went the full twelve. Gennadiy Golovkin lasted thirty-six rounds with him across three meetings, including the trilogy finale when Golovkin was forty. Different styles produce different results, but boxing history shows that defensive openings do not immediately guarantee a blowout.

Bradley fought in that very same era, so his viewpoint might lean on respect for his peer group. That does not discount his technical breakdown, but it does raise questions about whether his prediction relies on an outdated version of the Mexican star.

Seeing an opening is completely different from exploiting it through twelve fast-paced rounds. Canelo might spot the exact counter he wants, yet lack the stamina to deliver it over and over. A single crisp shot might turn heads, but it will not magically halt the next wave of pressure if Canelo cannot command real estate.

“As long as Canelo keep his back up off the ropes and keep the fight in the center of the ring,” Bradley added, suggesting Canelo should handle the assignment smoothly.

The eye test over the past few years undercuts any idea that Canelo is going to command the center of the ring against a relentless motor like Mbilli. Ever since the Jermell Charlo fight, Canelo’s legs have steadily abandoned him. What used to be deliberate ring generalship has turned into an older fighter looking for a place to lean.

Once the clock hits round six, his default setting is backing straight into the ropes, shelling up behind the high guard, and letting the ropes do the work of keeping him upright.

Against Jaime Munguia, Edgar Berlanga, William Scull, and Terence Crawford, that exact pattern played out. Canelo cannot sustain footwork to dictate geography anymore, and he certainly lacks the conditioning to maintain the work rate required to keep an aggressive dog off his chest. His stamina dictates that he fights in brief, explosive bursts, spending the remaining two minutes of every round resting and waiting to time a single big counter.

That strategy works when hand-picking opponents who either freeze under the lights or lack the punch volume and inside craft to make him pay for taking rounds off. Munguia had the volume but zero defensive awareness or punching power; Berlanga was hesitant and limited; Scull had nowhere near the offensive pop or pedigree to capitalize. They were tailor-made style matchups designed to let Canelo coast on reputation and single heavy shots.

Mbilli is the complete opposite of a hand-picked rest stop. He does not care about getting countered; he never stops throwing, and he thrives precisely where Canelo now camps out: on the inside, chest-to-chest, hammering away at the ribs and arms.

If Canelo’s only plan is to retreat to the ropes and look for single uppercuts while Mbilli fires non-stop for twelve rounds, relying on the judges to favor low-volume potshots is going to be a very dangerous game.

Sports.title: O’Shaquie Foster Reveals Shakur Stevenson Vanished After Ring Stunt
Sports.content:
Shakur Stevenson gathered all the buzz for a potential O’Shaquie Foster bout without stepping into the ring. By stepping through the ropes following Foster’s win over Raymond Ford in May, Stevenson ignited major public anticipation. Yet Foster reveals his team pushed for the bout, waited, and met total silence.

That recent past demands a sharper look at Stevenson’s latest words. Foster just took down Emanuel Navarrete, and Stevenson quickly voiced fresh interest. Boxing enthusiasts ought to pause before celebrating, keeping Foster’s prior experience in mind.

“We kept asking. We didn’t hear nothing. We didn’t hear nothing,” Foster said on the Ariel Helwani show. “We held out for a little bit. We didn’t hear nothing. Tyrone didn’t hear nothing.”

Foster explained that talks never progressed to discussing weight classes. He expressed total readiness to step up to lightweight or junior welterweight, clearing away a major hurdle for a 130-pound titleholder looking upward.

“We didn’t even get that far, but I didn’t care,” Foster noted. “Like, I honestly didn’t care whether it was 135, 140. Either one. It didn’t matter to me.”

It looked like pure clout chasing from Shakur, plain and simple. Walking into another man’s spotlight right after a hard-earned victory creates the illusion that you want the fight next. Fans get excited, the broadcast cameras lock onto you, and you get all the free publicity without taking an ounce of risk. Then, the second Foster’s camp actually reached out to make the fight happen, Shakur vanished into thin air. Total silence.

Once Foster beat Navarrete, Stevenson offered public compliments along with a fresh challenge.

“Hell of a fighter. He will never give me my credit, but I’ll be real tonight. He showed his level,” Stevenson stated in a social post read on air. “That’s a challenge that would get me out of bed. Let’s do it whenever he’s ready. I’ll be here after his undisputed run.”

That is what makes Stevenson’s latest comment after Foster beat Navarrete look so empty. Saying he will fight Foster “whenever he’s ready” completely flips the reality of what happened. Foster was ready months ago, even offering to jump up in weight to make it effortless for Stevenson. Shakur was the one who went missing.

For now, Foster’s sights remain locked on unifying all four belts at 130 pounds. Chasing undisputed status puts Foster in control rather than hanging on Shakur’s schedule. Foster can hunt the remaining belt while Stevenson figures out whether his online comments translate into real business.

Sports.title: David Benavidez Gives PBC More Years Without Becoming A Star
Sports.content:
David Benavidez is locking in more of his prime with PBC, even though his run with the outfit has not turned him into a household name. He has collected belts in three divisions. Casual fans still have little reason to tune in, and facing Michal Cieslak on December 5 will not change that.

Benavidez turns thirty next year. He burned through his twenties chasing Canelo Alvarez. Then he cleared out of light heavyweight without ever facing Dmitry Bivol or Artur Beterbiev. Now he sits at cruiserweight, stacking belts while marquee opponents remain out of reach.

“I’ve always wanted to stay with PBC. I feel like what we’ve built, obviously PBC is PBC before I got there, but the work I’ve put in for this promotional company, I’m not going to get that anywhere else,” Benavidez told FightHubTV. “I feel comfortable with Luis De Cubas. I feel comfortable with Al Haymon. This is my family. I’m one of the pillars that helps PBC stand.”

He sounds like someone trapped by sunk costs. Pouring years into a promotional stable is no reason to surrender the rest of his career. If mainstream fame is the actual target, he needs to look honestly at what loyalty has given him.

He has put on solid bouts. Caleb Plant provided genuine heat. Demetrius Andrade came undefeated. David Morrell was a dangerous test. Gilberto Ramirez offered the chance to pick up cruiserweight hardware. The resume is legitimate.

The box office numbers tell a different story. Reports put the Morrell clash at 150,000 to 160,000 pay-per-view buys. The Andrade fight reportedly landed around 60,000 buys. Those figures are not official numbers, but they prove he has not developed into an elite pay-per-view draw.

Canelo was the matchup that could have launched him into superstardom. It never happened, even with both fighters under the PBC umbrella. Canelo walked his own road, while Benavidez paid the bill in wasted time. Sharing a promotional banner provided zero leverage to force the biggest draw into the ring.

Bivol chose his own path too, giving up the WBC belt rather than facing Benavidez in 2025. Promoters cannot force anyone to sign. Yet Benavidez is the one creeping toward thirty without those career-defining names on his record.

Cieslak brings another strap to the table, but offers zero buzz for American fans. Winning might give Benavidez three cruiserweight titles, yet leave him completely invisible to general sports culture. That is the exact loop he must break.

Launching DB Promotions once his deal with Sampson Lewkowicz wraps up gives him real leverage. Sticking with PBC feels familiar, but familiarity seems to be his main motivation for staying put.

Benavidez has shown he can win titles with this team. He has not shown he can become a crossover sensation with them. Betting the remainder of his peak on this same routine is risky. He needs Jai Opetaia or another opponent people will actually pay to watch. Cieslak is just another belt while the real clock keeps ticking.

Ghana News.title: Galamsey fight will fail without mindset change — Young Dee Group CEO
Ghana News.content:
Young Dee Group Chief Executive Officer Desmond Darko has urged Ghana’s leaders to address what he describes as the mindset driving illegal mining (galamsey), arguing that enforcement alone cannot end the menace.

He said efforts to stop illegal mining would remain ineffective if authorities failed to understand why people in some communities continued to depend on gold extraction for their livelihoods.

Speaking on Joy FM’s Personality Profile with Lexis Bill on Thursday, October 29, Mr Darko said the problem went beyond the enforcement of laws and required a change in attitudes, alongside practical alternatives for affected communities.

“Ghana is struggling to solve galamsey because the leaders are refusing to understand that galamsey is a psychological problem. It's a mindset problem,” he said.

“And until they deal with the mindset, they can never solve galamsey in this country,” he added.

Alternative livelihoods

Mr Darko said some people in mining communities had spent much of their lives depending on rivers and other natural resources in their search for gold.

He questioned the effectiveness of demanding that such people abandon the activity without first addressing the economic circumstances and beliefs that sustained it.

“You are dealing with people in a community where their lifetime, the only way they know, is to go to the riverside and go and look for gold,” he said.

“And you are not giving them any alternative. You are not working on their mindset, and you think you can just go there and tell them to stop what they are doing,” he added.

He maintained that a lasting response to illegal mining required leaders to engage with the communities involved and address the factors that made the activity attractive to them.

Beyond enforcement

Mr Darko’s comments add to calls for approaches to galamsey that look beyond arrests and operations against illegal miners to consider the livelihoods of people who depend on mining.

His argument is that communities cannot be expected to abandon an established source of income without viable alternatives and efforts to change attitudes towards illegal mining.

Galamsey has remained a major environmental concern in Ghana because of the damage associated with illegal mining, including pollution of water bodies and the degradation of land.

Mr Darko said unless leaders recognised and addressed the mindset underpinning the activity, efforts to bring it to an end would continue to fall short.

Ghana News.title: AFCON back to every two years as CAF reverses decision
Ghana News.content:
AFCON trophy

The Confederation of African Football (CAF) has reversed its decision to hold the Africa Cup of Nations every four years, restoring the tournament’s two-year cycle.

In a post on X, CAF said its Executive Committee unanimously approved the return to the biennial schedule.

“The Confédération Africaine de Football (‘CAF’) Executive Committee (‘EXCO’) today unanimously decided that the CAF Africa Cup of Nations (‘AFCON’) will return to taking place every Two Years,” the statement said.

The Confédération Africaine de Football (“CAF”) Executive Committee (“EXCO”) today unanimously decided that the CAF Africa Cup of Nations (“AFCON”) will return to taking place every Two Years. The President of CAF Dr Patrice Motsepe announced at the CAF Strategy Conference in Cabo Verde which was held from 7-9 October 2026, that the CAF EXCO would be re-assessing and reconsidering the decision it took last year, for the AFCON to take place every Four Years. https://t.co/fYNKBPhPae — CAF Media (@CAF_Media) October 30, 2026

The decision follows an announcement by CAF President Dr Patrice Motsepe at the CAF Strategy Conference in Cabo Verde, held from October 7 to 9, 2026.

At that conference, Motsepe said the Executive Committee would reassess the decision it took last year to stage AFCON every four years.

The unanimous vote now overturns that move. However, CAF’s post did not specify which edition would mark the start of the restored two-year cycle.

Ghana News.title: Minerals Commission tells Northern Ashanti Mines to fight lease termination in court, not media
Ghana News.content:
The Minerals Commission has urged Northern Ashanti Mines Limited to pursue its legal challenge against the termination of its mining leases and prospecting licences in court rather than commenting publicly.

The Commission says the company acknowledged receipt of the termination notice but subsequently instituted legal action against the Minister responsible for Lands and Natural Resources, the Commission and the Attorney-General.

The dispute follows an operation on Thursday, October 22, during which Commission officials, accompanied by military personnel, entered the company’s concession to enforce the termination of its mineral rights.

The Commission cited the company’s failure to pay statutory fees and undertake meaningful mining operations for more than two years as grounds for the decision.

It says Northern Ashanti Mines owed US$8.33 million in outstanding Annual Mineral Right fees for its mining leases covering 2010 to 2025, as well as US$49,928 in fees relating to prospecting licences between 2019 and 2025.

The Commission maintains that it followed the Minerals and Mining Act, 2006 (Act 703), the Minerals and Mining (Licensing) Regulations, 2012 (L.I. 2176), and the terms of the agreements with the company. It also says the company was given several opportunities to regularise its position but failed to do so.

Speaking at a press conference on Thursday, October 29, the Minerals Commission's Chief Executive Officer, Isaac Tandoh, said the company should let the judicial process determine the dispute.

“The company duly acknowledged receipt of the termination notice, and yet it has chosen the courts. So we advise that they should pursue the courts and not the court of public opinion,” he said.

Mr Tandoh also rejected the company’s position that it was seeking dialogue, arguing that its decision to sue the relevant authorities while making public statements amounted to pursuing the dispute in court and through the media simultaneously.

“We state plainly, a company that sues the Honourable Minister, the Minerals Commission and the Attorney General is not a company that is seeking dialogue. It is a company seeking to litigate in court and in the media simultaneously. This is improper, and it is contemptuous of the judicial process,” he said.

He added that the termination had caused the mineral rights to revert to the state but did not extinguish the company’s outstanding financial obligations. The Commission said it will continue pursuing recovery of the outstanding fees.

Ghana News.title: 2027 Budget to prioritise jobs, productivity and higher incomes – Nyarko Ampem
Ghana News.content:
Thomas Nyarko Ampem

The government is expected to place job creation, increased productivity and economic growth at the centre of its 2027 Budget as it seeks to turn recent improvements in economic stability into tangible benefits for Ghanaians.

Deputy Finance Minister Thomas Nyarko Ampem says the next phase of the government's economic programme will focus on expanding employment opportunities, raising incomes and building a competitive economy driven by technology and value addition.

The 2027 Budget is scheduled to be presented to Parliament on November 12. Speaking at the maiden launch of Ghana in Numbers 2025 in Accra on Thursday, October 29, Mr Nyarko Ampem said economic stability must now translate into improved livelihoods.

“Stability is the foundation. Productivity is the engine. Jobs and prosperity must be the destination,” he said.

He cited economic growth of 6% in 2025 and 6.2% in the first half of 2026, alongside a decline in inflation from 23.8% in December 2024 to 5.2% in September 2026, as indicators of the progress made in stabilising the economy.

Mr Nyarko Ampem said the government would use the next phase of its economic agenda to strengthen local businesses, add value to Ghana's natural resources and create more opportunities for young people.

He argued that the country must move away from relying heavily on raw material exports and build its capacity to produce and export higher-value goods and services.

“We must move from exporting raw materials to exporting value and from producing job seekers to nurturing innovators, entrepreneurs and job creators,” he said.

The November 12 presentation is expected to set out the government's policy and spending priorities for 2027, with particular attention to productivity, employment and ensuring that macroeconomic gains lead to better living standards.

Ghana News.title: Mahama says social media criticism helps him become a better leader
Ghana News.content:
President John Dramani Mahama

President John Mahama has disclosed that social media platforms, including TikTok, help him pick up public complaints and feedback on government performance, which he forwards to ministers for attention.

He says criticism from citizens, regardless of their political affiliations, is an important tool for improving governance and helping him become a better leader.

Speaking during an engagement with the Ghanaian Community in Moscow, President Mahama said he does not take offence when citizens accuse his administration of heading in the wrong direction, insisting that constructive criticism helps him identify problems and demand answers from his ministers.

"I don't mind if people tell me that I'm leading the country in the wrong direction. I'm trying to do my best. Criticism helps me to do better," he said.

The President disclosed that he sometimes comes across complaints social media and contacts ministers directly to seek explanations about developments in their respective sectors.

"Sometimes I go on the media and I see something, and I call the minister and I say, 'Hey, my friend, what is happening in your sector?'" he recounted.

He assured citizens that their videos and complaints do not go unnoticed.

"So all your TikToks and things, don't think I don't see them. I see them," President Mahama said.

To illustrate how social media feedback informs government action, he cited a complaint about a bridge in the Ashanti Region which had reportedly been affected by illegal mining activities and washed away.

The President said he saw the information on social media and immediately forwarded it to the minister responsible, requesting that the situation be died

According to him, the minister subsequently visited the location and reported that a blocked channel was contributing to the problem, with an excavator being deployed to clear it and allow water to flow.

"That is how you solve some of these things," he said. President Mahama believes the growing influence of new media presents an opportunity for government to receive information directly from citizens and respond to challenges as they emerge.

"The new media is an advantage because it gives us information in real time," he added.

He urged citizens to speak up whenever they identify warning signs in the country's governance, stressing that holding leaders accountable should transcend partisan political considerations.

"The more we see the danger signs that somebody is leading us the wrong way, we must, all of us, not based on partisan leanings, all of us must say no, we're not going in the right direction," he said.

Ghana News.title: CAA, NFA, Copyright Ghana to lead dialogue on creatives’ pension scheme
Ghana News.content:
created by photogrid

The Creative Arts Agency (CAA), National Film Authority (NFA) and Copyright Ghana will lead stakeholder discussions on a sustainable pension and social security programme for Ghanaian creative professionals.

The dialogue, dubbed “My Art, My Ark! Dialogue”, is scheduled for Monday, 2 November 2026, at the British Council in Accra, beginning at 12:30 p.m.

The initiative is being organised by the CAA and NFA in partnership with Copyright Ghana and its Collective Management Organisations (CMOs): CopyGhana, ARSOG and GHAMRO, with support from the British Council, Accra.

The engagement seeks to develop a roadmap towards establishing a social security programme that responds to the financial security and long-term welfare needs of Ghanaian creative professionals.

Pension schemes provide a mechanism for individuals to build financial security for retirement through contributions accumulated during their working lives. However, creative professionals often face distinctive employment and income challenges, including freelance engagements, irregular earnings and limited access to conventional employment benefits.

These realities raise an important question: How can Ghana develop a sustainable pension arrangement that accommodates the diverse working conditions and income patterns of its creative workforce?

Beyond individual contributions, the proposed initiative brings into focus the role of government, relevant public institutions, industry organisations and other stakeholders in creating the policy, regulatory and administrative conditions necessary to make such a programme possible.

The dialogue is expected to provide a platform for brainstorming practical, inclusive and sustainable approaches to extending social security opportunities to creatives across Ghana’s diverse creative arts and cultural industries.

The initiative is linked to a manifesto commitment under the Black Star Experience to establish and promote “career security through legal and financial protection and mass pension schemes”.

Translating this commitment into a workable programme will require coordination among relevant government agencies, collective management organisations, creative industry associations and the professionals who stand to benefit from the proposed arrangement.

Key considerations include how creatives with irregular incomes can participate, the potential contribution structure, the institutional framework for implementation and the measures required to ensure the programme’s long-term sustainability.

The stakeholder dialogue is intended to contribute to a roadmap for addressing these issues and advancing discussions towards a social security framework tailored to the realities of Ghana’s creative economy.

As Ghana continues to explore ways of strengthening its creative economy, the proposed dialogue places an important issue on the industry agenda: ensuring that the people whose talents, ideas and intellectual contributions generate cultural and economic value can also work towards a more financially secure future.

Ghana News.title: Namibia President urges Africa to harness natural resources, youth for global influence
Ghana News.content:
Namibian President Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah

Namibian President Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah says Africa must harness its vast natural resources and youthful population to strengthen its economic power and influence global decisions, rather than allow others to determine the continent’s future.

She argues that Africa’s population of more than a billion people and its rich natural resources give the continent considerable economic leverage, which could be better utilised through stronger regional cooperation and increased trade among African countries.

In an interview on Diplomatic Affairs with Harriet Nartey on Joy Prime, President Nandi-Ndaitwah said Africa must recognise its strengths and take greater responsibility for shaping the rules governing its participation in the global economy.

“I believe that Africa needs to recognise their strength. First and foremost, we are a useful continent as we are now, and that is our biggest resource. That is complemented by our natural resources,” she said.

The Namibian leader believes the continent must move beyond dependence on decisions made by external powers and build the confidence to set its own economic priorities.

“Africa can take its own decisions and defend their decisions. And let others come in, if they want to come in,” she stated.

President Nandi-Ndaitwah said Africa’s large population represents a significant market that could promote trade, strengthen local industries, and attract partners seeking to participate in the continent’s economic growth.

She called for a stronger African Continental Free Trade Area, arguing that deeper economic integration would encourage countries to trade more among themselves and strengthen their collective position in the global marketplace.

“If you really will see that we have been squeezed in this global village, and we strengthened our continental free trade area, and really decide to trade among ourselves, the others who come and join us,” she said.

The President also questioned the tendency of African countries to approach international trade negotiations using rules and frameworks developed elsewhere, rather than defining arrangements that reflect the continent’s priorities.

She cited rules of origin as an example, suggesting African countries should consider how to shape such rules to serve their interests.

Diplomatic Affairs with Harriet Nartey is aired every Sunday at 7:30 pm on Joy Prime

World.title: Trump pleads not guilty to 34 felony counts
World.content:
News outlets will not be allowed to broadcast former President Donald Trump’s arraignment on Tuesday in a New York state court, a judge said Monday night, but he will allow some photographers to take pictures in the courtroom before the proceedings formally begin.

Acting New York Supreme Court Judge Juan Merchan rejected the request by several media organizations, including CNN, for permission to broadcast the historic proceedings. Trump’s arraignment — like most arraignments in the Manhattan courthouse — is a public proceeding, but news cameras are not usually allowed to broadcast from inside the courtroom.

However, the judge is allowing five pool photographers to take still photos at the beginning of the proceedings “until such time as they are directed to vacate the jury box by court personnel.”

Earlier on Monday, Trump’s lawyers urged the judge to reject the media’s request for live cameras in the courtroom. The Manhattan District Attorney’s office told the judge they didn’t have a position.

The media outlets that tried to get cameras into the courtroom argued that “the gravity of this proceeding … and, consequently, the need for the broadest possible public access, cannot be overstated.”

Trump is now in Manhattan ahead of the arraignment. A grand jury indicted the former president last week.

The arraignment is also expected to bring the unsealing of the criminal charges against Trump, which have not yet been seen by his lawyers or the public.

The indictment stems from Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg’s investigation into hush-money payments, made during the 2016 presidential campaign, to women who claimed they had extramarital affairs with Trump, which he denies.

Trump denies all wrongdoing and his lawyers said last week that they’ll fight to get the charges dropped.

A Ukrainian tank is seen near the frontline area amid the Russia-Ukraine war, in Bakhmut, Ukraine, on April 02. (Muhammed Enes Yildirim/Anadolu Agency/Getty Images)

The Ukrainian military has reported little change to the front lines but heavy fire from Russian forces at various parts of the front line in the Donetsk region.

The General Staff said that more than 45 enemy attacks had been repelled over the past day, with the focus on Lyman, Bakhmut, Avdiivka and Mariinka.

It said there were 17 air strikes and more than 20 strikes by multiple launch rocket systems.

“In the Bakhmut direction, the enemy is trying to take full control over the city of Bakhmut and continues to storm it,” the General Staff said.

West of the city, Ukrainian defense forces repelled about 20 enemy attacks, according to the General Staff.

Oleksandr Syrskyi, commander of Ukrainian Land Forces, posted on Telegram that in Bakhmut he had met with “soldiers and commanders who destroyed the myth of invincibility of the Wagner fighters and Russian paratroopers.”

“The enemy is weakening and trying to cover up its failures with new fakes about the capture of Bakhmut,” Syrskyi said.

Syrskyi referenced the possibility of a future counter-offensive, saying that “the forward movement of our entire army depends on what every soldier is doing right now on their section of the front.”

Some of the most intense fighting is to the northwest and west of the city of Donetsk – as the Russians continue months-long efforts to dislodge Ukrainian defenses in Avdiivka and Mariinka. The General Staff said that some 20 assaults had been repelled.

“There are also some operational successes of our military in the Donetsk area. Our military have taken some positions. They have taken a more strategic and favourable position,” said Oleksii Dmytrashkivskyi, spokesperson for the military in that zone.

He also noted that Russian special forces had been introduced in the area.

“The enemy is trying to attack our positions between Avdiivka and Marinka. These attempts do not stop. It should be noted that the enemy has suffered quite significant losses,” Dmytrashkivskyi said.

He also claimed that the Russians “don’t have the same amount of equipment and, as they themselves say, they are on a ‘diet’ of ammunition for assaults.”

Social media video showed both sides engaged in heavy fire in the Avdiivka area, which the Russians have surrounded on three sides.

Denis Pushilin, the leader of the self-declared Donetsk People’s Republic, claimed that Russian forces were still advancing in the Avdiivka direction.

“It is still premature to speak of encirclement, but the situation is being created, if not critical, then extremely difficult for the enemy… After clearing Kamianka, our units are moving further. There are difficulties both with the terrain, which must also be overcome, and there are also similarities with weather conditions. But these difficulties are mutual — both for the enemy and for us,” Pushilin said.

World.title: Suspected Chinese spy balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing
World.content:
Washington —

The Chinese spy balloon that transited the US earlier this year was able to capture imagery and collect some signals intelligence from US military sites, a source familiar with the matter tells CNN.

The balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing in real time, the source said, and the US government still does not know for sure whether the Chinese government could wipe the balloon’s data as it received it. That raises questions about whether there is intelligence the balloon was able to gather that the US still doesn’t know about.

Still, the intelligence community has not been overly concerned about the information the balloon was able to gather, the person said, because it is not much more sophisticated than what Chinese satellites are able to glean as they orbit over similar locations.

A US intelligence official told CNN on Monday that “although analysis of the wreckage of the High Altitude Balloon remains ongoing, thus far, its flight over the United States does not appear to have provided critical new insights to the People’s Republic of China.”

The US also knew what the balloon’s path would be and was able to protect sensitive sites and censor some signals before the balloon was able to pick them up, officials have said.

As CNN has reported, the US intelligence community last year developed a method of tracking what it says is a fleet of these Chinese balloons operating across the globe, controlled by the Chinese military.

The FBI is still examining the balloon, but so far officials have been able to glean additional information about how the device worked, including the algorithms used for the balloon’s software and how it is powered and designed.

CNN has reached out to the National Security Council at the White House and the Pentagon for comment. NBC was first to report on the new intelligence.

Video Ad Feedback Justin Trudeau on what the world needs to do to handle China's threats 1:33 • Source: CNN Justin Trudeau on what the world needs to do to handle China's threats 1:33

The balloon first crossed into US airspace over Alaska in late January before passing through Canada and down into Montana, where it hovered for a few days, leading the US to believe it was trying to surveil sensitive military sites, like Malmstrom Air Force Base in Montana. It was eventually shot down by the US off the East Coast on February 4, and the incident further escalated tensions between Washington and Beijing, including the postponement of a diplomatic visit by US Secretary of State Antony Blinken to China.

A senior State Department official said in February that, as the balloon floated across the US, it “was capable of conducting signals intelligence collection operations.”

Gen. Glen VanHerck, the commander of US Northern Command and NORAD, said at the time that the US “did not assess” that the balloon “presented a significant collection hazard beyond what already exists in actionable technical means from the Chinese.”

The surveillance program, which includes a number of similar balloons, is in part run out of the small Chinese province of Hainan, officials told CNN. The US does not know the precise size of the fleet of Chinese surveillance balloons, but sources tell CNN that the program has conducted at least two dozen missions over at least five continents in recent years.

Roughly half a dozen of those flights have been within US airspace, although not necessarily over US territory, according to one official familiar with the intelligence.

China has maintained that the balloon was actually just a weather balloon thrown off course, and the US has been assessing the possibility that it was not deliberately maneuvered into the continental US by the Chinese government, CNN has reported.

Still, China did maintain some ability to maneuver the balloon, officials believe. And once the balloon was over Montana, China appeared to take advantage of its position to loiter over sensitive sites and try to collect intelligence.

This story has been updated with additional reporting.

World.title: Beijing promised to 'fight back' over Taiwan leader's US visit. But this time it has more to lose
World.content:
Hong Kong —

An anticipated meeting between Taiwan’s President Tsai Ing-wen and US House Speaker Kevin McCarthy in California this week has sparked concerns of a repeat of the pressure campaign China launched last year when then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi visited Taipei.

At that time, Beijing encircled the island democracy with unprecedented military drills – firing multiple missiles into its surrounding waters and sending dozens of warplanes speeding across a sensitive median line dividing the Taiwan Strait.

It also cut off contact with the United States over a number of issues from military matters to combating climate change, in retaliation for what it viewed as a violation of its sovereignty.

This time, Beijing has already threatened to “resolutely fight back” if a Tsai-McCarthy meeting goes ahead.

Video Ad Feedback See why tensions are rising between US and China over Taiwan 2:32 • Source: CNN See why tensions are rising between US and China over Taiwan 2:32

It also slammed Washington for allowing Tsai to stopover in the US while en route to and from official visits in Central America, warning it could lead to “serious” confrontation between the two powers.

A defiant Tsai staked out her own ground, pledging as she took off on her 10-day trip not to let “external pressure” stop Taiwan from connecting with the world and like-minded democracies.

But the optics of the meeting, taking place in California and not Taiwan, and its timing – at a particularly thorny moment in China’s foreign relations and ahead of a presidential election in Taiwan that could reset the tone of its relationship with Beijing – may see Beijing tread more carefully this time, or at least not escalate further, analysts say.

“This puts the burden on China not to overreact, because any overreaction is only going to push China further away from the world,” said Yun Sun, director of the China Program at the Stimson Center think tank in Washington.

That doesn’t mean, however, that Beijing won’t be closely watching Tsai’s movements as it calibrates its response – and decides how much military might to flex over her meeting with an American lawmaker on American soil.

The opacity of China’s system – and the potential for competing interests within its vast bureaucracy – also make it difficult to accurately predict its response.

“Every time Taiwan does anything that China doesn’t like, the Chinese react with their own military coercion,” Sun said. But in the current situation, “they have to consider the consequences of overreaction,” she added.

House Speaker Kevin McCarthy talks to reporters at the Capitol in Washington on March 24, 2023. J. Scott Applewhite/AP

Rising pressure

The expected meeting, which McCarthy’s office announced earlier this week would take place on Wednesday, also comes at a precarious moment in US-China relations.

Washington and Beijing are struggling to stabilize their communication amid flaring tensions over issues from a downed suspected Chinese surveillance balloon to semiconductor supply chains – raising the stakes of potential damage to that relationship if Beijing lashes out as it did when Tsai met Pelosi.

Taiwan is still feeling the fallout of that response last August, with Chinese military forces now regularly making incursions over what had previously been an informal but largely respected border of control between Beijing and Taipei in the Taiwan Strait. Taiwan’s official Central News Agency also reported Monday that Tsai would meet with McCarthy, citing Tsai’s presidential office.

Video Ad Feedback See image of a Chinese balloon hovering over Taiwan 3:05 • Source: CNN See image of a Chinese balloon hovering over Taiwan 3:05

But a meeting between Tsai and the leader of the Republican majority in the US House of Representatives, who ranks second in line to the Presidency, would mark another symbolic moment for Taiwan and the US, which only maintain unofficial ties.

For Tsai, who is entering the final year of her two-term presidency, “it’s clearly a capstone event,” according to Wen-Ti Sung, a political scientist at the Australian National University’s Taiwan Studies Program. “She has this image as the Taiwanese president who has taken US-Taiwan relations to new heights, and who … has been able to give Taiwan almost unprecedented international visibility,” he said.

That increased visibility – and enhanced cooperation with the US – has followed China’s mounting pressure on the island, which sits fewer than 110 miles (177 kilometers) from the mainland coast.

China’s Communist Party claims the self-governing island democracy as its own despite never having controlled it, and has vowed to take the island, by force if necessary.

The party has undertaken a sweeping expansion of its military capabilities over the past decade under leader Xi Jinping – and ramped up its pervasive economic, diplomatic and military pressure on Taiwan.

That’s driven concerns, among some in Washington, that Beijing is preparing for an invasion, though China’s official language still suggests that scenario is not its preferred option for achieving the claimed goal of “reunification.”

It is those pressures – and how to support Taiwan against unilateral actions by Beijing – that are likely to be on the table when Tsai, McCarthy and a bipartisan group of US lawmakers sit down on Wednesday.

Congress has been a pillar of increasing American support for Taiwan in recent years. Lawmakers regularly visit the island and drive bipartisan legislation enhancing support and cooperation.

While the US switched its diplomatic relations to Beijing decades ago, it maintains unofficial ties with Taiwan and is bound by law to provide the democratic island with the means to defend itself.

Under Washington’s longstanding “One China” policy, the US acknowledges China’s position that Taiwan is part of China, but has never officially recognized Beijing’s claim to the island of 23 million.

Though McCarthy does not have Pelosi’s decades-long record of advocacy regarding China, the California Republican is now a leading voice pushing for closer scrutiny of Beijing, and meeting Tsai could help him to burnish that image.

Last month, McCarthy told reporters that meeting Tsai in the US would not impact whether he travels to Taiwan in the future – something he had earlier said he wanted to do.

Fighter jets of the Chinese People's Liberation Army Eastern Theater Command conduct joint combat training exercises around Taiwan on August 7, 2022 in this photo released by Xinhua News Agency. Gong Yulong/Xinhua/AP

Beijing watching

A meeting in California, on US soil, is widely seen as less likely to provoke Beijing than a McCarthy visit to Taiwan.

Pelosi’s trip – the first from a lawmaker of that rank to the island in 25 years – generated a fever pitch of nationalist and anti-US rhetoric in mainland China.

This time, so far, domestic conversation in China’s heavily controlled media sphere has been significantly muted.

But the stakes remain high – including for Beijing itself – over how it responds, analysts say.

As Taiwan prepares for a presidential election in January, a fierce response could push voters away from Taiwan’s main opposition party Kuomintang (KMT), widely seen as more friendly toward Beijing.

It could also jar with another high profile trip happening now: a tour of mainland China from former Taiwan president and senior KMT member Ma Ying-jeou, the first visit from a current or former Taiwan leader since the end of the Chinese Civil War in 1949.

Ma’s tour is a “once in a half a century opportunity to send a conciliatory message between the two sides, Beijing shouldn’t want to tank that,” said Sung, the political scientist.

China is also acutely aware that its actions toward Taiwan are under a significantly brighter global spotlight following the invasion of Ukraine by Russian President Vladimir Putin, a close diplomatic partner of Xi. Putin’s rhetoric over Ukraine has echoes of how Xi speaks of Taiwan.

Beijing has recently sought to position itself as an agent of peace in that conflict – especially as it aims to repair frayed ties with Europe.

This week, as Tsai is expected to meet with McCarthy, French President Emmanuel Macron and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen will head to China – an important opportunity that Xi may not want to overshadow with military posturing.

An aggressive response also risks stoking confrontation with the US, not yet six months after Xi and US President Joe Biden called to enhance communication during a face-to-face meeting in Bali.

“(A less overtly aggressive response) would imply that Beijing does not wish to escalate tension with the US to a level that can risk getting out of hand,” said Steve Tsang, director of the SOAS China Institute in London.

“A reset in US-China ties is not on the agenda, but an easing of tension is not beyond the realm of possibility.”

World.title: AI’s real bottleneck is electricity. Who will pay for it?
World.content:
As Big Tech turns to nuclear power to fuel its AI ambitions, the cost of keeping data centers running raises a question that extends far beyond Silicon Valley.

Within a week, two of the three largest cloud computing companies in the world signed 20-year contracts for nuclear electricity. Amazon has taken 690 megawatts from Constellation’s Calvert Cliffs plant in Maryland, including 190 megawatts of additional generating capacity expected between 2030 and 2032. Google has signed an agreement that will bring 890 megawatts of additional nuclear capacity into the United States. Constellation is investing more than $4.3bn to upgrade 11 reactors across Illinois, Pennsylvania, and New Jersey. Neither agreement, however, involves building a new nuclear reactor. Rather, they are paying to generate more output from reactors that already exist – some of which are even older than the companies themselves.

A few years ago, such agreements would have seemed inconceivable. Nuclear power had fallen out of favour following accidents at Three Mile Island in 1979, Chornobyl in 1986 and Fukushima in 2011. Germany phased out nuclear power, while Japan shut down its reactors after Fukushima, although it has since begun restarting them. In many democratic countries, advocating for nuclear energy became politically difficult.

Today, an undamaged reactor at Three Mile Island is being brought back into service, with Microsoft contracted to buy its output for 20 years. The US Department of Energy is providing up to $4.4bn in loans to support the restart of three shuttered plants, with the aim of restoring about 2.25 gigawatts. Palisades in Michigan, which was closed in 2022, is contracted to be generating again by March 2027. If successful, it would become the first US commercial nuclear plant to restart after entering decommissioning.



What has changed?

The quiet reversal

In the last decade, the industry’s answer to AI’s energy problem was efficiency – things such as better chips, smaller models and smarter cooling seemed appealing and feasible. Industry conferences featured discussions about performance per watt, with modern artificial intelligence (AI) chips performing more computation per unit of electricity than their predecessors.

Yet those efficiency gains did not reduce overall electricity demand. Instead, each gain was quickly put towards something larger. Even when DeepSeek demonstrated that a competitive model could be trained at a fraction of the computing cost many had expected, the result was not a reduction in industry spending. Instead, laboratories continued planning more training runs, models that reason for longer, agents that work continuously in the background, and video generation.

This would not be the first time something like this has happened in history. In 1865, William Jevons observed that more efficient steam engines made Britain burn more coal, not less, because cheaper power created uses that had not existed before. The International Energy Agency estimates that global data centre electricity demand will more than double to around 945 terawatt-hours by 2030, even assuming continued improvements in efficiency.

Hence, the industry has changed strategy – unable to shrink demand, companies are now buying up supply.

The arithmetic of waiting

Money, however, cannot solve every problem quickly.

A new large reactor takes a decade or more from decision to electricity. Tech companies are investing in small modular reactors to power their data centres, although many of these projects are not expected to deliver electricity until the early 2030s. So far, very few of these have been built anywhere in the world. Thus, while reactor restarts and upgrades are the faster option, the “fast option” still means 2027, 2028, 2029, or beyond.

AI capital expenditure, however, does not operate on that same calendar. The chips being installed this year could be overtaken by newer technology long before the 20-year electricity contracts powering them expire. This discrepancy underpins all of these announcements, yet the industry has not addressed the implications if demand weakens while contractual obligations remain.

Who pays in the meantime

This is where the story stops being about technology.

Most of these deals sit inside PJM, the grid operator serving roughly 67 million people across 13 American states and Washington, DC. PJM uses capacity auctions to secure sufficient electricity-generating resources for future demand, with the associated costs ultimately passed on to consumers through their electricity bills. Capacity prices have reached the regulatory price cap in three consecutive auctions. According to the grid operator’s independent market monitor, data centre demand contributed approximately $29.4bn in capacity costs across the four most recent auctions. In the latest auction alone, around $6.3bn of these costs were attributed to data centre demand, including forecasts for facilities that have yet to be built.



In effect, households are already paying higher electricity capacity charges, partly because of projected demand from facilities that may never become operational. The Natural Resources Defense Council estimates that, by 2028, the typical household within PJM could face an additional $70 per month in electricity costs if current trends continue. These rising costs are also having political consequences. Recent US polling shows growing public dissatisfaction with data centres, with electricity bills among the main concerns. In response, Virginia has established a separate electricity rate class for data centres, Ohio has introduced minimum billing requirements, and Illinois is debating legislation.

The aim of the Google agreement is to tackle this objection. Its underlying principle is that major new electricity consumers should bring additional generation capacity rather than compete with existing users for an already constrained supply. This approach represents a constructive step towards mitigating the pressure that data centres place on electricity systems.
