Over 13 months, from June 2025 to July 2026, this reporter travelled across Kano, Kaduna and Niger states, tracing the origin of the genetically modified TELA maize from research laboratories and demonstration farms to grain markets, flour processors, roasted maize vendors and household kitchens.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

But what is TELA maize made of, and do Nigerians know what they consume as food?

To answer these questions, PREMIUM TIMES interviewed regulators, scientists, seed companies, farmers, grain traders, processors, consumers, nutrition experts and biotechnology critics, and reviewed regulatory documents and scientific assessments to trace the crop’s journey from laboratory development to household consumption.

What emerged was a story that extends beyond science and agriculture to questions of transparency, consumer awareness and Nigerians’ right to informed choice.

From devastating pest to scientific solution

Maize is one of Nigeria’s most important staple crops, consumed daily in different forms, including tuwo, pap, roasted corn, boiled corn and livestock feed. Millions of farmers depend on it for income. But for years, two major challenges have threatened maize production: prolonged drought associated with climate change and the destructive fall armyworm (FAW).

First detected in Nigeria in 2016, FAW spread rapidly, destroyed farms, and forced farmers across states to spend heavily on pesticides while still experiencing significant losses.

According to the Federal Ministry of Agriculture and Food Security (FMAFS), the pest can destroy an entire maize field if left uncontrolled, threatening food production and farmers’ livelihoods. To establish a baseline, 2020 ministry data put annual local maize production at about 10.5 million metric tonnes, against a demand of about 15 million tonnes. The ministry also warned that pests such as FAW could cause losses of up to 70 per cent of maize production.

Scientists believed biotechnology could help address the problem, which led to the creation of the TELA maize project.

The TELA maize project is a multi-country research initiative coordinated by the African Agricultural Technology Foundation (AATF) in partnership with the International Maize and Wheat Improvement Centre (CIMMYT), Bayer Crop Science, and National Agricultural Research institutes across Nigeria, Kenya, Ethiopia, Mozambique, and South Africa.

The Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation (now the Gates Foundation) and the United States Agency for International Development (USAID) fund the project and support the development of drought-tolerant and insect-resistant maize for smallholder farmers in sub-Saharan Africa.

A 2019 Product Launch Collaboration agreement between AATF, CIMMYT, and Monsanto Company—an agricultural business later acquired by Bayer—provided a framework for commercialising the TELA maize technology in participating African countries. Under the arrangement, AATF obtained a royalty-free licence to oversee deployment and commercialisation and sub-licence the technology, subject to national regulatory and stewardship requirements.

The TELA Maize Project, built on more than a decade of research under the Water Efficient Maize for Africa (WEMA) project, sought to develop drought-tolerant maize for African farmers.

According to AATF, the name TELA comes from the Latin word “tutela”, meaning protection, reflecting the crop’s ability to protect itself against destructive insect pests while also tolerating periods of drought.

TELA maize contains a Bt gene from Bacillus thuringiensis, a soil bacterium, which produces proteins that target specific pests such as fall armyworm and stem borers.

Muhyideen Oyekunle, Traits Pipeline Testing Lead at the Institute for Agricultural Research (IAR), who evaluated the traits, explained that the Bt proteins disrupt the digestive systems of targeted pests when they feed on the plant, protecting the crop from damage. In contrast, the drought-tolerance trait allows the crop to withstand periods of water stress.

In Nigeria, the Institute for Agricultural Research (IAR) developed and adapted the technology at Ahmadu Bello University in Kaduna in collaboration with AATF.

But while scientists worked on the crop for years, questions remained about how much Nigerians understood about the technology and the variety of food they consume.

Nigeria’s road to commercial cultivation

TELA maize passed through years of research and assessment. The National Biosafety Management Agency (NBMA), Nigeria’s statutory regulator for genetically modified organisms (GMOs), said it assessed the crop and found it safe for human consumption and the environment.

Hauwa Ahmed, director of Biosafety Enforcement and Operations at the NBMA, explained that the crop underwent extensive scrutiny.

“The approval of TELA maize followed a rigorous, multi-stage biosafety risk assessment in line with the NBMA Act and Nigeria’s obligations under the Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety,” Mrs Ahmed told PREMIUM TIMES.

She added that researchers conducted years of Confined Field Trials (CFTs) in Nigeria to generate agro-ecological data, assess environmental risks and examine possible effects on non-target organisms before applying for commercial release.

She also noted that the regulatory process involved public participation, as the agency published notices in three national newspapers and made the application dossier available at designated locations for 21 days for public comments. The National Biosafety Committee and National Biosafety Technical Sub-Committee subsequently reviewed the scientific dossier and made recommendations to the agency.

In October 2021, NBMA granted IAR a permit to environmentally release TELA maize following assessments that included molecular characterisation, toxicology, allergenicity, nutritional equivalence, environmental risks, and comparisons with conventional maize. The assessment also considered socio-economic issues.

“The pre-approval risk assessment ensures that all potential risks are identified and management measures proffered before approval for commercial release,” Mrs Ahmed disclosed.

The assessment drew on evidence and experience from countries, including Argentina, Brazil, Canada, China, Japan and South Africa, as well as European Union member states.

Multi-location trials were also conducted across Nigeria’s ecological zones before the National Committee on Naming, Registration and Release of Crop Varieties, Livestock Breeds/Fisheries considered them.

On 11 January 2024, the committee officially approved the release of four varieties in Nigeria, including SAMMAZ 72T, SAMMAZ 73T, SAMMAZ 74T, and SAMMAZ 75T.

Mr Oyekunle explained to PREMIUM TIMES what the varieties mean. SAMMAZ is derived from “Samaru maize”, which refers to the institute’s location in Samaru, Zaria. The numbers identify the individual varieties, while the letter “T” distinguishes the TELA varieties from conventional SAMMAZ varieties.

Although the four varieties share the same biotechnology traits, they differ slightly in adaptation zones, plant characteristics, and yield potential. They were recommended for different agro-ecological zones, including the Guinea savannah, Sudan savannah, and rainforest zones, and have potential yields ranging from about 9.4 to 10.4 tonnes per hectare under good agronomic practices.

The developers described the technology as an important tool for improving food security, reducing pesticide use and helping farmers adapt to climate change.

The federal government formally launched TELA maize in 2024 to encourage nationwide adoption.

According to the NBMA, the FMAFS serves as the agricultural policy and deployment interface for TELA maize in Nigeria, including its adoption and farmer support programmes, while the NBMA oversees biosafety approval.

PREMIUM TIMES contacted the Federal Department of Agriculture under the ministry to understand its role in the TELA maize programme and the government’s position on its deployment and adoption.

An official of the department, who requested anonymity because he was not authorised to speak publicly, said the ministry does not independently approve GMOs; rather, it provides an enabling environment for agricultural technology.

He said the ministry reviews findings from the IAR, which operates under its mandate, and other relevant research agencies to determine whether a technology aligns with agricultural policy.

Meanwhile, the NBMA handles GMO regulatory approval and the National Agricultural Seeds Council certifies varieties for seed multiplication. He said TELA maize’s resistance to FAW, stem borers and drought could help boost production and reduce Nigeria’s food supply deficit.

On adoption, the official said uptake of TELA maize is increasing, as Agricultural Development Programmes (ADPs) sensitise farmers through demonstration plots that allow them to compare TELA maize with conventional varieties. However, he identified seed availability and affordability as major challenges. He stressed the need for farmers to follow recommended agronomic practices, including proper spacing and nutrient application, to achieve expected yields.

Data provided by AATF to PREMIUM TIMES indicate that approximately 8,000 to 10,000 farmers accessed and planted TELA maize during the 2024 cropping season. However, the figure did not include farmers who may have saved seed for subsequent planting.

Kaduna, Kano, and Niger recorded the largest numbers, with about 1,800 farmers in Kaduna, 1,500 in Kano, and 1,200 in Niger. Benue ranked fourth with about 1,100, and Katsina fifth with 1,000 farmers. Other states across the federation, including Kwara, Oyo, Ogun, Edo, Delta, Nasarawa and the FCT, accounted for about 3,400 farmers combined.

Muhammad Yahaya, a plant breeder and geneticist at IAR, said developing TELA maize took more than a decade.

“The development of TELA maize took over a decade, approximately 10 to 15 years.”

The process involved gene discovery, laboratory work, confined field trials, multi-location trials and regulatory assessments covering toxicity, allergenicity, nutritional equivalence and environmental risks.

The trials and subsequent deployment covered areas including Kaduna, Kano, Niger and Jigawa.

Mr Yahaya said post-release monitoring was also important because regulators and researchers continued to assess field performance, environmental effects, farmer experiences and compliance with stewardship requirements.

“Commercial release comes with stewardship obligations,” he said, describing biosafety as “an ongoing process rather than a one-time event.”

Yet while regulators declared the crop safe and farmers increasingly embraced it, another question remained unanswered: After leaving research stations and demonstration farms, who are the end consumers of TELA maize? Do Nigerians know they are already eating it?

Following the seed

Agric Seed Care Limited is a licensed distributor of TELA seed through AATF.

Mr Ochoche, whose company is based in Hotoro, Kano, said TELA seed was initially imported into Nigeria, which delayed its availability to farmers during the first planting season in 2024. By the time the seed arrived, some farmers had already planted other crops. He said the situation has since improved as the seed is now being multiplied locally.

Its chief executive officer (CEO), Oyaje Ochoche, said his company recalled that TELA maize seed was sold for as much as N9,500 per kilogramme during the first two years of commercial distribution. He added that the price has since dropped to between N4,500 and N7,000 per kilogramme.

For conventional hybrid maize seed, the company’s current comparison is between N1,200 and N1,500 for a two-kilogramme pack in many locations, Mr Ochoche said

Another licensed producer and distributor of TELA maize seed, Nagari Seed Company Limited in Kaduna, also obtains foundation seed for multiplication into certified seed for farmers. The company’s marketing manager, Tachio Boman, told PREMIUM TIMES that the seed is produced in two stages: foundation and certified seed.

Mr Boman said the foundation seed was initially imported from South Africa when TELA maize was commercialised, while local production systems were being established. Now, EcoBasic Seed Company collaborates with IAR to produce seeds locally for certified multiplication and supplies them to licensed Nigerian seed companies, including Nagari. The certified seeds are distributed to farmers through AATF-provided channels.

AATF Hybrid Seed Market Development Manager Olawale Ojo said the organisation operates a licensing system that involves qualified Nigerian-owned seed companies.

AATF, alongside EcoBasic Seed Company Limited, sub-licenses TELA maize hybrids to qualified seed companies that meet the criteria, including Agric Seed Care Limited, Nagari Seed Company Limited, Premier Seed Nigeria Limited, Techni Seed, Chinmade Nigeria Limited, Da-Allgreen Seeds Limited, Lifted Agro Limited, Boom Seed Limited, GoldAgric Nigeria Limited, Ingachi Seed Company Limited, Mastrotun Global Limited and Beta Seed Company Limited.

But after the seed entered Nigeria’s farming system, misinformation began to set in.

“There were many rumours. Some believed the maize was brought to harm Africans. Others claimed crops would never grow again on land where TELA maize had been planted,” Mr Ochoche recalled.

To counter the misinformation, AATF and FMAFS, through their agricultural development programmes, and seed companies established demonstration plots where farmers could observe the crop and receive training on cultivation and stewardship practices.

Mr Ojo said demonstration plots and farmer training helped address some of the concerns.

“People are often afraid of what they do not understand. Once farmers see the crop themselves and ask questions, many of the misconceptions disappear,” Ojo disclosed.

He added that the National Agricultural Seed Council certification tags, QR codes and SeedCodex authentication are imprinted on the certified TELA maize seeds to reduce counterfeiting.

Salisu Buhari, an official of the Kaita Agricultural Multipurpose Cooperative Society in Kano and an agro-dealer, stated that members first learned about TELA maize at a 2024 stakeholders’ meeting organised through the Kano ADPs in collaboration with FMAFS.

He explained that only a limited number of farmers initially received the seed because commercial quantities were not yet available. Distribution expanded in 2025 through demonstration plots in communities including Bichi and Bagwai LGAs in Kano State.

Mr Buhari said TELA maize had also begun appearing in local grain markets, although it still accounted for a small proportion of the maize sold.

“The biggest challenge now is availability and affordability. Many farmers want the seed, but they don’t know where to buy it, and when they find it, it is expensive,” Mr Buhari said.

Farmers report better yields, fewer pests

Abdullahi Muhammad, a farmer in Bichi Local Government Area of Kano State, was among the early farmers to plant TELA maize.

He farms almost one hectare and has worked as an extension officer for more than 20 years.

“I asked many questions because they told us from the beginning that it was genetically modified,” he said.

“After the explanations, I was satisfied.”

Mr Muhammad planted TELA maize in 2025 and again in June 2026.

He received training on refuge planting, spacing, fertiliser application and stewardship requirements.

He said the crop showed resistance to FAW and stem borers and required little pesticide treatment.

“Conventional maize suffers heavy pest attacks, but with TELA maize we hardly needed pesticides for fall armyworm,” he stated.

Under good management, he estimated that TELA could produce between 80 and 100 bags per hectare, compared with about 40 to 60 bags for conventional maize.

His 2025 harvest fell short of expectations because of poor rainfall, which he attributed to the weather rather than the seed.

He later planted cowpea on the same land and said it grew. He refuted claims that TELA seeds damage soil.

Mr Muhammad said he has trained other farmers, including 363 in Bichi through AATF programmes.

But he said awareness remained a major barrier.

“Whenever a new agricultural technology is introduced, people are naturally afraid of it. That is why more education is needed,” he said.

His family has consumed TELA maize since 2025, including roasted and boiled maize and Tuwo, without experiencing health problems, contrary to claims attributed to the seeds.

Seed cost remains an issue. TELA seed costs about N4,500 to N7,000 per kilogram, compared with about N1,500 for a two-kilogram pack of conventional seed.

Other farmers interviewed in Kano, Kaduna and Niger also reported better harvests, fuller cobs, reduced pest damage and tolerance to dry spells, although their experiences varied.

Cost and availability were common concerns.

Tajudeen Gambo, a farmer in Marke village, Makarfi Local Government Area of Kaduna State, said he recorded better yields after planting TELA maize.

He had farmed for about 15 years. He planted the seed from the AATF programme on about 0.3 hectares in 2025 and also used fertiliser supplied by the programme.

“I got better yield when I harvested my TELA maize,” he said.

He wanted to plant TELA again in 2026 but lost access to the rented farm.

He also raised concerns about the seeds’ cost and availability.

“People are worried about the seeds’ marketing monopoly, that farmers must purchase seed every year at an exorbitant price. Other than that, I do not have any problem with TELA maize,” he said.

In Niger State, Tamiru Danbaba planted TELA maize for the first time.

He said the crop survived a long dry spell in July while neighbouring farms suffered losses. He estimated that his harvest was about 25 to 30 per cent higher than what he would normally expect under similar conditions.

“It’s a relief to see a crop that doesn’t get ravaged.”

Mariya Lawal, a farmer in Bagwai LGA, Kano State, and Ismail Ibraheem in Zaria, Kaduna State, also reported improved harvests.

Ms Lawal said TELA produced fuller cobs, larger grains and more flour.

Tamatu Idi, a small-scale farmer in Kano, said her TELA maize survived a two-week dry spell.

But farmers, including Ms Lawal and Mrs Idi, continued to raise concerns about the cost of the seeds.

In response to the farmers’ concerns, the official from the Federal Department of Agriculture at the FMAFS said the government was seeking to increase seed production, including through subsidy interventions.

The official added that increased investment could expand supply and reduce price constraints.

After the 2025 harvest, however, the crop was no longer confined to farms.

It began moving through grain markets, flour mills and food vendors, eventually reaching Nigerian households.

This investigation is published in two parts. The second part will examine how TELA maize reaches consumers and whether they receive enough information about what they are buying.

World.title: Beyond the battlefield: Crisis communication as a national security imperative, By Mukhtar Ya’u Madobi
World.content:
In the digital age, protecting Nigeria increasingly means protecting the integrity of the information environment in which Nigerians make decisions. The institutions that understand this earliest, prepare for it seriously and communicate most credibly will be better positioned not merely to manage crises, but to prevent misinformation from becoming a crisis of its own.

When false reports travel faster than verified facts, a fabricated video can trigger panic, contradictory official statements can erode confidence, and prolonged silence can leave citizens vulnerable to manipulation. In Nigeria’s evolving security environment, the battle for public trust is increasingly being fought in the information space as much as on the physical battlefield.

That reality dominated the Second National Symposium on Crisis Communication organised by the Centre for Crisis Communication (CCC) on 27 and 28 October at the Nigerian Air Force Club in Kaduna. The gathering, themed “Inter-Agency Collaboration, Public Trust and Cyber Threat Management in Crisis Communication,” brought together more than 150 participants from the military, security and intelligence agencies, emergency services, government institutions, academia and media organisations.

The fundamental lesson from Kaduna was simple: operational cooperation among security agencies is no longer sufficient. It must be matched by communication cooperation. In an age of artificial intelligence, deepfakes and instant social media distribution, the institution that controls the facts but communicates too slowly may still lose the narrative.

Major General Chris Olukolade (rtd), chairman of the CCC, captured the challenge succinctly. He warned that delayed or contradictory official information creates vacuums in which rumours and manipulated narratives thrive. Citing DataReportal, he said Nigeria had about 109 million internet users at the end of 2025, while figures he attributed to the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime estimated losses of ₦1.1 trillion to cybercrime between 2017 and 2023. His prescription was equally direct: “one crisis, one coordinated response.”

That philosophy deserves serious attention.

During national emergencies, Nigerians should not have to choose between competing official versions of the same incident. Neither should security institutions allow an information vacuum to persist until speculation acquires the appearance of fact. Coordination in the field must extend to what agencies say publicly, when they say it, and how rapidly verified information reaches citizens.

Representing the Chief of Defence Staff, Brigadier General Murtala Abu expressed the principle memorably: “Operational collaboration without communication collaboration is incomplete.” He warned that AI-generated videos, audio recordings and images could be manipulated to deceive the public, while terrorism, kidnapping, cybercrime, oil theft and communal conflicts increasingly demand collective institutional responses.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

This is particularly important as Nigeria approaches the 2027 general elections. AI tools have dramatically lowered the barriers to producing convincing fake videos, recordings and images. A fabricated statement attributed to a security chief, electoral official or political actor could circulate to millions before verification catches up. Participants at the symposium consequently warned that deepfakes and coordinated disinformation could threaten national security, public trust and democratic stability.

But technology is only one part of the challenge. Public trust is the other.

Representing Kaduna State Governor Uba Sani, Commissioner for Information and Culture Ahmed Maiyaki argued that the battle for public trust has become as consequential as the battle against insecurity. He cited the Kaduna Peace Model, which emphasises dialogue, community participation, intelligence sharing and early-warning mechanisms, while making an important observation: “Silence creates a vacuum. Credible information creates confidence.”

That statement goes to the heart of crisis communication. Silence may sometimes be operationally necessary, especially where sensitive information could endanger lives. But unexplained silence can also breed fear. The challenge is therefore not simply to communicate more, but to communicate responsibly: quickly enough to prevent dangerous speculation, accurately enough to preserve credibility, and carefully enough not to compromise operations.

The symposium also reinforced the importance of institutional architecture. Its communiqué recommended an Integrated National Crisis Information Architecture supported by standard operating procedures and clear protocols for harmonising information-sharing and public communication. Participants also called for technological tools capable of detecting disinformation and AI-generated deepfakes, stronger digital literacy and regulatory safeguards that protect national security without undermining freedom of expression, fundamental rights and due process.

That balance is critical. Fighting disinformation must never become an excuse to criminalise legitimate criticism. Public trust cannot be manufactured through censorship. It is earned when institutions communicate truthfully, correct themselves when wrong, provide evidence where possible, and respect the citizen’s right to question authority.

The CCC also unveiled the Nigerian Journal of Crisis Communication, conceived as a platform for research, case studies and practical insights for professionals and policymakers. Olukolade further disclosed that the Crisis Communication Hub, established following the Centre’s inaugural symposium in November 2025, had received the 2026 Golden World Award of the International Public Relations Association.

The progression from the first symposium to Kaduna is important. It suggests that crisis communication is gradually being treated not as an afterthought attached to security operations, but as part of the architecture of national resilience.

Yet conferences and recommendations are only useful when they change institutional behaviour.

The real test will come during the next major security emergency. Will agencies share verified information rapidly? Will conflicting casualty figures be avoided? Will a designated lead institution communicate clearly? Can authorities detect a deepfake before it provokes panic? Will journalists have credible information quickly enough to resist publishing speculation? And will citizens trust the official account when it arrives?

These are the measurements that matter.

Nigeria’s evolving threat environment demands more than weapons, intelligence and operational capacity. It requires institutions capable of understanding that information itself can become a security asset or a security vulnerability. A falsehood can redirect emergency resources, inflame communal tension or undermine confidence in a legitimate operation. The symposium’s communiqué explicitly recognised that misinformation during emergencies can trigger panic, divert resources, endanger lives and weaken public confidence.

That is why the concept of “one crisis, one coordinated response” should not remain a conference slogan. It should become an operational philosophy.

Nigeria needs security agencies that cooperate before crises, not merely during them; spokespersons who understand both operational sensitivity and public accountability; journalists equipped to verify sophisticated digital manipulation; and citizens sufficiently media-literate to pause before forwarding potentially harmful content.

The Kaduna symposium has helped define the problem and propose a direction. The responsibility now lies in implementation.

Beyond the battlefield, credibility has become a strategic national asset. A government may possess accurate intelligence and formidable security capabilities, but if citizens do not trust the information accompanying its actions, an important part of the battle remains unfinished.

In the digital age, protecting Nigeria increasingly means protecting the integrity of the information environment in which Nigerians make decisions. The institutions that understand this earliest, prepare for it seriously and communicate most credibly will be better positioned not merely to manage crises, but to prevent misinformation from becoming a crisis of its own.

Mukhtar Ya’u Madobi is a Research Fellow at the Centre for Crisis Communication, Abuja.

World.title: Samson Adamu makes history as CAF confirms Nigerian as General Secretary
World.content:
Samson Adamu has been confirmed as the substantive General Secretary of the Confederation of African Football (CAF), becoming the first Nigerian to occupy the position in the organisation’s 70-year history.

The confirmation was announced on Thursday, with the Nigeria Football Federation (NFF) congratulating Mr Adamu on his appointment.

Emmanuel Ikpeme, the NFF’s acting general secretary, described the development as good news for Nigerian football administration and expressed confidence in Mr Adamu’s ability to succeed in the role.

“This is, indeed, very good news. I am so happy for Samson Adamu on his confirmation, and I know he is going to make Nigeria and Africa proud,” Mr Ikpeme said.

“He is a highly knowledgeable individual who has never stopped improving himself, and he is well-rounded in the business of football administration.”

Mr Ikpeme said the NFF was pleased with the appointment and pledged the federation’s support for Mr Adamu in his new role.

“The NFF is delighted with this appointment, and we will give him all the necessary support as a Member Association under CAF. We wish him tremendous success in the job,” he said.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Mr Adamu joined CAF, the continent’s football governing body headquartered in Cairo, Egypt, as director of competitions before being appointed director of tournaments and events.

On 29 March, he became acting general secretary after Veron Mosengo-Omba, a Swiss-Congolese football administrator, resigned.

His confirmation as substantive General Secretary is widely seen as a big boost for Nigeria’s representation in African football administration.

World.title: Gunmen kill four in Plateau community
World.content:
By Golok Nanmwa, Jos

Four persons were reportedly killed when gunmen attacked Sabon Angwa community, around Bet/Zat in Barkin Ladi Local Government Area of Plateau State, on Thursday night.

The attackers were said to have stormed the community at about 8pm and opened fire on residents, despite the curfew imposed in parts of the state to check attacks and restore security.

A resident of Barkin Ladi, Mr Bulus Jok, who confirmed the incident, said, “The gunmen struck the community around 8pm despite the curfew in place and started shooting sporadically.”

Jok said, “They were shooting at anything they saw. The attack created panic in the community, and four people were killed.”

He added, “The incident is very sad, especially as there had been an early warning alert sent to the relevant authorities a day before the attack.”

Also confirming the incident, Publicity Secretary of the Berom Youth Moulders-Association, BYM, Mr Rwang Tengwong, said, “Terrorist gangs reportedly attacked Sabon Angwa, around Bet/Zat in Barkin Ladi Local Government Area, and shot four people dead.”

Tengwong condemned the attack, describing the killing of innocent residents as unacceptable, adding, “We condemn this latest attack in strong terms and lament the loss of these lives.”

He said, “It is disturbing that communities are still being attacked despite the security measures and curfew put in place to protect residents.”

The BYM spokesman urged security operatives to intensify surveillance and take proactive measures to prevent further attacks on vulnerable communities, saying, “We call on security agencies to strengthen their presence and respond promptly to early warning alerts.”

Efforts to reach security operatives for more details were unsuccessful as of the time of filing this report.

World.title: 10 phones with biggest battery specs in Nigeria
World.content:
By Prince Osuagwu

The life of a Nigerian phone user is funny. With power cuts and long days on the road, battery life is no longer just a specification on a phone’s spec sheet, it is peace of mind.

This is because, a dead phone can mean missed calls, stranded commutes and lost work.

So, for a user, searching for phones with the biggest battery specs is inevitable.

TechXtra now xrays some of the models to watch.

The list ranks the phones by their listed battery capacity, starting with the first 10,000mAh smartphone available in Nigeria today.

REDMI Note 17 Pro Max 5G — 10,000mAh

The REDMI Note 17 Pro Max 5G leads the pack with a 10,000mAh silicon-carbon battery, the largest listed capacity for a smartphone sold in Nigeria.

The device combines the massive battery with 100W HyperCharge and up to 27W wired reverse charging. It also features a 6.83-inch 1.5K AMOLED display and 5G support.

REDMI Note 17 Pro 5G — 8,340mAh

The REDMI Note 17 Pro 5G comes with an 8,340mAh silicon-carbon battery and 67W HyperCharge, as well as up to 22.5W wired reverse charging.

It features a 6.83-inch 1.5K AMOLED display, Snapdragon 6s Gen 4 platform and IP66/IP68/IP69/IP69K ratings under specified test conditions.

realme C100 4G — 8,000mAh

The realme C100 4G is listed on realme Nigeria’s website with an 8,000mAh Titan battery and 45W fast charging, alongside up to 10W reverse charging.

The smartphone uses a 6.8-inch 120Hz display and MediaTek Helio G92 Max chipset and is available through Nigerian retail channels.

REDMI Note 17 — 7,700mAh

The standard REDMI Note 17 carries a 7,700mAh silicon-carbon battery with 45W Turbo Charging and up to 22.5W wired reverse charging.

Xiaomi Nigeria lists the phone with a 6.99-inch FHD+ AMOLED display, Snapdragon 6s 4G Gen 2 platform and TÜV SÜD five-star battery performance certification.

REDMI 17 — 7,500mAh

The REDMI 17 comes with a 7,500mAh typical battery, 45W Turbo Charging and up to 22.5W wired reverse charging.

It is positioned as an accessible large-battery option within the REDMI 17 lineup and is available through Xiaomi Nigeria’s official channels and authorised partners.

Vivo Y31D — 7,200mAh

The vivo Y31D packs a 7,200mAh typical BlueVolt battery with 44W FlashCharge and up to 6W reverse charging.

The device is sold in Nigeria with a 6.75-inch 120Hz LCD, Snapdragon 6s Gen 2 4G platform and IP69-rated dust and water resistance.

TECNO Spark 50 — 7,000mAh

The TECNO Spark 50 is listed with a 7,000mAh battery and 18W fast charging, targeting users seeking long daily battery life at an entry-level price.

TECNO Nigeria describes it as one of its latest 2026 phones, with more than 28 hours of continuous video playback claimed under laboratory conditions.

itel A300+ — 7,000mAh

The itel A300+ comes with a 7,000mAh battery and 22.5W fast charging, alongside a secondary 2.01-inch interactive rear display.

It is sold in Nigeria with a 6.78-inch HD+ 120Hz LCD, Helio G81 Ultimate chipset, IP65 rating and Android 16 (Go Edition).

Infinix Hot 70 Pro — 7,000mAh

The Infinix Hot 70 Pro is listed in Nigeria with a 7,000mAh battery and fast charging.

It also features a 6.78-inch 120Hz IPS display and MediaTek Dimensity 7100 5G chipset and is officially available through Infinix Nigeria’s retail stores and major online platforms.

TECNO Spark 50 4G — 6,700mAh

The TECNO Spark 50 4G variant is listed with a 6,700mAh battery and 18W fast charging, placing it below the 7,000mAh Spark 50 in the same series.

The phone targets value-focused buyers who want a large battery combined with a modern display in an entry-level package.

Big batteries become a selling point.

World.title: Dollar to Naira exchange rate today, October 30, 2026
World.content:
The Nigerian Naira opened today, Friday, October 30, 2026, holding firm against the United States Dollar across both the official foreign exchange window and the parallel market, following sustained liquidity interventions by the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) and healthy diaspora inflows.

At the official Nigerian Foreign Exchange Market (NFEM), the spot exchange rate traded at N1,346.86 per dollar during early morning transactions. Commercial banks and corporate importers observed orderly liquidity conditions as FX demand for trade obligations, tuition fees, and capital repatriation continued to be met across authorized channels.

In the parallel market, commonly referred to as the black market, street traders and Bureau De Change operators across major economic centers, including Lagos, Abuja, and Kano, quoted buying rates around N1,375 per dollar, while selling rates hovered around N1,385 per dollar.

The price gap between the official market and the parallel window remains narrow. Financial analysts attribute the relative stability of the local currency to Nigeria’s solid foreign reserve buffer, which remains well above $55 billion, enabling the central bank to cushion short-term demand shocks and maintain stability across trading channels. Market experts expect trading to remain steady throughout the business day as routine demand is steadily absorbed by market liquidity.

World.title: PSC promotes 2 DIGs, 10 AIGs, 17 CPs, 3,800 others
World.content:
By Kingsley Omonobi

The Police Service Commission (PSC) has approved the promotion of more than 3,800 senior police officers, including two Deputy Inspectors-General of Police (DIGs), 10 Assistant Inspectors-General of Police (AIGs) and 17 Commissioners of Police (CPs).

The promotions followed the officers’ successful participation in promotion examinations and oral interviews conducted by the commission.

A statement issued by the PSC on Thursday said the approvals were granted at its plenary meeting in Abuja, presided over by its Chairman, DIG Hashimu Salihu Argungu (rtd).

The two officers elevated to the rank of DIG are AIG Olaolu Adegbite, Head of INTERPOL National Central Bureau, Abuja, and AIG Dankombo F. Morris, who heads Zone 4 Headquarters, Makurdi.

Adegbite holds a BA in Russian Language from the University of Lagos and an MA in Philology from the Pushkin Institute, Moscow. He is a recipient of the national honour of Member of the Order of the Federal Republic (MFR), a member of the FBI National Academy Associates and an alumnus of Harvard Kennedy School.

He previously served as Director of Operations at the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC).

Morris, who hails from Gombe State, holds a BA in History from the University of Maiduguri and a Diploma in Police Science. He has served as Commissioner of Police in Adamawa State.

Alani, DC CID Delta; Wuwa Auwal Muhammad, DC Airwing; and Benedict U. Agbo, DC Forensic.

The commission also approved the promotion of 85 officers from Assistant Commissioner of Police (ACP) to DCP.

Among them are ACP Dr Ruth Oyinmearelu Okunbo, Medical Director of MD Abubakar Police Hospital, Deidei, and ASR Police Reference Hospital, Utako, Abuja; ACP Isah Adejoh, Assistant Director, Liberal Studies, Police Staff College, Jos; and ACP Mannir Yusuf Gafai of Kano State Command.

World.title: NESG: Nigeria’s high production costs threaten industrial competitiveness
World.content:
By Favour Ulebor

The Nigeria Economic Summit Group has warned that high production costs, unreliable electricity and poor logistics infrastructure are undermining Nigeria’s industrial competitiveness, calling for a council within the Presidency to coordinate industrialisation policies.

Co-facilitator of the NESG, Lumun Feese, said Nigeria needed a coordinated approach to industrial development to address structural challenges and enable local manufacturers to compete effectively in African markets.

She spoke at a breakout session on building an integrated industrial ecosystem during the 32nd Nigeria Economic Summit in Abuja.

Feese said Nigeria had dropped from eighth to 14th position on the African Development Bank’s Africa Industrialisation Index, although she noted that the methodology had changed and more countries had been included in the latest ranking.

She said, “We are not maximising our potential and our large economy.

“How do we go and compete in South Africa when our cost of production is so high?

Feese said the proposed industrialisation, competitiveness and regional integration council would provide a central coordinating platform within the Presidency to align government policies, improve implementation of the National Industrial Policy and strengthen private-sector participation.

She said Nigerian businesses needed reliable power, efficient transportation systems and lower production costs to take advantage of the African Continental Free Trade Area, which offers access to a wider continental market.

Feese said the recommendations followed consultations on mining, the blue economy, power, oil and gas, and industrial competitiveness.

She urged businesses and other stakeholders to sustain their engagement with the NESG’s Industrial Policy Commission, saying coordinated policies and consistent implementation were necessary to achieve measurable industrial growth.

Other stakeholders at the session identified limited access to finance, skills shortages, regulatory bottlenecks, security concerns and inadequate export infrastructure as major obstacles to industrial growth.

Special Assistant on Strategy to the Minister of State for Industry, Gerald Okunsebor, called for greater awareness of the National Industrial Policy and a clear implementation framework with defined responsibilities, timelines and accountability mechanisms.

He said a central knowledge-management system was also needed to ensure continuity in industrial development policies across successive administrations.

World.title: Nigeria’s export earnings rise 23.7% to $35.6bn in H1’26
World.content:
By Babajide Komolafe

Nigeria’s total export earnings rose by 23.7 per cent year-on-year, YoY to $35.64 billion in the first half of 2026 (H1’26), from $28.82 billion in the corresponding period of 2025, driven largely by a surge in petroleum products exports.

Analysis of data from the quarterly statistical bulletin, of the Central Bank of Nigeria’s (CBN) for Q2’26, showed that the country’s export earnings increased by $6.82 billion during the six-month period, with petroleum products accounting for about 65 per cent of the growth.

Petroleum products exports jumped by 238.7 per cent YoY to $6.31 billion in H1’26 from $1.86 billion in H1’25, representing an increase of approximately $4.45 billion.

Crude oil remained Nigeria’s largest individual export category, generating $17.51 billion, up 7.7 per cent YoY from $16.25 billion in the corresponding period of 2025.

Gas exports also increased, rising by 4.2 per cent YoY to $6.22 billion from $5.97 billion.

Consequently, total exports of crude oil, gas and petroleum products rose by 21.9 per cent YoY to $30.03 billion from $24.63 billion in H1’25.

The performance indicates that petroleum-related exports remained the dominant source of Nigeria’s export earnings, accounting for about 84.3 per cent of total exports during the period.

Meanwhile, non-oil exports increased by 18.2 per cent YoY to $5.60 billion from $4.74 billion in H1’25.

Despite the increase, non-oil exports accounted for about 15.7 per cent of total export earnings, down from approximately 16.5 per cent in the corresponding period of 2025.

World.title: Living Through the Heat: Lifestyle changes you must make
World.content:
By Josephine Agbonkhese

STEPPING outside lately can sometimes feel like walking into an oven. Before long, you’re burning up, sweating, feeling thirsty and wishing you could return to the comfort of your home. While this may be a familiar experience for many Nigerians, rising global temperatures are making the heat a more serious health concern.

A recent Climate Impact Lab report projected that Nigeria could record 31,400 additional heat-related deaths between September 2026 and February 2027 as the El Niño weather pattern intensifies.

Beyond fatalities, extreme heat can cause dehydration, heat exhaustion, heatstroke, headaches, dizziness, fainting, skin rashes, sunburn, poor sleep and difficulty concentrating. Although this is only a projection, the warning underscores the need to take extreme heat seriously by adjusting our everyday habits.

Know When Heat Is Becoming Dangerous

Severe weakness, dizziness, headaches, nausea or heavy sweating may indicate heat exhaustion and should not be ignored. Move the affected person to a cooler place, loosen any unnecessary clothing and help them cool down. If they are fully alert and can swallow safely, offer them water.

Heatstroke is a medical emergency. Call emergency medical services immediately and begin cooling the person while waiting for help. Do not give fluids to someone who is confused or unconscious. Pay particular attention to older adults, young children and people with health conditions such as diabetes.

Drink Water Before You Feel Thirsty

Keep safe drinking water within reach, whether you’re at your desk, in transit or at the market. Drink regularly rather than waiting until you feel thirsty. Water-rich foods such as watermelon, oranges and cucumber can also contribute to hydration, but they should not replace drinking water. People on medically prescribed fluid restrictions should follow their healthcare professional’s advice.

Dress for the Weather

Loose-fitting clothing made from lightweight, breathable fabrics such as cotton and linen can help you stay cooler. Choose lighter colours and comfortable footwear where possible. A wide-brimmed hat, sunglasses and an umbrella can provide additional protection outdoors. If your work requires formal attire, opt for breathable fabrics and lighter layers.

Rethink Your Daily Schedule

Must that errand happen at noon? Could your walk, outdoor exercise or market visit be scheduled for earlier in the morning or later in the evening? Where possible, plan strenuous activities for cooler parts of the day and reduce exposure to direct sunlight during the hottest hours.

If you work outdoors, take regular breaks in shaded or cool areas. Parents should also pay attention to children’s outdoor play, sports and school activities. Never leave a child alone in a parked vehicle, even for a few minutes.

Make Your Home More Comfortable

Not everyone can afford air conditioning, particularly given the cost of electricity. However, keeping curtains or blinds closed to block direct sunlight during the hottest hours can help. Where safe and practical, open windows when the outdoor air is cooler to improve ventilation, and use fans to circulate air. Also, avoid activities that generate unnecessary indoor heat during the hottest hours.

Wear Sunscreen

Protecting your skin is another important part of managing hot weather. Apply a broad-spectrum, water-resistant sunscreen with an SPF of 30 or higher to exposed skin before going outdoors. Reapply it at least every two hours and after swimming or heavy sweating, following the product instructions.

Sunscreen does not replace shade, protective clothing or measures to limit prolonged exposure to intense sunlight. Combine these precautions to reduce the risk of sunburn and harmful ultraviolet radiation exposure.

WHAT SCHOOLS, WORKPLACES AND GOVERNMENT MUST DO

SCHOOLS must reconsider strenuous outdoor activities, sports and assemblies during the hottest periods of the day while ensuring that pupils have access to drinking water and cool spaces.

EMPLOYERS, particularly those whose workers spend long hours outdoors, should adjust work schedules where possible, provide adequate breaks and take heat warnings seriously.

GOVERNMENT must also make public spaces safer for people who are exposed to the sun daily. This includes providing adequate shade at bus stops and motor parks, where commuters and transport workers often spend considerable time waiting in the heat. The government must also prioritise the construction of covered waiting areas.

Vanguard News

World.title: From ‘Miracle Girl’ to Purpose: How Esther Longe turned survival into life of impact
World.content:
Esther Longe

*SHE survived the 2006 crash that claimed 96 lives, battled survivor’s guilt, and spent a decade building a career in marketing before embracing a divine call to ministry. Today, she is redefining leadership through faith, strategy and legacy.

By Nkiruka Nnorom

The first thing that hits you about Dr Esther Longe is how ordinary she looks. No burn scars. No limp. No visible reminder of a tragedy that wiped out 96 lives in minutes.

Only a small scratch. A literal scratch, she calls it.

On October 29, 2006, 21-year-old Esther was aboard ADC Airlines Flight 053 from Abuja to Sokoto. The Boeing 737-2B7 crashed shortly after take-off after encountering wind shear, broke up, and burst into flames in a cornfield near Tungar Madaki village, Abuja.

20 YEARS AFTER THE ADC AIR CRASH

There were 105 souls on board — 100 passengers and five crew members. Ninety-six died, including the Sultan of Sokoto, Alhaji Muhammadu Maccido; his son, Senator Badamasi Maccido; and Deputy Governor Alhaji Garba Muhammed. Nine survived. Of all the survivors, Esther Kemmer Amoda, now Longe, was the only one without physical injuries.

The burden of a miracle

Newspapers the next morning called her the Miracle Girl. Television vans camped outside her home. Everybody said the same thing: “God has saved your life for a reason.”

At 21, she did not want a reason. She wanted to disappear.

“From the onset, I understood that my survival came with a responsibility. But it came with panic attacks and survivor’s guilt,” she tells Weekender.

“As a 21-year-old, that was daunting. I did not know what that purpose was. I did not think I had done anything to deserve being saved or singled out.”

The years she ran

For the next ten years, she ran. She ran into lecture halls and boardrooms.

She bagged a BSc in Mass Communication from the University of Lagos, a master’s in Marketing from the University of South Wales, UK, a master’s in Research, and a PhD in Marketing, both from the University of Bath, UK.

She became a trained marketing strategist, working with some of the biggest global brands — PwC, GTBank, Pizza Express, and Wrigley’s. She served as a Super Mentor for FCMB SheVentures and a facilitator for the Africa Green Grant Award. She was on track to become a Chief Marketing Officer at a Fortune 500 company.

She wanted to be known for what she built, not what she survived.

“If I am being honest, I ran and hid,” she confesses. “If you look at me, you would not know I had been through such an experience. It was easy to hide. I did not want to be known for something I had nothing to do with. I wanted to be known for what I had accomplished.”

But purpose does not need permission.

People who lost loved ones on that flight began to find her. Not to blame her, but to connect. In their eyes, she saw a question she could not run from: If you were saved, what are you doing with the life taken from us?

“I have had the opportunity to interact with people who lost loved ones on that flight. Those encounters reinforced my desire to live intentionally. I cannot bring their loved ones back, but I hope when they see how I am living, they will believe some good can come out of such a horrible experience.”

The disruption

In December 2016, exactly ten years after she began building a new identity, came the disruption she never planned.

God told her to leave marketing and minister full-time.

“I was very upset because that was not the life I had planned for myself,” she says. “I had written my first life plan at 19. I am Type A. I prided myself on control. Here was God asking me to walk on water with no blueprint.”

She surrendered, albeit reluctantly at first. Then, wholly.

What followed is a portfolio she never imagined. Today, she describes herself as a transformative leader whose mission is to reconnect people to an intimate relationship with God and free individuals, families, and nations from the strongholds of their past.

She is a speaker, author, teacher, marketplace pastor, trainer, and coach. She is the lead coach for the Unicorn Programme, her flagship coaching programme, through which she helps people embrace their God-given uniqueness, break limiting beliefs, heal trauma, and align with God’s will to shine in every area of life.

From strategy to sanctuary

She channels that assignment through five ministry expressions.

God in Real Life Outreach helps people experience intimacy with God in everyday life. Broken serves the broken-hearted who seek to reconnect with God after life’s challenges. The Alternative Business School (TABS) is a life business school for believers in Christ, teaching them how to do business, govern, and minister with integrity.

The 7000 Movement celebrates individuals who lead, govern, and minister with integrity, righteousness, and justice. Adullam Fellowship is a monthly virtual gathering for kings and priests in the marketplace — a place for God’s army to be refreshed.

Her edge is her unique ability to simplify complex issues. Faith meets strategy. Marketing precision meets ministry passion.

Whole Leadership: Her survival code

She calls her model Whole Leadership. It rests on three pillars: identity, radical candour, and authentic leadership. For her, it is not theory. It is a survival strategy.

“I cannot separate my faith from who I am. I lead from values. I don’t just make business decisions; I make value-based business decisions. I don’t see people who work with me as employees. I see them as individuals entrusted to my care.”

Vanguard News

World.title: Former Postmaster-General Calls for Independent Audit of Voters’ Register
World.content:
Ayodeji Ake



A former Postmaster-General of the Federation and Chief Executive Officer of the Nigerian Postal Service (NIPOST), Bisi Adegbuyi, has called for an independent technical audit of Nigeria’s voters’ register to strengthen its accuracy, integrity and credibility ahead of future elections.

Adegbuyi said the proposed review should go beyond confirming voters’ identities to examine the accuracy of their locations, the consistency of registration records and the verifiability of information in the register.

He made the call in a statement yesterday amid renewed concerns about the integrity of the voters’ register, including questions surrounding some voter records.

According to him, strengthening the electoral register requires as much attention to the accuracy of geographic data as to voter identification and the transmission of election results.



Adegbuyi recalled that he had proposed a technical framework on February 27, 2026, to modernise existing voter addresses without disrupting established electoral arrangements.



The framework recommended machine-assisted interpretation, geographic resolution and digital location referencing to improve the quality and reliability of voter-location data.



He said the proposed system could help electoral administrators detect inconsistencies, identify unusual concentrations of registrations in particular locations and improve the verification of polling-unit assignments.



Adegbuyi explained that the framework would complement existing electoral systems rather than replace Permanent Voter Cards (PVCs) or biometric verification.

He said geographic verification could provide an additional layer of assurance by helping authorities establish whether the location information attached to voter records was accurate and consistent.

The renewed call comes amid concerns about questionable voter photographs and possible procedural lapses in the handling of voter information.

Adegbuyi, however, acknowledged that geographic verification alone would not resolve every issue relating to voter identity or data integrity.

He maintained that the approach could complement existing safeguards and help identify records requiring further investigation.

“Nigeria’s electoral infrastructure deserves a verification framework in which identity, geography, provenance and accountability reinforce one another,” he said.

The former NIPOST chief urged the relevant authorities to subject his earlier recommendations to an independent technical assessment to determine their feasibility and potential benefits.

He stressed that any review or implementation must comply with electoral laws, data-protection requirements and the statutory responsibilities of the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC).

Adegbuyi said the objective should be to improve the reliability of the voters’ register without undermining existing voter-identification and biometric verification arrangements.



He argued that the credibility of the register depended not only on establishing who was registered but also on confirming the accuracy and consistency of the information associated with each registration.



“The credibility of a voters’ register depends not only on who is registered, but also on whether the information associated with each registration is accurate, consistent and verifiable,” he said.

Under the proposed approach, geographic information would complement identity and biometric data as part of a broader framework for strengthening Nigeria’s electoral infrastructure.

Adegbuyi said the current concerns surrounding the register presented an opportunity to examine technical solutions that could enhance verification, transparency and accountability before future elections.

World.title: FHFL Unveils New Corporate Identity
World.content:
Raheem Akingbolu

Family Homes Funds Limited (FHFL), key institution advancing affordable housing finance in Nigeria, has unveiled its new corporate identity, reflecting its evolution into a broader housing finance platform and its continued commitment to addressing Nigeria’s estimated 15 million-unit housing deficit.

The new identity represents FHFL’s expanding role in mobilising capital, structuring housing finance solutions and building partnerships that enable affordable housing delivery, create jobs and widen access to homeownership across Nigeria.

Since commencing operations, FHFL has financed more than 15,900 homes, created 104,000 direct and indirect jobs and established a presence across 70 project sites in 19 states and the FCT. The institution also has more than 18,000 homes in its development pipeline, reflecting its ongoing efforts to scale housing delivery through sustainable financing and strategic partnerships.

Speaking on the significance of the new identity, Chairman of FHFL, Mr. Ademola Adebise, said the organisation’s evolution reflects the importance of building a stronger housing finance system capable of delivering lasting social and economic value.

“Access to decent, affordable housing remains a critical development priority for Nigeria. Addressing the scale of the challenge requires institutions that can mobilise capital, strengthen partnerships and create the conditions for housing delivery at scale. FHFL has an important role to play in this process, and its new identity reflects our ambition to deepen that role and deliver greater value to Nigerian families and the wider economy,” he said.

FHFL’s work spans construction financing for affordable homes, mortgage financing for eligible homebuyers, purpose-built rental housing, including student accommodation, land and infrastructure development, and social housing initiatives for vulnerable communities. Through these solutions, the institution works with government, private developers, financial institutions and development finance partners to expand housing supply and improve access to affordable financing.

Speaking on the strategic direction behind the rebrand, Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of FHFL, Mr. Abdul Mutallab Mukhtar, said the new identity reflects the organisation’s growth and its projections for the coming years.

“Our previous identity served us through the early years of our operations, and our growth has created the need for a brand that reflects the organisation we have become, where we are today and where we want to be. Since 2018, FHFL has evolved in its operations. While we initially relied heavily on government funding, we have since expanded our funding base to include private capital, and other funding sources. Our new identity reflects this evolution and the broader role we are building within Nigeria’s housing finance landscape.

“Looking ahead, our projection for the next three to five years is to establish FHFL as a more resilient, well-structured and key player among Nigeria’s development finance institutions, with the capacity to mobilise capital, build strategic partnerships and contribute meaningfully to addressing the country’s housing deficit,” he said.

FHFL’s impact extends across its Affordable Housing Fund, Home Ownership Fund, Rental Housing Fund, Land and Infrastructure Development Fund, and Social Housing Programme. These initiatives address different stages of the housing value chain, from enabling developers to build affordable homes to helping eligible households access mortgage financing and supporting purpose-built rental accommodation.

The institution’s approach also recognises housing as a driver of wider economic activity. Housing development creates demand across construction, building materials, transportation and related services, generating employment and supporting livelihoods within host communities. FHFL incorporates sustainability considerations into its financing activities, including environmental, social and governance requirements for developers it finances.

As FHFL advances its strategic projections, the new corporate identity provides a clearer expression of its institutional direction, housing finance expertise and commitment to measurable outcomes. Its work will continue to focus on expanding access to affordable housing, strengthening partnerships across the housing ecosystem and mobilising investment towards solutions that respond to the needs of Nigerian families.

World.title: Police Charge  Abia Man over Fraudulent Allegations against Benjamin Kalu
World.content:
Alex Enumah in Abuja

The Inspector-General (IG) of Police, has filed a six count criminal charge against one Emenike Okorie, an indigene of Amazu, Umuhu Ezechi, Bende Local Government Area of Abia State, for making fraudulent allegations and questioning the record of the Deputy Speaker of the House of Representatives, Benjamin Kalu.

The six count charge dated October 26 was filed on behalf of the Police by Anthony Egwu of the Police Directorate of Legal Services.

The Police in the charge marked: FHC/ ABJ/ CR/710/2026, alleges that Okorie circulated messages on the Umuhu Ezechi Development Union WhatsApp group in violation of provisions of the Cybercrimes (Prohibition, Prevention, Etc.) Act 2015, as amended in 2024.

According to the prosecution, the messages contained information Okorie allegedly knew to be false and were transmitted for purposes including bullying, threatening or harassing the Deputy Speaker.

The disputed posts reportedly contained allegations relating to a N348 million garri-processing project in Umuhu Ezechi, as well as criticisms of Kalu’s representation of Bende Federal Constituency.

According to the police, the defendant intended to cause reputational damage to Kalu.

Count one of the charge reads:That you Emenike Okorie ‘M’ 49 years old of Amazu, Umuhu Ezechi, Bende, Abia State did knowingly and intentionally transmit or cause the transmission of communication in the form of a post through computer system or network on the Umuhu Ezechi Development Union Whstsapp Grouwp wherein you stated, “ yes, OUK is a striker, but I can’t say the same thing about a man that used the name of Umuhu Ezechi to steal N348 million in the name of an inexistent Garri Processing Plant in Umuhu Ezechi.

So, Ben Kalu is not a striker but Scam, and therefore, must be changed before he sells and liquidate Bende Federal Constituency…”, a post you made referring to Rt. Hon. Benjamin Okezie, the Deputy Speaker, House of Representative as a scam and irresponsible representative of Bende Federal Constituency, knowing same to be false, for the purpose of causing a breakdown of law and order, and posing a threat to life of the said Rt. Hon. Benjamin Okezie, the Deputy Speaker, House of Representative and you thereby committed an offence contrary to and punishable under section 24 (1) (b) of the Cybercrimes (Prohibition, Prevention, Etc) Act 2015 ( as amended) 2024

Count 2

“That you Emenike Okorie ‘M’ 49 years old of Amazu, Umuhu Ezechi, Bende, Abia State did knowingly and intentionally transmit or cause the transmission of communication in the form of a post through — computer system or network on the Umuhu Ezechi Development Union Whatsapp Group wherein you stated, “ yes. OUK is a striker, but I can’t say the same thing about a man that used the name of Umuhu Ezechi to steal N348 million in the name of an inexistent Garri Processing Plant in Umuhu Ezechi. So, Ben Kalu is not a striker but Scam, and therefore, must be changed before he sells and liquidate Bende Federal Constituency…”, a post you knowingly or intentionally transmitted to bully, threaten or harass the person of Rt. Hon. Benjamin Okezie, the Deputy Speaker, House of Representative, placing him in fear of violence or bodily harm and you thereby committed an offence contrary to section 24 (2) (a) of the Cybercrimes (Prohibition, Prevention, Etc) Act 2015 ( as amended) 2024 and punishable under section 24 (2) (c(i) of the Act.

Meanwhile, human rights lawyer, Deji Adeyanju, in a statement yesterday said he had intervened in the matter to secure Okorie’s release.

the allegations contained in the charge remain unproven, and the charge sheet does not establish that Okorie committed the offences alleged against him.

The case has drawn attention to the growing tension between online political commentary, demands for accountability and the application of Nigeria’s cybercrime laws to alleged harassment and reputational attacks.

The court document reviewed in connection with the case did not establish an arraignment date, plea, bail decision or final judicial determination.

Okorie remains presumed innocent until proven guilty by a competent court.

World.title: Borno Parents Seek Tinubu’s Intervention as 78 Children, Teacher Remain in Captivity
World.content:
Amina Hassan in Abuja

Parents in the Margi community of Askira/Uba Local Government Area of Borno State have appealed to President Bola Tinubu to intensify efforts to secure the release of 78 schoolchildren and a teacher abducted from Mussa and Lassa communities in separate incidents.

Speaking at a press briefing in Abuja yesterday, the Chairman of the Margi community, Malla Gadzama, said 42 children were abducted from Mussa on May 15, 2026, while 36 children and a teacher were taken from Lassa on June 29 during the National Examinations Council (NECO) examinations.

The community said the victims had remained in captivity for months despite repeated appeals to the government and other relevant authorities.

Another community member, Frank Kudla, said the abductors had communicated with the government but had not contacted the victims’ families directly.

He noted that the community understood that the government was the only party aware of the kidnappers’ demands, leaving the families without direct information about the situation. “We asked the government to resolve quickly so that our children can be released,” he said.

Kudla added that the families had received assurances from the Borno State Government that the children would be returned, but they were still awaiting their release months later.

Gadzama said the community had previously held press conferences in Maiduguri, the state capital, and at the National Assembly to draw attention to the abductions, but the efforts had yet to secure the victims’ freedom.

The community’s Secretary, Gambo Kadiri, expressed concern that President Tinubu might not have been fully briefed about the situation, although the community could not establish whether the president had received information about the incidents.

Kadiri said the community had also written to the National Security Adviser but had yet to receive a response. He called on the relevant authorities to treat the matter with urgency and sustain efforts to secure the victims’ release.

Kudla said attempts to secure an audience with the Senate President and other National Assembly authorities had also been unsuccessful, prompting the community to hold another press briefing to draw attention to the matter.

The community said it might consider a procession to the National Assembly to press lawmakers to engage the presidency and security agencies over the continued captivity of the children and their teacher.

The community called for coordinated rescue efforts involving federal and state authorities, as well as regular communication with affected families without compromising the safety of the victims.

It also urged the government to establish a designated liaison arrangement through which families could receive verified information and raise concerns about the situation.

The community called for psychosocial and welfare support for affected families, alongside medical care, rehabilitation and educational assistance for the children upon their return. It further urged the authorities to strengthen security around vulnerable schools and communities to prevent future abductions.

Appealing to civil society organisations, religious and traditional leaders, professional associations, women’s and youth groups, and the media, the community called for sustained public attention to the victims’ plight.

It also cautioned journalists against publishing information that could endanger the children or compromise rescue efforts.

World.title: Kaduna: The Road to Continuity and Prosperity
World.content:
Stanley Nkwocha writes that last Saturday’s flag off of the re-election of President Bola Tinubu and Vice President Kashim Shettima in Kaduna signifies road to continuity and prosperity ahead of the January 16, 2027 presidential poll in the country.

History does not merely look at Kaduna; it waits for it. On Saturday, October 24, 2026, this legendary crucible of Nigerian politics became the epicentre of a looming national showdown. Before a roaring sea of party faithful, President Bola Tinubu, flanked by Vice President Kashim Shettima, officially drew the battle lines for the 2027 general elections.

Igniting the All Progressives Congress (APC) presidential campaign on the very soil where empires and republics have been forged, the Tinubu administration sounded a definitive battle cry: the march to tomorrow has officially begun.

The campaign flag-off became an epicentre of raw political parley as governors, ministers, and lawmakers converged with party faithful from every corner of the federation. In that charged political atmosphere, the sheer scale of the APC’s machinery was undeniable. Fuelled by a roaring base, the administration sent an unmistakable message to the nation: as the next electoral storm gathers, the governing party is mobilised, locked in, and ready to consolidate its democratic gains for the future.

Beyond the crowds, colours and excitement, Kaduna offered an opportunity to demonstrate how the Tinubu administration is connecting difficult but necessary economic reforms with infrastructure development, improved public services and the long-term prosperity of Nigerians.

The Renewed Hope Agenda has entered a phase in which the foundations laid through reform are increasingly being complemented by investments and programmes with direct implications for citizens’ livelihoods. That is the work of national development, and it is the responsibility to which the administration has committed itself.

One of the most significant highlights of the presidential campaign flag-off was President Tinubu’s symbolic inauguration of the completed 81-kilometre section of the Abuja–Kaduna–Zaria–Kano Dual Carriageway. The project marks an important milestone in the administration’s commitment to improving Nigeria’s transport infrastructure and strengthening economic connectivity.

For decades, the Abuja–Kaduna corridor has served as a major route connecting the Federal Capital Territory with commercial and agricultural centres across Northern Nigeria. Farmers depend on the corridor to transport produce to markets. Manufacturers rely on it to move raw materials and finished goods, while traders, transport operators and other businesses require efficient road networks to sustain their activities.

The President’s decision to inaugurate the project during the campaign flag-off brought infrastructure delivery into the national political conversation. It demonstrated the place of transport connectivity in the administration’s strategy for building a more productive and competitive economy.

President Tinubu assumed office in May 2023 amid serious economic challenges, including fiscal pressures, foreign exchange distortions, infrastructure deficits, and longstanding structural weaknesses.

His administration responded with reforms designed to address these difficulties and establish a more sustainable foundation for growth. The removal of petrol subsidies and changes to the foreign exchange system were among the most consequential decisions.

While these sweeping policies demanded painful sacrifices from families and enterprises alike, the administration remains unyieldingly committed to a singular mission: ensuring the hard-won victories of reform directly transform Nigerian lives with revitalised services, soaring investment, and unprecedented economic opportunity. Today, the latest economic indicators offer undeniable proof—the tide is turning, and progress is real.

Nigeria’s economy recorded growth of 4.43 per cent in the second quarter of 2026, compared with 4.23 per cent in the corresponding period of 2025. The Federal Ministry of Finance also reported headline inflation of 15.39 per cent in August 2026, while external reserves reached approximately $54.7 billion in September. These developments strengthen the conditions under which businesses can invest, governments can plan, and citizens can pursue opportunities with greater confidence.

Progress is also taking shape through interventions across critical sectors. The Nigerian Education Loan Fund (NELFUND) is expanding access to tertiary education financing, while the Nigerian Consumer Credit Corporation (CREDICORP) is working to improve access to consumer credit.

The Presidential Initiative on Compressed Natural Gas is supporting the transition to alternative transportation fuels, with the potential to reduce operating costs for transport providers and commuters.

In healthcare, the administration is pursuing the revitalisation of primary healthcare facilities, improved financing and expanded access to essential services. Agricultural interventions, investments in food production and ongoing road projects, including the Lagos–Calabar Coastal Highway and Sokoto–Badagry Superhighway, form part of a broader effort to strengthen domestic productivity, connect markets and create economic opportunities across the federation.

The task ahead is to consolidate these gains while addressing the cost-of-living pressures that continue to affect many families. This explains the emphasis the Renewed Hope Agenda places on infrastructure, agriculture, healthcare, education, transportation and other sectors with direct consequences for household welfare.

The Ranchers Bees Stadium in Kaduna was a boiling cauldron in which these Renewed Hope policies were explained, the air thick with the dust of a thousand stomping feet and the deafening roar of the APC faithful. President Tinubu, launching his bid for a second term, waited for the thunderous cheers to subside. When he spoke, he did not offer a defensive shield. He drew a sword.

“I hear my opponents talking about hunger and poverty,” the President’s voice cut through the stadium, sharp and unyielding. He leaned into the microphone, pausing just long enough to let the weight of the accusation hang over the crowd.

“Who created it?” He didn’t wait for the opposition to answer. He pointed a finger straight into the political ether, directly at the legacy of his rivals. “They did!” he thundered. “They created the hunger. They created the poverty. And we are trying to eradicate it!”

The crowd erupted. Behind him, the political elite watched the raw theatre of a President aggressively shifting the battleground of the 2027 election. He implored the sea of supporters not to be swayed by the sudden empathy of past leaders, specifically targeting those who now weaponise the cost-of-living crisis against his administration.

“Don’t let them lie to you,” he declared, drawing a definitive line in the sand over his economic overhauls. “What is past is in the past. Fuel subsidy is in our past: no more corruption, no more lies, no more smuggling!” It was a deliberate, high-stakes gamble. Facing severe public anxiety over inflation, President Tinubu chose not to soften his rhetoric, but to weaponise the narrative, challenging his critics to look in the mirror before speaking of the nation’s pain.

His remarks brought into focus the structural problems inherited by successive administrations and the responsibility of leadership to confront them. The Tinubu administration has chosen reforms intended to address the underlying conditions that have constrained economic growth. The President’s message in Kaduna was that these efforts must be sustained to achieve the broader objectives of economic stability, productive investment and poverty reduction.

Vice President Kashim Shettima reinforced the political and historical significance of the gathering by recalling President Tinubu’s longstanding relationships with leaders from Northern Nigeria. In his speech, he highlighted the President’s support for northern presidential candidates across different electoral periods, citing former President Muhammadu Buhari, former Vice President Atiku Abubakar and Mallam Nuhu Ribadu as examples of political relationships built over time.

These dynamics underscore a fundamental truth: a nation defined by its diversity requires constant, active engagement across regional and religious divides. Unity demands cooperation, mutual respect, and deliberate political understanding. Throughout his journey, President Tinubu has consistently forged strategic alliances far beyond his immediate constituency—proving that national objectives are best achieved by building common ground.

The Vice President also acknowledged Kaduna State’s contribution to the APC’s political development and commended its people for their support.

Governance thrives on these connections. Nigeria cannot develop without regional cooperation and political institutions focused on a shared national agenda. In this federation, the prosperity of one region is inextricably linked to the opportunities of another.

This core understanding anchored the remarks of Kaduna State Governor, Senator Uba Sani, who lauded President Tinubu for supporting states as they execute critical development agendas.

Governor Sani reported progress in reopening schools and primary healthcare centres previously affected by insecurity.

He also highlighted investments in transport infrastructure and other development initiatives. Such interventions are especially important in communities where insecurity has disrupted education, healthcare and economic activity. Restoring these services helps families regain the confidence to rebuild their lives and plan for the future.

At its core, the promise of Renewed Hope is more than a vision; it is a strategic blueprint. Real hope demands both the fierce determination to pursue meaningful goals and the clarity to build credible pathways toward them. When people can trace a direct line from their current sacrifices to a better tomorrow, uncertainty fades, and confidence takes its place.
