World.title: Liberia: AML Reaffirms Support to Liberia’s Future, Says Country Ready for Global Mining Boom
World.content:
Unification Town, Margibi County— ArcelorMittal Liberia, one of the country’s largest investors in the mining sector, has reaffirmed its commitment to Liberia’s development agenda, highlighting its investments in iron ore production, railway infrastructure, and industrial expansion as key drivers of economic growth.

By Emmanuel Weedee-Conway

The company’s Chief Executive Officer, Michiel van der Merwe, said ArcelorMittal Liberia is helping position the country as a strategic supplier of premium iron ore to global markets while creating opportunities for industrial development and long-term economic growth.



Speaking at the Liberia International Mining and Energy Conference and Expo (LIMEC), held at the Farmington Hotel, van der Merwe stated that Liberia has the mineral resources, strategic location, and investment potential needed to compete in the global mining and energy sectors.

The conference marks the return of a major mining and energy gathering in Liberia after approximately 15 years.

Mining and Energy as Drivers of Economic Growth

Van der Merwe told the gathering that the future of Liberia’s economic growth depends partly on the country’s ability to capitalize on its natural resources while building strong partnerships among government, investors, industry players, and local communities.

He noted that countries capable of providing stable investment conditions, strong partnerships, and high-quality mineral resources are better positioned to attract investment and compete in international markets.

According to him, Liberia possesses many of these advantages but must strengthen collaboration and demonstrate sustained commitment to translate its potential into lasting prosperity for its citizens.

He also emphasized the importance of developing Liberian talent, saying investments in human capital would help ensure that future generations can lead and sustain the industries being established today.

Phase II Expansion Positions AML for Growth

Van der Merwe explained that ArcelorMittal Liberia’s experience demonstrates the benefits of long-term partnerships built on trust, commitment, and a shared development vision.

He pointed to the company’s Phase II Expansion Project as evidence of its long-term commitment to Liberia, describing the investment as a major transformation of the country’s iron ore industry.

He recounted that the commissioning of Liberia’s first large-scale iron ore concentrator represents a significant milestone for both the company and the country.

“It enables Liberia to move higher up the value chain by producing premium iron ore concentrate for international markets for current steel mills as well as the next generation of steel mills with lower carbon emissions technology.”

For him, the project demonstrates Liberia’s ability to attract and execute large-scale industrial investments capable of creating jobs, building local capacity, and strengthening national infrastructure.

US$800 Million Invested in Railway and Port Infrastructure

Beyond its investment in the concentrator, the AML chief threw light on the rehabilitation and expansion of the railway linking the company’s mining operations at Tokadeh to the Port of Buchanan.

Although the railway and port facilities are government-owned assets, van der Merwe maintains that ArcelorMittal has invested approximately US$800 million to date in rehabilitating the railway and expanding its capacity to accommodate the company’s planned growth.

He described the railway as critical infrastructure for supporting future mining operations and creating opportunities for other investors to transport minerals through the corridor.

The company’s investment, he asserted, has laid the groundwork for a multiuser railway system intended to support broader mining development in Liberia.

AML Targets More Than 20 Million Tons in 2027

Van der Merwe revealed that ArcelorMittal Liberia is preparing to increase its iron ore exports to more than 20 million tons in 2027, up from less than five million tons exported in 2024.

The projected increase follows the introduction of the company’s new concentrator and the expansion of supporting infrastructure.

“That’s a quadrupling of tonnage exported from Liberia,” he declared.

He added that the company is also planning to increase production capacity at its mines to 30 million tons, noting that the current railway expansion already accommodates this anticipated growth and could allow other users to access surplus capacity in the interim.

The planned expansion is expected to strengthen Liberia’s position in the international iron ore market while increasing demand for supporting services and infrastructure.

Government Reaffirms Multiuser Railway Commitment

Van der Merwe reiterated ArcelorMittal Liberia’s commitment to working with the Government of Liberia to ensure that the Tokadeh-to-Buchanan railway remains accessible to other mining companies.

He indicated that the company supports the position maintained by successive presidential administrations that the railway should operate as a multiuser asset, allowing other investors to benefit from the infrastructure.

The Third Amendment to the company’s Mineral Development Agreement, ratified earlier this year, provides for the railway to be open to other users, with the Government of Liberia determining which additional companies may access the corridor.

He told the gathering that prospective users would be responsible for financing their own expansion requirements, while benefiting from the foundational investments already made by ArcelorMittal Liberia.

“The recent Third Amendment to our Mineral Development Agreement, that was ratified earlier this year ensures that this is a railway open to all users, with the Government of Liberia deciding who else can utilize this infrastructure.”

Van der Merwe further disclosed that the operating framework for the multiuser railway, discussed by three successive administrations over the past decade, is being formalized through the Rail Systems Operating Principles (RSOP).

He accentuated that the principles provide for the railway to be operated by an independent company beginning in 2030.

Calls for Independent Railway Operator

The AML chief called for the establishment of an independent railway operator, describing the move as an important step toward transforming Liberia’s economy and expanding access to critical infrastructure.

He intoned that the cooperation among the government, investors, and industry could create the conditions necessary for sustainable economic growth.

“More importantly, it lays the foundation for a truly shared infrastructure platform that can unlock new mining opportunities, attract further investment, and accelerate national development,” van der Merwe said.

He added that the vision of shared infrastructure and prosperity extends beyond mining and rail transportation, requiring a collective commitment to national development.

Van der Merwe also disclosed that ArcelorMittal Liberia is in agreement with the government on the establishment of a National Rail Authority that would eventually oversee the development and management of additional railway corridors across the country.

The AML CEO clarified that the company wants the operating principles governing the Tokadeh-to-Buchanan railway to be recognized when the proposed authority is established.

AML Pledges Long-Term Partnership

, van der Merwe informed the conference that Liberia’s development ambitions could not be achieved by any single company, government institution, or investor acting alone.

At the same time, he is of the conviction that sustained cooperation could help create an environment in which investment flourishes, industries expand, and communities benefit from economic opportunities.

“ArcelorMittal Liberia remains committed to playing its part in that journey. We’ve played this part for the last twenty years and we are ready to do so for another forty years or more.”

World.title: Liberian Journalists Challenged to Turn China Training Into Action
World.content:
Monrovia-Twenty-three Liberian journalists have returned from a two-week media training program in China with new professional insights, international connections and a challenge that could prove more difficult than the journey itself, turn what they have learned into better journalism for Liberia.

By Willie N. Tokpah

The challenge came from Bai S. G. Best, leader of the Liberian media delegation, and Vice President of the Publisher Association of Liberia, whose closing remarks at the end of the October 14–28 seminar went beyond the usual expressions of gratitude that accompany international training programs.



Instead, Best left his colleagues with a question rooted in a familiar idea of growth, responsibility, and accountability.

“If I plant you, will you grow?”

It was a question directed at 23 media practitioners drawn from Liberia’s state-run and private media institutions who had spent two weeks in China studying media communication, international reporting, cultural exchanges, media convergence and approaches to combating fake news.

For Best, the significance of the trip would not be determined by the certificates participants received in Beijing, the institutions they visited, or the experiences they shared abroad.

It would be measured by what happens when they return to their newsrooms, face editorial deadlines, and resume reporting on the problems confronting ordinary Liberians. “Our Chinese hosts have planted seeds of knowledge, friendship, and possibility in each of us.

The question now is what we will do with them,” Best told the gathering. “To our Chinese friends, thank you for planting these seeds. To my Liberian colleagues, let us return home determined to make them bear fruit.”

The seminar, organized by the Research and Training Institute of China’s National Radio and Television Administration, concluded on October 27, with participants receiving certificates and gifts.

Gabriel Mills, Minister Counselor for Press at the Liberian Embassy in China, also urged beneficiaries to put the knowledge and practical skills acquired during the program to use.

He commended the Chinese government and the Chinese Embassy through the Ministry of Commerce for providing the training opportunity.

But beyond the official speeches and closing ceremony, the central concern remains relevant to Liberia’s media landscape, what changes will the training produce in the way Liberian journalists report, question those in power and serve the public.

Beyond Certificates and Photographs

Best’s address was notable for its emphasis on the work waiting for participants at home. He described the two-week experience as physically demanding, intellectually challenging, and culturally enriching.

Participants had to adjust to Beijing’s autumn weather, an eight-hour time difference with Monrovia, unfamiliar foods and customs, and a demanding schedule of lectures, excursions, and professional discussions.

At the same time, they were expected to keep up with responsibilities in Liberia, including filing stories and meeting newsroom deadlines. Yet Best said the most important transformation was not simply what participants had learned about China, it was what they had learned about themselves, their profession, and one another.

The delegation brought together journalists from different institutions, backgrounds, and professional circles. Some arrived knowing little about one another; they leave, Best said, with deeper friendships, greater mutual respect, and a stronger sense of shared purpose.

“We arrived as colleagues, some of us barely acquainted. We leave with deeper friendships, greater mutual respect, and a stronger sense of shared purpose,” he said.

He described the experience as an opportunity to look beyond the distance separating Liberia and China and engage directly with another country’s institutions, culture, and media environment.“And somewhere along this journey, it ceased to be simply about Liberians coming to learn from China. It became about all of us, Liberians and Chinese alike, exchanging perspectives on our professions, our cultures, our nations, our people, and our ways of life,” Best said.

For a profession that often operates under intense deadlines, institutional pressures, and competing demands, the exchange offered participants an opportunity to reflect on the broader purpose of journalism and the responsibilities that come with it.

A Call for Journalism That Does More Than Find Fault

Best called on his fellow journalists to embrace constructive journalism, an approach that examines public problems while also investigating possible solutions.

He said he hoped participants would return to their newsrooms with a renewed determination to produce reporting that helps society understand its challenges rather than simply identifying what is wrong.

“I hope we return to our respective newsrooms with renewed determination to practice constructive journalism, journalism that does not merely identify problems, but helps society understand them and explore solutions,” he said.

He also stressed that constructive journalism must not mean avoiding difficult questions or protecting powerful interests from scrutiny. Instead, he argued that journalism must continue to challenge prevailing narratives, ask uncomfortable questions, and ensure that the voices of the least heard are not drowned out.

The distinction is important for Liberia, where journalists play a critical role in informing citizens, scrutinizing public institutions, and bringing issues affecting communities to national attention.

A focus on solutions, if applied rigorously, can complement investigative and accountability reporting by examining whether proposed interventions work, who benefits, who is left behind, and what evidence supports claims of progress.

But the test will be whether the lessons from the seminar can be incorporated into everyday newsroom decisions without compromising editorial independence, accuracy, or the media’s watchdog role. He warned that participants could face skepticism, pushback, and resistance when attempting to introduce new ideas in their newsrooms, communities, and institutions.

“Meaningful change has never been easy,” he said. That acknowledgment gave his message a practical edge international exposure may introduce new ideas, but implementing them requires commitment, professional discipline, and an environment in which journalists can put those ideas into practice.

The Leaf, the Seed, and Liberia’s Next Chapter

Best’s most memorable message came when he drew on an idea associated with Chinese President Xi Jinping’s development philosophy, using the image of a leaf to describe how one small contribution can help enrich an entire community.

“One leaf. One person. One idea. One commitment to doing things differently,” he said.

He then turned to what he described as a simple but powerful Liberian proverbial question, “If I plant you, will you grow?” The imagery captured the responsibility accompanying the opportunity offered to the delegation.

Training, he suggested, is only the beginning.

Knowledge must be applied, professional relationships must be sustained, and new ideas must produce results beyond the conference room.

The question is whether the experience will lead to more rigorous reporting, stronger newsroom practices, more informed public, debate, and greater attention to the concerns of Liberian communities. Those outcomes cannot be guaranteed by certificates or international exchanges alone.

They depend on how participants use what they have learned, the support they receive from their employers, and the professional standards they uphold.

For Best, however, the responsibility is clear. The participants have received an opportunity, and what they do with it is now up to them.

China-Liberia Media Ties

The closing ceremony also highlighted the broader relationship between Liberia and China, particularly cooperation in media, communication, and cultural exchange.

Liu Linhai, Vice President of the Research and Training Institute of the National Radio and Television Administration, described the seminar as an important platform for deepening exchanges between the two countries.

He said the 14-day program brought participants into discussions with experts and scholars from China’s National Radio and Television Administration, China Media Group, the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, the Communication University of China and China Foreign Affairs University.

Topics included international communication, cultural exchange, innovation in media convergence, and combating fake news.

Liu expressed hope that the participants would share their experiences with colleagues in Liberia and help strengthen practical cooperation between the two countries in media and culture.

He also encouraged the journalists to continue serving as cultural ambassadors, building bridges of friendship and understanding between Liberia and China.

The program forms part of a series of training opportunities the Chinese government has provided to Liberian media practitioners over several years.

Such initiatives offer participants exposure to China’s governance structures, media institutions, and approaches to communication.

For Liberia, the value of these exchanges will depend not only on the knowledge acquired but also on how journalists critically assess and apply relevant lessons within the country’s own political, social, and media environment.

Lessons From Anji

The seminar extended beyond lectures and classroom discussions, with participants spending a week visiting Anji County in China’s Zhejiang Province.

The delegation visited Yucun Village, associated with China’s philosophy that “lucid waters and lush mountains are invaluable assets,” as well as the Bamboo as a Substitute for Plastic Center and the White Tea Cultural and Creative Complex.

The visits offered a look at how local initiatives connect environmental protection, economic activity, cultural promotion, and community development.

Participants also visited Anji’s County-level Governance Center and Public Creative Platform, where they learned about the use of integrated media in local governance and the development of new media and creative industries.

Liu said he hoped the delegation would take home lessons on green development and the use of media to support social development.

Liberia’s natural environment and ecological resources provide a local context for examining such experiences, particularly in environmental reporting and public communication.

But any application of lessons from China would need to reflect Liberia’s own institutions, resources, and development priorities.

The visits offered examples for reflection, but their longer-term value will depend on whether participants can translate what they observed into reporting that helps Liberians better understand environmental challenges, public policy, and community development.

World.title: Liberia: Kemayah Urges Global Youth to Move Beyond Climate Talk, Demand a Seat at Policy Table
World.content:
Speaking at the IHRC-COP31 Simulation Conference, Liberia’s former Foreign Minister calls for meaningful youth participation in climate diplomacy, stronger climate financing, renewable-energy innovation and accountability as Türkiye prepares to host COP31 in November.

MONROVIA — Former Foreign Minister Dee-Maxwell Saah Kemayah Sr. has called for a fundamental shift in global climate governance, urging governments and international institutions to move young people beyond symbolic participation and give them a meaningful role in climate negotiations, policymaking and implementation.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh

Delivering the keynote address at the opening of the International Human Rights Commission (IHRC)-COP31 Simulation Conference 2026 on Saturday, October 24, Kemayah argued that young people must be recognized as active partners in addressing climate change rather than treated merely as future leaders who will inherit its consequences.



“The future of our planet is being shaped by decisions we make today, and young people must have a meaningful voice in those decisions,” Kemayah told participants at the two-day online conference held under the theme, “Global Youth, Climate Diplomacy, and a Sustainable Future.”

The conference brought together students, young professionals, diplomats, scholars and civil society representatives to explore international climate negotiations and the challenges of reaching agreements on climate finance, technology transfer, energy security and climate-related displacement.

Kemayah, who served as Liberia’s Minister of Foreign Affairs and Dean of the Cabinet, said climate change had evolved beyond an environmental concern into a global development challenge affecting food security, public health, livelihoods, economic growth and human dignity.

Quoting former United Nations Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon, he reminded delegates: “There is no Plan B because there is no Planet B.”

He said the interconnected nature of climate risks requires coordinated international action, adding that no country or generation can afford to ignore the consequences of a warming planet.

Climate Justice for Vulnerable Countries

Kemayah placed particular emphasis on the challenges facing developing countries, many of which must confront climate vulnerability while struggling with poverty, unemployment, inadequate infrastructure and limited financial resources.

He cited changing rainfall patterns, droughts, coastal erosion, flooding and extreme weather events as threats to agricultural productivity, infrastructure, water supplies and public health systems.

For vulnerable countries, he argued, responding effectively to climate change requires more than commitments to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. It also demands adequate financing, access to technology, stronger adaptation programs and international cooperation that reflects differences in national circumstances.

He pointed to the principles of equity and common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities under the international climate framework, including the Paris Agreement.

These principles recognize that countries differ in their historical contributions to greenhouse gas emissions, financial and technological capacity, and exposure to climate risks.

“A fair international response must therefore combine environmental ambition with development needs,” Kemayah said, emphasizing that climate justice should provide vulnerable countries with a realistic pathway toward sustainable development.

His argument reflects a longstanding challenge in international climate diplomacy: how to reconcile the urgency of reducing emissions with developing countries’ demands for financing and support to adapt to climate impacts and pursue economic growth.

Youth Inclusion Must Go Beyond Conferences

A central theme of Kemayah’s address was the gap between inviting young people to climate conferences and giving them the power and resources to influence decisions.

He identified young people as researchers, entrepreneurs, community organizers, technical professionals and emerging diplomats whose contributions could strengthen climate planning and implementation.

University students, he said, could investigate local climate risks, while young entrepreneurs could develop renewable-energy solutions and sustainable businesses. Young diplomats and professionals could contribute technical expertise and help bridge differences among countries during negotiations.

However, he warned that meaningful participation requires more than representation at international gatherings.

Governments and international institutions, he said, must provide young people with access to information, technical training, mentorship, financing and opportunities to participate in national climate consultations, international negotiations and environmental research.

He also stressed the importance of including rural youth, young people with disabilities, economically disadvantaged students and those living in climate-vulnerable communities.

“The principle is straightforward: young people should not simply inherit the consequences of climate decisions. They should help shape those decisions,” he said.

Climate Diplomacy Must Produce Results

Kemayah also challenged governments to measure the success of climate diplomacy by tangible outcomes rather than the number of declarations signed or promises announced.

He acknowledged that international negotiations are complicated by competing national interests, different energy systems, economic priorities and unequal financial capacities.

Some countries prioritize rapid emissions reductions, while others must balance climate commitments against the need for affordable electricity, industrial development, employment and poverty reduction.

Effective diplomacy, he argued, must recognize these differences without weakening the urgency of climate action.

He outlined four essential requirements for effective climate negotiations: sustained dialogue and mutual understanding, credible scientific evidence, equity in international cooperation, and stronger implementation and accountability mechanisms.

The ultimate test, he said, should be whether agreements produce cleaner energy, stronger climate resilience, protected ecosystems, effective adaptation and improved access to climate finance.

“The ultimate purpose of climate diplomacy is not simply to reach agreement. It is to reach agreements that make a measurable difference,” Kemayah said.

He described the IHRC-COP31 Simulation Conference as an opportunity for participants to develop negotiation skills, understand competing national interests and explore solutions that are equitable, practical and capable of implementation.

Five Priorities for Youth-Led Climate Action

To translate climate commitments into practical results, Kemayah proposed five strategic priorities for governments, educational institutions, development partners and young people.

The first is strengthening climate education and research. He called on schools, universities and professional institutions to equip young people with the knowledge and skills needed to assess climate risks, evaluate evidence and develop solutions.

Second, he urged greater investment in renewable energy and sustainable innovation, including affordable energy systems, energy-efficient technologies, sustainable agriculture and improved waste management.

Third, he called for stronger protection of forests, water resources and biodiversity through reforestation, watershed protection, ecosystem restoration and community environmental education.

Fourth, he emphasized investment in climate-resilient communities, including early-warning systems, resilient infrastructure, improved water management, disaster preparedness and climate-resilient agriculture.

Fifth, he called for transparency and institutional accountability, urging governments to report progress on climate commitments, businesses to assess their environmental impacts and institutions to monitor how climate resources are used.

He said young people could contribute to these efforts through research, responsible advocacy, public consultations and civic engagement.

According to Kemayah, the five priorities are interconnected: education builds knowledge, innovation develops solutions, conservation protects natural systems, resilience reduces vulnerability, and accountability helps ensure that commitments deliver results.

Stewardship and Responsibility to Future Generations

Beyond policy and diplomacy, Kemayah framed climate action as an ethical responsibility to protect the natural environment and preserve opportunities for future generations.

He argued that forests, water, energy, agriculture and infrastructure must be managed with consideration for their long-term effects on human well-being and environmental security.

Referring to environmental protection as a responsibility to care for God’s creation and one’s neighbors, he said sustainable development should not be treated as a choice between economic progress and environmental preservation.

Instead, he argued, development must be pursued in ways that protect human dignity while sustaining the ecological systems on which life depends.

“Environmental stewardship is an expression of our responsibility to care for God’s creation and our neighbors,” he said.

Focus Turns to COP31 in Türkiye

The IHRC-COP31 Simulation Conference was held online on October 24–25, 2026, ahead of the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference, commonly known as COP31, scheduled for Antalya, Türkiye, from November 9–20, 2026.

According to the conference background materials, the simulation was designed to give university students, youth leaders, young professionals and civil society representatives practical experience in international negotiations.

Participants were assigned roles representing countries, international organizations, businesses and civil society groups to discuss issues expected to shape the global climate agenda.

The simulation featured four negotiation areas: fossil fuel transition and energy security; critical minerals and green industrial competition; climate finance and adaptation; and loss and damage and climate displacement.

The exercise aimed to strengthen participants’ understanding of global climate governance, international cooperation and climate justice while developing their negotiation and public-speaking skills.

Kemayah urged participants to use the opportunity to move beyond theoretical discussions and develop practical proposals that could inform international climate action.

He concluded with three central messages: climate change requires international cooperation and responsible governance; young people must have meaningful influence in climate policymaking; and commitments must translate into measurable improvements in environmental protection and human well-being.

“Let us learn with intellectual discipline, negotiate with integrity, and take action with determination,” he said.

For Liberia and other climate-vulnerable countries, the issues raised in the address carry particular significance. The challenge extends beyond participating in international discussions to ensuring that global commitments translate into resources, policies and practical interventions that strengthen communities against climate risks.

As the world prepares for COP31, Kemayah’s message was that young people must be equipped not only to understand the climate crisis but also to influence the decisions, negotiations and investments that will determine how countries respond to it.

World.title: Faith Kesselly Inducted as LICO President, Pledges Unity and Accountability
World.content:
In her inaugural address, Kesselly outlined a leadership agenda centred on community welfare, youth empowerment, cultural preservation and accountability, emphasizing the need to ensure that every member of the Liberian community feels represented and supported.

LONDON, United Kingdom — Faith Kesselly has been inducted as president of the Liberian Community Organisation (LICO), pledging to lead with compassion, transparency, accountability, unity and service as she begins a four-year tenure running from 2026 to 2030.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh

Kesselly was elected unopposed on Saturday, July 11, 2026, and formally inducted on Saturday, October 17, at St John’s Angell Town Church in Brixton, London. Her inauguration was held under the theme, “One Community, One Vision, One Future,” reflecting her commitment to strengthening unity, promoting inclusion and improving the welfare of Liberians living in the United Kingdom.



In her inaugural address, Kesselly outlined a leadership agenda centred on community welfare, youth empowerment, cultural preservation and accountability, emphasizing the need to ensure that every member of the Liberian community feels represented and supported.

“Our elders must never feel forgotten. Our vulnerable members must know they are not alone. Our young people must see opportunities for their future, and every Liberian must feel that this organisation belongs to them,” she said.

She pledged to promote a leadership culture grounded in compassion, transparency, accountability, unity and service, identifying these values as the foundation of her administration.

Kesselly also announced plans to showcase Liberian culture in schools across the United Kingdom, with a particular focus on involving young people in promoting and appreciating their heritage.

“I promise to showcase Liberian culture throughout schools in the UK, and to involve our young future leaders in promoting and appreciating their roots and heritage and bringing the community together,” she stated.

The initiative is intended to help younger generations maintain connections with Liberia’s cultural identity while encouraging greater interaction and cohesion within the diaspora community.

Kesselly’s administration takes office under the banner of “The New Standard Leadership Agenda,” with its stated priorities aligning with LICO’s longstanding mission to promote unity, integrity and progress among Liberians in London.

Established in 1994, LICO is a not-for-profit organisation founded by Liberians living in London in response to the challenges confronting members of the community. It serves as an umbrella organisation for Liberians in the British capital, providing a platform for support, representation and advocacy.

Over the years, the organisation has focused on community welfare, education and development, youth and women’s empowerment, health and well-being, economic empowerment and networking. It also works to build constructive partnerships with public authorities, voluntary organisations and other stakeholders.

LICO describes itself as non-political, non-sectarian and non-discriminatory, welcoming individuals who share its commitment to unity, integrity and progress.

As Kesselly begins her four-year tenure, her stated priorities place particular emphasis on ensuring that older people and vulnerable community members receive support, young people have opportunities to develop, and Liberians in the United Kingdom remain connected to their cultural roots.

Her leadership agenda now sets out the direction for her administration as it seeks to strengthen community bonds and sustain LICO’s role in supporting Liberians in London.

“One Community, One Vision, One Future,” she declared.

World.title: From Double Market To The Liberian Senate: The Journey of Senator Botoe Kanneh
World.content:
Gbarpolu County Senator Botoe Kanneh

A story of humble beginnings, community trust, perseverance and grassroots leadership in Gbarpolu County.

Before the Senate Chamber and the responsibilities of national leadership, Senator Botoe Kanneh’s story was rooted in the marketplace.

By Augustus D.R [email protected]



Her journey from trading pepper, dried meat and other goods at Double Market to serving in the Liberian Senate reflects years of hard work, personal sacrifice and engagement with ordinary citizens.

Building trust at Double Market

For years, she traded at Double Market while helping fellow citizens from Gbarpolu County sell their agricultural produce and other products. Beyond conducting her own business, she developed relationships with people who depended on the market to earn a living and support their families.

Through these interactions, she became familiar with the everyday struggles of traders and rural families. Helping fellow citizens market their products created opportunities for mutual support and strengthened relationships that extended beyond business.

Over time, these connections helped build a foundation of trust and familiarity with many people from Gbarpolu County. For those who knew her through her years of trading and community engagement, her story was not simply about selling goods; it was also about maintaining close ties with people at the grassroots level.

Her supporters describe her as reliable and trustworthy, pointing to her longstanding relationships with community members as part of the basis for that confidence. In their view, the trust she enjoys was built over years of personal interaction rather than appearing only when she entered politics.

From the marketplace to politics

Her early life was shaped by responsibility and hard work. Accounts of her background indicate that she sold pepper, dried meat and other goods to help support her younger siblings’ education.

As she traveled through Gbarpolu C ounty, she encountered the difficulties facing rural communities, including limited access to essential services, economic hardship and challenging transportation routes.

These experiences contributed to her interest in public service. Inspired in part by Ellen Johnson- Sirleaf’s Election in 2005, she eventually decided to enter electoral politics. In 2017, she contested the representative seat for Gbarpolu District Three.

Although that election was reportedly followed by a legal dispute, the setback did not end her political ambitions. Instead, she continued preparing for another opportunity to serve.

A challenging road to the Senate

In 2020, she contested the Gbarpolu County senatorial election as an independent candidate. According to accounts of the race, she was the only woman among ten candidates. The election faced controversy following disruptions in Nomadatanou, a community described as one of her political strongholds.

The National Elections Commission postponed voting there and conducted a rerun on December 8, 2020. Subsequent legal challenges took the matter to the Supreme Court, which ruled against the challenge to her victory. She was subsequently recognized as the winner, becoming Gbarpolu County’s first female senator.

Her journey illustrates the difficulties that can accompany a bid for elected office and highlights the importance of women’s participation in Liberia’s political institutions.

From community relationships to public service

Since entering the Senate, she has identified education, healthcare, women’s economic empowerment, and road infrastructure among her priorities.

Accounts of her work report the construction of two schools intended to improve access to education for children who otherwise face long journeys to school.

She has also reportedly supported patients receiving specialized medical care at Emirates Hospital and pursued other community-focused initiatives, including market development.

Improving the road to Nomadatanou is another of her stated goals. Having traveled through the Gola Forest during her trading years, she understands from personal experience the transportation challenges affecting residents and traders in the area.

These priorities address issues that matter to many communities across Gbarpolu County. Their lasting impact will depend on effective implementation, sustainability and measurable benefits for the people they are intended to serve.

A legacy still being written

Her journey from Double Market to the Liberian Senate illustrates how grassroots relationships can become an important part of a person’s public life.

The relationships she developed while helping fellow citizens sell their products helped establish connections that, according to her supporters, contributed to the trust she enjoys among many people in Gbarpolu County.

Her supporters regard her as a dependable figure whose engagement with ordinary citizens began long before she entered elected office. Her continued public service provides an opportunity to demonstrate how those relationships can translate into effective representation, accountability, and sustainable development.

Ultimately, the significance of her journey will be measured not only by how far she has traveled, but also by the extent to which her work improves the lives of the people she represents.

From Double Market to the Senate, Senator Botoe Kanneh’s story reminds the Liberian People that leadership can begin with ordinary work, grow through relationships and find expression in public service. For Gbarpolu County, it is a story about the connection between the marketplace, community trust and the pursuit of representation.

World.title: LERC’s Commissioner Advances Regional Power Cooperation during courtesy call on TRANSCO CLSG in Abidjan
World.content:
Hon. Kamara (m) with Mr. Bailly (2nd from right) and other senior officials of TRANSCO CLSG

Abidjan, Côte d’Ivoire, October 21, 2026 – Hon. Amara Kamara, Commissioner of the Liberia Electricity Regulatory Commission (LERC), paid a courtesy visit to TRANSCO CLSG headquarters in Abidjan on Wednesday, underscoring the two institutions’ commitment to regional power cooperation.

Commissioner Kamara was received by General Manager Etienne Bailly; Director of Finance and Administration Josephus Jigba Yilla; Acting Technical Director Erick Achi; Procurement Specialist and Contract Manager Mohamed Keita; and Communications Officer Sidiki Trawally.

On behalf of LERC Chairman Claude Katta and the Board of Commissioners, Commissioner Kamara congratulated Mr. Bailly on his appointment as General Manager of TRANSCO CLSG. He pledged LERC’s full support for the organization’s work. “We admire the work being done here at TRANSCO CLSG,” Commissioner Kamara said.



The discussions centered on the performance and long-term sustainability of the regional power system. Both sides emphasized the importance of regular institutional dialogue as West Africa works toward a more reliable and interconnected electricity market.

TRANSCO CLSG operates the Côte d’Ivoire–Liberia–Sierra Leone–Guinea interconnection, which facilitates cross-border electricity exchange. As Liberia’s electricity regulator, LERC plays a key role in promoting reliable supply, effective oversight and sustainable regional power trade.

During the meeting in the Main Conference Room, LERC and TRANSCO CLSG reaffirmed their commitment to expanding electricity trade and strengthening the reliability of the CLSG transmission network.

Participants reviewed system performance, commercial sustainability and deeper market integration. They noted that closer coordination among regulators, utilities and transmission operators is essential to address operational requirements and support future growth.

Both institutions identified reinforcement of the CLSG corridor as a priority as new generation projects emerge across the region. Commissioner Kamara encouraged greater knowledge sharing, targeted training, staff secondments and cooperation agreements with neighboring utilities to improve maintenance response and strengthen national capacity.

The parties also called for sustained capacity building, stronger donor coordination and accelerated studies and investment to reinforce the corridor. The visit reaffirmed their shared commitment to practical cooperation and dependable regional electricity trade.

Commissioner Kamara further emphasized the need for continued coordination between the two institutions to advance integration under the ECOWAS Regional Electricity Market.

World.title: Liberia: Water Advocacy Group Launched in Liberia
World.content:
MONROVIA – A new water advocacy group has been launched in Liberia, with a call on government to ensure the equitable and affordable provision of safe drinking water to citizens across the country.

By Obediah Johnson

The group named and styled Liberia Water Justice Forum was launched at the climax of a capacity building workshop held at the New Water in the Desert Apostolic Pentecostal Church in Brewerville, outside Monrovia.



The Forum was launched by Church Aid International (CAI, in collaboration with the Fellowship of Christian Councils and Churches in West Africa (FECCIWA) and Africa Water Justice Network based in Togo and Accra, Ghana respectively.

Speaking during the launch, CAI Chairman Bishop Kortu Brown disclosed that the Forum would advocate and ask hard questions surrounding access to water in Liberia.

He said those who would not listen and respond to inquiries being raised by others to address social and other challenges confronting Liberians, should not be leaders here.

“No matter how hard the questions are, we can find solutions to those hard questions. If you are leading people you must be ready to answer the hard questions. All those who are running away from the hard questions should not be leaders because leaders speak to the rock. You must find answers to the hard questions.”

Bishop Brown maintained that church and other religious leaders of the Liberia Council of Churches (LCC) must speak out and ask hard questions to find solutions to societal issues.

“We have to face the hard questions because if Moses does not speak to the rock, the water will not come. The are things that we God servants would like to pray Moses prayed and God said to find solution you have to speak to the rock.”

He said many leaders in Liberia get worrisome when asked the hard questions. He vowed that the church would not relent to continue to advocate for the supply of accessible and affordable safe drinking water to citizens across the country.

Bishop Brown noted that regardless of geographical locations or boundaries, all Liberians, especially women and children, should have access to water.

He called for concession companies operating in Liberia to pay fees for allegedly polluting rivers, creeks and other sources of water in their respective areas of operations.

He stressed that citizens in the leeward areas used the creeks and rivers to fetch water for drinking, cooking and other purposes and as such, these waters should not be polluted by mining companies.

“Where ever the difficulties are, we have to go there and speak. If you don’t know where the problem is, you can never find the solution. It is on this premise that I come to formally launch the Liberia Water Justice Forum.”

For his part, the Secretary General of the Liberia Council of Churches (LCC) Rev. Christopher Toe observed that though water covers a substantial percentage of the land space in Liberia, access to safe drinking water remains a challenge in households across the country.

He pointed out that the launch of the Forum is in promoting pillar six of the global Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), which amongst other things calls for the provision of clean water and sanitation.

He maintained that with 70% of the human body comprising of water, it (water) should always be a component of every human life.

Rev. Toe emphasized that church leaders have a roll to play towards ensuring that there is justice for water in the Liberian society.

“Water is life, water is dignity. Our land space gets so much water but yet still we don’t have water in our homes or access to water. I think this forum is a justice component of water. God gives us water to make use of it (water) so that it benefits you. There are many a lot of people who are getting rich out of water. In everything we do, the politicians are aware that the Church is the lead.”

He said through advocacy, the church should speak with one voice on the significance of access to water to citizens across the country.

“There is a conversation about the third land. On that third lane we must ensure that water is in all our homes. Anybody who will be on that third lane, you will have to take water as a priority.”

He cautioned against attacks and suppression of the Church by politicians in the country. Also speaking, the acting Secretary General of the Fellowship of Christian Councils and Churches in West Africa (FECCIWA) based in Lome, Togo, Mr. Michael Tettey, observed that access to water remains one of the biggest challenges on the African continent.

He said the idea of the Forum in Liberia was birthed in Benin a a result of expressed interest and willingness of Bishop Brown to drive the initiative.

He disclosed that it took just two months to plan and ensure that the Forum was established in Liberia to advocate justice for access to water in the country.

Mr. Tettey added that access or citizens’ right to affordable water remains critical to support development and social initiative for their well-being. He said Christians should advocate towards the promotion of good sanitation accountability.

Mr. Leonard S. Quartey, Coordinator of Africa Water Justice Network based in Accra, Ghana, commended CAI for leading the initiative. He pointed out that approximately 400million people on the African continent do not have access to safe drinking water.

He said with a very meager population of Liberian population having access to safe drinking water, the launch of the Forum would help raise awareness and advocate for the provision of safe drinking water to citizens.

“We are fighting against a system that wants to normalize the situation (of the lack of safe drinking water). Quartey said various water systems across the African continent should be improved for the betterment of the citizenry.

The capacity building workshop marking the launch of the Forum brought together participants and facilitators from Sierra Leone, Ghana, Togo, Guinea, amongst others.

World.title: Makembo backs Mufalali as Sports Minister
World.content:
Zambia Sports Fans Association (ZASPOFA) Chief Pastor Peter Makembo has welcomed the appointment of Senanga South Member of Parliament Likando Mufalali as Minister of Sports.

Mufalali was among several Ministers appointed and sworn in by President Hakainde Hichilema on Wednesday as a new Cabinet took shape after the 2026 General Elections.

He has succeeded Elvis Nkandu, who has been appointed Minister of Information and Media.

Speaking to Lusaka Times Sports, Makembo said he expects Mufalali to support all sports disciplines equally and fairly.

Makembo said Mufalali has the potential to excel as Minister of Youth and Sports.

“At last, we have been given the Minister of Sports. We say welcome to our newly appointed Minister of Sports Honourable Mufalali. We know the sports ground is fertile for success, and we need to maintain that” Makembo said.

“All sports disciplines need his guidance and support. Let’s move in a positive way as a sports fraternity in Zambia,” he said.

He called for support for Mufalali.

“I am confident our new Minister of Sports won’t find it difficult to operate and excel. As stakeholders in the sports fraternity, we need to give him the necessary support. Let’s give him the support we have been giving the previous Sports Ministers like Honourable Elvis Nkandu,” Makembo said.

Meanwhile, Mufalali officially reported for duty at the Ministry of Youth and Sports and was warmly welcomed by the management team, Heads of Departments and Units.

“I am grateful for the warm welcome and the thoughtful gesture from the staff, who marked the occasion with a cake-sharing ceremony,” Mufalali said.

“I look forward to working with the entire team to advance youth empowerment and sports development across the country,” he said after reporting for duty.

Mufalali is a business executive and computer technician by profession.

World.title: High Court Nullifies Mapatizya MP’s Election
World.content:
The Livingstone High Court has nullified the election of Mapatizya Constituency Member of Parliament, Emelda Munashabantu following a successful election petition over irregularities in the tallying and declaration of the August 13, 2026 parliamentary election results.

High Court Judge, Kazimbe Chenda ruled that the declaration of Ms Munashabantu as winner was premature because results from 10 of the constituency’s 74 polling stations had not been included when the returning officer announced the outcome.

In his judgment, Judge Chenda held that the irregularities in the post-voting electoral process were serious enough to have affected the outcome of the election.

“I therefore invoke sections 97(2) (b), 97(4) and 99(a) of the EPA, and hold that the election result for Mapatizya constituency, following voting on 13th August 2026, is void,” Judge Chenda ruled.

“Consequently, the declaration of the First Respondent as MP, made on 16th August 2026, is hereby nullified,” he added.

The court heard that Ms Munashabantu was declared winner with 14,812 votes against 14,330 votes for the petitioner, Clive Miyanda, giving her a margin of 482 votes.

However, Judge Chenda observed that the 10 polling stations whose results were not included had a combined potential vote of 6,238, a figure significantly higher than the margin between the two candidates.

The judge noted that the returning officer had acknowledged during his testimony that the electronic system could not close the results because the outstanding polling station results could potentially place the petitioner ahead of Ms Munashabantu.

“It was a serious irregularity and outright illegality for the returning officer to declare a parliamentary election winner in the absence of results from all 74 polling stations,” Judge Chenda stated.

He further held that electoral officials had a duty to ensure that the will of all voters who validly cast their ballots was reflected in the final result, adding that an agreement between parties could not be used to circumvent statutory electoral procedures.

The court, however, dismissed the allegation of misconduct against Ms Munashabantu, finding that no instance of misconduct had been proved against her.

“There is no instance of misconduct that has been proven against the First Respondent. It follows that the first ground of the petition lacks merit and is hereby dismissed,” the judge ruled.

Judge Chenda attributed the irregularities to the Electoral Commission of Zambia’s handling of the post-voting process, stating that the blame lay with the commission and the returning officer.

The court ordered the Electoral Commission of Zambia to bear the petitioner’s costs, to be taxed if not agreed upon.

Ms Munashabantu was spared from any costs burden arising from the commission’s actions, apart from her own costs.

The judgment rendered the declaration of Ms Munashabantu as Mapatizya Member of Parliament null and void.

World.title: Minister of Finance urges Ministers to defend the national budget
World.content:
Minister of Finance and National Planning Situmbeko Musokotwane has urged Ministers to fully understand and defend the National Budget in Parliament as it is a collective Cabinet position.

Dr Musokotwane said the budget to be presented in Parliament is not for the Minister of Finance alone but for the entire Cabinet, hence all Ministers must be ready to defend it.

He was speaking during a Budget Orientation Meeting for Ministers in Lusaka today ahead of the budget presentation next week and the Cabinet meeting to approve the budget tomorrow.

“That budget presentation is for Cabinet. The Minister of Finance is just the messenger, the deliverer. By the time we go to Parliament, we would have unified our positions. The debates and arguments remain in the Cabinet room in State House. What is delivered in Parliament is an agreed position,” he said.

Dr Musokotwane said once the budget is presented, the House will adjourn to allow committees to scrutinise the estimates, noting that the most critical debates take place in committees.

He said each Minister will be required to present their ministry’s budget to the relevant Parliamentary Committee and face rigorous questioning.

“These days, there is a lot of debate within the committees, infact, the most critical debate takes place in the committees. This is why we are having this orientation so that you get prepared,” he said.

“You must know your ministry’s budget from bottom to top, ask your Permanent Secretaries, your directors, to explain everything to you, because everything in the budget is subject to question, subject to challenge.”

Dr Musokotwane warned Ministers against treating the budget as the responsibility of chief accountants, stressing that the Minister is the person in charge and accountable.

He said Ministers should not go to Parliament to complain about being given too little or too much, as those arguments belong to the Cabinet room.

He further cautioned that there will be no additional funding to ministries after Cabinet approval tomorrow unless Cabinet directs otherwise, but Ministers can propose reallocations within their ceilings.

“If you feel that certain priorities are more important than those provided for, that is a discussion you can have with officials. When the time comes in Parliament, you can actually make a proposal for amendment to the Speaker,” he said.

The Minister of Finance emphasised the need for Ministers to understand government financial regulations on contracting and spending.

“Please pay careful attention to that. Otherwise people will be taken to court, people will be arrested because of ignoring what government regulations say in terms of how to spend money,” Dr Musokotwane warned.

He said the budget will outline revenue estimation, critical must-pay expenditures such as salaries, debt, social insurance and CDF, and the remaining resources available for other priorities.

Meanwhile, Secretary to Cabinet Patrick Kangwa said the national budget is more than a statement of revenue and expenditure but a principal instrument through which the government translates its policies and development aspirations into concrete programmes.

“The 2027 national budget is particularly important as it seeks to consolidate the gains made in restoring macroeconomic stability while shifting greater attention towards accelerating economic growth, increasing production, creating employment opportunities and transforming the livelihoods of our people,” he said.

He emphasised that while each Minister is responsible for a particular portfolio, the budget is a collective government undertaking and Ministers must appreciate the broader economic and fiscal considerations informing allocations.

Mr Kangwa pointed out that the orientation covers economic developments such as debt restructuring, macroeconomic objectives and outlook underpinning the 2027 budget, details of the budget framework and resource envelope, preparation of the Ninth National Development Plan, and public financial management.

He said annual budgets must be anchored in a coherent medium term development framework with clearly defined targets and stressed that achievement of objectives depends not only on allocation but on effective and transparent management of resources.

Government will present the 2027 National Budget to Parliament on Friday, 6th November 2026.

World.title: First Lady receives hospital beds, sewing machines
World.content:
First Lady Mutinta Hichilema has received 200 hospital beds from the Chinese Chamber of Commerce in Zambia (CCCZ) aimed at improving maternal health delivery in the country.

Mrs Hichilema also received 200 sewing machines meant to support women through skills empowerment.

Speaking when she received the donation in Lusaka today, Mrs Hichilema said the gesture will significantly contribute to improved health care service delivery as well as women empowerment through skills development.

Mrs Hichilema noted that the government remains committed to improving the lives of vulnerable communities through initiatives that support health care and economic empowerment adding that the donation is important as it supports such efforts.

She added that the hospital beds will help improve patient’s care comfort especially in health facilities that have not yet received such support.

“We are grateful for this donation as it will improve health care services especially in facilities that have not yet received such donations,’’ she said.

And on the 200 donated sewing machines, Mrs Hichilema noted that the machines will provide individuals and cooperatives with opportunities to develop skills and start small businesses which will help them earn income.

“This is more than just a present, they present hope, dignity and opportunity from people who benefit from them,’’ she said.

Mrs Hichilema further observed that improving the lives of people cannot rest on government alone adding that it requires strong partnership with organisations such as CCCZ which has helped reach more communities.

Speaking at the same event, Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation Permanent Secretary for International Relations and Cooperation, Etambuyu Gundersen, noted that the donation symbolises the warm relation that exists between Zambia and China.

Ms Gundersen noted that the relationship between the two countries borders on mutual respect on cooperation and shared aspirations for the wellbeing of the people.

She stated that the donation is more than friendship but an investment in human development, community empowerment and spirit of solidarity that binds the two nations together.

Ms Gundersen commended Mrs Hichilema for her unwavering commitment to developing initiatives that touch the lives of vulnerable and ordinary Zambians who will directly benefit from this donation.

Meanwhile, CCCZ President, Lie Tie, explained that the aim of the donation is to support women development and health in Zambia.

Mr Lie noted that the 200 beds will help improve maternal health for women before, during and after maternal births.

“Welcoming a new life should be a joyful experience, but safety remains our concern and it deceives our shared attention hence the donation,’’ he said.

Mr Lie noted that improving childbirth conditions and reducing maternal deaths requires sustained efforts by government and corporation partners.

And on the donated sewing machines, Mr Tie explained that the machines are aimed at supporting women economically for them to be independent and self-reliant through business support.

“This sewing machine is an important tool and can open another path to employment through entrepreneurship hence this donation,’’ he said.

World.title: Small holder farmer implored to embrace technology
World.content:
Small Scale Farmers Network has emphasised the vital need to enhance agricultural technology and support systems in the country.

This is in a move to drive growth and sustainability for smallholder farmers across the country.

Speaking in an exclusive interview with the media, Small Scale Farmers Network Chief Executive Officer Edward Nsama said while various government pronouncements have been made regarding agricultural transformation and the adoption of modern technology, continuous efforts are needed to ensure the initiatives directly benefit small scale farmers.

Mr Nsama said that among the core pillars advocated by the Small Scale Farmers Network is the pressing need for the government to focus intensely on modernizing equipment and technology for small scale farmers, moving beyond traditional methods like hand hoes and ox ploughs.

He pointed out that reliance on seasonal rainfall has become increasingly unreliable, making innovative approaches to irrigation essential for safeguarding food security.

“The only pure way of doing agriculture without disruption is by tapping from the groundwater,” Mr. Nsama stressed.

He recommended that farmers embrace borehole and irrigation systems powered by solar technology to navigate dry spells effectively.

Mr Nsama emphasised that policy implementation must remain a collaborative effort between the government and the farming community.

“Government formulates policies, but those policies should be centered at the people, the poor people or the small-scale farmers,” he said.

Mr Nsama added that the Small-Scale Farmers Network remains committed to encouraging grassroots participation so that agricultural policies translate into tangible resources, helping farmers transition from subsistence farming to medium and commercial scales.

World.title: President Hichilema implores newly appointed Ministers
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema has directed the newly sworn-in ministers of Transport and Logistics and Housing to accelerate infrastructure development and improve access to affordable housing.

Speaking during the swearing-in ceremony of Charles Milupi and Christopher Kalila, President Hichilema said the two ministries were critical institutions that will support the grow Zambia Agenda and should deliver tangible results.

He urged the two ministers to ensure that bureaucratic procedures did not delay the implementation of key infrastructure projects.

On transport and logistics, President Hichilema called for accelerated development of railway networks and economic corridors to facilitate the movement of goods, reduce pressure on roads and stimulate investment.

“We need to move beyond discussions about infrastructure projects and focus on implementation,” he said.

“These are functional areas for delivery, investment to fulfil the Grow Zambia Agenda,” Mr Hichilema said.

President also highlighted the importance of developing the Tanzania -Zambia Railways (TAZARA) and other rail links to facilitate the transportation of heavy cargo.

He said improved railway infrastructure would help reduce damage to roads caused by heavy vehicles while enhancing the efficiency of cargo transportation.

President Hichilema further called for progress on railway rehabilitation and the development of transport corridors, urging the new minister to work closely with relevant stakeholders to ensure that planned projects moved forward without unnecessary delays.

On housing, President Hichilema called for measures to address unplanned settlements and improve access to affordable homes.

He directed the Ministry of Housing to work with local authorities to ensure that residential areas were properly planned, with designated roads and appropriate infrastructure before construction began.

He said Zambia could not continue allowing settlements to develop without proper road networks and essential services, warning that such conditions could make it difficult for ambulances and garbage collection vehicles to access communities.

He said local authorities needed to ensure that new residential developments complied with planning standards and that existing settlements were progressively improved.

President Hichilema also called for standardised housing designs to help control construction costs and ensure that public resources were used efficiently.

He said government housing programmes should provide practical and affordable homes suited to the needs of public service workers and other citizens.

The President further called for improvements in housing finance and mortgage systems, saying properly structured housing schemes could allow public officers to access homes without having to spend excessive time overseeing construction.

Transport and Logistics Minister, Charles Milupi said transport was central to all economic activities and pledged his ministry’s commitment to advancing the objectives of the Grow Zambia Agenda by ensuring the efficient movement of goods and services.

Meanwhile, newly appointed Housing Minister, Dr Christopher Kalila thanked President Hakainde Hichilema for entrusting him with the role, describing housing as a key driver of economic development.

He said access to quality, affordable housing with essential amenities would enable communities to thrive.

World.title: HRC urges the public to report human rights violations
World.content:
The Human Rights Commission (HRC) Chairperson Pamela Sambo has urged members of the public to report alleged human rights violations to the Commission through its toll-free line 8181, following a review of 100 alleged human rights violation cases.

Dr Sambo says the Commission will continue pursuing remedies for individuals whose rights are allegedly violated and follow up on outstanding cases.

“The Commission will continue to pursue remedies in individual cases, follow up on outstanding matters and use findings to guide institutional engagement, monitoring and public reporting,” she said.

She was speaking during a press conference on the outcome of the Commission’s third cases review meeting held from October 27 to 28, 2026, at Sarovar Hotel.

Dr Sambo said the Commission has reviewed 100 alleged human rights violation cases involving law enforcement agencies, justice sector institutions and other public and private entities, highlighting that 66 had been resolved while 34 remained under active consideration.

Dr Sambo, however, has acknowledged that the review revealed persistent concerns over prolonged detention and delays in the administration of justice, with 83 cases relating to protection of the law and personal liberty.

Dr Sambo cited a case in which three people were detained at Shang’ombo Central Police for approximately one year and seven months before their first court appearance.

“The three remained in custody for a further two months and eight days after a court ordered their release because the prosecution had failed to serve the order on the detention facility,” she said.

Meanwhile, the Commission has identified barriers to accessing police bond citing the case of a convicted person who waited approximately four years for sentencing after committal to the High Court.

Dr Sambo has called on the Zambia Police Service to ensure that bond conditions do not unnecessarily restrict the rights of suspects.

She has also raised concern over the treatment of children in conflict with the law, citing eight cases allegedly handled contrary to the Children’s Code Act No. 12 of 2022.

She cited the case of a 14-year-old child in Choma who was detained for 54 days on allegations of theft, while two 17-year-olds in Namwala were held for 16 and 58 days, respectively.

Dr Sambo has called for sustained corrective action by institutions to address recurring human rights concerns.

She has urged members of the public to report alleged violations to the Commission through its toll-free line, 8181.

World.title: HH bans councils from allocating unplanned plots
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema has barred local authorities from allocating unplanned land, saying the practice has turned large parts of the country into shanty compounds. The President issued the directive at State House in Lusaka on Thursday while swearing in Lukulu South Member of Parliament Dr Christopher Kalila as Minister of Housing. He said all 116 councils must ensure that land set aside for housing is properly planned before any plot is handed out. Planned land, he said, must come with properly designed roads and clear standards for the houses to be built on it.

“We cannot continue allowing councils to allocate plots which are unplanned, essentially continuing building up shanty compounds, unplanned settlements. No,” President Hichilema said.

The President also ordered the construction of roads and drainage in existing residential areas that were developed without them. He said those areas must also be provided with water, sanitation and other basic amenities. The directive places the newly created Ministry of Housing at the centre of a push to bring order to how land is allocated and developed. It marks a break from a pattern in which residents build first and wait years for services to follow.

President Hichilema questioned why houses built for teachers, nurses and agricultural officers in rural areas were often bigger than necessary. He said the same resources could instead produce two smaller but decent units. They could also go into homes designed specifically for couples with children or for single officers. Once national housing standards are in place, he told the minister, the Government would be able to monitor and control construction costs with precision.

“Once we have the standards, minister, then we can monitor and control the cost of those houses because we know how many bricks or blocks go into that house,” he said.

On affordable housing, the President said Zambia’s mortgage system must become functional. He said public service workers spend a great deal of time at their construction sites, time they never account for at work. Under proper housing schemes backed by financing, he said, workers would no longer need to supervise their own plots. A worker would choose a house that meets the standards, a developer would build it and the worker would pay through a mortgage while remaining at their desk.

“The mortgage system must work,” President Hichilema said.

The President told Dr Kalila that his background as a medical doctor would not hold him back, saying a person with intellect could take on many tasks. He described the problems in the housing sector as basic matters that required practical solutions. Housing previously fell under the Ministry of Infrastructure, Housing and Urban Development. Its former minister, Charles Milupi, was sworn in at the same ceremony as Minister of Transport and Logistics.

The President has also turned his attention to land under traditional authority. During a courtesy call on Senior Chieftainess Nkomeshya Mukamambo II of the Soli people at her palace in Chongwe District, he committed the Government to resolving chiefdom boundary disputes dating back to the 1958 demarcation. The Senior Chieftainess raised the boundary question alongside the problem of her chiefdom falling under more than one council. She also cited the difficulties traditional leaders face in attending council meetings following the 2025 amendment to the Constitution.

“We have committed to resolving the boundary question, which affects many other chiefdoms as well,” President Hichilema said.

To ease the burden on chiefs, the President directed that traditional leaders whose chiefdoms straddle several districts should nominate proxies to attend council meetings on their behalf. He said the Government brought traditional leaders back into councils so they could contribute directly to the development of their areas. The proxy arrangement means chiefs can keep a voice in every council covering their land without attending each meeting in person. Senior Chieftainess Nkomeshya is a former Member of the Central Committee of UNIP and a former Member of Parliament for Chongwe.

Disorderly land allocation has long troubled local authorities. The Ministry of Lands and Natural Resources has in the past revoked the land agency of councils including Lusaka City Council, Kafue Town Council, Chongwe Municipal Council and Kitwe City Council over illegal allocation. Illegal allocation has often left more than one person claiming ownership of the same plot. Unplanned settlements also frequently lack roads, drainage, toilets and water, making it difficult for ambulances to reach residents during emergencies. Zambia’s housing deficit is estimated at 1.5 million units.

The directive comes as the Government pursues a national programme to regenerate cities. Vice-President W.K. Mutale Nalumango this week said the Government favours urban upgrading that improves living conditions in informal settlements without unnecessarily displacing residents. In a speech read on her behalf by Local Government and Rural Development Minister Gift Sialubalo at the National Urban Planning Conference, she said land was often occupied, subdivided or developed before planning frameworks and essential services were in place. She said the Grow Zambia Agenda depended on well-planned settlements, reliable infrastructure and access to markets.
