World.title: Ethiopia: As Tens of Thousands Flee Ethiopia to Kenya, UN Agency Warns of Growing Humanitarian Needs
World.content:
A map showing the location of Kenya (in orange) and Ethiopia (in green).

Geneva — The UN Refugee Agency (UNHCR) says humanitarian needs are growing in an unfolding crisis on the Kenya–Ethiopia border as ongoing clashes on the Ethiopian side have forced tens of thousands of people to cross into Kenya in search of safety.

Significant cross-border movements at Moyale have been reported since Oct. 22.

“According to local authorities, up to an estimated 50,000 people have crossed into Kenya,” said Fatima Mohammed-Cole, the UNHCR Representative in Kenya.

“The figure remains fluid as registration and verification efforts continue, amid reports of further crossings,” she said in a statement.



Many of those fleeing are women and children.

The UN official said that while some affected people are staying with relatives and in host communities, others have sought shelter in temporary locations such as schools and churches.

- FOOD: THE URGENT NEED

“Food remains the most urgent need, alongside safe drinking water, emergency shelter, sanitation and health care,” said Mohammed-Cole.

UNHCR has deployed an emergency team to Moyale and is working closely with the Kenyan government.

It is working alongside the UN migration agency, IOM; the UN children’s agency, UNICEF, the UN World Food Programme, the Kenya Red Cross Society, and other humanitarian partners, to support the national and local response.

UNHCR said it is mobilising emergency relief supplies, including essential household items and temporary shelter materials, to support nearly 12,000 people, with efforts underway to increase assistance as needs grow.

The agency is supporting ongoing assessments of protection and humanitarian needs.

“We are also working with the authorities and partners to identify safer accommodation options, further away from the border, for those fleeing violence,” the UNHCR official said.

According to Chatham House researchers, “Although Tigray has seen conflict before, this time there is a risk that hostilities could extend into Eritrea and Sudan,” they wrote.

World.title: Congo-Kinshasa: Global Nursing Head Flags Dangers of Misinformation After Killing of Congo Ebola Nurse
World.content:
A nurse prepares a bed for a suspected case of Ebola in the isolation unit at Bwera Hospital, Kasese District (file photo).

Geneva — The International Council of Nurses (ICN) head has warned of the lethal dangers that misinformation poses to the nursing profession following the killing of a nurse in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), who was responding to an Ebola case.

ICN chief executive Howard Catton said the “tragic news” was a reminder that prevalent misinformation was particularly dangerous for healthcare staff after young men armed with machetes killed the nurse.

“Health misinformation and the breakdown of trust in science is now a deadly risk for nurses and health workers,” Catton posted on the media platform X on Oct. 29.

The UN’s Ebola coordinator and the head of the World Health Organization (WHO) on Oct. 29 deplored the killing of the nurse working to fight the disease in the DRC four days earlier.



In an interview with AllAfrica, Catton also warned that community health workers often supplant nurses and may be seen as an easy, cheap substitute for a skilled nursing workforce in parts of Africa.

“There is both the migration of registered nurses from the continent of Africa and unemployment of nurses in Africa,” said Catton.

“So, as we see this growth in community health workers, we also know that registered nurses continue to leave Africa for high-income countries in Europe or North America.”

At the same time, many nurses on the continent remain unemployed.

Catton cited UN figures showing Africa’s health workforce grew to 5.72 million in 2024, up from 4.3 million in 2018, noting that such progress is not keeping pace with demand.

ONLY 46 PERCENT OF WORKFORCE NEEDS

“The African region currently has only 46 percent of the health workers it needs,” said the head of the international nursing group.

Catton visited African countries last year, and some leaders said what is happening is making it harder for them to improve their healthcare systems.

“To us, this is starting to feel like a form of neo-colonialism because we're having valuable resources which are being taken; we're not being adequately compensated for them,” said the nursing head, conveying the sentiment some African leaders expressed to him.

The WHO's Africa 2026 report says an estimated 943,000 trained health workers across the African region were unemployed in 2024.

That is, as the continent faces severe staffing shortages and meets only 46 per cent of its overall health workforce needs.

“We are training more health workers than ever before, yet too many remain unemployed while millions go without care,” said Dr Mohamed Yakub Janabi, the WHO regional director for Africa.

Close 

“Without bold investment and coordinated reform to plan, train and retain health workers, progress toward universal health coverage will remain out of reach,” said Dr Janabi, speaking in Ghana in May.

The WHO estimates a global shortage of at least ten million healthcare workers by 2030, and some organizations project an even larger shortfall, writes Pooja Kumar, a global leader at the McKinsey Health Institute.

She notes, though, that the global healthcare workforce shortage is not evenly distributed.

“For example,” Pooja says, “Africa has 17 percent of the world’s population but accounts for 52 percent of the global shortage.”

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - October 30, 2026
World.content:
Rwandan Man Convicted in U.S. for Lying About 1994 Genocide Role

A Rwandan man, Eric Nshimiye, has been convicted in the United States of perjury and obstruction of justice after lying under oath about his involvement in the 1994 Rwandan genocide. A federal jury in Boston found that Nshimiye concealed his alleged participation in attacks against the Tutsi community while testifying in the 2019 immigration fraud trial of his former university classmate, Jean Leonard Teganya. Nshimiye fled Rwanda for Kenya in 1994 and was admitted to the U.S. as a refugee the following year. Evidence presented at his trial showed that, while a student at the University of Rwanda in Butare, he took part in attacks on the Tutsi people, including by striking them on the head with a club. Nshimiye faces up to five years in prison for each of four perjury counts and up to 10 years for obstruction of justice. He is expected to be sentenced on 26 January 2027.

Tinubu Heads to Saudi Arabia to Pray for Nigeria



Nigerian President Bola Tinubu has travelled to Saudi Arabia to perform the lesser Hajj pilgrimage, known as Umrah, where he is expected to pray for Nigeria's peace, unity and stability. The presidency said that the visit will provide an opportunity for spiritual reflection and prayers for the country's continued progress. Tinubu's trip comes as Nigeria prepares for general elections, with insecurity and economic challenges expected to dominate the campaign. His media aide has dismissed speculation that the visit is intended for medical checks, insisting that it is a religious journey. The next elections are scheduled for 16 January 2027. Tinubu's main challengers will again be former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar and former Anambra State Governor Peter Obi.

U.S. Seizes $750,000 in Kenyan-Linked Student Aid Fraud Probe

US authorities have seized more than $750,000 in cryptocurrency linked to an alleged international student financial aid fraud scheme involving Kenyan nationals. The seizure forms part of Operation Ghostbusters, an investigation into a network accused of using stolen American identities to submit fraudulent student aid applications and divert millions of dollars in grants and loan refunds. The US Justice Department has charged five defendants, with investigators alleging that Kenyan-based conspirators worked with individuals in the US to transfer proceeds through bank accounts and overseas networks. Authorities said that the wider investigation has identified more than $32 million in losses. Cooperation with Kenyan law enforcement agencies is continuing to trace funds and pursue suspects.

Rights Group Urges Mali to Release Missing Junta Critic and Son

Human Rights Watch has called on Mali's military authorities to disclose the whereabouts of former government minister and junta critic Mountaga Tall and his son, Cheick Mamadou Tall, six months after their abductions. Unidentified gunmen reportedly seized Mountaga in Bamako on 2 May. His son disappeared two weeks later after being told he could deliver belongings to his father. Their whereabouts and condition remain unknown, with authorities yet to acknowledge detaining them. Human Rights Watch said that the disappearances reflect a wider crackdown on political opposition and dissent under Mali's military junta. He urged authorities to ensure their safety and release them.

Sudan Accuses Ethiopia of Backing Drone Attacks

Sudanese authorities claim that 162 drone attacks launched from Ethiopian territory have killed more than 400 civilians and 102 military personnel, amid allegations that Ethiopia is supporting the Rapid Support Forces (RSF). Officials said that the attacks have targeted several locations across Sudan, destroying schools, hospitals, health centres and fuel stations. However, the claims have not been independently verified. Sudan has accused Ethiopia of allowing drones to operate from bases near its border. He warned that the attacks threaten regional stability and efforts to enable displaced people to return home. Ethiopia has previously rejected allegations of supporting the RSF, describing them as unfounded. Sudan's Defence Minister has also accused more than 20 countries of providing the paramilitary group with logistical support, funding, mercenaries and drones.

Close 

Guinea-Bissau Busts Trafficking Ring Behind Fake Migration Scheme



Police in Guinea-Bissau have dismantled an alleged human trafficking network that lured approximately 70 people from across West Africa with promises of employment and opportunities to migrate to Europe. More than five suspects have been arrested following an operation on 21 October. Authorities allege that victims from countries including Mali, Sierra Leone, Guinea, Senegal and Côte d'Ivoire were defrauded, held against their will and pressured into recruiting others into fraudulent pyramid schemes. Some women were reportedly threatened with sexual exploitation and prostitution. Victims have been rescued; however, many remain stranded in Guinea-Bissau because they cannot afford to return home. Human rights organisations have raised concerns about inadequate shelters, psychological support, and financial assistance for survivors.

World.content:
Seemingly every other game in the NFL these days, there's a scary injury that requires transportation and tests at the hospital. Just in the past few weeks, Jalen Hurts' blood clots and Terry McLaurin's awful leg injury were major stories around the league.

During Thursday night's game, that injury went to Green Bay Packers star wide receiver Christian Watson. On a play that also hurt a defensive back.

Watson was in the middle of a huge night against the Carolina Panthers at Lambeau Field, racking up six catches for 100 receiving yards in the first half. His big play came when he brought in a 53-yard catch on a deep ball from Jordan Love about midway through the second quarter, setting the Packers up in great field position as they drove down for another score.

But he hit the ground hard while colliding with Panthers cornerback Will Lee III, and was slow to get up. Lee himself also had to be helped to his feet thanks to a hamstring injury, eventually needing the cart to leave the field.

Multiple customers at a Chili's Grill & Bar reported experiencing chemical burns Wednesday after consuming margaritas that had been prepared with an industrial cleaning chemical that was mistaken for sugar or salt.

According to preliminary findings, the mix-up began Monday when an employee received an industrial degreaser from a contracted worker and placed it in an unmarked container.

The container was then brought inside the restaurant and left in the bar area.

Two days later, an employee preparing the bar for lunch service discovered the unlabeled container and, believing its contents to be sugar or salt, used the chemical to prepare the margarita station, the health district said.

Shortly after the restaurant opened, three customers consumed the contaminated beverages and "immediately experienced discomfort and chemical burns in and around their mouths."

After the customers alerted staff, two employees also tasted the substance and reported similar symptoms.

CHILI'S REVIVES ICONIC RED BOOTHS AND CLASSIC DESIGN IN NATIONWIDE RESTAURANT OVERHAUL

In a statement to Fox News Digital, Chili's said the company took immediate action to support those affected.

"We are aware of an isolated incident at our restaurant in Forest City, North Carolina that resulted in injuries to two of our guests and Team Members. Our team took immediate action to support those affected and avoid any further injuries. We are actively investigating the circumstances related to this incident as the health and wellbeing of our guests and Team Members remain our top priority," the company said.

The company’s account differed from the Foothills Health District’s preliminary findings, which said three customers experienced chemical burns after consuming the margaritas.

After the Foothills Health District launched an investigation, the restaurant's food service permit was immediately suspended.

It was quickly reinstated on Thursday after specialists determined the restaurant met all other food safety standards.

World.title: June Jones, former Hawai'i and Atlanta Falcons head coach, dead at 73
World.content:
June Jones, a longtime football coach who made an impact at the college level, died at the age of 73 on Thursday.

Jones was placed in hospice care two weeks ago, as he’s dealt with health issues earlier this year, per the Honolulu Star-Advertiser.

The University of Hawai’i, where Jones served as head coach from 1999-2007 after playing quarterback for the Rainbow Warriors, confirmed his death.

Timmy Chang, Hawai’i’s current head coach, became the NCAA’s all-time passing yards leader under the tutelage of Jones. He said "words can’t express the sorrow" he feels learning of his old coach’s passing.

"Coach Jones was a father figure, a mentor, and a visionary who revolutionized the game," Chang said in a statement, per ESPN. "He believed in a young kid from Hawai’i and gave me the opportunity of a lifetime to run his offense. And his impact didn’t stop when my playing days ended. He guided me every step of the way as I transitioned into coaching, always making time to share his wisdom and support me when I took over this program.

"He put Hawai'i football on the map and showed us all what was possible. We lost a true legend today, but I will spend the rest of my career trying to honor his legacy, his passion for this university and the Aloha he shared with everyone he touched. My deepest condolences go out to his 'ohana and all those who he impacted."

After playing college ball at Hawai’i, Portland State and Oregon, Jones signed as an undrafted free agent with the Atlanta Falcons, whom he spent four seasons with, backing up quarterback Steve Bartkowski. He started five games in his NFL career, winning just one.

Jones’ coaching career began right after his playing days were over. He eventually worked his way to become the Falcons’ head coach from 1994-96, and he would be named the interim head coach of the San Diego Chargers in 1998.

He had an opportunity to remain in place, but he decided to head back to Hawai’i to become its head coach. Jones led the Rainbow Warriors to conference titles in 1999 and 2007, the latter season being a historic one.

World.title: A ghost story in the nation's Capitol
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

They always ask if I felt something. "Across your foot? Your shin?" My shin?

"Yeah. Your ankle. Did you feel it?" Not really. But before I respond, they ask again.

What was it like?" they inquired. "Or did you just fall?" Then they speculated I might be clumsy.

Hmmph. Clumsy. I truly don’t think so.

REPORTER'S NOTEBOOK: CONGRESS BRACES FOR POST-ELECTION GAME OF MUSICAL CHAIRS AS LEADERSHIP BATTLES LOOM

Oh. I fall like everyone else. I work out daily. I’ve taken a couple of tumbles on predawn runs in Alexandria, Virginia. You never know when one of those sidewalk snakes will slither up from the asphalt and nip you on the ankle. I used to snow ski. I studied martial arts for years and hold a second degree black belt.

Clumsy? Nah.

"But, what do you think it was?" they follow up. Well, I have my theories.

I was a little tired that day. I noted the lip on the small staircase near the Memorial Door of the U.S. Capitol where I may have caught the edge of my brown loafers.

I remember my shoes. Rubber soles. Slight scuff on the toes. Perfectly matched with my crisp tan summer suit. Not quite an "Obama" tan suit. But appropriate for summer. And I thought at least reasonably dapper for traipsing around the U.S. Capitol and covering Congress on a sweltering July day.

Was it the shoes? My fatigue? Or how about my haste to "get the story." I spotted then-Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau and his small coterie of aides and a security detail descending a spiral staircase after a meeting with then-House Speaker Nancy Pelosi. D-Calif.

I would try to ask Trudeau a question.

No. This really doesn’t have anything to do with Trudeau. Or the fact that I recalled that there was a picture of him, aged about 14 or 15, at Olympic Stadium in Montreal, rooting for the Expos. He’s there with his father — the most storied of all Canadian prime ministers — the late Pierre Trudeau.

Of course, the Expos no longer play in Montreal. They don’t play at all. They moved to Washington in 2005 and are now the Nationals. And this was before the tariff wars. Montreal has been bereft of Major League Baseball ever since.

What would Youppi! Say?

Look him up, kids.

No, there wasn’t something across my shin or ankle. I didn’t feel anything. I was there, on those steps, in the U.S. Capitol, because I’m a baseball fan. And I found out that Justin Trudeau watched those old Montreal Expos teams in the 1980s. Stocked with Andre Dawson, Warren Cromartie and Steve Rogers. And even though Trudeau was there to discuss affairs of state with Pelosi and others, I was there to ask him about the national pastime.

Ironic, I know, to pose such an interrogative to a Canadian.

However, the reason was that there was a report that the Tampa Bay Rays might consider splitting their season each year between Florida and Montreal. Big league baseball would return to Quebec. It would be international news if Trudeau commented. It would appear on Fox. FS1. ESPN. TSN in Canada. And Montreal — famously robbed of perhaps winning the World Series in 1994 with the best team in the game that year because of the player’s strike — might have a shot again at baseball glory.

But journalism is like baseball. A game of failure. You sometimes swing and miss. You’re doing great if you’re successful three out of ten times.

THE HITCHHIKER'S GUIDE TO WHY REMOVING ILHAN OMAR FROM CONGRESS COULD BE HARDER THAN TRUMP EXPECTS

And sometimes, in journalism, the question is never asked.

That was this day. On those steps. Questions about the Rays and Montreal were muted. All because of whatever got me.

Absolutely got me.

I stepped toward Trudeau, mumbled something about Tampa Bay and bought it.

I fell on those steps. Directly in front of the Canadian Prime Minister. On the hard Capitol marble.

I quickly realized I was about to fall. With a microphone in one hand, I couldn’t catch myself. I was confident I’d break a wrist or a hand if I tried to catch myself.

So, I just went with it and fell.

And because I studied martial arts for all of those years from Master Kim and Master Yang back at the Tae Kwon Do dojang, I knew how to fall without hurting myself.

I rolled onto my right shoulder toward Trudeau.

My feeling flew up absurdly high in the air.

"Oh Chad! Oh Chad! Oh Chad!" hollered my photographer, Robert Fetzer. "Chad!"

Trudeau stopped briefly. But I leaped to my feet after the roll, hoping he might say something about baseball.

I struck out. And Trudeau departed.

"But what tripped you?" they ask. "Were you all right?"

Physically, I was fine. Mentally, kind of garbled. I’ve worked daily at the U.S. Capitol for decades. I had a sneaking suspicion of what got me. Or better yet, who?

In the latter years of the 19th Century, Rep. William Taulbee, D-Ky., did not get along with reporter Charles Kincaid. Taulbee thought Kincaid wasn’t an honest broker, writing screeds about his personal affairs.

Taulbee was tall, towering over the diminutive Kincaid. Taulbee was known to sometimes physically pummel Kincaid.

Taulbee was out of federal office. But Kincaid knew Taulbee would be at the Capitol. Kincaid packed a pistol with him. And on Feb. 28, 1890, the reporter shot the Bluegrass Congressman square in the eye.

Taulbee leaked blood all the way down the House’s "Y" staircase, the plasma blending with marble. Through a miracle of chemistry, the splotches are still visible today.

The Kentucky Democrat succumbed to his injuries 11 days later.

It probably goes without saying that Taulbee does not like the congressional press corps. And, so, his phantasm is known to lurk around the Capitol.

Sometimes low bridging reporters on ornate staircases.

"What tripped you?" they ask.

CLICK HERE TO GET THE FOX NEWS APP

And before I can answer, my inquisitors jump to a conclusion, albeit an interrogative one.

"Was it a ghost?" they giddily exclaim, like they had just figured out Final Jeopardy.

As I say, I have my theories. I’ll let you come to your own conclusions.

But I don’t want to trip you up.

World.title: Criminal probe launched into alleged noncitizen voting in California
World.content:
The Justice Department has opened a criminal investigation in California as it continues its effort to prove that as many as 20,000 noncitizens are on the state’s voter rolls, a U.S. official confirmed to NBC News on Thursday.

The official said the Justice Department has issued federal grand jury subpoenas to local election officials across the state. It’s unclear how many subpoenas were sent out and exactly who received them.

The New York Times first reported the new subpoenas.

In response to an inquiry from NBC News on Thursday, the Justice Department declined to comment on “leaks about alleged grand jury subpoenas” but said federal courts have said voting unlawfully results in criminal exposure.

The U.S. official told NBC News that receiving a subpoena doesn’t mean a person is necessarily a target, just that the person may have information relevant to the investigation. The official added that the Justice Department rarely subpoenas people it intends to charge with crimes.

The new subpoenas follow a federal judge’s ruling Wednesday to deny the Trump administration’s request to segregate 20,000 mail ballots from alleged noncitizens in California, calling into question the accuracy of the administration’s process to identify such people.

Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder and County Clerk Dean Logan touted the decision Thursday.

“At every step, the U.S. Department of Justice has taken a confrontational, adversarial approach. Election officials are acting in accordance with state and federal law,” Logan said in a statement, adding that “clear court rulings” by both the federal judge and an appeals court have confirmed that.

Last week, Justice Department officials sent letters to 57 of California’s 58 counties warning local election officials to cooperate with federal investigations into illegal voting or face investigations themselves.

The Justice Department expanded the efforts this week, sending similar letters to officials in Washington state and asking its secretary of state to review a list of 400 registrants whom it believes to be noncitizens. It also asked that the state sequester any ballots those people cast.

The Trump administration faced two legal setbacks in the efforts this week when an appeals court denied its request Monday to block California from counting mail ballots from the alleged noncitizens and a federal judge Wednesday rejected its request to segregate those ballots.

The Trump administration has pressured state officials to assist in investigations of allegations of voter fraud for months, having sued 30 states and the District of Columbia for refusing to hand over their voter registration list data.

While noncitizens can appear on voter rolls, it is rare. In addition, newly naturalized citizens are often mistakenly flagged as noncitizens, especially since there is no comprehensive list of U.S. citizens.

Election experts have argued that the Trump administration’s lawsuits rely on flimsy legal arguments, particularly as the Justice Department doesn’t have legal authority to intervene in election certification.

World.title: Vivek Ramaswamy’s attack ad against Amy Acton’s ends TV run
World.content:
Republican Vivek Ramaswamy’s ad featuring the estranged mother of Amy Acton, his Democratic opponent for Ohio governor, is leaving the state’s airwaves, the Ramaswamy campaign confirmed Thursday.

The ad, which debuted last week to wide bipartisan condemnation, is rotating out after completing its intended run, according to the campaign. The campaign has other ads running in the final days of the race.

In the now-completed ad campaign, Donna Arthur — the mother whom Acton says she has not seen since her then-stepfather was charged with raping her as a young child nearly 50 years ago — calls her daughter a liar and urges Ohioans not to vote for her. The ad does not address details of the rape case. But critics panned the Ramaswamy campaign’s decision to use Arthur as a character witness and dredge up painful family history.

“I’m learning things even about my childhood right now that I did not know,” Acton told reporters Tuesday during a campaign stop in Youngstown. “I think it is despicable. … I’m sure someday I’ll unpack everything that I’m learning here. But I’m just grateful to Ohioans and everyone, really so much support and love that we’ve received.”

The Ramaswamy campaign said last week that the ad would be backed by $4 million in airtime. It began as a minutelong spot but was eventually shortened to a 30-second version. Many, including term-limited Gov. Mike DeWine, a Republican who has endorsed Ramaswamy, had called on him to take down the ad.

“Vivek Ramaswamy should never have run his despicable ad in the first place, and it’s totally unsurprising that he took it off the air in the most cowardly way possible, without even the hint of an apology to Dr. Acton, her family, or to the people of Ohio,” Acton campaign spokesperson Addie Bullock said in a statement Thursday.

The Columbus Dispatch first reported that the ad was ending its run.

“It ran to completion, and we’ve put up four other ads,” Ramaswamy said at a Thursday campaign stop, according to the newspaper.

World.title: Israel’s final election results show neither Netanyahu nor rival can immediately form government
World.content:
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s right-wing bloc won 53 seats in Israel’s 120-member Knesset, or parliament, results released by election officials on Thursday showed, well below the 68 it had controlled at its peak in the previous parliament.

The bloc supporting Netanyahu’s main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, won 48 seats in an extremely tight election race, meaning neither secured the 61 seats needed to form a government.

The count is complete, but the results still need to be certified and submitted to President Isaac Herzog next Wednesday.

Herzog will then consult with party chairs and choose a candidate ⁠who he thinks has the best chance to form a government.

Yashar Party leader Gadi Eisenkot at a polling station in Herzliya on Tuesday. Amir Levy / Getty

Parties led by Israel’s Arab minority made historic gains, winning a combined 19 seats in a race in which Palestinians with Israeli citizenship headed to the polls in record numbers Tuesday, many hoping to oust Netanyahu and far-right members of his coalition, including Bezalel Smotrich, his finance minister, and National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir.

Both leading blocs have ruled out the possibility of forming a government with the two main Arab parties, Ra’am and the Joint List. But their rise as potential kingmakers has brought the complex realities faced by Palestinian Israeli nationals into fresh focus.

Ahead of the election, Netanyahu and other members of his coalition amplified allegations of foreign election interference, referring Arab parties to the domestic security service, the Shin Bet, for investigation over allegations of Qatari intervention.

Ra'am party leader Mansour Abbas votes Tuesday with his family in Maghar. Mahmoud Illean / AP

Qatar denied the allegations. Mansour Abbas, the head of Ra’am, said his party had “no connection” to such conduct and urged a full investigation. He also accused Netanyahu of a “campaign of incitement and delegitimization” against Arab citizens.

Dean Livne, the acting director general of Israel’s Central Elections Committee, said in a published letter sent to a member of parliament that there was “no basis for allegations of systematic violations of electoral integrity.”

Before the election, both Netanyahu and Eisenkot ruled out forming a government with the Arab parties.

Yair Golan, the leader of Israel’s Democrats. Gil Cohen-Magen / picture alliance via Getty

But Yair Golan, the head of the smaller left-wing Democrats party, called for a government formed “in partnership” with Arab parties. “We must no longer accept Netanyahu’s racist division between Jewish votes and Arab votes,” he said Wednesday on X.

The majority of Palestinians with Israeli citizenship are the descendants of those who remained within what became Israel during the war that led to the country’s founding in 1948. At the time, hundreds of thousands more fled or were expelled from their homes.

World.title: Binance targeted in $6.3 billion crypto heist, the largest ever
World.content:
The digital currency exchange Binance says it was the target of a $6.3 billion crypto heist Thursday, believed to be the largest ever recorded.

The company has suspended all deposits and withdrawals while it works with law enforcement to secure its infrastructure and locate stolen funds.

The hack originated from a compromised laptop, it said, which allowed “an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions.”

“The estimated total impact sits at around $6.3B,” Binance said late Thursday on X.

About $3 billion of crypto assets that transited through wallets connected to the hackers have so far been identified and frozen, the company said.

Binance will “cover all losses” from the hack, it said, adding, “User funds are safe.”

“We are working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of these criminals and bring them to justice,” it said.

Binance is the world’s largest cryptocurrency trading platform by volume, with hundreds of thousands of users who buy, sell and store billions of dollars’ worth of digital currencies on the exchange.

Unlike traditional bank deposits, funds kept in accounts with companies like Binance are not automatically insured against losses, potentially leaving any refunds up to the discretion of individual exchanges.

The previous record for a crypto heist was $1.5 billion that hackers from North Korea stole from Bybit in February 2025.

Binance cautioned that the full value of assets affected by the hack, as well as assets recovered or frozen, could change.

“This figure may continue to increase as our teams work closely with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace and freeze additional assets,” it said.

As word of the hack spread online Thursday, major cryptocurrencies traded lower. Bitcoin was down about 4.3%, while Ethereum lost 4.6% of its value.

Two major stablecoin issuers, Tether and Circle, said they had identified billions of dollars in assets connected to the hackers and had frozen them.

Tether froze more than $1.567 billion worth of its digital currency, CEO Paolo Ardoino said on X.

Jeremy Allaire, CEO of stablecoin issuer Circle, said the company had also frozen hundreds of millions of dollars of assets and was coordinating with law enforcement.

The massive breach of Binance occurs at a moment when cybersecurity defenses around the world are on high alert about the possibility of novel attacks facilitated by recent advances in artificial intelligence.

Digital currency has been a primary target of hackers for years. In 2025, Coinbase disclosed that thieves had stolen customers’ personal information and tried to extort the company for $20 million. Coinbase refused to pay and offered a bounty for information leading to arrests, instead.

Binance’s founder, Changpeng Zhao, said, “As a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered.”

Zhao stepped down as the CEO of Binance in 2023 and pleaded guilty to breaking U.S. anti-money-laundering laws. President Donald Trump later granted him a full pardon.

World.title: The former youth pastor leading one of the NFL’s best offenses
World.content:
When Nate Scheelhaase was promoted to offensive coordinator of the Los Angeles Rams last winter, he stepped into one of the NFL’s most auspicious jobs, and for a Super Bowl contender, no less.

Not bad for a former youth pastor.

Fresh out of college, Scheelhaase moved to Louisville, Kentucky, in 2014 to work with teenagers at Southeast Christian Church, one of the largest megachurches in the U.S. During that time, he regularly stopped by a few dozen high schools to visit with students. For two high schools’ football teams, he volunteered as a chaplain. The role entailed building trust, finding common ground and helping those he spoke with work for something bigger than themselves.

“An impactful year,” said Scheelhaase, 35.

It wasn’t the typical starting point for a career in coaching — because even though Scheelhaase had been a four-year starting quarterback at Illinois, he wasn’t initially interested in that career path at all.

Without intending to, though, Scheelhaase honed skills while he was a youth pastor that he says helped him rise quickly within the coaching industry.

“I would say that there’s a lot of carryover,” Scheelhaase said in an interview. “From a ministry standpoint, just being around people from all different walks of life, different journeys, being able to meet them where they’re at — that’s also a football locker room. That’s a staff locker room.”

Los Angeles Rams offensive coordinator Nate Scheelhaase during training camp at Loyola Marymount University this summer. Ric Tapia / Getty

The growth of sports in the U.S. is often a story of their crossover with faith. James Naismith, basketball’s inventor, is said to have believed he could better embody what it meant to be a Christian using sports than the pulpit. Many of football’s conventions, including the huddle, numbered jerseys and padded goalposts, came from Amos Alonzo Stagg, who had gone to Yale to study divinity and began coaching to fulfill a vision of “muscular Christianity.”

Careers in sports have often led to careers in religious roles. Rocky Seto won national championships at the University of Southern California and a Super Bowl with the Seattle Seahawks during 16 years on Pete Carroll’s coaching staffs. In Seattle, Seto’s role eventually evolved to include a weekly address delivered in front of the entire roster and staff. He obsessively prepared his material.

“How am I going to capture the whole room?” Seto said. “It’s basically convincing them that if you learn this, this is going to help us win, help us be better.”

That experience made him feel prepared to give his first sermon. It was 2017, and Seto had just left the Seahawks to become the pastor-in-waiting at Evergreen Baptist Church, in suburban Los Angeles. Standing in front of another packed room of congregants, Seto felt his new job’s mission mirrored that of his last one — to deliver hope.

“You come to church in some ways to take a peek into heaven for a moment, and then we break. It’s like a huddle, and then we break out to basically fulfill the Great Commission outside this building, right?” he said. “And so coaching is no different. The information has to be almost like, ‘This is the greatest thing you need to know.’”

As Scheelhaase’s career was ending in late 2013, all he knew was that he didn’t envision a future in coaching.

He had gotten married a few months earlier, and he had seen enough coaches get fired and hired to question raising a family in an industry with fleeting job security and a nomadic career path. Meetings with Illini alumni in corporate jobs in Chicago also failed to inspire him. Unsure what to do, Scheelhaase called Jason Epperson, a local pastor who served as Illinois football’s team chaplain.

Scheelhaase was a four-year starting quarterback at the University of Illinois. Michael Hickey / Getty

Epperson had just taken a job at Southeast in Louisville, where there was a youth pastor role open. The idea intrigued Scheelhaase, who had grown up outside Kansas City, Missouri, as a devout Christian. When he arrived at Southeast in early 2014, he was trying “to figure out different ways to just connect with people in the area and show them that I was interested in just who they were more than just what they were doing,” Scheelhaase said. “Which I think is always a good spot to start.”

Chris Burke, an ESPN baseball analyst who lived in the area, first noticed Scheelhaase because of his athleticism during pickup games inside Southeast’s gym. Other things about Scheelhaase soon stood out, too.

“He looked perfectly suited for that job,” Burke said. “You can tell he got a kick out of being around young people. He communicated well with them. He had the patience.”

When a local mother told Scheelhaase that her eighth grade son’s father had recently died and that she needed others to be there for her son, Scheelhaase gave him rides and went to practices. The son was Nate Hobbs, the future San Francisco 49ers defensive back whom Scheelhaase still describes as one of his closest friends.

Scheelhaase stopped by Trinity High School, a local powerhouse, with a “confident humility,” said Andrew Coverdale, Trinity’s offensive coordinator at the time, who is now the passing game coordinator at Kentucky. Scheelhaase didn’t expect students to listen to him just because he had been a college quarterback.

“As somebody who taught in high school for a long, long time, I can’t really emphasize enough that kids need every form of mentorship and positive adult presence they can have, because it is brutal to be a teenage kid right now,” Coverdale said. High schoolers are “just dealing with so much and carrying so much. And so I just think having a guy like that around that you can talk to, who has life experience that he’s willing to share in a really winsome way, it was just great.”

Scheelhaase spent a relatively brief year and a half in Louisville, but he said that time shaped him immeasurably. Scheelhaase, who now has three children, said spending time around church leaders and attendees gave him role models for how he wanted to act as a husband and a father. It also changed his career path.

While he was leading a chapel service for football players at Eastern High School in 2014, he gave what he thought was a compelling, relatable speech that pulled in his athletic background and life story. It was received, he said with a smile, by proverbial crickets.

Taking a seat, he was stunned to see the reaction when the school’s head coach stood up to deliver his own pregame speech.

“Everybody was on the edge of their seat,” Scheelhaase said. “And in that moment, I thought, man, there is a cool ability to impact as a coach. And it was probably the thing that triggered the thought of, man, what would it look like to be able to impact in that way and influence in that way.”

Scheelhaase celebrates against the Buffalo Bills at SoFi Stadium near Los Angeles on Oct. 12. Katelyn Mulcahy / Getty

By the start of the 2015 football season, Scheelhaase was at Illinois coaching running backs. Technically, he was new to the profession. Yet recruiting players to campus and developing them once they were on the roster didn’t feel any different, at its core, from how he’d worked to build trust in Louisville.

“You are going to ask people to do really hard things as a coach, things that are counterintuitive to what you want to do,” he said. “Stand in a pocket where you know somebody’s going to hit you in the side of your helmet. To be somebody who loves to catch the football, but you got to go and block. To be somebody that’s willing to do the dirty work, and you’re going to ask them to do it, and the only way I know how to do that is to connect with them on a deep level. They know I not only understand what we’re asking them to do, but I care and I see them in that. And so connection, fortunately for me, it’s how I’m wired. That’s the part I enjoy the most about my job. ...

“And there probably is an element of that’s what I enjoyed even about the job as a high school pastor in Louisville, too, is just connecting with people and seeing there’s oftentimes more common ground than you think.”

In 2023, he became a coordinator at Iowa State. A year later, he left to become an offensive assistant for Sean McVay and the Rams, which to some may have seemed like a backward step; his job revolved around using software to manually draw the plays McVay wanted called each week. In the NFL, however, just being around McVay is a career springboard: The last four Rams offensive coordinators are now head coaches, and Zac Taylor was drawing McVay’s plays before Cincinnati hired him as its head coach. In 2025, a full year before Scheelhaase’s promotion to Rams offensive coordinator, McVay had called him “a special coach” and “a rising star, without a doubt.”

Last winter, as Scheelhaase was interviewing for NFL head coaching jobs, he called interim Stanford coach Frank Reich to ask about the school’s opening. The two had more in common than football. After he retired from a long career as a backup NFL quarterback, Reich attended seminary and worked as a pastor before he became an NFL head coach.

He saw carryover between the two industries, too.

“In coaching or seminary or pastoring, there are a lot of hours,” Reich said in 2019.

The hours Scheelhaase put in in Louisville have paid off in ways he didn’t expect, he said. There, his life revolved around Sundays. In ways he could never have predicted, it still does.

World.title: Peltola says she "knew nothing about" the other Dan Sullivan
World.content:
Juneau, Alaska — Democratic Alaska Senate candidate Mary Peltola told supporters Thursday she is "not interested in tricking voters," after two days of intense questions about how a man with the same first and last name as her Republican opponent ended up on the ballot.

The state's toss-up Senate contest has drawn nationwide scrutiny since The New York Times alleged Thursday that operatives linked to Peltola's campaign helped recruit a candidate named Daniel J. Sullivan — who has the same first and last name as GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan. The Justice Department has sued to potentially block the election from being certified if the senator loses due to "voter confusion," and it issued subpoenas in a separate criminal probe.

In a rally at the state capital of Juneau on Thursday, Peltola offered some of her fullest public remarks on the controversy, denying any connection to Daniel J. Sullivan.

"I just want to clear the air. I knew nothing about any other candidates on the ballot except for me and the incumbent. That is all I have ever known about. I am not interested in tricking voters. I know I can beat Dan Sullivan," she told supporters.

Peltola decried the "smears and attacks" she said she has faced.

"I just feel like I'm dodging bullets left and right, you know? Just, you know, with all the nonsense," said Peltola, who previously represented Alaska in the House. "And when did The New York Times become the National Enquirer? Inquiring minds want to know."

She vowed to "stay focused on affordability, affordability, affordability."

Daniel J. Sullivan's presence on Alaska's ballot has frustrated Republicans for months, with Sen. Sullivan calling him a "sham candidate" intended to confuse voters and siphon votes away from the incumbent Republican. The other Sullivan, a retired teacher, has denied those allegations in the past, insisting he is genuinely interested in running.

State courts in Alaska allowed the other Sullivan to stay on the ballot. The Justice Department filed suit last week, asking a federal court to intervene.

Then, the Times reported on the alleged effort by Democratic operatives to get other candidates on the ballot in Alaska, including Daniel J. Sullivan, citing a former Peltola campaign manager and text messages reviewed by the newspaper. Spokespeople for the Peltola campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee denied that they had any hand in recruiting Daniel J. Sullivan.

President Trump reacted furiously, saying Peltola and Daniel J. Sullivan should be removed from the ballot and prosecuted. "The Democrats cheated!" he said.

In addition to the Justice Department's investigation, Alaska's Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy ordered a separate probe into "whether this scheme violated Alaska's laws and whether criminal charges or civil action are warranted." He later said in an interview that the probe could impact whether a winner is certified in next week's Senate race.

A Peltola campaign spokesperson said in response: "Dunleavy's threat to overrule the will of Alaskan voters exemplifies what Alaskans hate about partisan politics and shows why he's the least popular governor in the country. Mary won't be intimidated by Dunleavy, Sullivan, or any of their DC allies who are trying to steal this election from Alaskans before votes are counted."

World.title: What to know about Alaska's Senate race with 2 Dan Sullivans
World.content:
Washington — A candidate bearing nearly the same name as sitting Sen. Dan Sullivan has drawn scrutiny in Alaska's Senate race, as Republicans and the Trump administration raise the alarm bells over the possibility of confusing voters.

And although the Democrat in the race, Mary Peltola, has denied any involvement, new reporting from The New York Times details an alleged secret effort by people aligned with her campaign to help recruit the second Dan Sullivan.

The race between Sullivan and Peltola has appeared closer than initially expected in a state that President Trump won by double digits in 2024. But the second Sullivan has added a wrinkle.

Here's what to know about the Alaska Senate race:

How did two Dan Sullivans end up on the ballot?

Alaska voted to change its election system in 2020, introducing a nonpartisan primary and a ranked-choice general election. The unique system, which was first implemented in 2022, aimed to move the state away from party primaries in an attempt to stymie polarization.

Now, as Alaska voters head to the polls, they face four options for Senate, after the state held a top-four primary in August. The incumbent Sullivan — identified on the ballot as Dan S. Sullivan — is facing off against a candidate by nearly the same name, Daniel J. Sullivan, another Republican, Gerald Heikes, and his main competitor, Democrat Peltola.

Alaska Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan (at left) is in a 4-way race that includes a challenger named Daniel J. Sullivan (right). AP Photo/Mark Thiessen; AP Photo/Katie Holmlund

Under Alaska's system, voters can rank as many or as few candidates as they'd like, rather than just selecting a single candidate. If any candidate is the top choice for more than 50% of voters, they win. If nobody wins an outright majority, the count goes to a second round and the candidate with the fewest votes is eliminated, with their supporters' votes redistributed to their second choice. The process continues until one candidate wins a majority.

Daniel J. Sullivan came in third place in the primary, winning just 2.5% of the vote. Peltola came in first, with 49.5%, followed by Sen. Sullivan, with 41.4%.

Who is the second Dan Sullivan?

Daniel J. Sullivan is a retired teacher from rural Alaska. He announced in June that he was entering the race, prompting a push by the incumbent senator to remove him from the ballot, calling him a "sham candidate" attempting to trick voters. But Daniel J. Sullivan has denied those allegations, insisting that he is genuinely interested in running for Senate.

After the second Sullivan announced his bid, an Alaska election official determined in June that he was not eligible to appear on the ballot, citing a "determined effort and a deliberate attempt" to confuse Alaska voters. Elections Director Carol Beecher said at the time that Sullivan's entry into the race was not done to "declare an actual good-faith candidacy for the office of United States Senator, but was instead filed with a purpose to confuse or mislead and to thereby compromise the ballot's fairness or neutrality."

Beecher noted that at one point, Daniel J. Sullivan tried to file as just "Dan Sullivan," despite never using that iteration of his name to vote, that he tried to list "S" as his middle initial — the same initial as the incumbent senator — and that the two campaign websites looked similar, suggesting a "deliberate" appropriation of Sen. Sullivan's campaign. Beecher also said he initially asked to be listed as a Republican, but the state had no record of affiliation with the GOP.

But the challenger appealed the decision, and a judge overturned Beecher's move to keep him off the ballot later that month, finding the state didn't have the power to decide whether a candidate is running in "good faith." The state Supreme Court upheld the decision days later, paving the way for both Sullivans' names to appear.

A sample ballot shows how the two Sullivans are listed, with Daniel J. Sullivan appearing first, as "Sullivan, Daniel J. Jr.," with no party affiliation, and Sen. Sullivan appearing next, as "Sullivan, Dan S. (Registered Republican) Incumbent."

For Republicans, the ballot differentiation is the best-case scenario — although they would prefer the second Dan Sullivan not to appear on the ballot. But as Election Day has approached, the GOP has been efforting to make that distinction clear and prevent any confusion, reaching out to voters throughout the state, including with a radio jingle that says, "Dan S., Daniel, Gerry – just don't rank Mary!"

Alaska Senate candidates, as shown on sample ballot from Justice Department court filing

Reported campaign ties spur questions

Republicans have claimed for months that Daniel J. Sullivan has ties to the Democratic Party. But after The New York Times reported that a Democratic operative who worked with Peltola's campaign and national Democrats helped encourage him to run, citing text messages and interviews, Alaska's Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy ordered an investigation into the Peltola campaign.

"Today's New York Times reporting reveals disturbing new evidence of an organized effort to manipulate Alaska's elections by recruiting candidates — including one with the same name as an incumbent U.S. Senator — to deliberately confuse voters and misdirect their votes," Dunleavy wrote in a post on X.

Dunleavy said the Alaska Division of Elections investigated "these very concerns" earlier this year, adding that the new reporting "substantially supports the Division's findings." He said he was directing the Department of Public Safety to investigate "whether this scheme violated Alaska's laws and whether criminal charges or civil action are warranted."

A spokesperson for Sen. Sullivan's campaign said in response to the Times' reporting that "Alaskans deserve the truth."

"Mary Peltola and her campaign have spent months gaslighting Alaskans, denying a scheme they were running all along," Nate Adams said.

The Times reported that the operative's work to encourage Daniel J. Sullivan to run appeared to be part of a wider effort to draw more candidates into the race. But Peltola's campaign has denied any involvement in getting Daniel J. Sullivan on the ballot, and a spokesperson for the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee said it "is not involved with Dan J. Sullivan."

In a campaign stop in Juneau on Thursday, Peltola said she is "not interested in tricking voters."

"I just want to clear the air," Peltola said. "I knew nothing about any other candidates on the ballot except for me and the incumbent. That is all I have ever known about. I am not interested in tricking voters. I know I can beat Dan Sullivan."

The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee has also argued that in the Senate primary and in prior elections, Republicans engaged in their own efforts to stack the Alaska ballot in order to help their preferred candidates.

Trump administration intervenes

The Times' report came after the Justice Department filed a lawsuit last week to preemptively challenge the certification of Alaska's Senate race if Sen. Sullivan loses.

If Sen. Sullivan were to lose because of votes unintentionally cast for Daniel J. Sullivan, the Justice Department argued that the election should not be considered valid. It alleged that he deliberately sought to confuse voters by running with the same ballot name — and, initially, party affiliation — as the incumbent senator.

Attorney General Todd Blanche emphasized on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" Sunday that the DOJ's lawsuit is "not saying, 'don't certify.'" But if a court determined that the race was decided "because of confusion, and not the will of the voters," then the Justice Department does not think the state should certify the election. He added that the Justice Department was looking to "put guardrails in place" with the move.

Blanche said it may "be obvious from the results and from the ballots that voters were confused," adding, "That could be obvious from the way that they rank the Dan Sullivans, or not including a Dan Sullivan on the ballot."

On Wednesday, Mr. Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social, "I don't think Mary Peltola, after perpetrating such a terrible scheme, should be allowed to run, because this is ELECTION FRAUD."

The administration has faced criticism for filing the lawsuit less than two weeks ahead of Election Day, a move that Mr. Trump said came at his direction. The Peltola campaign called the DOJ's move "a despicable political threat to overturn an election."

GOP Sen. Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, the state's other senator who's not up for reelection this cycle, opposed the lawsuit, saying, "Alaskans don't need any help voting for their preferred candidates and the State of Alaska has already handled this by clearly distinguishing the candidates on this year's ballot."

But after The New York Times' reporting, Murkowski was critical of the Peltola campaign, saying, "Alaskans deserve the honest truth from Mary and her campaign," calling the revelations a "pattern of lies and coverups and a culture of deception that belongs nowhere in our elections or among our elected officials."

The pushback isn't expected to change much ahead of Election Day. Under the Constitution, states have the primary authority when it comes to the "times, places, and manner of holding elections."

"The Alaska courts have already considered whether or not this might be shenanigans, and they've ruled on this under Alaska state law," election law expert and CBS News contributor David Becker said. "The DOJ's lawsuit doesn't have any legal basis, it's not going to stop certification. The voters of Alaska are still going to decide this race."

Becker said there is "almost certainly no crime committed here or nothing illegal about what's happened."

"These kind of shenanigans unfortunately happen quite a bit. This has happened on both sides of the aisle," Becker said. "This isn't unusual — it's unfortunate."

World.title: 3 killed in midair collision involving 2 choppers near Oregon airport
World.content:
Three people were killed when two helicopters collided in midair Thursday afternoon in a community near Portland, Oregon, authorities said.

The collision involving an Airbus H125 and a Robinson R22 occurred near McMinnville Municipal Airport at about 2:15 p.m. local time, according to a statement from the Federal Aviation Administration provided to CBS News.

Only the pilot was aboard the Robinson R22, while the Airbus H125 was carrying two people, the FAA said.

The Yamhill County Sheriff's Office later said in a statement that all three people aboard the aircraft were killed in the crash. The two people aboard the Robinson R22 were identified as 22-year-old flight instructor Maddie Aasbo of Texas and a British student pilot whose name was not immediately released.

The pilot of the Airbus was identified as 38-year-old Tyler Delane Sturdevant of Newberg, Oregon.

One of two helicopters involvd in a midair collision near McMinnville, Oregon, on Oct. 29, 2026. Yamhill County Sheriff's Office

One of the two choppers belonged to Jerry Trimble Helicopters, an aviation school based at the McMinnville Municipal Airport, the school said in a statement.

"Our hearts and thoughts are with the individuals involved, their families and everyone affected by the event," the school said.

The circumstances of the collision were unclear. The sheriff's office said multiple agencies responded to the crash site in a field near a highway southeast of McMinnville. Surrounding roads were closed, officials said.

The FAA reported that the National Transportation Safety Board would lead the investigation into the crash. The NTSB also confirmed it was investigating.

The city of McMinnville is located about 35 miles southwest of Portland.

World.title: Guilty plea on federal charges in deadly Boulder firebomb attack
World.content:
The man who already pleaded guilty to more than 100 state criminal charges, including first-degree murder, for an attack on the Pearl Street Mall in June 2025, appeared in federal court on Thursday, where he changed his plea to guilty on a dozen charges.

"I'm always nervous for someone to say, 'No' until they finally say, 'Yes,' so it's just like finally to get to that element was...you know...I wrote down the time when he said, 'Guilty,'" said Ed Victor a survivor of the attack.

Mohamed Soliman admitted to the attack during last summer's peaceful demonstration in support of Israeli captives held by Hamas. According to prosecutors, Soliman threw two Molotov cocktails at the group, killing one person and injuring more than a dozen others.

"He admits that he acted because of the actual or perceived Israeli national origins and the actual or perceived Jewish religion of the victims," United States Attorney for the District of Colorado, Peter McNeilly said during a news conference. "Anti-Semitism erodes the common ties that bind our great nation together, and there is no place for it in America."

Mohamed Sabry Soliman Boulder Police Department

At the time of the attack, the organization known as Run for Their Lives had been marching through downtown Boulder every Sunday for more than a year. Each week, the group marched along the Pearl Street Mall and ended their gathering at the historic Boulder County Courthouse.

Soliman pleaded guilty to state charges in May of this year. The judge handed down a life sentence without the possibility of parole for the first-degree murder conviction, in addition to 2,128 years in prison for the other charges he pleaded guilty to.

"I was there that day, and I told him, 'You're going to jail,' and I want to be here, each time something happens to put him there," said Aaron Brooks, another survivor of the attack. "I still think about my friends that when through it. I still think about Karen Diamon. I don't think that will ever go away. I want to make this about supporting my friends. Many people feel unsafe, and I don't want people to feel unsafe."

Mohamed Soliman in Boulder County Court on May 7, 2025. CBS

Soliman also faced 12 federal hate crime charges. He appeared before a judge in the Arraj Courthouse for the change-of-plea hearing at 10 a.m. Thursday. The judge found Soliman competent to plead guilty to every count. He had previously pleaded not guilty to the federal charges on June 27, 2025.

The 12 charges include:

1 count - hate crime resulting in death - Karen Diamond

7 counts - violation of hate crime involving bodily injury and intent to kill - willfully caused bodily injury

1 count - hate crime involving attempt to cause bodily injury and attempt to kill - willfully caused bodily injury with an explosive or incendiary device

2 counts - using fire or an explosive to commit a felony

1 count - carrying explosive during commission of a felony

"Here is why the federal case is important in addition to the state case: The federal case holds Mohamed Soliman responsible for the hateful ideology that drove his violent acts in June 2025 in Boulder, Colorado. He has pleaded guilty to federal hate crimes, which accounts for the fact that he was motivated by the fact that he thought these people were Jewish and Israeli, and that is why he did violence that day," said U.S. Attorney for the District of Colorado Peter McNeilly.

The judge has not made up his mind about sentencing but did say the guidelines are just a guide and he may not follow them. Prosecutors and Soliman's defense team were requesting life in prison plus 50 years.

The sentencing has been scheduled for 10 a.m. on Jan. 7, 2027.

This statement was provided to CBS Colorado by Susan Rona, the Regional Director of ADL Mountain States, after the change of plea hearing, "The attacker in last year's Boulder, Colorado, firebombing pleaded guilty today to federal hate crime charges, admitting that he targeted people because of their religion or national origin. That admission, made in a federal courtroom, confirms what the facts already showed: This was an antisemitic attack. He planned this act of terror for over a year and targeted people simply because they were Jewish.

"No legal outcome can bring back Karen Sorin Diamond, who died from injuries she suffered in the attack, or undo the trauma the attacker inflicted on the other survivors and the Boulder Jewish community. This plea is an important step toward justice, and we are grateful to the federal prosecutors and law enforcement who pursued it."

Many survivors also mentioned the significance of the admission that this was an attack with motives due to perceived Israeli national origins and the actual or perceived Jewish religion.

"I know people injured who are still going through that injury. Still the trauma and the emotions that is still continuing, so it's weird. That's what I mean by, 'It's a chapter, but not an ending," Victor added.

World.title: Patrick Stewart, best known for "Star Trek" and "X-Men," dies at 86
World.content:
Legendary actor Sir Patrick Stewart, best known for his work in the "Star Trek" and "X-Men" franchises and his prolific award-winning stage career, has died at 86 years old, his spokesperson confirmed.

Stewart died at home on Wednesday, spokesperson Kelly Bush Novak said in a statement. His death followed "a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer's Disease and Lewy Body Dementia," Novak said.

"He has been held in the warm embrace of family and friends, surrounded by live music, prayer, tears, laughter, and the kind of profound emotion that only he could inspire after a lifetime of devotion to us all," Novak said.

Patrick Stewart attends the premiere of "Star Trek: Picard" on Jan. 13, 2020, in Hollywood, California. Rich Fury/Getty Images

Stewart began his acting career doing stage plays in the United Kingdom, joining the Royal Shakespeare Company in the 1960s.

Stewart's most recognizable role began in 1987, when he started playing Enterprise Captain Jean-Luc Picard on "Star Trek: The Next Generation." The show ran for seven seasons and also spawned four "Star Trek" films featuring Stewart as Picard and the rest of the "Next Generation" cast. Stewart later reprised the role for Paramount+ series "Star Trek: Picard," which ran for three seasons.

In a 2023 interview with "CBS Mornings," Stewart said "Star Trek" creator Gene Roddenberry initially turned him away.

"He was talked into employing me by the other producers," Stewart said.

Fellow "Star Trek" legend William Shatner posted: "Sir Patrick Stewart was a friend, a colleague, and a magnificent actor. From the stage to the bridge of the Enterprise, he brought intelligence, grace, and a deep sense of humanity to everything he did. Captain Picard stood for the best of us, and so did the man who played him. I was filled with affection and admiration for him and his work."

George Takei, who played Hikaru Sulu in the original "Star Trek" series, said on Threads that "Stewart took the starship Enterprise to places it had never gone before, and he inspired a whole next generation of star-gazers who looked longingly ahead to a brighter future for all humanity. Our hearts are heavy, indeed. Rest in the heavens, Captain."

Stewart also played "X-Men" leader Charles Xavier in over half a dozen films in the "X-Men" franchise. He reprised the role for the upcoming "Avengers: Doomsday," which will be released in December 2026. Marvel Studios said on social media that it was "deeply saddened" by Stewart's passing, calling him a "singular talent" who defined the character "for generations of fans."

"X-Men" co-star Hugh Jackman said in a social media post "We lost one of the greats of stage and screen today. And, in my book, a tremendous friend and man. I learned so much from him. I will miss you, Patrick Stewart, all of my days."

Stewart appeared in dozens of other film and television roles, including voice work on Seth MacFarlane's animated shows "Family Guy" and "American Dad."

"Patrick was one of those icons who we somehow all took for granted would always be with us," MacFarlane wrote on social media Thursday. "... He was that rare actor who could take any bit of dialogue and elevate it, making a good writer sound great, and a great writer sound masterful. He was also as humble as they come ... We have lost a legendary actor today, and for many of us, a good friend. He will be deeply missed by the entire planet."

The bulk of Stewart's work was on the stage: He was a frequent presence on Broadway and in London's West End, where he played characters from Shakespearean villains to Charles Dickens' Ebenezer Scrooge. He appeared with "X-Men" co-star Ian McKellen in "Waiting for Godot" in London in 2010, then again in New York City in 2013. He also performed his one-man version of "A Christmas Carol" frequently over the decades.

Stewart appeared in over 60 Royal Shakespeare Company productions. The company named him an "Honorary Associate Artist" to celebrate his contributions to their work. He has also been awarded three Olivier Awards for his London stage performances and received one Tony nomination for his work on Broadway.

Stewart was nominated for multiple Emmy, Golden Globe and SAG awards for his on-screen roles. He won a Grammy Award in 1995 for "Best Spoken Word Album for Children."

In 2001, Queen Elizabeth II appointed Stewart an Officer of the Order of the British Empire. In 2010, Stewart received a knighthood, again from Elizabeth II, for his services to drama.

In 2023, Stewart published the memoir "Making It So." The book landed him on the New York Times' best-sellers list. He also recorded a companion audiobook.

Stewart was actively working until 2026. In addition to his role in "Avengers: Doomsday," he recorded an audiobook where he narrated and commented on all 154 of William Shakespeare's sonnets. He also had a voice role in the animated comedy "The Sheep Detectives."

Stewart was married three times. He wed Sheila Falconer in 1966. The pair had two children — Daniel and Sophia — before divorcing in 1990. From 2000 to 2003, he was married to producer Wendy Neuss. In 2008, he began dating singer-songwriter Sunny Ozell. The two married in 2013 and were wed until his death. Novak said Ozell was at Stewart's side when he died.

In that 2023 interview with "CBS Mornings," Stewart reflected on what he believed made a successful relationship.

"I think it's being open and a good listener and to make connection," he said. "You don't have to be exactly the same but it's necessary that you can share – I think very important. So sharing and respecting."

Stewart was also "a fierce advocate for causes he strongly believed in," his spokesperson said. Those causes included social justice, women's rights, domestic abuse advocacy, veterans' rights, the refugee crisis, animal rights and political reform.

"We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace," Novak said. "His sonorous voice and singular talent will forever be synonymous with indelible performances in every genre. … He will be remembered for the dignity, compassion and humanity he brought to every role — in his art and life."
