World.title: Sheinbaum and cabinet pay tribute to Cuauhtémoc Cárdenas: Thursday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Listen to this article

Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

🕊️ Government pays tribute to Cuauhtémoc Cárdenas after his death: The centerpiece of Thursday’s mañanera was a tribute to Cárdenas, a three-time presidential candidate, co-founder of the Democratic Revolution Party (PRD) and former Mexico City mayor, who died at age 92. Interior Minister Rosa Icela Rodríguez said “Mexico is in mourning,” while Minister for Women Laura Itzel Castillo praised his commitment to democracy and social justice. Asked what legacy Cárdenas leaves for “the left” in Mexico, Sheinbaum answered: “Honesty and democracy.”

The centerpiece of Thursday’s mañanera was a tribute to Cárdenas, a three-time presidential candidate, co-founder of the Democratic Revolution Party (PRD) and former Mexico City mayor, who died at age 92. Interior Minister Rosa Icela Rodríguez said “Mexico is in mourning,” while Minister for Women Laura Itzel Castillo praised his commitment to democracy and social justice. Asked what legacy Cárdenas leaves for “the left” in Mexico, Sheinbaum answered: “Honesty and democracy.” 🗳️ Sheinbaum says Taddei “betrayed the trust of the people of Mexico”: Three days after Guadalupe Taddei resigned as president of the National Electoral Institute (INE), the president offered a blunt assessment of her conduct. Taddei stepped down after media reports that companies linked to a businessman close to her received lucrative INE contracts. Sheinbaum noted that Taddei was chosen by the Chamber of Deputies, not by the president, and reiterated her support for a comprehensive audit of the INE by the Federal Auditor’s Office.

Three days after Guadalupe Taddei resigned as president of the National Electoral Institute (INE), the president offered a blunt assessment of her conduct. Taddei stepped down after media reports that companies linked to a businessman close to her received lucrative INE contracts. Sheinbaum noted that Taddei was chosen by the Chamber of Deputies, not by the president, and reiterated her support for a comprehensive audit of the INE by the Federal Auditor’s Office. 🖨️ Sheinbaum wants state-owned printer Talleres Gráficos de México to supply “most electoral materials”: The president asserted that “two or three” INE suppliers of items such as ballot papers and ballot boxes are “intermediaries” that don’t produce the materials themselves. Sheinbaum said that next week her government will formally propose turning the government-run printing agency Talleres Gráficos de México into a state-owned company with its own board of directors and “external observation.”

Why today’s mañanera matters

President Claudia Sheinbaum’s Thursday morning press conference came the day after the death of Cuauhtémoc Cárdenas Solórzano, a three-time presidential candidate (1988, 1994 and 2000), a co-founder of the leftist Democratic Revolution Party (PRD) and the son of former President of Mexico Lázaro Cárdenas del Río.

Cárdenas, a major figure in Mexican politics who served as a federal senator in the 1970s, governor of Michoacán in the 1980s and mayor of Mexico City in the 1990s, passed away at the age of 92.

Sheinbaum acknowledged his death in a social media post on Wednesday night.

“With deep sorrow, we lament the passing of the engineer Cuauhtémoc Cárdenas Solórzano, a man of steadfast principles who transformed the political life of our country,” she wrote.

“His role in Mexico’s contemporary history is fundamental. In 1988, he led a peaceful democratic movement that channeled the yearning for change of millions of Mexican women and men. That historic electoral day, in which he should have been recognized as president, marked the beginning of the democratic transformation,” Sheinbaum wrote, alluding to allegations that Cárdenas was denied victory in the 1988 presidential election by electoral fraud.

A tribute to Cárdenas was the centerpiece of today’s mañanera, at which government officials honored his life and political legacy.

Beyond the tribute, Sheinbaum spoke about the allegedly corrupt conduct of Guadalupe Taddei, former president of the National Electoral Institute (INE).

Taddei resigned earlier this week after media outlets reported that companies linked to a businessman with whom she has a close personal relationship had received lucrative INE contracts.

‘Mexico is in mourning,’ says Interior Minister Rosa Rodríguez

Sheinbaum announced at the start of the press conference that the government would pay tribute to “the engineer” Cuauhtémoc Cardenas Solórzano, who obtained a degree in civil engineering from the National Autonomous University of Mexico.

“From here we send an affectionate hug to Lázaro, Cuauhtémoc and Camila, his children, and to all the people who were close to the engineer,” she said.

#LoÚltimo 🕊️La presidenta Claudia Sheinbaum anunció que la mañanera de este jueves estará dedicada a rendir homenaje a Cuauhtémoc Cárdenas, tras darse a conocer su fallecimiento a los 92 años. “Hasta siempre, Cuauhtémoc Cárdenas”, expresó la mandataria. https://t.co/DNTvdCAtcq — xevt – xhvt (@xevtfm) October 29, 2026

Interior Minister Rosa Icela Rodríguez was the first official to speak at length about Cardenas.

“The journey of Cuauhtémoc Cardenas Solórzano has historical significance for Mexico and for the people of the Americas and the world,” she began.

Rodríguez said that his political “struggle” greatly influenced “the Mexico of today.”

Cárdenas was a man who “shaped the transition to democratic life” in Mexico and he “left a mark on the transformation of our country,” she said.

“His example demonstrates that convictions take on meaning when they are placed at the service of the people,” Rodríguez said.

At the end of her address, the interior minister said that “Mexico is in mourning,” but added that Cárdenas’ “teachings, his love of the homeland, his principles and his ideals will remain with us.”

“Long live the great democrat of Mexico, Cuauhtémoc Cárdenas Solórzano,” Rodríguez said.

Minister for Women Laura Itzel Castillo called Cárdenas “a great Mexican” and a “dear friend” of her family.

She said his life was “marked by the strength of his convictions and his commitment to democracy, social justice and the defense of national sovereignty.”

“His career is part of the contemporary history of Mexico. His struggle opened paths for democratic participation and he contributed to the transformation of political life in our country,” Castillo said.

After a video tribute to Cárdenas was played, a reporter asked Sheinbaum about the legacy he leaves for “the left” in Mexico and Latin America.

“Honesty and democracy,” she responded.

“Democracy that comes from below, not democracy of the elites,” Sheinbaum said.

Sheinbaum: ‘I believe that Guadalupe Taddei betrayed the trust of the people of Mexico’

Three days after Guadalupe Taddei resigned as president of the INE, Sheinbaum offered a blunt assessment of Taddei’s conduct.

“I believe that Guadalupe Taddei betrayed the trust of the people of Mexico,” she said. “That’s the way it has to be said.”

Sheinbaum reiterated that Taddei was elected by the Chamber of Deputies, rather than by the president. She also reiterated her support for a comprehensive audit of the INE by the Federal Auditor’s Office.

In 2023, during the presidency of Andrés Manuel López Obrador, Taddi was elected via sortition — also known as selection by lottery — as none of the candidates for president of the INE had the support of the required two-thirds of lawmakers in the lower house of Congress. At the time of her election, questions were raised about her family links to both the government and Morena.

Sheinbaum says state-owned company should supply ‘most electoral materials’

Electoral materials suppliers linked to José Alfredo Hernández Casillas — the businessman who is reportedly a close friend of Taddei — received lucrative INE contracts.

Sheinbaum asserted that “two or three” companies that received contracts to supply materials such as ballot papers and ballot boxes to the INE didn’t actually produce the materials themselves but rather acted as “intermediaries.”

She told reporters that “most electoral materials” should in fact be made by Talleres Gráficos de México, a government-run printing agency.

To that end, Sheinbaum said that next week her government will formally propose turning Talleres Gráficos de México into a state-owned company with its own board of directors and “external observation.”

MEXICO · SECURITY

Key Facts The country Mexico, in the border city of Matamoros, Tamaulipas, across the river from Brownsville, Texas.

What happened Soldiers and National Guard arrested a man known as Axel, second in command of the Ciclones, on Thursday 29 October 2026.

The aftermath Blockades and burning vehicles hit Matamoros, Río Bravo and the Victoria highway; a girl died and classes were suspended.

Who he is Son of a cartel commander known as El Contador and nephew of jailed ex-boss Osiel Cárdenas Guillén.

Power Index Mexico ranks 2nd of 14 in Mexico ranks 2nd of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 71.4 points (October 2026 edition).

Mexican soldiers and National Guard special forces arrested Axel, second in command of a Matamoros cartel faction called the Ciclones, on Thursday 29 October 2026. Matamoros sits on the Texas border opposite Brownsville, so blockades there can disrupt travel and trade.

Within hours, armed groups blocked roads and burned vehicles in Matamoros, Río Bravo and on the Victoria highway. A girl died, and afternoon classes were suspended.

What Happened

The Defense Ministry (Defensa), Army special forces and the National Guard arrested Axel Alfredo and one other man in Matamoros on Thursday 29 October 2026. Mexican authorities name suspects by first name and an initial, so the federal statement says Axel Alfredo N.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Mexico ranks 2nd of 14 with 71.4 points. Strongest pillar: economic relationships (90); weakest: state capacity & security (46). Alignment group: Hedging. Watch21 homicides per 100,000; organised crime at 7.7 of 10. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

Defensa says the operation followed military intelligence work and that both men were caught in the act. Forces seized weapons, magazines, ammunition, drugs and a vehicle.

A Mexican Air Force plane flew both men to Mexico City, where federal prosecutors for organized crime (FEMDO) hold them at their disposal. The Ciclones are a Matamoros faction of the Gulf Cartel, one of Mexico’s oldest criminal groups.

Axel is the son of José Alfredo Cárdenas, a former Ciclones commander known as El Contador. He is also a nephew of Osiel Cárdenas Guillén, the jailed former Gulf Cartel boss.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Blockades and Violence in Matamoros

From about 11:00, blockades and burning vehicles appeared across Matamoros, in Río Bravo and on the Victoria–Matamoros highway. Attackers used hijacked cargo trucks and spiked strips that burst tyres.

The Tamaulipas state prosecutor’s office confirmed that a girl died near the Reynosa road, and her mother was shot and taken to hospital. Reports say the girl was hit by a stray bullet, but the cause has not been officially established.

The city’s civil protection coordinator was injured while helping to put out a burning truck. Afternoon classes were suspended and many shops closed.

Federal forces moved the prisoners under armored escort and with a helicopter overhead. Residents were told to rely on official channels for road information.

Why It Matters

Defensa links Axel to homicide, kidnapping, extortion, fuel theft and the smuggling of drugs, weapons and people toward the United States. Security Secretary Omar García Harfuch’s office also presumes him responsible for an attack on 17 May 2026 that killed a federal protection officer.

The officers were assigned to protect the US consulate, and the American consul condemned the killing, so the Matamoros cartel faction is a US concern. Axel was first arrested on 7 May 2023, and on 18 January 2024 a judge let him face trial in freedom.

The city was also the scene of the abduction of four Americans, covered in our report on the 25-year sentences. Joint border patrols are described in our Operation Mirror coverage, and our Mexico security guide explains how these groups work.

What It Means for You

If you plan to cross between Matamoros and Brownsville, check official crossing and road status first. Avoid the Victoria and Reynosa highways at night while reinforcements stay.

Past arrests of cartel figures in Tamaulipas have been followed by new blockades. Follow the Tamaulipas security office and the American consulate’s alerts.

For US companies with factories or freight in the border region, delays at the bridges are the main risk. No attack on American citizens was reported on Thursday.

What Is Not Known

Some early accounts called Axel the leader of the Ciclones, but the federal statement calls him second in command. It is not known who now leads the Matamoros cartel faction.

Authorities have not said where Axel is held or when a judge will hear him. The number of blockades and burned vehicles, and the cause of the girl’s death, are not established.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who was arrested in Matamoros?

Soldiers and National Guard special forces arrested a man known as Axel Alfredo N on Thursday 29 October 2026. The Defense Ministry says he is second in command of the Ciclones, a Matamoros cartel faction.

What happened after the arrest?

After the Matamoros cartel faction arrest, blockades and burning vehicles hit Matamoros, Río Bravo and the Victoria highway. A girl died and afternoon classes were suspended.

Is it safe to travel to Matamoros?

Check official alerts before any trip, because roads were blocked on Thursday and reinforcements are on the streets. Avoid the Victoria and Reynosa highways at night until the situation calms.

World.title: São Paulo Nightlife Tonight: Four Shows on Paulista — October 30, 2026
World.content:
São Paulo · Nightlife

Tonight, Friday 30 October 2026, São Paulo’s best-documented plan is live music on Avenida Paulista, the city’s central avenue. Blue Note São Paulo (a jazz and live-music club on the second floor of the Conjunto Nacional building) lists four shows, from a Maysa tribute and an OBMJAZZ set at 8 p.m. to a Rolling Stones tribute and an acoustic Vanguart show at 10:30 p.m. Showers are likely at 6 p.m. but should fade by 10 p.m., so bring a jacket for the cooler evening.

Tonight at a Glance — Date Friday, 30 October 2026. Times are São Paulo time (UTC-3, three hours behind Greenwich Mean Time).

— Weather Open-Meteo, a free weather service, forecasts 18.6°C (65°F) at 6 p.m. with an 84 per cent chance of rain, and 17.2°C (63°F) at 10 p.m. with 9 per cent.

— Top pick Vanguart Acústico, Blue Note São Paulo, 10:30 p.m. The club’s site marks it as last tickets available.

— Neighborhood in focus Avenida Paulista, São Paulo’s central avenue on the border of Bela Vista and Consolação, with a club and Metro stations close together.

— Entry prices Ticket prices are not shown on the venue pages we checked. Rate: US$1 = R$5.37 (PTAX, the central bank’s official daily dollar rate, 29 October).

— Safety note Rain eases late, but the evening is cool, so dress in layers and use a ride app for the trip home.

Planning more nights? Read our São Paulo Nightlife Guide 2026, with neighborhoods, costs, safety and how the scene works.

If You Only Go to One Place Vanguart Acústico, Blue Note São Paulo, 10:30 p.m. Vanguart is a Brazilian indie-folk band, and tonight’s show is an acoustic set at the Paulista club. Blue Note’s own page marks it as last tickets available, so book before you travel; we could not confirm the price.

Tonight’s Top 5 (All Tonight)

1. Vanguart Acústico, Blue Note São Paulo, Paulista Blue Note São Paulo is a jazz and live-music club inside the Conjunto Nacional building. Its programme lists an acoustic Vanguart show tonight and flags last tickets. When Friday 30 October 2026, 10:30 p.m.

Genre Brazilian indie-folk, acoustic.

Entry We could not confirm the price on the venue’s page.

Address Avenida Paulista 2073, Conjunto Nacional, 2nd floor (the border of Bela Vista and Consolação).

Verdict The show the club flags as nearly sold out. For foreigners: lyrics are in Portuguese, but the acoustic format makes the music easy to enjoy without it.

2. RS Experience, “Tribute to the Rolling Stones”, Blue Note São Paulo, Paulista The club’s programme lists a Rolling Stones tribute show, billed as “Stones Weekend”, for the late slot. When Friday 30 October 2026, 10:30 p.m.

Genre Classic rock tribute.

Entry We could not confirm the price on the venue’s page.

Address Avenida Paulista 2073, Conjunto Nacional, 2nd floor (the border of Bela Vista and Consolação).

Verdict A familiar songbook for visitors who know the originals. For foreigners: the show is billed in English, so little Portuguese is needed.

3. Ná Ozzetti and Marcelo Ghelfi, “Maysa 90 Anos”, Blue Note São Paulo, Paulista The programme lists this show under the title “Maysa 90 Anos”. Ná Ozzetti and Marcelo Ghelfi, two Brazilian musicians, perform in a tribute to the Brazilian singer Maysa. When Friday 30 October 2026, 8 p.m.

Genre Brazilian song, tribute.

Entry We could not confirm the price on the venue’s page.

Address Avenida Paulista 2073, Conjunto Nacional, 2nd floor (the border of Bela Vista and Consolação).

Verdict A calm early-evening option before the late shows. For foreigners: the repertoire is in Portuguese, so a quick search on Maysa helps.

4. OBMJAZZ Jamaica 2.0, Blue Note São Paulo, Paulista The programme lists this show under the title “OBMJAZZ Jamaica 2.0”. OBMJ stands for Orquestra Brasileira de Música Jamaicana, a Brazilian band; we could not confirm the line-up. When Friday 30 October 2026, 8 p.m.

Genre Billed as jazz.

Entry We could not confirm the price on the venue’s page.

Address Avenida Paulista 2073, Conjunto Nacional, 2nd floor (the border of Bela Vista and Consolação).

Verdict An early jazz slot on a busy avenue. For foreigners: an 8 p.m. start leaves time for dinner nearby afterwards.

5. Rodrigo Barba, “25 anos do Bloco do Eu Sozinho”, Casa Natura Musical, Pinheiros Casa Natura Musical is a concert hall in Pinheiros, a west-side district known for bars and music. Its programme lists Rodrigo Barba, the original drummer of the Brazilian rock band Los Hermanos, in a show marking 25 years of the band’s 2001 album “Bloco do Eu Sozinho”. When Friday 30 October 2026. We could not confirm the start time.

Genre Brazilian popular music.

Entry We could not confirm the price; tickets are sold through Sympla, a ticket platform.

Address Rua Artur de Azevedo 2134, Pinheiros.

Also Tonight

— Blue Note São Paulo, Paulista Four shows tonight: two at 8 p.m. and two at 10:30 p.m., as listed above.

— Casa Natura Musical, Pinheiros One show tonight, Rodrigo Barba; the next is Agnes Nunes on Saturday 31 October.

Later This Week

— Saturday 31 October Blue Note lists the Tears for Fears Experience, a tribute show, at 8 p.m. and Elton John Diamonds, billed with Mizinho Carvalho, at 10:30 p.m. Casa Natura lists Agnes Nunes, billed with the Cultura Inglesa Festival.

The Night in Context

Tonight’s verified calendar is built around one avenue. Blue Note alone lists four shows, which makes Paulista the simplest place for a first-time visitor.

Blue Note runs an early session at 8 p.m. and a late one at 10:30 p.m. tonight and tomorrow, so you can choose the one that suits your dinner plans.

The weather shapes the plan. Open-Meteo gives 84 per cent chance of rain at 6 p.m. and 9 per cent at 10 p.m., so the late sessions are the safer choice if you must walk.

BOLIVIA · CORRUPTION PROBE

Key Facts The country Bolivia, an Andean nation led by President Rodrigo Paz, arrested ex-defense minister Edmundo Novillo in La Paz.

What happened Novillo was held on Thursday 29 October 2026 after giving a statement to prosecutors.

The case A 2016 air-defense contract of more than US$213 million, with a possible state loss of US$123 million.

His answer Novillo says he is innocent and calls the arrest unjust. No court has found anyone guilty.

Power Index Bolivia ranks 12th of 14 in Bolivia ranks 12th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 28.4 points (October 2026 edition).

Bolivia arrested ex-defense minister Edmundo Novillo on Thursday 29 October 2026 in La Paz, in a corruption probe over 13 radars bought in 2016. Novillo says he is innocent, and no court has found anyone guilty.

The case matters to US readers because Bolivia’s new government is auditing old state contracts while it seeks closer ties with Washington. Companies selling to Bolivian state buyers should expect past deals to be reviewed.

What Happened

The ex-defense minister went to the prosecutors’ office in La Paz shortly before noon on Thursday to give a statement. A prosecutor ordered his arrest when he finished, and police took him to cells at about 3:30 p.m.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Bolivia ranks 12th of 14 with 28.4 points. Strongest pillar: military means (55); weakest: diplomatic & cultural influence (13). Alignment group: Hedging. WatchRating below investment grade (CCC+); economy contracting (-1.2%); inflation of 20%. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

The cells belong to the Felcc, Bolivia’s special police force against crime, and he now waits for a precautionary-measures hearing. At that hearing a judge decides whether he stays in custody.

Novillo came in voluntarily, and he said, “I am innocent, I have presented all my defences.” He called the arrest unjust, and his lawyers say they will take legal action.

The case concerns Sidacta, a Spanish abbreviation for an integrated air-defense and air-traffic-control network. Bolivia signed the contract in August 2016 with the French company Thales Air Systems, as our explainer describes.

The deal covered 13 radars and control centres for more than 191 million euros (about US$213 million). It was meant to be delivered in 31 months and took about 98.

The Defense Ministry filed a criminal complaint on Thursday 15 October 2026 after an internal audit, covered in our first story on the complaint. It names 19 people, including four former defense ministers, and alleges a possible state loss of Bs 1.478 billion (about US$123 million).

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Bolivia Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

What the Investigators Say

Novillo served under President Luis Arce, who governed until November 2025, and signed two of the seven amendments to the contract. Vice-Minister Yamil García, the government’s transparency official, spoke about them on Thursday.

García said one amendment added reimbursable expenses for the contractor, although a turnkey contract fixes one price for a finished system. He also said an on-site inspection found that about 60 percent of the project does not work.

The ministry’s audit counted only two of the 13 radars as working without observations. Nine work with observations and two do not work at all.

Accounts of the exact offences differ and include breach of duties, uneconomic conduct, contracts harmful to the state and economic damage. The complaint lists four alleged offences, and a complaint asks prosecutors to investigate, which is not a finding of guilt.

Why It Matters

This ex-defense minister’s arrest reaches across three governments, since the contract was signed under President Evo Morales and amended under Áñez and Arce. It also tests President Rodrigo Paz, in office since November 2025, who says his government will pursue officials of every camp.

Deputy Claudia Bilbao of the PDC party called the arrest due process, not political persecution. She asked why other former ministers are not held.

The radars are meant to watch Bolivian airspace, including for illegal flights linked to drug trafficking. The government says a technical audit will aim to repair the system while the probe continues, as our guide to the next steps explains.

What It Means for You

If you are a US traveler, nothing changes, because no authority has said flights or airport operations are affected. The US State Department’s usual advice on Bolivia still applies.

If you sell equipment or services to Bolivian state bodies, expect auditors to look again at old contracts and their amendments. Investors in Bolivian debt or state firms can read the case as a sign that the Paz government will act against past officials.

What Is Not Known

The date of the precautionary-measures hearing has not been announced, and it is not clear whether the judge will order jail, house arrest or release. Prosecutors have not published the full list of charges in the arrest order.

It is not known whether the other three ex-defense ministers named in the complaint will be summoned or detained. The calculation of the Bs 1.478 billion loss (about US$123 million) is unexplained, and the French contractor has not commented in the sources we reviewed.

More: Bolivia news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is Edmundo Novillo?

He was Bolivia’s defense minister under former President Luis Arce, who governed until November 2025. He was arrested on 29 October 2026 in the radar case and says he is innocent.

What is the radars case?

It is a probe of a 2016 contract for 13 air-defense and air-traffic radars worth more than US$213 million. The government alleges a possible loss of about US$123 million and says many radars do not work as agreed.

Has Novillo been convicted?

No. He has been arrested and awaits a hearing on precautionary measures. No court has found anyone guilty in this case.

Sources: Ministerio de Defensa del Estado Plurinacional de Bolivia, 29 October 2026; Procuraduría General del Estado de Bolivia, 29 October 2026; Ministerio Público de Bolivia (Fiscalía General del Estado), 29 October 2026.

COLOMBIA · CÚCUTA

Key Facts The country Colombia, led by conservative President Abelardo de la Espriella, shares a long border with Venezuela.

Power Index Colombia ranks 6th of 14 in Colombia ranks 6th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 51.9 points (October 2026 edition).

What happened On Thursday 29 October 2026 the president ordered the temporary militarization of the border city Cúcuta.

What starts next An army and police campaign called Esparta, plus an urban security team, begins on Tuesday 3 November.

The legal basis No decree is public; the president’s constitutional powers over public order and the armed forces apply.

Cúcuta militarization became official policy on Thursday 29 October 2026, when President Abelardo de la Espriella sent the army into this border city. He gave no troop numbers or map, and no decree is public.

US readers should care because Cúcuta is the main crossing to Venezuela, a route for trade, migrants and armed groups. The order follows a political killing on Monday 26 October and an explosive attack on Tuesday 27 October.

In Plain English

Militarization means the army, and not only the police, takes a visible lead in keeping order. The president calls the step temporary, lasting only while public order is stabilised.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Colombia ranks 6th of 14 with 51.9 points. Strongest pillar: military means (91); weakest: diplomatic & cultural influence (28). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. WatchRating below investment grade (BB-); 26 homicides per 100,000; organised crime at 7.8 of 10. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

Cúcuta is the capital of Norte de Santander, a Colombian department (the equivalent of a state) on the Venezuelan border. BOSUR is the Urban Security Operational Bloc, a tactical team the president created to pursue criminal networks in cities.

What Happened

President de la Espriella spoke to the media on Thursday 29 October with the military high command beside him. He said he had ordered the Defence Minister and security chiefs to carry out the Cúcuta militarization immediately.

The army will reinforce its presence in coordination with the National Police, he said, to confront criminal and narcoterrorist groups. On Tuesday 3 November a military and police campaign called Esparta and the BOSUR team begin work in the city.

He listed their aims as recovering territorial control, dismantling criminal structures and hitting their finances. He also said he would travel to Cúcuta next week to check progress.

The trigger was the killing of mayoral hopeful Miguel Castellanos on Monday 26 October, as our report on the killing covered. A blast in El Escobal on Tuesday 27 October then wounded police officers and civilians, as our explosion report describes.

Why It Matters

The target area is the city of Cúcuta, which sits beside the main bridge to Venezuela. The announcement came with no map, so the zone’s boundaries are not defined.

The legal basis for the Cúcuta militarization is Article 189 of the Constitution, which makes the president armed forces commander and keeper of order. Article 296 adds that his public-order orders override those of governors and mayors.

No state of exception, the emergency regime that widens a president’s powers, was announced. The president described the army as acting in coordination with the National Police.

It is the second city in five weeks to get more soldiers, after Santa Marta, which our report on the armed group there covers. He has also said parts of Bogotá need military control, a plan we described in our report on troops for Bogotá.

Cúcuta has seen this before: a truck bomb wounded 11 people on Saturday 1 August 2026, and the military sent about 250 extra soldiers. The military command blamed the ELN, a leftist guerrilla group.

What It Means for You

If you plan to visit Cúcuta or cross to Venezuela, expect a heavier military presence and read the US State Department’s Colombia travel advisory first. Nothing in the announcement closes the border or the bridge.

For US policy, the Cúcuta militarization tests a conservative government that has now turned to troops in two cities. Companies with staff or cargo on the Cúcuta route should ask local partners about delays.

What Is Not Known

The government has published no troop numbers or decree text for the Cúcuta militarization. On 1 August the military command gave a figure of about 250 extra soldiers, so a number may follow.

The government has not named the legal provision it relies on, so the constitutional articles above are our reading of the president’s powers. It is also unclear whether residents will face checkpoints or curfews.

No boundary has been given for the Cúcuta militarization, and the end date is unknown. No group has claimed the explosion of 27 October.

More: Colombia news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Cúcuta militarization?

On Thursday 29 October 2026 President de la Espriella ordered the immediate, temporary militarization of Cúcuta, with the army working alongside the police. An army and police campaign called Esparta starts on 3 November.

How many soldiers are going to Cúcuta?

No number has been published for this order. In August the military command sent about 250 extra soldiers after a truck bomb, but that is a different deployment.

Is there a decree or a state of emergency?

No decree text has been made public, and no state of exception was announced. The president’s constitutional powers over public order and the armed forces are the apparent basis, though the government has not named an article.

BRAZIL · DIPLOMACY

Key Facts The country Brazil, Latin America’s biggest economy, sends Foreign Minister Mauro Vieira to the talks.

What happened Brazilian diplomats say Vieira left for Atlanta on 29 October; no ministry note confirms it yet.

The question No one-on-one meeting with Rubio or Argentina’s foreign minister, Pablo Quirno, is confirmed so far.

The backdrop Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, who lost Brazil’s runoff, landed in Miami on Wednesday 28 October.

Power Index Brazil ranks 1st of 14 in Brazil ranks 1st of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 75.0 points (October 2026 edition).

Brazil’s foreign minister, Mauro Vieira, is due at the Atlanta G20 meeting that opens on Friday 30 October 2026. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio chairs it, and no private meeting between the two is confirmed yet.

It matters to US readers because it comes days after Senator Flávio Bolsonaro landed in Miami on 28 October. Our report on the Atlanta G20 talks explains what Washington wants from the meeting.

What Happened

Brazilian diplomats say Vieira left on Thursday 29 October for the G20 foreign ministers’ meeting in Atlanta, Georgia. Itamaraty, Brazil’s foreign ministry, had published no note on the trip by Friday morning.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Brazil ranks 1st of 14 with 75.0 points. Strongest pillar: military means (100); weakest: state capacity & security (56). Alignment group: Hedging. WatchRating below investment grade (BB); public debt at 93% of GDP. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

The Atlanta G20 runs on Friday 30 and Saturday 31 October, and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio chairs it. The same diplomats expect Argentina’s foreign minister, Pablo Quirno, to attend, although we found no confirmation from Buenos Aires.

Brazilian diplomats say no one-on-one meeting with either man is scheduled, though sideline talks could happen. The US State Department says Washington wants the ministers to discuss open sea lanes, energy and food security, resilient supply chains, economic growth and technology.

The US State Department says Washington wants the ministers to discuss open sea lanes, energy and food security, resilient supply chains, economic growth and technology. The talks prepare the G20 leaders’ summit that President Donald Trump hosts in Miami on 14 and 15 December.

The talks prepare the G20 leaders’ summit that President Donald Trump hosts in Miami on 14 and 15 December. Neither the State Department nor Itamaraty had published a list of one-on-one meetings by Friday morning.

In Plain English

The G20 is the group of 20 large economies, and Brazil is a full member. Its foreign ministers meet before each leaders’ summit to settle the agenda.

Itamaraty is the name Brazilians use for their foreign ministry, and Vieira has led it since January 2023 under President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Rubio, a former US senator from Florida, is America’s top diplomat, and Quirno holds the same job for President Javier Milei of Argentina.

Why the Backdrop Is Tense

Flávio Bolsonaro, a senator and the son of ex-president Jair Bolsonaro, lost the 25 October runoff to Lula. Brazil’s Supreme Court had ordered him to hand over his passports, and he landed in Miami on Wednesday 28 October anyway.

A senior State Department official said on 27 October that Washington would issue visas to him and his family. President Donald Trump said he “would approve”, and our reports on his Miami arrival and his thank-you letter give details.

Argentina’s migration agency says he crossed from Brazil into Argentina on Tuesday 27 October. That is why Vieira and Quirno sitting in the same room as Rubio draws attention.

What Brazil Has Said So Far

Itamaraty had posted no statement on Atlanta that we could find by Friday morning, so Brazil’s line is not on the record. Brazilian diplomats describe it as pragmatic: keep talking to Washington and avoid a public confrontation.

Vieira and Rubio know each other, having held talks in October 2025 during the earlier tariff dispute, as our coverage of that reset shows. No new trade or tariff step between the two countries has been announced this week.

Why It Matters

The United States is the host, the chair and the country that has just welcomed a defeated Brazilian candidate who disputes the vote. Whatever Vieira and Rubio say at the Atlanta G20, or leave unsaid, will signal how far Washington and Brasília want to keep the relationship stable.

Argentina matters because Bolsonaro thanked Milei publicly for his help. The tone between Brazil’s and Argentina’s top diplomats at the Atlanta G20 is the first test of whether that episode costs the two neighbours anything.

The US midterm elections take place on Tuesday 3 November, four days after the Atlanta talks end. That keeps Washington’s attention split between domestic politics and the G20 agenda.

What It Means for You

For US investors, the Atlanta G20 gauges political risk in South America’s biggest economy, whose main stock index fell 13.88% on 26 October. A calm Vieira-Rubio exchange would point to limited spillover into trade talks, while a public clash could add to market nerves.

For travellers and businesses, nothing changes on Friday 30 October, because visas, tariffs and flight rules are not among the priorities the State Department listed. Street closures in Atlanta start at midnight on Thursday, which affects anyone visiting the city on Saturday 31 October.

What Is Not Known

It is not known whether Vieira will sit down with Rubio or Quirno, or only speak to them on the sidelines. Neither Itamaraty nor the State Department had published a schedule for such talks by Friday morning.

It is also unclear whether Flávio Bolsonaro will be raised in any official exchange. We found no Itamaraty note on the trip, so the travel details rest on diplomats’ accounts until the ministry confirms them.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Mauro Vieira meeting Marco Rubio at the G20?

Brazilian diplomats expect Vieira at the G20 foreign ministers’ meeting in Atlanta on 30 and 31 October 2026, which Rubio chairs. No separate one-on-one meeting has been confirmed so far.

Who is Mauro Vieira?

Vieira is Brazil’s foreign minister and a career diplomat who has led the ministry since January 2023. He serves under President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.

Why does the Flávio Bolsonaro case matter to this meeting?

Bolsonaro, who lost Brazil’s runoff, landed in Miami on 28 October after Washington promised him visas. Argentina’s help on his route also makes the Brazil, US and Argentina ministers’ presence in Atlanta politically sensitive.

ARGENTINA · HEALTH POLICY

Key Facts The country Argentina, a South American republic with a two-chamber Congress: the Senate and the Chamber of Deputies.

Power Index Argentina ranks 4th of 14 in Argentina ranks 4th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 61.2 points (October 2026 edition).

What happened Argentina’s Senate approved a rewrite of its 2010 mental health law, 42 votes to 21.

What changes Involuntary treatment is allowed when there is a grave risk to life, not only an imminent one.

What is next The bill now goes to the Chamber of Deputies, which can approve or change it.

Argentina’s Senate passed a mental health reform 42 to 21 on Friday 30 October 2026, making it easier to treat people against their will. The bill came from the government of President Javier Milei, and it now goes to the Chamber of Deputies.

For US readers, the vote shows that Milei can still build a Senate majority, as the chamber also passed an investment-incentives bill that night. It also touches a debate Americans know well, namely when the state may hospitalise someone who refuses care.

In Plain English

Law 26.657, passed in 2010, treats mental illness mainly as a community matter and bans building new psychiatric asylums. It allows hospitalisation against a person’s will only when danger is certain and imminent, a test known in Spanish as riesgo cierto e inminente.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Argentina ranks 4th of 14 with 61.2 points. Strongest pillar: future resources (68); weakest: economic relationships (23). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. WatchRating below investment grade (B-); inflation of 42%; public debt at 80% of GDP. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

Families of people with severe addictions or psychosis have argued for years that this test is too strict and that doctors cannot act in time. The mental health reform answers those complaints, while its critics say it risks bringing back the asylum.

What Happened in the Senate

The Senate approved the mental health reform 42 to 21 after a session that ran past midnight on Thursday 29 October. Debate on the mental health reform began after 10:30 p.m., following votes on the investment bill and a voluntary carbon market bill.

The votes in favour came from Milei’s party La Libertad Avanza (Liberty Advances), the centre-right PRO, the centrist Radical Civic Union and several provincial blocs. The 21 votes against came from the Peronist bloc, the Independencia group and the Convicción Federal group.

Committee chair Ivanna Arrascaeta of La Libertad Avanza summed up the aim as “arriving in time”, meaning acting at grave risk, not imminent danger. She said more than 70 experts, associations and families had addressed the committees.

What the Mental Health Reform Changes

The central change replaces the “certain and imminent” test with “grave risk of harm” to the life or physical integrity of the patient or others. In an emergency, one doctor, preferably a psychiatrist, can order hospitalisation, and an interdisciplinary team must confirm it within 48 hours.

The risk assessment needs two professional signatures, and a judge must be told, so courts keep oversight. A psychiatrist can join by video call where none is available in person.

Hospitals can be general hospitals or specialised psychiatric centres, which the reform treats as legitimate, but building new asylums stays banned. Addictions, including gambling, are folded into mental health policy.

Children and teenagers must be treated by teams trained for their age and housed apart from adults. Every patient needs a discharge plan from the first diagnosis, and a stay longer than 180 days triggers a review by the national oversight body.

Who Opposes the Mental Health Reform

The human rights group Centro de Estudios Legales y Sociales (CELS) says the bill returns to the asylum model. It notes that Argentina has fewer than 5,000 psychiatrists.

Senator Guillermo Andrada, a doctor from the Convicción Federal group, said the 2010 law failed for lack of money, not principles. Senator Gerardo Zamora of Santiago del Estero asked how the new duties would be paid for by provinces that already run the hospitals.

Why It Matters

Argentina is one of the largest economies in South America, and its Congress decides how far Milei’s reform agenda can go. A 42-vote majority for the mental health reform on a hard social issue suggests that the government’s alliances with governors and centrist parties are holding.

The funding clause is the part to watch. The reform says the national government will help provinces through bilateral agreements, with the money written into the national budget.

What It Means for You

If you live in or visit Argentina, nothing changes yet, because the bill is not law. Emergency rules for hospitals stay as they are until both chambers approve the text and the president signs it.

For investors in Argentine assets, the vote is a sign of legislative momentum rather than a market event. It does not change the budget, taxes or the currency.

What Is Not Known

No date is set for the Chamber of Deputies to take up the bill. If Deputies change the text, it goes back to the Senate for a final decision.

The cost of the national support for provinces is not stated in the text of the mental health reform. How many psychiatrists the provinces can add, and how fast, is also open.

More: Argentina news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Argentina’s Senate vote on?

On 30 October 2026 the Senate voted 42 to 21 to rewrite Law 26.657, the 2010 mental health law. The bill was proposed by the government of President Javier Milei.

Does the reform allow people to be hospitalised against their will?

Yes, when there is a grave risk to the life or physical safety of the person or others. One doctor can order it in an emergency, and a team must confirm it within 48 hours.

Is the reform now law?

No, it has passed only one chamber. The Chamber of Deputies must now vote, and the president must sign the final text.

COLOMBIA · ECONOMY

Key Facts The country Colombia, South America’s fourth-largest economy, is led by conservative President Abelardo de la Espriella.

What happened The government filed its 106-article Rescue Law in the lower house on Thursday 29 October 2026.

The goal The bill would cut 2027 spending by about US$12.7 billion, equal to 2.2% of the economy.

The deadline Congress must pass it before its regular session ends on Wednesday 16 December 2026.

Power Index Colombia ranks 6th of 14 in Colombia ranks 6th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 51.9 points (October 2026 edition).

Colombia’s government filed its Rescue Law in Congress on Thursday 29 October 2026, and lawmakers have about six weeks to decide. The bill, in Spanish the Ley de Rescate Económico, would cut about 40 trillion pesos (about US$12.7 billion) of spending in 2027.

For US readers, the Rescue Law tests whether Colombia’s new conservative government can calm debt worries without a revolt in Congress. Our guide to Colombia’s key players explains who holds the votes.

What Happened

Finance Minister Miguel Gómez Martínez and Vice President José Manuel Restrepo delivered the Rescue Law to the lower house on Thursday afternoon. They described five pillars: public finances, a sales tax refund, health care, investment and a smaller state.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Colombia ranks 6th of 14 with 51.9 points. Strongest pillar: military means (91); weakest: diplomatic & cultural influence (28). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. WatchRating below investment grade (BB-); 26 homicides per 100,000; organised crime at 7.8 of 10. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

Restrepo said the previous government of Gustavo Petro left a time bomb, since one of every three tax pesos now pays debt interest. He said about 70% of the effort would come from the state itself and about 30% from the richest tenth of Colombians.

What the Bill Says

The government says the bill cuts professional-services contracts by 50% in 2027 and payroll by 20% in 2028, with the armed forces excluded. It also gives the president extraordinary powers for six months to merge, split or close ministries and agencies.

The government would refund sales tax to about 19 million people, or 38 of every 100 Colombians, through a scheme called EfectIVA. The size of each refund would depend on household income.

Health care would receive 30 trillion pesos (about US$9.5 billion) over four years, according to the government’s summary. Officials have also described tax changes for companies and the wealthiest households, but the exact rates are still being read in the 106 articles.

The Vote Calendar

The Rescue Law starts in the economic committees, the groups of lawmakers who handle money bills, and then goes to the floor of both houses. Regular sessions end on Wednesday 16 December 2026, so the whole path must fit into about six weeks.

The deadline leaves little room for a long fight over the 106 articles. Any delay beyond 16 December would push the bill into a special session or into next year.

Why It Matters

The government says public debt reached 1,185 trillion pesos (about US$377 billion), or 61.4% of output, at the end of September. The finance ministry’s own plan projects a record deficit of 9.4% of output in 2027 if nothing changes.

Economists have already questioned whether such a large cut can be made in one year. Opposition lawmakers are expected to challenge the extraordinary powers, because they would let the president reshape the state without a vote on each change.

What It Means for You

If you hold Colombian bonds or stocks through US funds, the Rescue Law decides whether the government can show a path to a smaller deficit. The peso trades near 3,147 per US dollar, so 1,000 pesos are worth about US$0.32.

Travelers need not change plans, because the bill sets no new rules for visitors. US companies in Colombia should watch the investment pillar, which the government says will offer tax incentives for large new projects.

What Is Not Known

It is not known whether the bill can pass in six weeks, or how many of its 106 articles survive. The government has not yet shown the detailed savings for each measure.

The start date of the sales tax refunds is not settled in the public summaries, and Congress may change the tax rates. It is also unclear whether the extraordinary powers over ministries will clear the constitutional limits that critics cite.

More: Colombia news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What Is Colombia’s Rescue Law?

It is a 106-article bill that would cut about US$12.7 billion of spending in 2027 and refund sales tax to about 19 million people. The government filed it on Thursday 29 October 2026.

When Will Congress Vote on the Rescue Law?

Regular sessions end on Wednesday 16 December 2026, so both houses must finish by then. The committees are expected to start work in the coming weeks.

Does the Rescue Law Raise Taxes?

The government says it also targets about 30% of the effort at the richest tenth of Colombians. It also promises a sales tax refund for poorer households, and Congress may change the details.

World.title: Costa Rica’s Cambronero Bridge to Reopen
World.content:
The Cambronero bridge on Route 1 is scheduled to reopen Tuesday, November 3, restoring traffic through a stretch of the Inter-American Highway closed since a truck damaged the structure in September. The reopening is planned for noon, nearly two weeks ahead of schedule. The bridge is at kilometer 71, on the road connecting San Ramón, Alajuela, with Esparza, Puntarenas.

The crossing has been closed since the night of September 7, when a tractor-trailer struck the modular steel bridge. Crews had to dismantle parts of the structure, replace damaged components and remove and reinstall the bridge deck. Before those repairs could begin, workers built a support tower to hold the bridge’s weight while damaged pieces were removed. Some parts of that temporary support had to be manufactured specifically for the work.

Additional work will continue after the bridge reopens, but those remaining tasks are not expected to interrupt traffic. Drivers should slow down and use caution around crews at the site. The reopening will restore passage through Cambronero while preparations continue for a permanent solution to the ground instability affecting this section of Route 1.

Bids for that project are under review, with construction expected to begin in early 2027. The planned work includes stabilizing the slope, removing the modular bridge and restoring the road’s two lanes. A possible third lane is also being studied, but it has not been approved for construction.

World.title: Tamarindo Celebrates Halloween Weekend With Costume Surfing, Parades and Beach Parties
World.content:
Tamarindo is getting ready for a Halloween weekend that promises everything from surfers riding waves in costumes to trick-or-treating, costume contests, live music and beach parties. The popular Guanacaste destination will host the fifth annual Tamarindo Halloween Fest, with its main celebrations taking place this Friday and Saturday.

Organized by the Tamarindo Development Association (ADIT), the festival brings together local families, tourists, businesses and community organizations for two days of activities designed to offer something for just about everyone. There will be events for children, contests for pets, a nighttime running race and plenty of entertainment for adults looking to celebrate Halloween at the beach.

The celebration has grown since it began in 2022, with Tamarindo’s hotels, restaurants and local businesses joining the festivities. Organizers hope the event will also bring more people to the community before Costa Rica’s busy tourism season gets underway. This year, Halloween falls on a Saturday, giving everyone a full weekend to enjoy the celebrations without having to rush home the next morning.

The main family activities begin Friday at 5 p.m. with a costume parade through downtown Tamarindo, starting near Hotel Tamarindo Diria and continuing toward Parque Oneida, where much of the evening’s entertainment will take place. Children and adults are encouraged to dress up, with costume competitions planned for kids and families. Even dogs will have their chance to compete, as organizers invite pet owners to bring their four-legged companions dressed in Halloween outfits.

The Friday celebration will feature a crazy hair competition, trick-or-treating, music and activities for younger children. The traditional Payasos Los Alegres will also join the parade, bringing a touch of Costa Rican entertainment to the festivities. For those who prefer something a little scarier, Journey School will operate a haunted house at Parque Oneida beginning at 6 p.m. Admission to the haunted house carries a fee, with proceeds supporting scholarships for students at the school.

Those looking for food will find local vendors participating in the Tama Market, offering a variety of dishes and refreshments throughout the evening. A dance competition will add another element to the celebration, with participants performing routines inspired by Halloween characters and popular horror-themed entertainment. Organizers are encouraging groups to put together their most creative performances for a chance to win prizes.

Friday will also feature a recreational 5-kilometer (3.1-mile) race organized by Tama Run. The event combines exercise with Halloween fun, rewarding runners who show up wearing the most creative costumes. After the family celebrations, Tamarindo’s nightlife will take over. Crazy Monkey will host its Haunted Paradise party on Friday beginning at 9 p.m., featuring several DJs and three stages with dancehall, reggaeton and electronic music.

The festivities continue Saturday morning with a free Halloween reading event at the Tamarindo Children’s Community Library. From 10:30 a.m. until 12:30 p.m., children can enjoy themed stories and collect candy. One of the weekend’s most unusual events takes place Saturday afternoon when surfers head into the Pacific Ocean wearing Halloween costumes.

The costume surfing event is scheduled from 3:30 p.m. to 4:30 p.m. in front of Witch’s Rock Surf Camp, bringing together local surfers, instructors, residents and visitors for an afternoon of waves, music and prizes. Participants will be judged in different categories, adding a playful twist to a sport that has helped make Tamarindo one of Costa Rica’s best-known surfing destinations.

Several local surfing organizations are participating, including the Tamarindo Surf Association, the Tamarindo Sports Committee and the North Pacific Surf Association. For anyone who would rather watch than paddle out, the beach will provide a chance to see surfers attempt to catch waves while dressed in costumes not normally associated with the ocean.

Saturday evening will bring another round of parties and competitions. Sharky’s is planning a Halloween celebration with $1,500 in costume prizes, while Iguana Surf and NAIA restaurant will hold a sunset gathering featuring music and additional costume contests. A pickleball tournament organized by 15 Love Tamarindo is also part of the festival’s activities, with prizes that include a two-night hotel stay for two people.

Beyond the entertainment, the festival is intended to support Tamarindo’s tourism businesses during a traditionally slower period of the year. Hotels including Pasatiempo, Mar Rey, Hideaway Costa Rica and Las Guapas are offering special accommodation promotions, with some deals extending into November.

Restaurants and shops are also participating, giving everyone more reasons to spend the weekend in town. Several beachwear and fashion retailers have announced discounts ranging from 10% to 70%. Elizabeth Cole, president of the Tamarindo Development Association, said the goal is to make the community a destination people associate with Halloween celebrations in Costa Rica.

The combination of beaches, restaurants, nightlife and family entertainment makes Tamarindo well suited for a festival that appeals to different age groups, while providing additional business for local merchants ahead of the high season. Although many of the community activities are free, some attractions, races and private parties may require advance registration or paid admission.

Anyone planning to attend should check individual event details, particularly for nighttime entertainment and competitions with limited participation. The main family celebration at Parque Oneida runs from 5 p.m. to 9 p.m. Friday, while the Saturday program offers activities from the morning through late evening.

For travelers already visiting Guanacaste, Halloween weekend provides another reason to spend time in Tamarindo. And for those living in Costa Rica who want something different from the usual Halloween party, watching costumed surfers catch waves in the Pacific might be difficult to beat.

The complete schedule, registration details and any last-minute changes are available through the Tamarindo Development Association’s official website and its social media accounts.

World.title: Costa Rica’s Native Stingless Bees at Center of Supreme Court Fight
World.content:
Costa Rica’s tiny native bees have become the center of a legal battle that could affect beekeepers, honey producers and efforts to protect some of the country’s most important pollinators. The Constitutional Chamber of the Supreme Court (Sala IV), has agreed to review a challenge against government regulations that limit the commercial use of native stingless bees. The case raises questions about whether the rules are protecting biodiversity or making it unnecessarily difficult for people who have raised these insects for generations.

Costa Rica is home to 58 recorded species of native stingless bees, but regulations introduced in November 2025 allow commercial production without additional scientific studies for only two species. Anyone hoping to commercially produce honey, wax or other products from the remaining species must first provide scientific evidence showing that doing so will not threaten their survival.

The legal challenge was accepted last week following a complaint filed by Yandry Johanna Alvarado Castro. The lawsuit questions several provisions of the Executive Decree which regulates facilities where stingless bees are raised and managed. Unlike the familiar European honeybee, Costa Rica’s native stingless bees lack a functional stinger. Many are much smaller, and some live in colonies inside hollow trees, fallen logs and other natural cavities.

Two of the best-known species are the mariola (Tetragonisca angustula) and soncuano (Scaptotrigona pectoralis). Both are included among the species permitted for commercial production under the regulations. Their honey is produced in relatively small quantities and has long been valued by Costa Rican families, particularly in rural communities where raising native bees has been passed down through generations.

The practice is known as meliponiculture, a type of beekeeping that focuses on stingless bees rather than the imported honeybees commonly used in large-scale commercial honey production. But these insects do much more than produce honey. They pollinate native plants and agricultural crops, helping forests regenerate and supporting the reproduction of vegetation throughout the country.

That ecological importance is one reason the government introduced the regulations. Officials say the rules are intended to protect native bee populations, prevent overexploitation and preserve genetic diversity. However, beekeepers and researchers have questioned whether some of the restrictions are supported by sufficient scientific evidence.

One of the most controversial measures limits commercial operations to 30 colonies and noncommercial operations to just five. The legal challenge argues that these limits fail to consider differences between species, regional environmental conditions and the availability of food sources.

A beekeeper working in the humid forests of Limón, for example, may face very different conditions from someone maintaining colonies in the dry forests of Guanacaste. Critics argue that applying identical limits to both operations may not make sense without additional research.

The regulations also require beekeepers to maintain minimum distances between their colonies and agricultural operations using pesticides. Depending on the size of the bee species, those distances range from 500 meters (1,640 feet) to 3.5 kilometers (2.2 miles). Even greater distances are required in some circumstances, including where aerial spraying takes place.

Although the intention is to protect bees from potentially dangerous chemicals, the lawsuit questions how those distances were established and whether they are practical for small farmers and rural families. Researchers at the National University’s Tropical Bee Research Center (CINAT) have also raised concerns about the scientific basis for the restrictions.

Of the 58 native stingless-bee species recorded in Costa Rica, researchers have documented 20 species being maintained in managed colonies. That is considerably more than the two species covered by the regulation’s simpler commercial approval process. Specialists agree that native bees need protection but have warned that more information is required before deciding how many colonies should be allowed or which species are appropriate for commercial production.

For traditional beekeepers, the rules could have financial consequences. Some families maintain several species and depend on the sale of small quantities of honey and other products to supplement their income. Others raise bees primarily to preserve traditional knowledge and maintain healthy populations of pollinators on their properties.

The National Chamber of Stingless Beekeepers has previously called for additional species to be included in the regulations, particularly the jicote gato (Melipona beecheii) and jicote barcino (Melipona costarricensis). The organization and other critics argue that overly restrictive rules could discourage beekeepers from registering their operations and push some producers into the informal market.

Another concern involves potential penalties. The lawsuit challenges provisions that refer violations to Costa Rica’s Wildlife Conservation Law, arguing that beekeepers could face legal uncertainty over activities involving insects that naturally move between managed colonies and the surrounding environment. The case now moves forward in the Constitutional Chamber, where judges will examine whether the disputed rules comply with Costa Rica’s Constitution and environmental protections.

The court has given the Attorney General’s Office and the ministries of Environment and Energy and the Presidency 15 days to respond to the legal challenge. Importantly, accepting the case does not mean the judges have ruled against the regulations. The existing requirements remain in effect while the court considers the arguments.

Beekeepers also face a registration deadline in November 2026, when the 12-month period established under the regulations is scheduled to expire. The dispute comes at a time when Costa Rica is already confronting broader concerns about the survival of native bees. Earlier this year, the Constitutional Chamber ordered authorities to enforce a nationwide ban on insecticides containing fipronil after a separate case involving damage to bee colonies in Lepanto, Puntarenas.

The complainants in that case reported losing at least 24 native bee colonies and serious damage to hundreds of additional hives. The ruling highlighted the risks that agricultural chemicals can pose to pollinators and reinforced the importance of protecting native insects that play an essential role in Costa Rica’s ecosystems.

For now, the latest legal dispute presents a difficult question for authorities: how to protect native bees without placing unnecessary burdens on the people who raise and care for them. With dozens of native species, a long tradition of small-scale beekeeping and an economy closely connected to agriculture and conservation, Costa Rica has considerable interest in finding the right balance.

The Supreme Court’s eventual ruling could help determine how the country manages its native bees for years to come, affecting not only honey producers but also the forests and farms that depend on these small but valuable pollinators.

World.title: Costa Rica’s President Invites Pope Leo XIV to Visit in 2027
World.content:
President Laura Fernández formally invited Pope Leo XIV to visit Costa Rica during a private audience at the Vatican, proposing a trip in 2027 that would make him the first pontiff to set foot in the country since John Paul II in March 1983. Fernández delivered the invitation in a letter and handed it to the pope in person at the Apostolic Palace. In it, she extended what she called a fraternal and respectful invitation on behalf of the people and government of Costa Rica, describing the country as a land where work and peace prevail.

The letter ties the proposed visit to two anniversaries Costa Rica will mark in 2027. One is the 203rd anniversary of the declaration of Our Lady of the Angels, known here as La Negrita, the patron saint. The other is the 180th anniversary of the Constitution recognizing Catholicism as the official religion of the state.

No date has been set and the letter leaves the timing to the pope, and Fernández offered to coordinate preparations for an eventual pastoral and official visit through the Vatican’s Secretariat of State and the Apostolic Nunciature in San José. The Vatican has not said whether the pope will accept.

Fernández also presented the pope with a replica of the Virgin of the Angels and coffees from several Costa Rican growing regions. It is not the first time Costa Rican coffee has reached Leo XIV. Speaking to Catholic media after the meeting, Fernández said she had invited the pope to come and greet La Negrita, and that it would be very special for Costa Rica to receive a pope again after 1983. She said the conversation lasted about 30 minutes, that she told him Costa Ricans had been praying for him, and that she felt at home.

She added that the pope appeared in good spirits and in good health following a recent medical procedure, though she said the two did not discuss his recovery directly. The Holy See Press Office said in a statement after the audience that Fernández also met with Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Vatican secretary of state, and Archbishop Paul Richard Gallagher, secretary for relations with states and international organizations.

According to the statement, those talks highlighted good relations between the Holy See and Costa Rica and between the state and the local Church and covered social and political issues in the country and the region, particularly security and migration. Fernández said she discussed with the pope the situation of Nicaraguan migrants, the largest migrant group in Costa Rica, as well as cooperation with the United States on people going through deportation proceedings.

On security, she said her government pairs investment in education, health and support for young people with measures against organized crime, including efforts to stop inmates from directing violence from inside prisons. The audience came two weeks after Fernández toured El Salvador’s CECOT mega-prison, and as Costa Rica moves inmates into its own maximum-security facility, the CACCO.

Bishop Bartolomé Buigues of Alajuela, vice president of the Costa Rican Episcopal Conference, said closer engagement between the Church and civil authorities is of great importance. The bishops’ conference thanked the president for promoting the meeting. The Vatican stop opened Fernández’s third official trip abroad since taking office in May, following visits to El Salvador and Colombia. Her schedule in Rome also includes a meeting with Italian President Sergio Mattarella.

She then travels to Madrid for the 30th Ibero-American Summit of Heads of State and Government on Nov. 4 and 5 and is scheduled to return to Costa Rica on Nov. 6. A papal visit would carry particular weight in a country where devotion to La Negrita draws pilgrims from every province to the Basilica of Our Lady of the Angels in Cartago each August. John Paul II’s 1983 stop, part of a tour of Central America, remains the last time a pope visited the country.

World.title: 46 US Veterans Tried Ayahuasca in Costa Rica, Where Rules Remain Murky
World.content:
Forty-six American military veterans and first responders spent a week at an ayahuasca retreat in Guanacaste in September, hoping the Amazonian brew would ease trauma they carried home from combat zones and emergency scenes. Their accounts, published Wednesday by the New York Post, describe former Army Rangers and Navy SEALs weeping in ceremony tents and returning home calmer.

The stories are moving. They also land in a place where the Ministry of Health has spent nearly two years warning the public against therapeutic ayahuasca use, while the best-known center that serves it holds a ministry authorization the ministry itself tried, and failed, to cancel.

The retreat ran from Sept. 5 to 12 at Rythmia Life Advancement Center near Tamarindo, in the area of Santa Cruz, spanning the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 attacks. It was organized with The Coming Home Project, a nonprofit founded in 2021 by Navy SEAL veteran Nate Brown to combat veteran suicide, and funded largely by the Birds Eye View Project, a Texas veterans charity, according to the organizers.

The Post put the group at 46, while a September press release from the organizers said 47 took part. Days combined yoga, individual and group counseling, classes and meditation, with ayahuasca ceremonies held at night in tents. Rythmia and Coming Home reviewed each participant’s medical history, medications and mental health beforehand, the Post reported.

The need behind such efforts is stark. A 2026 Department of Veterans Affairs report counted 6,488 veteran suicides in 2024, an average of nearly 18 a day. Participants described the week as a turning point. A 44-year-old firefighter and former Army Ranger, identified only as Dave L., told the Post that the constant inner conflict he lived with had grown much quieter since he returned home. He stopped short of calling a single retreat a cure.

Jeff McNairy, Rythmia’s chief medical officer and a psychiatrist, told the paper that trauma is the condition he considers ayahuasca best suited to treat. He said roughly half the participants vomited on any given night, a reaction the center describes as a psychosomatic release of trauma.

What the coverage does not include is outcome data. No standardized symptom scores, follow-up assessments or comparison group were reported for the group. Rythmia advertises a self-reported success rate above 97% among more than 23,000 guests since 2016, a figure drawn from its own guest surveys rather than independent clinical measurement.

The broader research is promising but young. An observational study run with the nonprofit Heroic Hearts Project followed 58 veterans who attended ayahuasca or psilocybin retreats in Peru and Jamaica between 2021 and 2024. Its research director, neuroscientist Grace Blest-Hopley, has said more than 80% of those who entered with PTSD no longer met the diagnostic criteria afterward.

The study’s published averages were more modest, with PTSD symptom scores falling about 26% among the ayahuasca group. Researchers at the University of Texas are now studying how brain responses in combat veterans change after ayahuasca treatment. None of this yet amounts to the large controlled trials regulators require before approving a treatment.

The risks are well documented. About 70% of users experience acute nausea and more than half report unsettling psychological effects, according to research cited by the Post. Combined with common SSRI antidepressants, the brew can trigger serotonin syndrome, which can be fatal, and it can provoke prolonged psychosis in people with underlying psychiatric vulnerabilities.

Those medications and histories are common among veterans with PTSD, which is why screening matters as much as the ceremony itself. Costa Rica has no law written for this industry. In January 2025 the Ministry of Health issued a health warning on ayahuasca and ibogaine, urging the public not to consume or promote either for therapeutic purposes, not to join rituals that use psychoactive substances for healing, and to report anyone offering them.

The ministry said no product based on either plant holds the sanitary registration it requires. Rythmia is the exception, and an awkward one. The center promotes itself as the world’s only medically licensed ayahuasca center, with a round-the-clock medical team that McNairy said includes five doctors and 12 registered nurses.

According to a February 2025 opinion from the Attorney General’s Office (PGR), the Ministry of Health told Rythmia in July 2022 that it could keep using ayahuasca for therapeutic purposes on a temporary basis until a regulation was issued. In October 2024, Health Minister Mary Munive asked the PGR to endorse annulling that authorization.

The PGR declined and said the ministry’s request contained extremely serious errors, including a failure to identify which rules the authorization violated, and noted that no regulation governed or banned ayahuasca when the permission was granted. It is not clear whether the ministry has revisited the case since.

Elsewhere, safeguards vary widely. A study published in January in JAMA Network Open interviewed representatives of 49 publicly advertised psychedelic retreat organizations, most of them based in the United States. About seven in 10 worked with a licensed health professional or someone trained in emergency response, but only about two-thirds had such a person present at retreats even some of the time.

By one estimate, Costa Rica hosts about 80 psychedelic retreat centers, some 60 of them offering ayahuasca, making it the second most popular destination for this kind of travel after Peru.

The consequences of thin oversight have already been felt here. Lauren Levis, a 40-year-old social worker from New Mexico, died in August 2024 after taking iboga at Soul Centro, a retreat in Paquera on the Nicoya Peninsula. Her brother has said she collapsed in a shower after an all-night ceremony, and that an electrocardiogram taken before the retreat showed marked abnormalities, yet she was allowed to attend.

Judicial investigators sent their findings to prosecutors in March 2025, nearly eight months after her death. A Norwegian woman died after taking ibogaine at another facility near Liberia in 2014. The veterans’ relief may prove genuine, and researchers are working to measure how much of it lasts. For now, the safeguards around ayahuasca in Costa Rica depend largely on the operators who serve it.

Researchers who study the retreat industry advise anyone weighing one to ask for a written medical screening that covers heart conditions, psychiatric history and every medication, a medical professional on site rather than on call, a clear emergency plan with transport to the nearest hospital, and straight answers about the legal status of what is being served. Medical experts also warn that safely tapering off antidepressants can take six to 12 weeks under supervision, far longer than many retreats allow.

World.title: All Three VIP Lounges at Juan Santamaría Airport Close Sunday
World.content:
If you are flying out of Juan Santamaría International Airport this Sunday, Nov. 1, plan on waiting at the gate. All three VIP lounges at Costa Rica’s main airport will be closed that day, and one of them has no date to reopen. The closures start Saturday, Oct. 31, and each lounge is on a different schedule. BAC Credomatic said the special hours are the result of an operational adjustment scheduled by the airport’s management and outside the bank’s control.

Here is how each lounge is affected:

Lounge BAC closes at 6 p.m. Saturday, Oct. 31, two hours earlier than usual. It reopens at 4 a.m. Monday, Nov. 2. That is 34 hours without service.

closes at 6 p.m. Saturday, Oct. 31, two hours earlier than usual. It reopens at 4 a.m. Monday, Nov. 2. That is 34 hours without service. VIP Santamaría , next to Gate 5, closes for Sunday, Nov. 1, only.

, next to Gate 5, closes for Sunday, Nov. 1, only. VIP Lounge Costa Rica, the Mastercard lounge that also operates as the Copa Club, closes Saturday, Oct. 31, until further notice.

That last closure is the one to watch. If you usually get in with a Mastercard card or a Priority Pass membership, you will lose that option for an open-ended period. The lounge’s own notice gives no reopening date, and Priority Pass now lists it as temporarily closed from Oct. 31 until further notice.

Aeris, the company that runs the airport, has not said what the adjustment involves. Asked whether the lounges would change operators, the company said it recognizes the lounges as an important part of the airport experience. It added that any official information will be released through its own channels.

The lounges normally open from 4:30 a.m. to 8 p.m. Priority Pass also lists VIP Santamaría as undergoing renovation work, and warns that space may be limited even when it is open. Nothing announced so far affects flight schedules. If you were counting on lounge food or a quiet place to work this weekend, eat before you head to the airport and bring a charged phone and laptop.

Check with your bank or lounge program before you leave home, since access rules differ from one lounge to the next. If you are heading to the United States, you will also need to sign a new passenger form starting Nov. 3. The lounge closures come a week after a power failure disrupted the airport’s control tower. From Monday, the BAC and VIP Santamaría lounges are expected back on normal hours. The Mastercard lounge may stay closed well beyond that.

World.title: Elena Rybakina Clinches Year-End World No. 1 Ranking After Tokyo Victory
World.content:
Elena Rybakina has won the year-end World No. 1 ranking for the first time in her career, defeating fellow Kazakh Yulia Putintseva 6-2, 6-3 at the Pan Pacific Open in Tokyo on Thursday. The 27-year-old needed just one more victory to guarantee that Aryna Sabalenka could not overtake her before the end of the season.
