World.title: Got beef? When politics meets meat
World.content:
Meat remains firmly at the center of the culture wars, especially in the U.S.

Trump this week poked fun at James Talarico, the Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate in Texas, saying he was absent from the campaign trail after being “food poisoned by meat ’cause he can’t stand it.”

Talarico has, in Republican eyes, committed the terrible crime of being a vegan. But the small issue there is that Talarico has said on multiple occasions that he is not vegan, or even vegetarian for that matter, and there are photos of him eating meat.

That doesn’t seem to matter, though, because the Venn diagram of vegans and members of the MAGA movement is presumably just two separate circles — especially in Texas, where the state vegetable is steak. The implication is that if you don’t eat meat, and preferably lots of it, you are somehow weak (not an issue here at POLITICO Towers, where we have kebabs available 24/7).

Trump, of course, has a famously balanced diet, with his favorite meal being two Big Macs, two Filet-O-Fish and a large chocolate milkshake.

And speaking of rump, Trump also used this week’s campaign speeches to comment on the “one hell of a beautiful ass” of rapper Nicki Minaj. “That’s hard to miss,” added the president of the United States of America.

World.title: Burnham tries to avoid a slavery reparations ‘disaster’
World.content:
The visit will be a test of how Burnham — who has a reputation for speaking off the cuff, especially on issues of moral justice — maintains a delicate U.K. government line that reparations are not “the answer,” as Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told POLITICO last month. And Burnham will face that challenge in a unique spotlight: It will be his first overseas visit with King Charles III, who is the head of the Commonwealth.

POLITICO spoke to a dozen U.K. officials or politicians who were involved in the 2024 summit or the planning for Burnham’s upcoming visit. They painted a picture of acute anxiety in the British state over how to deal with calls for reparations from its former colonies; tensions between Downing Street and the Foreign Office over the handling of 2024; and serious questions in Whitehall about whether the summit is even useful for No. 10 — despite the king’s role leaving U.K. prime ministers little choice but to attend.

Burnham will not have to deal with the extreme jetlag and communications hurdles that dogged Starmer’s trip, which involved a 28-hour flight in each direction. But like Starmer, he will fly out at a time when his in-tray is crowded by other issues — not least the U.S. midterms happening at the same time and the domestic aftermath of his first budget, just unveiled this past Wednesday.

Keir Starmer attends a a state banquet during the CHOGM summit in Samoa, on Oct. 24, 2024. | Pool photo by Fiona Goodall via Getty Images

The first U.K. official quoted earlier in this story said: “There’s a sense that there can’t be a repeat of [2024] this time around.” The third U.K. official quoted above said: “I don’t understand why they’re making the same mistake. Does the prime minister really have to go?”

A No. 10 official, however, said Burnham made clear soon after taking power on July 20 that he was “very keen” to attend the summit. Miliband has “laid the groundwork so that things hopefully won’t be as tricky as they were in 2024,” this person added.

“Andy’s style is that he is an honest broker with people, and he will give an instinctive response to things,” the official said. “But the government’s position is clear that reparations are not seen as the right route. It’s a careful balancing act, but one that we’re well prepared for.”

World.title: Who’s afraid of whom in Brussels?
World.content:
Here’s our guide to who is terrified of whom in the Brussels bubble.

Everyone is scared of Marine Le Pen

The person haunting EU diplomats, officials and lawmakers is French presidential front-runner Marine Le Pen. Will she really halve Paris’ contribution to the EU budget, as promised? Will she pull Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni away from the Brussels mainstream? And will she demand von der Leyen’s head?

The bubble had warmed (slightly) to the idea of Jordan Bardella in the Élysée Palace, after his years leading the National Rally’s European operation revealed a certain pragmatism toward Brussels — only for those hopes to be shattered when a Paris appeals court cleared Le Pen to be a candidate for the presidency.

The next ECB chief is scared of Jean-Luc Mélenchon

The European Central Bank president is the euro’s last line of defense against unorthodox national economic decisions — but that could be tested by French presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who is on course to reach the runoff after vowing to set billions of euros of French debt “on fire.” His incendiary plan calls on the Frankfurt-based ECB to waive interest payments on a vast tranche of French bonds — an unorthodox, perhaps impossible, maneuver that critics warn could even see France kicked out of the euro.

Now that we know Christine Lagarde will step down as ECB president in February, what France’s presidential candidates want to do about its monumental debt pile will haunt the race for her successor, with Dutchman Klaas Knot and Spaniard Pablo Hernández de Cos as the two frontrunners.

Lobbyists are scared of ChatGPT

The number of amendments lawmakers have filed has exploded since generative AI arrived, with key EU laws now facing thousands of proposed text changes. Parliament officials don’t think it’s a coincidence, with some pointing to amendments written in suspiciously bot-like language, and others saying sometimes amendments cite legislation that does not even exist.

World.title: Britain by numbers: everything we don’t know about the country
World.content:
Budgets are all about numbers: growth, inflation, unemployment, headroom. So this week on Westminster Insider, Sascha and Pat look into the numbers behind Britain’s economy — and just how much government policy is really made up of guesswork, rather than solid measurements.

Sascha talks to Dr Laura Gilbert, the former director of data at Number 10 Downing Street, who explains exactly why the numbers we have on measurements like immigration or the workforce are often wrong by hundreds of thousands of people.

Ben Warner, who was chief advisor on data and digital at Number 10 during the pandemic, explains why this uncertainty spells chaos for political decision-making and says he believes most ministers don’t know how to use data.

World.title: Canada and Europe share challenge of diversifying without antagonizing US and China
World.content:
One of the core EU interests in Canada, the official explained, is a chance for the bloc to diversify its supply of critical raw materials and sources of energy to further reduce its dependence on China and Russia, respectively.

“They have most of what we need,” the official said about Canadian minerals. “There’s also a huge opportunity to bring Canadian fossil fuels and gas to the EU.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney dismissed the controversy over whether the EU should label the relationship with Canada as an “associate membership,” saying on Thursday it was a sideshow to what’s been billed as a landmark summit.

Earlier this week, Germany, France, Greece and other countries opposed the definition in a joint EU-Canada statement to be issued in Montreal. That came after European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen put forward the “associate membership” label in September.

But Carney told reporters on Thursday that the new alliance wasn’t “a marketing exercise” and that the name doesn’t matter. “What matters is that the complementarities of our two jurisdictions strengthen our sovereignty, strengthen Europe’s sovereignty, various strategic autonomies, critical minerals, energy, other aspects — AI,” he said.

A tricky political road lies ahead as Carney and von der Leyen make moves to draw the EU and Canada closer in a partnership that doesn’t include its southern neighbor. They’ll need to tiptoe forward with an “association without accession” work plan in the last years of the U.S. President Donald Trump’s time in office.

World.title: DR Congo: MSF celebrates Ebola patient discharges in Ituri province
World.content:
Health workers and local residents danced and sang outside an Ebola treatment centre in Mongbwalu, in the Democratic Republic of Congo's Ituri province, to celebrate the discharge of its last remaining patients. In footage published by Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) on 28 October, staff and members of the community gather outside the facility, moving to the rhythm of the celebrations.

 

According to the medical charity, it is the first time since May that the centre has had no confirmed Ebola patients under treatment. The joyful scenes mark a welcome moment for healthcare workers and residents in a region that has been grappling with the deadly virus for months.

The celebrations come despite the continuing Ebola epidemic in the region. On 27 October, Congolese health authorities reported that Africa's latest outbreak had surpassed 10,000 confirmed cases, the vast majority recorded in the Democratic Republic of Congo.

Ebola is a severe viral disease that can cause life-threatening illness and spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of infected people. Although the discharge of the final patients represents an important milestone for the MSF facility in Mongbwalu, it does not mean the outbreak has ended or that new cases cannot emerge. The charity's announcement concerns patients being treated at this particular centre, rather than the wider situation across Ituri province or the country.

World.title: ‘A living hell’: The occupied town of Oleshky captures the world’s attention — including Melania Trump’s
World.content:
But first some news: Former Ukrainian Prime Minister Arseniy Yatseniuk just told Europe Today that “there is no way to trust Russians” over an ongoing temporary ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia focussed on one small town.

 

“What is happening right now in Oleshky is a humanitarian disaster and it's actually a living hell,” he said of the Russian-occupied community on the morning programme. Watch.

As Sasha Vakulina writes, a rare humanitarian mission is expected to reach the Russian-occupied Oleshky, the town Yatseniuk is referring to, on Friday to change this. It would mark the first operation of its kind in years, with evacuations of residents and aid distribution scheduled to last until the afternoon. An accompanying ceasefire for the town to make this operation possible lasts until Sunday.

But for around 2,000 residents, the deadline presents a frightening choice: risk leaving through Russia or occupied Crimea, without assurances they can reach Ukrainian-controlled territory, or remain in a town where basic necessities are increasingly scarce.

Tetiana Hasanenko, head of the Oleshky city military administration, previously painted a frightening picture to Euronews of the situation on-the-ground. “People have been forced to eat weeds,” she said. “The city is practically destroyed.”

Help from Washington? The humanitarian mission was agreed to with the involvement of US First Lady Melania Trump. Despite the good tidings, however, the former Ukrainian prime minister has accused Moscow of using civilians as "hostages" and staging the humanitarian operation to portray itself as their rescuer.

All eyes will be on Oleshky to see if the operation goes off without a hitch.

Another bloody conflict: "We're not leaving. We're going to stay. We will resist," said Mustafa Barghouti, General Secretary of the Palestinian National Initiative, speaking about Palestinians living under the immense weight of far-right Israeli sentiment. The United Nations Independent International Commission of Inquiry found Israel committed genocide in the Gaza Strip.

Barghouti was speaking on Europe Today in the wake of the Israeli legislative elections on Tuesday, which, among other things, showed Arab parties making immense gains. But does this win forebode any future for the two-state solution, and hope for peace?

"The only way to save the two-state solution is to remove the illegal Israeli settlements from the West Bank," he said. This has been made more challenging due to the the "lack of response" from the international community to apply sanctions on Israel for these actions, Barghouti said. Watch.

Meet me in Montréal: The second day of the EU-Canada summit kicks off Friday with a meeting between European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, European Council President António Costa and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney.

The love-in is expected to expand cooperation across multiple areas, including trade, investment, supply chains, AI, quantum, and other topics, most notably support for Ukraine.

Context matters: Much of the meeting will occur in the long shadow of US President Donald Trump, whose abrasive “America First” policies and turbulent policies towards Kyiv have brought the two sides closer, making this summit possible, Jorge Liboreiro writes in a curtain-raiser.

What's noticeable, however, is that von der Leyen dug her heels in and renewed her push to make Canada the bloc’s first-ever “associate member”. This is despite a forceful push by Germany that killed the wording from the joint declaration. Speaking at an event in Montréal, the Commission president described her pitch as a “new frontier together”. “Our idea is simple: it is an association without accession,” von der Leyen said.

Try to keep up: In the hours following, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz published a cryptic tweet endorsing the “alliance for the future” concept instead.

But then Carney threw a spanner in the works by declaring that “we’re in the process of forging a new alliance for the future, with Canada as an associate member”. So, is the idea of “associate membership” dead, and should it be resuscitated? Luca Bertuzzi explores.

The summit’s concluding press conference is scheduled for 5:25pm CET, which should hopefully answer these questions.

Did the EU just get its own ICE? The EU's border and coastguard agency, Frontex, is set to gain unprecedented powers to deport irregular migrants, monitor social media and respond to mass arrivals at EU borders under a sweeping reform proposed by the European Commission.

According to reporting by Vincenco Genovese, the overhaul would significantly expand Frontex's mandate, triple its workforce and give it a much greater role in deportations beyond EU territory. How’s that for a Halloween scare?

But the proposal has already sparked controversy, with critics warning that the agency's expanded powers and budget could lead to further fundamental rights violations and intrusive surveillance. For Member of the European Parliament Cecilia Strada, it inches closer towards resembling Trump’s controversial ICE operation.

Trouble in Albania: Albania introduced heavy fines on Wednesday for people present at demonstrations that turn violent. It comes as officials in Tirana try to manage daily protests demanding the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama in the capital.

The fines — which can go as high as 500,000 leks (€5,500) — are not limited to people directly engaged in violence and will be imposed on "anyone who chooses to remain in a crowd" that is carrying out acts of violence or looting in a public space, or that is "concealing their identity". Important to note: The average monthly salary before tax in Albania stands at €930.

Albania has seen months of anti-government protests, with demonstrations in recent days escalating into clashes between protesters and security forces on the streets of Tirana. It follows trends of similar public demonstrations gripping France, Spain and Belgium.

Taking a leaf out of Paris’ note: Rama said he had drawn inspiration from a French bill passed by the upper house of parliament on Wednesday, which would hold protesters financially responsible for damage caused during demonstrations.

In France, the proposed legislation would require protesters to pay up to €10,000 for damage caused during demonstrations.

This is important because: Next week the Commission will deliver scorecards for each EU accession country, such as Albania. Will the elephantine fines factor into the report, and is the bloc’s enlargement boss, Marta Kos, taking stock? Time will tell.

Brussels hopes unspent defence loans may help plug Ukraine’s budget hole

The European Commission has opened a new round of low-interest defence loans and is urging member states to spend them on joint ventures with Ukraine, as Kyiv faces a €70 billion budget gap.

On Thursday, €21.3 billion of unspent funding under the Security Action for Europe (SAFE), the EU’s financing programme for strategic defence investment, was made available, with the Commission hoping to steer some of it towards Ukraine.

“Using the remaining funds from SAFE, we will be setting up a new programme for joint projects with Ukrainian companies,” Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said in her annual State of the Union address to the European Parliament last month.

Is this hot air, or will Kyiv actually get the defensive capabilities it has been promised? Luca unpacks it all in this story.

More from our newsrooms

Deadly train crash puts Sánchez on the ropes a month before elections. Wednesday's accident happened in the middle of the pre-election campaign, adding pressure to Sánchez's government. With a month to go, parties are locked in a blame game. Christina Thykjaer has the analysis.

‘I cannot remain neutral’: Lagarde finally explains her early ECB exit. Christine Lagarde is leaving the European Central Bank (ECB) early because she no longer wants to stay silent. Piero Cingari explores why.

EU countries push back against Brussels plan to tax gas more than electricity. More than a dozen EU countries are challenging Brussels' plans to favour electricity over gas, warning that the proposals would undermine national control over energy taxation and grid charges. Marta Pacheco has more.

We’re also keeping an eye on

The final day of the EU-Canada summit wraps up in Montreal. Press conference to be expected at 5:45pm CET.

European Commissioner for the Economy Valdis Dombrovskis represents the EU at the NATO Fuse event in Riga.

European Commissioner for Equality, Preparedness and Crisis Management Hadja Lahbib visits Brussels’ famed Manneken Pis and Jeanneke Pis ahead of the European Civil Protection Forum.

That’s it for today. Sasha Vakulina, Jorge Liboreiro and Vincenzo Genovese contributed to this newsletter.

World.title: Netanyahu bloc first but without majority as Arab parties hold balance of power in Israel election
World.content:
Final results from Israel's pivotal legislative election this week showed there was no clear winner, with both of the two main blocs well short of a majority in the 120-seat Knesset.

 

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc finished on 53 seats, while the opposition camp, led by the centrist Yashar party of rival Gadi Eisenkot, ended on 48.

Netanyahu's right-wing Likud party remained the largest party, with 27 seats, while the Arab parties secured a record 19 seats between them.

The result means Israel is now set to face a lengthy and likely tricky period of negotiations as party leaders work to form a government. Failure to do so would see Israelis head back to the polls.

‘Ra’am-gate’

Netanyahu has accused Arab parties of "stealing" the election, calling on police and Israel's domestic security service Shin Bet to carry out a "thorough investigation into election fraud."

The Likud party also pushed claims that foreign funding had been used to influence voters in the election. The allegations focused on claims that the Ra'am party had received money from Qatar.

"The ‘Ra’am-gate’ scandal is an earthquake. The Israeli elections have been stolen," Likud said in a statement on Thursday.

Ra'am party leader Mansour Abbas reportedly denied any wrongdoing and said he would welcome an investigation.

In a post on social media, Eisenkot said foreign interference was "unacceptable and extremely serious" and called on Shin Bet to investigate the allegations "fully and immediately, without bias."

Next steps

Moving forward, Israeli President Isaac Herzog will consult with leaders of the parties elected to the Knesset before assigning the task of trying to form a government to the candidate he believes has the best chance of securing sufficient support to do so.

Under Israeli law, that individual will have 28 days to carry out the job. The president is able to extend this by a maximum of 14 days if necessary.

Should that fail, the president can give a second leader the chance to form a government, this time with a maximum deadline of 28 days. If this second round were also to fail, then the Knesset can request a third candidate be given a go. They would have 14 days to complete the task.

If all attempts fail, another election is called.

World.title: Knot for eating: Welcome to the Italian restaurant where every meal is knitted
World.content:
Layers of lasagna bursting with bolognese, pistachio-filled cannoli dusted in icing sugar, and a seductive slab of pillowy tiramisu.

 

These are just some of the mouth-watering dishes available at Kate Jenkins' new 'Knitalian' restaurant.

But here's the catch: none of them are edible.

Instead, Jenkins has knitted, crocheted, embroidered and sewed every single recipe, hand-crafting a feast of fiber art for her new exhibition at the Air Contemporary gallery in London, United Kingdom.

The gallery has been re-modelled accordingly, fitted with traditional trattoria-style gingham tablecloths, rustic wall art and a giant gelato fridge. If it weren't for a lack of baked dough wafting through the air, you could almost swear you've teleported from the bustling streets of Soho to a charming Italian deli.

An interior view of 'Kate's Knitalian'. Kate Jenkins

This immersive element is an integral part of Jenkins' work, which has previously included knitted replicas of fishmongers, bakeries, supermarkets, bagel bars and more.

Her latest installation feels much more personal, however — inspired by frequent trips to Italy with her Italian partner.

"I always feel inspired [in Italy] because there's so much culture there in terms of food," Jenkins told Euronews Culture.

"There are all these amazing different parts of Italy and they're famous for different things. So, looking at the food culture in Venice, you've got cicchetti, which is like the equivalent of the tapas. And then there's Crotone, which is famous for its red onions."

The diversity of Italy's foods combined with Jenkins' interest in their subtle regional differences became a starting point for a year-long project that features more than a thousand fabric food and drink replicas.

The knitted tiramisu was one of the most complex foods to complete. Kate Jenkins

Among them are slices of salami, various cheeses, bottles of Chianti, and hundreds of individual pasta pieces in bowls. No detail is left untouched, with Jenkins treating the process of knitting a lasagna as if she was actually cooking one.

It requires really looking at how things are constructed and then breaking it down and then rebuilding it. Kate Jenins British artist

"I was knitting the sheets of pasta, then making the Ragú, so that's crocheted, and then layering it all up, as you would when you're making your own cooked lasagna," Jenkins explains.

"It requires really looking at how things are constructed and then breaking it down and then rebuilding it, but knitted."

Getting the colours and textures correct also required endless experimentation, mixing yarns and trialling different stitch techniques to make it look as believable as possible.

"Making things like ravioli, it has to have a certain puffiness to it, and then it's got the little serrated edge and that has to be a certain stitch," she said.

"Or when I'm making an ice cream cone that's a 3D waffle structure, there's some things I use a crochet technique for and then others I'll use a knitting machine to get it to look right."

Knitted cannoli (knot for eating) © Emma Wood/Kate Jenkins

Ever since her grandma taught her how to knit as a child, the craft has been a major part of Jenkins' life.

She began her career as a knitwear designer in the late '90s, working with big fashion designers including Ralph Lauren, Marc Jacobs and Kate Spade before later founding her own label, Cardigan.

Then, while brainstorming ways to promote an accessories line, she started knitting foods — mostly for fun, but also as a way to get people to view things in a different way.

It proved so popular that Jenkins was able to open her first food-themed exhibition in 2007, 'Comfort Food', which ultimately changed the entire trajectory of her career.

"I think people love seeing food," she said, believing there's something universally joyful about seeing and creating replicas of pre-existing things.

"I find it very satisfying once I've set myself a goal and I go, right, I'm going to make a bagel and make it look identical to an actual bagel."

Exhibition guests can visit a build-your-own pizza station. Kate Jenkins.

The exhibition also opens at a time when so-called "grandma hobbies" like knitting have soared in popularity among younger generations, with 86% of Gen Z now identifying as "crafters" or "makers", according to a survey by Mintel Group Ltd.

"The internet has opened the world up to people being able to learn online," Jenkins said.

"It's amazing and I can see why there's such a massive interest because it's more accessible and it's not too taxing. You don't need massive amount of tools or money to make something."

The communal nature of crafty hobbies has also allowed Jenkins to make her exhibitions more sociable and interactive, encouraging people to knit their own cakes at her 2022 'Cafe Kate' show in the Netherlands.

"It's nice to have that excitement, for people to go and just hang out and do a bit of knitting, or feel absorbed in the exhibition in that way."

There's a similar sense of conviviality at 'Kate's Knitalian', although guests can rest assured they won't need any knitting (or cooking) skills to visit the build-your-own-pizza station.

They will, however, need to exercise a lot of self-restraint not to take a bite out of anything...

'Kate's Knitalian' opens at Air Contemporary gallery in London, United Kingdom, from 30 October until 5 December 2026.

World.title: Inside Copenhagen’s swanky new ‘water culture house’ with 10 pools, three saunas and an onsen
World.content:
Rain or shine (or even snow), nothing can get between Danes and going for a swim.

 

Soon, Copenhagen residents will have a new spot for doing so – and it’s seriously swanky.

Part of a wider project to revitalise Copenhagen Harbour, KAI will open on Paper Island on 5 December.

Designed by Japanese practice Kengo Kuma & Associates, the name is both a reference to the Japanese word for sea and the Danish word for quay (kaj), a nod to its location.

Described as a “water culture house”, the facility has 10 swimming pools plus direct access to designated swimming and dipping zones in the harbour and will host cultural experiences that “invite people to explore water in new ways”.

“It is part of the ongoing transformation of the city and its harbour from an industrial port into a cultural waterfront, where new functions have helped bring the surrounding areas of the Inner Harbour to life,” Yuki Ikeguchi, lead architect and partner in charge at Kengo Kuma & Associates, said.

“As Paper Island’s cultural cornerstone, the House is a civic institution dedicated to water and community, embraced by a public harbour bath.

“Open to all, it creates new settings for everyday life in Copenhagen, where physical and mental wellbeing can become a natural part of urban life.”

What to expect at KAI

Spanning some 5,800 square metres, the complex consists of five brick towers, each of which is shaped according to the outline of the pools beneath it.

The ground floor has a 25-metre fitness pool, a teaching pool and three children’s play pools, with access to the harbour bathing areas which include a swimming zone overlooking the Opera Park, and a plunge zone with views of the Royal Danish Playhouse.

The first floor is dedicated to wellness, with a therapy pool, a hot pool, and a cold plunge pool. It’s also where you’ll find the open-air valley pool, as well as the outdoor onsen, which boasts fantastic views of the harbour.

Able to handle 380 bathers at any given time, the facility also has three saunas, a heated stone and a steam bath.

World.title: ‘Historic milestone’ for Greenland as new international airport opens in Ilulissat
World.content:
A new international airport opened on Thursday in Greenland's third-largest town, Ilulissat, following approval by the Danish Civil Aviation and Railway Authority.

 

Built with the aim of better connecting the vast Arctic island to the rest of the world, it is the third new airport to open in Greenland since 2024. This puts the “final piece in place” in the country’s “historic airport expansion”, said operator Greenland Airports.

Ilulissat Airport is the last to open under the Danish autonomous territory’s expansion programme, following Nuuk in November 2024 and Qaqortoq in April 2026. Together, these airports “form a new backbone” for the country’s infrastructure, the operator said.

"The opening is a historic milestone for Ilulissat, for North Greenland, and for all of Greenland," said Jens Lauridsen, CEO of Greenland Airports.

“The three new airports in Ilulissat, Nuuk, and Qaqortoq fundamentally change how the country is connected internally and how Greenland is connected to the rest of the world.”

The new airport has a 2,200-metre runway capable of accommodating larger aircraft, enabling direct international services to Ilulissat, a hub for Disko Bay and North Greenland.

Air Greenland operates domestic flights between Ilulissat Airport and destinations including Nuuk, Aasiaat, Qaarsut and Upernavik. On the same day as the airport’s opening, Air Greenland launched a direct route between Ilulissat and Denmark’s capital, Copenhagen.

Following the launch, the regular winter schedule begins in November. The route between Copenhagen and Ilulissat will initially be operated by Jettime using a Boeing 737-800. Flights will primarily operate on Wednesdays, with selected additional Monday departures around Christmas and New Year, as well as in March.

Meanwhile, Icelandair will operate a seasonal service between Keflavík and Ilulissat from 3 June to 16 October 2027.

Operations at the airport will “ramp up gradually”, with opening hours and activity expanding in phases. “The goal is for the airport to be fully operational by the summer 2027 season,” Greenland Airports said.

The airport infrastructure upgrades, partly funded by Denmark, are intended to support the development of the local economy and tourism.

“Infrastructure is a long-term investment, and its real impact is measured in decades,” said Jens Wittrup Willumsen, chairman of the board of Greenland Airports.

“With the three new airports, Greenland has a foundation that future generations can build on.

“Now the task is to ensure that the new facilities benefit the entire country, including the towns and settlements around the airports, as part of the future development of business and tourism.”

Located on Greenland's west coast, about 250 kilometres north of the Arctic Circle, Ilulissat is situated next to Disko Bay, known for its enormous icebergs.

For tourism, the new airport means that international visitors can fly directly to Ilulissat to visit its UNESCO-listed icefjord. The airport also creates new opportunities for business, cargo, and regional development throughout North Greenland.

World.title: The new time lord: Wei Koh on his first year as GPHG jury president
World.content:
White T-shirt, visible tattoos, large sunglasses, Wei Koh cuts through the crowd to greet us in the sweltering heat of the Geneva Watch Days pavilion, where dozens of fine watchmaking houses have gathered to show off their latest releases.

 

"Hey dude, what’s up?", he asks. Behind the infinitely laid-back energy, he's about to preside, for the first time, over the jury of the luxurious industry’s most prestigious competition, the Grand Prix d'Horlogerie de Genève (GPHG).

This year, 84 nominated timepieces are competing for 19 prizes, including the coveted Aiguille d'Or, awarded every year since 2001 to the single most remarkable watch of the year. The 2026 awards ceremony will be held on 7 November in Geneva.

"The creativity is extraordinary this year. You've got watches that are executed at such a level of finesse that, as a watch lover, it makes you want to weep," promises the 54-year-old Singaporean.

What is the jury actually looking for?

The final list of 84 pieces in the running was published early September. Most are genuine feats of technical artistry, often produced in tiny numbers by confidential workshops most people outside the industry have never heard of.

So what makes a watch better than another? "I think singularity, right? Like a voice that's really unique," Koh says. "Remember the first time you listened to John Coltrane, or Miles Davis, or Tupac? Even if that person was relatively young, they were making a fundamental contribution to music. It's the same with watches."

He borrows a line from watchmaking legend François-Paul Journe, who once described the craft as one continuous wall. "If you want to enter this métier, your mission is to add at least one brick, a vital contribution," Koh explains. "That's what we're looking for."

Revolution founder and GPHG jury president Wei Koh Credit: Cyril Fourneris

Mechanical watchmaking know-how, sometimes billed as the 12th art, has been on UNESCO's list of intangible cultural heritage since December 2020.

Among this year's contenders, he quotes the first ever grand sonnerie able to play two different melodies for the quarter-hour chimes, a watch reviving a century-old balance-wheel technique thought lost to history, and a chronograph that reinvents how we physically interact with the complication altogether.

Behind closed doors

Choosing which timepiece deserves top honours is no small task. The 24-member jury will meet behind closed doors early November in Geneva, just days before the ceremony, to physically examine each of the 84 nominated pieces, to discuss and vote by secret ballot.

"We're kind of on an honour system, so we don't really talk much about what happens behind closed doors," Koh says, though he's quick to credit his predecessor, Nick Foulkes, for setting the tone: rigorous exchange, real disagreement, open dialogue.

"Nick has always believed in debate," Koh, who has been a jury member during the previous editions, remembers. "There are extraordinary moments where you're like, wow, I've just had a revelation. Someone explained it so well it completely changed my mind about a specific timepiece."

Wei Koh built his reputation the hard way. Back in 2005, he was handing out magazines at Baselworld. Some 21-years and a thriving media company later, he's one of the most recognisable names in the business, and the producer of Man of the Hour, one of the first documentary-style series dedicated to watchmaking.

"What I've learned over these years is that this industry is a meritocracy," he says. "If you strive for excellence, if you're consistent and honest in your efforts, you will succeed. But what this industry really rewards is when you try to contribute meaningfully to its survival, by protecting its principles."

The luxury watch market has hit historic highs over the past decade. The result of a careful balancing act between honouring heritage and pushing technical innovation. In the exhibition room of the Geneva Watch Days, centuries-old complications sit alongside breakthrough materials.

An industry in motion

This edition of the GPHG comes with real changes: the old "men's" and "women's" watch categories have been scrapped in favour of new categories built around technical criteria. On 7 October, adieu French, the ceremony will be held in English for the first time. A shift that echoes something Koh has spent two decades pushing for.

Put your hands in the air: All the winners at the 2025 Grand Prix d'Horlogerie de Genève Courtesy: GPHG

"The whole idea with Revolution was to uplift the founding ethics and principles of watchmaking while connecting it with a much bigger audience," he says. "For this craft, for this industry to survive, we have to keep growing the audience and bring in the next generation."

The renewed obsession with mechanical watches might seem surprising in the age of artificial intelligence. Koh states that they are more relevant than ever, and points to what he calls "tech and AI oligarchs, the people who built the hyper-digitised world we now live in, who have become huge watch collectors."

The most famous example is Mark Zuckerberg, CEO of Meta, who has been seen wearing high-end independent watchmakers such as Patek Philippe to F.P. Journe, H. Moser & Cie., and De Bethune.

"I think it's because a mechanical watch is the opposite of everything ephemeral. It outlives you. It only takes the energy you give it, by winding it or wearing it. There's something magical about that."

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has been seen wearing this Greubel Forsey, which won the GPHG Men's Complication Watch Prize 2020 Courtesy: GPHG

Wei Koh saves his best line for last: "Watchmaking gave me everything: a job, and my friendships, which are incredibly international. Because watchmaking transcends where you're from, your age, your religion, even your language. I find that to be this incredible force that binds us together." In the world we live in today, he suggests, that might matter more than it ever has.

The winners of the 2026 GPHG will be announced at the Bâtiment des Forces Motrices in Geneva on Saturday, 7 November and live on Euronews Culture and gphg.org.

World.title: US judge narrows Macrons' defamation lawsuit against American podcaster
World.content:
A judge in the United States has ruled that French President Emmanuel Macron and his wife Brigitte ​could continue their defamation lawsuit against the companies of the American podcaster Candace Owens, but not against Owens herself.

Advertising Read more

The Macrons had filed a lawsuit in July 2025 against Owens and two companies, accusing her of helping fan online rumours about whether Brigitte is a transgender woman.

Owens, 37, an influencer with a large following on social media platforms, has claimed that Brigitte was a man.

Delaware Superior Court Judge Sheldon Rennie said in a ruling on Tuesday that Owens could not be held personally liable in the case.

But Rennie allowed the suit against two companies associated with her – Candace Owens LLC and GeorgeTom Inc – to continue.

Question of jurisdiction

Rennie said the Delaware court did not hold jurisdiction over Owens because her residence was in another state, Tennessee.

The ruling means that if the French first couple were to eventually win the case, Owens' personal assets would be shielded.

In their lawsuit, the Macrons said Owens ⁠touted ​false claims and conspiracy theories ​against them "to promote her independent platform, gain notoriety, and make money".

Rennie deferred judgment on Owens' motion to dismiss ‌the ⁠Macrons' litigation until he was briefed on how French defamation law and statutes of limitation intersect with US law.

"I am in the absolute best mood over this Macron dismissal," Owens said on X on Wednesday.

'Centuries of patriarchal history': why trans rumours are wielded against women

Damages to Brigitte Macron

Brigitte Macron, 73, has taken to the courts in France to combat claims she was born a man.

Two French YouTubers, Natacha Rey and Amandine Roy, were convicted in September 2024 of spreading false claims after they posted a video in December 2021 alleging that Brigitte Macron had once been a man named Jean-Michel Trogneux – who is actually her brother.

Rey and Roy were ordered to pay €8,000 in damages to Brigitte Macron and €5,000 to Jean-Michel Trogneux.

The defendants were also given a suspended fine of €500.

Did French media silence enable Brigitte Macron fake news story to go viral?

Brigitte Macron had filed a libel complaint against the two women after their claim went viral, triggering conspiracy theories notably among the far right.

Roy, an online fortune-teller, interviewed Rey, a self-described independent journalist, for four hours on her YouTube channel in December 2021.

The women discussed the unsubstantiated rumour that Brigitte Macron had undergone gender reassignment, with Rey claiming to have uncovered a “state lie” and “scam”.

The claim went viral just weeks before France's 2022 presidential election, spreading even to the US where Owen derided the first lady in a now deleted YouTube video.

World.title: Egypt's mahrganat music: from the streets to five-star hotels
World.content:
Born in Egypt’s working-class neighbourhoods, mahraganat music is loud and raw, and these days it is practically impossible to escape. But for the artists behind it, mahraganat is more than just party music: they see it as the latest chapter in Egypt’s rich musical history.

Advertising

In this third episode of the season, we travel to the Egyptian capital, Cairo, to discover the origins of a genre that has become the soundtrack to urban life, despite receiving no official airtime.

Mahraganat evolved from shaabi: music by the people, for the people. Although it rose to prominence during the revolution of 2011–12, it has since become less overtly political.

It remains the music of happiness, partying, joy, and celebration.

Its fast rhythms and loud beats may be a far cry from the golden age of Egyptian music, but mahraganat has been on the scene since the early 2000s and it isn’t going anywhere, any time soon.

We trace its origins and evolution as we speak to one of the godfathers of the movement, his musical partner and a specialist in the genre.

Mid-East Junction is produced by RFI's English-language service. This episode was mixed by Vincent Pora. Special thanks to Elisa Schouten for her contribution.

World.title: The dachshund, a humorous icon with political symbolism
World.content:
From Picasso to Andy Warhol, a surprising number of artists have portrayed the German breed. But the dachshund has also at times been co-opted as a political symbol.

Pablo Picasso was renowned for having numerous muses — mostly women with whom he also had harmful relationships. But there's at least one of these muses who was freed from toxic romantic entanglement: a cute dachshund called Lump.

Before becoming his most famous canine model, Lump originally belonged to US photojournalist David Douglas Duncan.

The dog and the photographer visited the painter at his villa in Cannes in 1967. According to Duncan, upon their first encounter, Lump jumped right onto Picasso's lap. He apparently "decided" to stay with the painter and they lived together for six years.

The story does not reveal how Lump's decision was communicated, but that immediate special bound was immortalized through art: Picasso painted the dachshund's portrait directly onto a ceramic dinner plate that day, and Duncan did a series of photos documenting them together while the work was created.

The plate and the photos are on show at the new exhibition "The Dachshund. An Icon off the Leash " held at the Kunsthalle Bremen until March 28, 2027.

The exhibition includes installations created for dogs Image: Sina Schuldt/dpa/picture alliance

Lump also appears in many of Picasso's series of paintings reinterpreting Diego Velazquez's masterwork "Las Meninas," in which the original work's large mastiff was replaced with his adoptive pet.

A particularly iconic animal

With their long ears and extreme length compared to their short legs, dachshunds have a silhouette that's instantly recognizable: "It's really a dog with an iconic shape, and that makes them interesting for many things" — from art to , says exhibition curator and art historian Annett Reckert.

Alongside Picasso, a surprising number of important artists, including Andy Warhol, Otto Dix, David Hockney, Max Liebermann and Rosemarie Trockel, have paid tribute to the dachshund. "It's striking how often the dachshund has served as a muse, model and studio accomplice for them," Reckert tells DW.

Combined with this prolific artistic career, the dachshund can equally be explored from a historical perspective, since "there's also the fact that we associate them with something German," the curator adds.

Germany's 'badger dog'

Bred to track and chase badgers, foxes, rabbits and other burrowing animals, the dachshund originated in Germany over 300 years ago. Breed standards were established in 1879, and the German Teckel Club (DTK) — one of the oldest dog breeding organizations in Germany — was founded in 1888.

A lithography from 1867 showing children feeding deer with a dachshund watching Image: Wolfgang Diederich/imageBROKER/picture alliance

The name combines the German words "Dachs" (badger) and "Hund" (dog), literally translating to "badger dog." But Germans more commonly call them Dackel or Teckel.

Because of their long, narrow build, dachshunds are also colloquially known in English-speaking countries as wiener dogs or sausage dogs.

An evolving cultural icon

Beyond their role as hunting dogs, dachshunds have a surprisingly rich place in German cultural history, from bourgeois stereotype to Olympic icon.

Germany's last emperor, Kaiser Wilhelm II, was an avid dachshund enthusiast and owned several of them.

Two of his dogs, Wadl and Hexlsome, made history by causing a minor diplomatic incident during a visit to the estate of Archduke Franz Ferdinand, Konopiste Castle, in 1908. The dachshunds reportedly killed one of the archduke's prized golden pheasants. The attack was widely commented in aristocratic circles, and Kaiser Wilhelm II was forced to issue a formal apology.

The pheasant incident was obviously not as consequential as another event involving Franz Ferdinand, heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne: his assassination in Sarajevo on June 28, 1914, which became the primary catalyst of World War I.

Still, the dachshund remained present throughout this global conflict. In propaganda maps and political cartoons, Germany was represented as a dachshund, while the British as a bulldog and the French, a poodle.

The popularity of the dachshund in the United States plummeted during the First World War because of this association; those who owned one called their dogs "liberty hounds" instead of using the German word.

Described as the 'Devil dog' in US propaganda from 1917 Image: akg-images/picture alliance

During World War II, dachshunds were used for military tasks such as mine detection.

However, their missions weren't as outlandish as the stories published by the UK's tabloid press relatively recently, which claimed that the Nazis aimed to build armies of talking dachshunds. The rumors followed the publication of a non-fiction book on dogs published in 2011, "Amazing Dogs: A Cabinet Of Canine Curiosities," which outlined Nazi research into dogs' — including dachshunds' — intelligence and personalities.

The dachshund definitely didn't fit into the Nazis' aesthetics: "They were used in the war, too, but not in the same way as other dogs. After all, they weren't the kind of dog a Nazi would have wanted to be seen with for the sake of appearances," notes Reckert. "Take Hitler, for instance: He famously made public appearances with his German Shepherd, Blondie. They would rather be seen with a Dobermann, or dogs that looked big and dangerous."

A symbol of the 'other' side Germany

The endearing potential of the dachshund is actually one of the ideas that guided Reckert in her curation of the exhibition. They "simply give the impression that they have a sense of humor," the art historian says. "That's an attribution, of course. But they really do spread good cheer and have a truly likable character."

In the 1970s, this slightly absurd and cheerful domestic companion inspired a figure embodying a new image for West Germany: the official mascot for the 1972 Summer Olympics in Munich, Waldi.

Waldi entered children's rooms worldwide as an ambassador of a colorful, democratic and friendly West Germany Image: Wolfgang Maria Weber/picture alliance

A stark contrast to the heavy symbols that represented Germany during the Third Reich — the eagle, Germania, forests, Wagner and Prussian discipline — the mascot created by renowned graphic designer Otl Aicher and his intern, Elena Schwaiger, was as iconic as the shape of the dachshund.

The designer was vehemently against including brown, or any of Germany's national colors — red, black and gold — in the brand identity. Instead, he went for delicate pastel shades: "The approach to color was truly visionary," notes Reckert. "Their intention was something we are still working on today — something we still haven't completely achieved: an open, cheerful, democratic and colorful Germany."

Still today, right-wing extremist groups attempt to co-opt the dachshund as a subtle nationalist fashion symbol that appears on ties or socks, inspired by accessories worn by Alexander Gauland. On the other hand, "Dachshunds Against the Right" has also emerged as a counter-protest movement.

But altogether, Reckert has focused on the dachshund as a symbol of friendliness and joy while conceiving "The Dachshund. An Icon off the Leash." The exhibition includes halls that are open to small dogs, and even features artworks and performances specifically designed for them.

The Bremen exhibition is on show until March 28, 2027 Image: Sina Schuldt/dpa/picture alliance

The feedback she's been getting in the run-up to the show also aligns with this cheerful image. She notes that hardly a day goes by without something arriving in the mail related to the dachshund — whether pictures, artworks or information about dachshund-related events: "It's really crazy," she says, showing examples of the stuff she's received. "I've never had an exhibition that was greeted ahead of its opening in such a friendly, diverse way. It's almost a bit uncanny, really."

Edited by: Brenda Haas

World.title: Germany news: Merz in Asia warns against weaponizing trade, calls for 'rules based' order
World.content:
Skip next section Merz in Seoul calls for new trade order, says supply chains cannot become 'political pawns'

The German chancellor has been calling for a new global free trade network Image: Kay Nietfeld/dpa/picture alliance

During his final day of a whirlwind Asia tour this week, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz told the Asia-Pacific Conference of German Business in Seoul on Friday that Germany and Europe are ready to cooperate with Asian economies to foster a rules-based economic order.

Merz said the European Union is ready to take the lead in shaping a better deal for countries in Asia feeling the pressure of a destabilized rules-based trade order.

"Competition between the US and China is ramping up. Tariffs, technological decoupling strategies and a tough race for critical raw materials and new technologies are fundamentally changing the rules of our global economy," Merz said.

"These conflicts and systemic shifts in power patterns concern us all. They particularly concern economically aspiring partners in the Indo-Pacific, as well as in Germany and in Europe."

During stops in Singapore and Japan this week, Merz pushed for free trade partnerships and greater European cooperation with Asian economies.

In Singapore on Wednesday, Merz called for a free trade agreement between the EU and the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP), a sweeping multilateral free trade agreement connecting the Asia Pacific and the Americas.

The UK is the single European signatory, albeit outside of the EU bloc. The US pulled out during the first administration President Donald Trump in 2017, scuttling the original version, the Trans-Pacific Partnership (TPP).

"We want to offer opportunities beyond bilateral agreements,"he said in Seoul on Friday.

"We are resolutely joining forces against unilateralism, autocratic power politics and violations of international law," Merz added.

"When supply chains become political pawns, when access to key technologies is obstructed or when efforts to secure raw materials resemble displays of power rather than fair partnerships, this jeopardizes growth, prosperity and ultimately the security of entire regions."

Citing Germany as an example, South Korean Prime Minister Han Seong Sook told the conference "German companies are using Korea as a central hub to expand their presence in the Asia-Pacific region."

Additional reporting by Nina Haase

10/30/2026 October 30, 2026 West Bengal, Assam on flood alert after glacial lake outburst in Bhutan

A part of Punakha-Gasa highway in Bhutan is washed away Image: Department of Surface Transport, Ministry of Infrastructure and Transport, Bhutan/REUTERS

Several districts in West Bengal, along with parts of Assam and Arunachal Pradesh, were placed on flood alert on Friday, media reports said.

The flood, triggered by a glacial lake burst at Sintaphu Lake in neighboring Bhutan, swept away infrastructure at the Gasa Tshachu natural hot springs in the Himalayan kingdom.

Indian authorities have stepped up monitoring along the Sankosh River, which flows from Bhutan through West Bengal and into Assam. Communities along the Brahmaputra River in Assam and Arunachal Pradesh have also been alerted over possible flooding.

In Bhutan, no casualties have been reported, state broadcaster BBS said.

According to Bhutanese media reports, two Bailey bridges, built in portable, pre-fabricated sections, may have been washed away, as well as a part of the road leading to Laya village, where the hot springs are located, had also been washed away.

World.title: Israeli election: Netanyahu, main rival fall short of majority after all votes counted
World.content:
10/30/2026 October 30, 2026 Tricky task of forming a working coalition begins

Ahead of the election, two clear coalitions had formed. On the one side, the ruling coalition of right-wing, far-right and religious parties centered around Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his Likud party.

On the other side was the anti-Netanyahu bloc, made up of a coalition of right-wing, centrist and liberal parties whose unifying principle was to oust Netanyahu from power.

However, neither of these blocs was able to secure a majority of seats, meaning a simple path to forming a government is off the table.

The task of figuring out a new working coalition is now beginning, with the question of whether the two Arab-Israeli lists, which together secured an unprecedented 19 seats, may form part of a future government or at least provide some form of support.

Yair Golan, chairman of the left-liberal Democrats, said he had met with opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot, former Prime Minister Yair Lapid and Mansur Abbas, head of the Arab Ra'am party.

He has called for discussions with the Arab-led parties, saying after his meeting with Eisenkot that "the rescue of Israel is at stake," in a post on X.

It remains to be seen if the right-wing factions of Eisenkot's anti-Netanyahu bloc would ultimately entertain the possibility of working with the Arab-led parties.

Another option that has been aired is the possibility of a unity government including both Netanyahu and Eisenkot, but such a move may be similarly distasteful for moderate voters.

World.title: Venezuela: Opposition leader Maria Corina Machado says US backs 2027 election
World.content:
The return of Maria Corina Machado, who says Trump opened the "floodgate to freedom" for Venezuela, presents a challenge for Washington as Trump has also backed interim President Delcy Rodriguez.

Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado said on Thursday that the country was moving towards a US-prescribed presidential election in 2027, in her first public remarks since returning from 10 months in exile.

Calling the transition to democracy "irreversible," Machado said, "US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has laid out a sequence of steps for moving toward a democratic transition that includes ​presidential elections in 2027."

"The date of the election is the date of liberation," Machado said in Caracas after returning home following 10 months in exile.

Machado also reiterated that her priorities included dismantling the country's repressive system and securing the release of the thousands of political prisoners. She denied having had any contact with interim President Delcy Rodriguez.

Shortly before Machado's public statements, Rodriguez announced that there "will be elections" in Venezuela, without specifying a date.

Machado says Trump helped open 'floodgate to freedom'

Machado, who famously "presented" US President Donald Trump with her Nobel Peace Prize, thanked Trump for his actions on January 3, leading to "the floodgate to freedom" being opened in Venezuela.

The opposition leader was referring to the US capture of former President Nicolas Maduro, currently facing US drug trafficking and torture charges, which he denies.

Machado, however, criticized a major oil deal Washington and Caracas agreed to earlier this year, under which Venezuela is expected to supply 20% of its oil reserves to the United States.

"This agreement does not reflect the levels of transparency that Venezuelan society wants," she said.

At the same time, she skirted questions that highlighted Trump's comments in January that she did not have sufficient support to immediately lead Venezuela, as well as his suggestion this week that the country could become the 51st US state.

US caught in a bind

Machado, who was barred from contesting the 2024 presidential election, backed opposition candidate Edmundo Gonzalez. His supporters said he had won by a wide margin, even though electoral authorities declared Maduro the winner.

Machado's recent return after nearly a year in exile complicates things for Washington which has said Machado has every right to be in Venezuela, but also praised acting President Rodriguez.

World.title: Bayer wins Roundup cancer trial after Supreme Court ruling
World.content:
The weedkiller Roundup has been accused of being carcinogenic to humans despite no warning on its label. Bayer is seeking to settle tens of thousands of further cases.

The German pharmaceutical giant Bayer won a trial on Thursday over claims the Roundup weedkiller, manufactured by subsidiary Monsanto, caused cancer in three women.

The Missouri jury sided unanimously with Bayer. It's the first trial since a US Supreme Court ruling that limits complaints over the product.

Bayer is waiting for a separate court ruling where the company is seeking a $7.25 billion (€6.5 billion) settlement in relation to tens of thousands of other Roundup cases.

Missouri decision could reshape Bayer's glyphosate fight To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What is the complaint against Roundup?

Thursday's court ruling follows a case brought to a St. Louis court by Theresa Aretino, Cynthia Fernandez and Betty Larkin in 2020.

The three women had said they were diagnosed with non-Hodgkin lymphoma after regularly using the weedkiller.

Their attorneys argued that Roundup was defectively designed and unreasonably ​dangerous, and that Bayer was negligent in selling it.

The three were not participating in the Bayer settlement. Some 65,000 other cases have been filed against the company, claiming Roundup gave them cancer.

What did the Supreme Court rule in regards to Roundup?

The US Supreme Court ruled earlier this year that plaintiffs could not argue that the Roundup label failed to warn users about the risk of cancer since the US Environmental Protection Agency had concluded the label does not require a cancer warning.

Bayer wins in US court, but at what cost to public health? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"We are pleased with the jury's favorable verdict for Monsanto validating our belief that there is no evidence to prove design defect, fraud or negligence claims in the Roundup litigation," Bill Dodero, the company's US general counsel and global head of litigation, said in a statement.

"This verdict should send a strong signal that plaintiffs who wish to pursue claims in the court system following the Durnell ruling will face significant challenges both in demonstrating they have viable claims and putting forth the necessary evidence to prove them in court," he added, using the name of the Supreme Court case.

The company has repeatedly defended the use of glyphosate, the active ingredient in Roundup, as safe, calling it "one of the most studied agricultural tools in history."

The EPA has previously concluded that glyphosate is probably not carcinogenic, but it is in the middle of a new review of its safety. The International Agency for Research on Cancer concluded in 2015 that the chemical was "probably carcinogenic" to humans, but Bayer has rejected the study's findings, calling it an outlier.

World.title: Binance crypto platform suspends trades amid suspected hack
World.content:
The platform suspended some trading while crypto companies froze billions in their respective currencies. The full extent of the possible hack was not yet clear.

The world's largest cryptocurrency platform, Binance, confirmed on Thursday that it was investigating a potential security breach that resulted in an estimated $6.3 billion impact.

Analysts said the breach could amount to the largest-ever crypto heist

"It does look like a hack on Binance," said former company chief Changpeng Zhao, who remains a major shareholder.

Binance said it worked to freeze the affected assets and that it had located about $3 billion so far. It did not provide information about the remaining $3.3 billion.

"Binance will cover all hacking losses," co-founder Yi He said, without providing more details about the incident.

Some $3 billion (€2.7 billion) had been frozen in response to the suspected hack.

Binance 'reviewing' possible hack

"Rest assured that user funds are completely safe," a company spokesperson said.

"Our security teams are reviewing all relevant information with urgency, and we will provide updates through official Binance channels as soon as we have verified information," the company statement said.

"Binance’s initial investigation suggests that the security incident may involve a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop, which allowed an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions," the company wrote. "We have found no evidence of any wallet private key leak."

How to avoid crypto losses To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The company, which is the world's largest platform in terms of daily crypto trading volume, suspended trading on certain products while the freezing came from cryptocurrency companies using the platform.

Tether froze around $1.6 billion in its USDT currency, according to CEO Paolo Ardoino, and Circle froze some $800 million-worth of USDC, boss Jeremy Allaire said.

Who is Binance ex-CEO Zhao?

The news of the possible hack sent Bitcoin's value tumbling by 3.2% on Thursday evening, dropping below $79,000.

Zhao, who founded the Binance platform in 2017, said "as a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered."

He stepped down as CEO after pleading guilty in 2023. to failing to prevent money laundering on his platform. US President Donald Trump pardoned him in 2025.

Zhao and Binance have been key supporters of cryptocurrency ventures by US President Donald Trump and his family.

World.title: Germany's Alexander Zverev clinches tennis No. 1 ranking
World.content:
Alexander Zverev is the second German man, after Boris Becker, to clinch the No. 1 spot in tennis.

German tennis star Alexander Zverev is set to become the new world No. 1 in tennis, capping a successful year where he won two Grand Slams.

Zverev is the second German man, after Boris Becker, to clinch the top spot in the sport. Becker reached No.1 some 35 years ago.

Zverev replaces Italy's Jannik Sinner, who previously held the world's No. 1 spot.

Zverev got there by reaching the quarter-finals of the Erste Bank Open in Vienna this week.

He is also the second-oldest first-time No. 1 ranked player after Australian John Newcombe.

"(It is) very special. To have the feeling to be on the top of the world is amazing," Zverev said.

"It is different than winning a tournament or a title, but it's such a special feeling to know that the No. 1 is going to be next to your name when the new rankings come out."

Among German female tennis players, only Steffi Graf and Angelique Kerber have achieved this in the WTA rankings.

Zverev beat Ben Shelton to win the US Open in September Image: Robert Deutsch/IMAGN Images/REUTERS

Two Grand Slams in 2026

Zverev's career had been defined by getting close to Grand Slam titles but never quite reaching them, facing stiff competition from Sinner and Spanish talent Carlos Alcaraz.

The Hamburg-born also won a gold medal in the 2021 Olympics.

But his tennis career finally had its breakthrough this year, when he won the Grand Slam at both the French and US Opens.

Known for his consistency, he was just the ninth man to reach at least the semifinals at all four majors in the same season.
