When Isaac Quaynor attended his first spring racing carnival back in 2023, what he wore was of little consequence. “I was a bit of a deer in the headlights,” the Collingwood player and G.H. Mumm ambassador admits. “I was just happy to be here, so I didn’t really pay attention to what people were wearing.” It’s a far cry from his approach to Derby Day 2026, for which Quaynor worked with his stylist Simon Finnegan and Australian tailor Oscar Hunt to design a custom-made pinstripe suit that suggests more spritzer than simpleton. Hannah Dal Sasso and Isaac Quaynor at the G.H. Mumm marquee in the Birdcage at Flemington Racecourse. Eddie Jim “When I started working with him he wore a lot of streetwear and colour. We still do that now but we lean a lot more towards men’s tailoring and focus on the silhouette,” Finnegan explains.



Quaynor is leading the new wave of young men approaching their race-day outfits with careful intent and experimental enthusiasm. Related Article Good Weekend Red-carpet looks influencing this year’s spring racing fashions “It’s a reflection on men taking more risks now but also brands are giving men more options,” says stylist Donny Galella. “Suiting used to be very black, white, grey, beige – you know, the same colours – so it’s great to see now a plethora of all these fun colours that guys can wear, and fun suit styles: the oversized ’90s jackets, wide-leg pants, double-breasted jackets. Guys have more options and have more fun.” Frankie Foster says he’s lost count of how many ties he has. The 30-year-old former Love Island UK contestant-turned-racing commentator and presenter found himself accumulating the accessory at a rapid pace once he became a race-day regular, leaning on the tie as a cost-effective way to update his look without needing a new suit.



Frankie Foster launched his own label, Franc James, specialising in 100 per cent silk ties. Eddie Jim “I was going racing all the time and I don’t have 20 suits in my wardrobe – but I can have 20 ties,” Foster says. “And with a different shirt, tie, pocket square, hat – whatever it is – you can wear the same suit as many ways as you want.” Loading Foster became such an aficionado that in 2022 he launched his own label, Franc James, specialising in 100 per cent silk ties, hand-stitched and printed in England.



“I once calculated the value of all of them, and that’s probably when I decided: let’s stop buying them and let’s start making them.” Related Article Caulfield Cup A lesson in elegance: The Caulfield Cup fashion winners Asked what advice they’d give men keen to make their mark this Derby Day, Quaynor and Foster echo similar sentiments: get a suit that fits properly, and stay sharp. “If you want to get with the times, go for a baggier pant and stay away from anything tight,” advises Quaynor, who says he’s taken to trawling Pinterest when he needs a spark of style genius. Foster offers dually sage wisdom: “The most frequent mistake happens after you’ve had a few drinks and your tie starts to loosen,” he says.



“It looks a bit scruffy. Readjust it, make sure it’s fastened tight to the collar of your shirt, give a little pinch to make a dimple and you’re good to go.” Make the most of your health, relationships, fitness and nutrition with our Live Well newsletter. Get it in your inbox every Monday.

World.title: Jess Wilson knows the SRL can’t be stopped. Pretending otherwise is political shenanigans
World.content:
Analysis PoliticsVictoriaVictorian election Jess Wilson knows the SRL can’t be stopped. Pretending otherwise is political shenanigans Kieran Rooney October 30, 2026 — 7:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The Coalition’s explanation of what a “pause and review” of the Suburban Rail Loop would actually entail is now as murky as the subterranean mud that tunnel boring machines are digging through. Both major parties are ensnared in an SRL conundrum wrapped in a political riddle – what to do with a major project that is too big to fail and increasingly expensive to build. Once tunnel boring machines like this one begin their work, it is extremely costly to stop them. The first stage of the under-construction rail line, running underground from Cheltenham to Box Hill, is too far gone to cancel or drastically alter without significant costs. This is not a comfortable reality for Opposition Leader Jess Wilson, who has made economic management her biggest virtue to voters. She has appointed herself shadow treasurer for this exact reason.



By repeating the mantra that they will pause and review the project with just a morsel of detail, the Coalition has, deliberately or not, allowed some wiggle room in the minds of voters. Related Article Exclusive

Victorian election Coalition says it will keep drilling Suburban Rail Loop tunnels as the massive cost of stopping is revealed Like a political Rorschach test, different groups have found their own meaning. Haters have clung to the hope that this process will find the underground line is too expensive and must be cancelled immediately. Others have rationalised that an incoming government will get their feet under the desk and accept that it has to be completed.



In this sweet spot, Wilson’s pause and review policy has allowed her to appear as a hard-nosed budget manager without being tied to any specific changes that could be criticised. Related Article Exclusive

Victorian election Victoria has ‘no choice’ but to confront growing debt problem Until this week, the word “pause” was never assumed to be the subjective part of the plan. Most people had a mental picture of tools being put down, tunnel boring machines unplugged and sites being padlocked while a Coalition government crunched the numbers. This was not quite right, the Coalition now says. Their strategy, clarified in a statement to The Age, actually does not involve sending workers home or halting digging while the review is under way.



Instead, it is a pause on signing further contracts similar to Premier Ben Carroll’s promise not to sign station-building contracts until a technical review of the project tries to find $1 billion in savings. Loading The Coalition’s statement says its policy has no technical or budgetary differences to the government’s own review decision. It would be disingenuous to now blame the media, the public or the Coalition’s political opponents for this supposed misconception. Speaking at parliament in May, when Wilson was asked on camera if pausing meant stopping work, she nodded and said yes.



When asked for how long, she said, “as long as it takes”. She has not been as unequivocal at other media appearances, but the conversation remains a matter of public record and is partly why the issue hasn’t been pressed further. Loading On Friday, shadow attorney-general James Newbury was sent out to clarify the issue and said: “Any works that can be paused will immediately be paused. “We’ve never said we’re going to breach any contract. What we have said is, tools will be down while we review the project,” he added. Later on Friday, a Liberal spokesperson sought to clarify again that “pausing the project means not committing to further contracts whilst the review about the project’s future is undertaken. Workers will continue to be paid”.



None of this makes a lot of sense when put together. It makes their position even murkier. Related Article Victorian election Deal or no deal? How the major parties are tackling the minority government risk When information is incomplete, imagination will fill the gaps. If the Coalition’s position was altered after May, they should have said so. They were given plenty of opportunities to explain the nitty-gritty of their policy and must wear the blame if it was misunderstood.



It may well be there was never an incentive to clarify the position until now. The shades of grey were better than the political realities, which are as follows: There are three tunnel boring machines digging their way under Melbourne’s east and south-eastern suburbs, and a fourth is being assembled to launch shortly;

Stopping them or terminating their work before they reach their next destination will be a logistical challenge rivalled only by the time I learned how to reverse the swing of my laundry door;

Across launch sites and the sites of six future underground stations, there are gigantic holes in the ground that have been excavated by workers believing that, at some point in the next two years, builders will come in and start building concrete platforms and walls. The opposition’s public transport spokesman, Matthew Guy, acknowledged this challenge on ABC Radio in August 2025. “If we’ve got tunnel boring machines which have gone six kilometres underground, then we can hardly fill it back in,” he said.



“The project will then proceed, there’s no doubt about it ... No government would have any choice.” Related Article Victorian election Opposition goes loco with $1.7 billion transport pitch This is an uncomfortable truth for both Wilson and Carroll, who is known to be sceptical about the project but, after becoming leader, ultimately decided to plough on with it and search for $2 billion in savings. Of these savings, $1 billion has been contested and the other $1 billion is yet to materialise. There are plenty of counterfactuals to be had about the Suburban Rail Loop, its merits and timing.



The Coalition can argue that proceeding with tunnel boring machines before the election has tied their hands, severely limited their options to manage the budget, and should have been reconsidered after the debt incurred during the pandemic. Related Article Exclusive

Suburban Rail Loop ‘Building the plane while it’s flying’: How the government rewrote the story of the Suburban Rail Loop Labor can argue that the project was already on the ballot of two elections, including one where the Coalition said they would scrap it, and it will only grow in cost the longer it is delayed. What cannot be disputed is that machines are digging underground, workers are on site, and any suspension or cancellation will not be easy. Alongside economic management, another huge part of Wilson’s pitch to voters has been restoring trust in government and being transparent.

World.title: Australia vs South Africa LIVE: Nathan Lyon, Aussies chase quick wickets as South Africa resumes batting at Newlands on day four
World.content:
South Africa are 40 runs in front, but they’re four wickets down. Who’s on top? Australia, according to Kerry O’Keeffe, Mark Waugh and David Warner. Here’s what they just said on Fox Cricket.

O’Keeffe: “It’s climax time, isn’t it? This is why we turn up (at Test cricket).

“I think Australia are well ahead in the game. The way the surface was being disturbed late yesterday, these six could fall over very quickly – and then it’s a walk to the line for Australia.”

Waugh wasn’t quite as emphatic, but still believes the tourists are favourites.

“Australia’s in the driver’s seat, aren’t they. I think South Africa need another 150-200 to be in the game. They’ve got a bit of batting to come, but I think Australia are in the driver’s seat.”

Warner: “I think it’s Australia. This first hour is a big one for Australia. It’ll be a balance of attacking and saving runs.”

World.title: Antisemitism alert raises critical alarm
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Jillian Segal is quoted in the article (“Progressive critics spur new wave of antisemitism: Segal”, October 30) as saying some “well-intended people who are concerned about the policies of the state of Israel and feel critical of them transfer that criticism to Jewish members of society in Australia”. That statement is a generalisation and requires further explanation. I, for one, criticise the Israeli government but do not transfer this to Jewish members of the Australian community. Many other Australian citizens feel the same way. Many Australian Jews criticise the Israeli government and clearly do not transfer their criticism to the Australian Jewish community. Some travelled to Israel recently to vote against the current Israel government! I have the right, as an Australian citizen, to criticise the Israeli government and not to be criticised for it. Peter Spencer, Castle Hill Does Jillian Segal include in her criticism of “progressives motivated by social justice” all those Jewish people who have voiced their abhorrence of the current policies of the Israeli government? She should not equate opposition to Netanyahu’s abuse of Palestinians, even to the extent of his absolute denial of the right to a separate state, with antisemitism. We can be critical of a nation’s policies and still respect the citizens of that country. That is how many of us see the current situation in Israel. Doug Hewitt, Hamilton Australia’s special envoy to combat antisemitism, Jillian Segal. Janie Barrett Jillian Segal’s updated road map, ASECA Priorities, represents an unacceptable overreach into Australia’s public institutions. By singling out progressives, human rights advocates, public schools, universities and broadcasters for “modern progressive antisemitism”, the report risks weaponising legitimate concern for human rights to stifle political speech. Demanding that universities, arts bodies and media outlets risk losing public funding or face independent oversight panels if they fail to align with a specific ideological filter is dangerous policy. Public institutions must remain independent. Subordinating them to partisan criteria undermines the very fabric of our multicultural democracy. In a successful multicultural society, social cohesion relies on open debate, shared values and fair application of the law – not on enforcing ideological conformity or policing domestic criticism of foreign governments. Robyn Dalziell, Kellyville It has little to do with political preferences but is more about the fact that treating Jews, based on their religious identity, with prejudice and hostility or discrimination goes against the basic longstanding human or social values of fairness, inclusiveness and empathy. Steve Ngeow, Chatswood I look forward to reading the empirical evidence for Jillian Segal’s claim that those she labels “progressive” critics of Israel or Netanyahu have spurred (is that “caused”?) anti-Jewish violence or discrimination. Reviewing the book On Antisemitism: A Word in History in The New York Review of Books recently, Jewish scholar Omer Bartov concluded: “Because the aim of today’s surging accusations of antisemitism is not to combat the actual phenomenon but to suppress anti-Zionism or criticism of Israel, the ‘new right’ has been handed a convenient opening.” Bartov is the dean’s professor of Holocaust and genocide studies at Brown University. The university is regarded as “progressive”, as are all universities committed to scholarship. I trust that Segal has taken a historically and conceptually sophisticated approach commensurate with Australian academic standards when composing her report. Philip Bell, Bronte I suspect I might be one of the social-justice-minded progressives that Jillian Segal accuses of antisemitism. I am so utterly hurt by this because I try to keep a balanced view, but how can I do that with what has happened in Gaza and continues today in the West Bank? How can I not be angry when I am continually told I am something that I am not? When I watch and read about the Holocaust do my tears count for nothing. Julie Robinson, Cardiff



Liberal senator James Paterson. Dominic Lorrimer Open embassy Following ASIO’s findings linking the Islamic Republic to two antisemitic attacks on Australian soil, Australia expelled its ambassador. Yet the embassy in Canberra remains open. During Senate estimates, Senator Paterson asked Foreign Minister Wong whether consular convenience should outweigh the safety of Iranian Australians. Wong said their safety was always front of mind, and that decisions would be guided by security agencies. That leaves unanswered why maintaining the Islamic Republic’s diplomatic presence remains justified following Australia’s own security findings. I recently spoke on ABC’s 7.30 about threats I received after publicly criticising the Islamic Republic. I reported them to the Australian Federal Police. I have no evidence linking those threats to the embassy, but they highlight the broader risk of transnational repression that the government has already acknowledged.

Iranian Australians have legitimate consular needs, which should not be dismissed. Alternative arrangements, including through third countries, deserve serious examination. Having publicly attributed attacks to the Islamic Republic and expelled its ambassador, Australia should close the Islamic Republic’s embassy in Canberra while ensuring access to essential consular services. The government owes Australians a clear explanation of why the embassy remains open. Saeid Zand, Director, Iranian-Australian Public Affairs Committee A stolen election? The extraordinary irony is that Benjamin Netanyahu and Gadi Eisenkot need the Palestinian bloc to become prime minister (“It’s deadlock in the Israeli election. Here’s how it could unfold”, October 30). In true Trump style Netanyahu says Palestinians have “stolen” the election. Michael Fox, Pacific Palms A tour group travelling on public transport arrives at Western Sydney International (Nancy-Bird Walton) Airport WSI on Thursday. Kate Geraghty ‘NBW’ airport taken



Hereward Dundas-Taylor’s concern that Nancy Bird-Walton’s legacy has been corporatised by the assignment of the IATA code WSI is understandable (Letters, October 30). Yet it is worth noting that IATA referencing shows the official name is “Western Sydney International Airport (Nancy Bird-Walton)” . Unfortunately, assigning, say NBW, was out of the question as it is already assigned to Leeward Point Field in none other than Guantanamo Bay, Cuba! Apparently, changing longstanding airport codes is rare. However, that didn’t deter the current POTUS, who recently convinced those in authority to change Palm Beach International Airport to President Donald J. Trump International Airport, and yes, you guessed it, PBI has become DJT! Allan Gibson, Cherrybrook Options to barrack for Highlighting the human cost of selling Victoria Barracks is important (“Price of Victoria Barracks is much higher than $200m”, October 30). Too often the human cost of government policy is discounted. Perhaps the most graphic example was the sell-off of public housing in Millers Point and the Sirius building. The human cost of the displacement was profound. A unique community was destroyed, social ties were torn asunder and many tenants, especially older tenants, found it difficult to cope in their new location. The human cost of any policy intervention should be front and centre. Alan Morris, Eastlakes Trump behind the teleprompter at a rally in Rock Hill, South Carolina on Thursday, where the Senate race is surprisingly competitive. AP Lessons from US midterm mess Waleed Aly’s examination of the wild ride of insurgencies in the US and Britain is a timely and interesting case for Australia (“Wild ride could be coming to an end”, October 30). One Nation’s insurgent attacks on traditional politics have caught the interest of those disgruntled by the Trump administration’s war on the world. Coalition voters have been attracted to One Nation due to the abandonment of common sense, traditional values and honesty by both the Liberals and Nationals. Perhaps it’s timely to ask what is One Nation offering? There is no evidence to suggest that One Nation is interested in the executive functions of government – quite the opposite, in fact. One Nation cannot or will not account for its own internal spending. One Nation’s attacks on minorities, on migrants, on individual politicians should be sounding alarm bells, even to the disaffected. One Nation attack cartoons are not satirical, they’re just nasty. Bluey has been misrepresented as an urban terrorist, instead of the positive role model she is. Pauline Hanson would learn a lot from digesting Bluey’s return message via Matt D’s cartoon published in Friday’s Herald. Geoff Nilon, Mascot



Opinion polls might well show that “moderates” are doing better than “progressives”. But will the “moderates” bring about change? After all, that is how Trump got elected in the first place. Voters thought that the establishment had repeatedly failed them, so they thought they’d try something different. But in his first term Trump was constrained by the establishment types who surrounded him. And then there was Biden. Now an uninhibited Trump has really failed them! But whoever is elected in the midterms, whether they are “moderates” or “progressives”, if they don’t produce the change that the electorate demands then voters are just as likely to swing back next time. David Rush, Lawson I am an admirer of Waleed Aly, but he has made the midterm situation unnecessarily complicated. It’s simple. If Trump and his cohort are successful in the midterm elections, things will get crazier and weirder. If Trump and friends are hammered, things will get crazier and weirder. Jim Croke, Stanmore Illustration by Matt Davidson Dignity for seniors Reading your editorial about the shocking lack of foresight in our system of aged care, juxtaposed with Matt D’s cartoon featuring Bluey dreaming of Pauline Hanson apologising for her incendiary attitude to our world, is a combined portent of what is coming to impact on all our lives. Having watched my mother in her final years deal with an overstretched health system, all I can say is: she deserved better. We are removing dignity for our seniors and we should be ashamed. Aged care is but one area of our wrongheadedly prioritised world that needs a complete shift in our collective mindset. While Hanson’s values are not mine, what she is doing is providing a very effective megaphone to all the collective rage brought about by either real or imagined change and imbalances in our system. And what we don’t understand is a vacuum that will vent itself. We all need to better understand ourselves through creative solutions. “PLEASE EXPLAIN” is a good place for the creatives to start. In not creating understandings, what we end up with are leaders that our collective intransigence so rightly deserves. It’s time for some self-reflection. Neville Williams, Darlinghurst Staff and nonsense James Massola exposes a fundamental flaw in our governance: the executive’s control over the resources of parliamentarians (“PM has gone too tribal this time”, October 30). When a prime minister can manipulate the staffing and advisory resources available to rival or crossbench MPs, the national interest is compromised. An independent body should determine resourcing for all parliamentarians, including the prime minister. Letting a partisan government decide who gets what support creates an obvious conflict of interest. In a modern democracy, the executive should not control the resources of those charged with holding it to account. Chris Rivers, Port Macquarie



Illustration by Matt Golding Fluoridation antics Liberal senator Alex Antic is the Australian equivalent of his US counterpart Robert Kennedy Jr, hawking conspiracy theories that spread panic and anxiety (“Guidelines over water fluoridation under review”, October 30). This time it is about fluoridation of water. Singapore has had fluoridation of its water supply for 68 years, and instead of causing lower intelligence in children, the country has for many years sat at or near the top of the PISA score list. Another high-score entity, Hong Kong, began fluoridation in 1961. Other high scorers, the PISA-assessed regions of China (Beijing, Shanghai, Jiangsu, Zhejiang), no longer fluoridate their water supplies but only because the water sources contain naturally high fluoride background levels. While many people might point to the fact that many other high-scoring countries prefer fluoridation of toothpaste, in support of their opposition to fluoridation of water, one should not confuse cause and effect in the low-high IQ debate. Low IQ or weak intellectual development in children may well be caused by regular consumption of alcohol by the mothers. In its review of Australia’s national guidelines for fluoride in drinking water, the National Health and Medical Research Council should study the effects of alcohol, too. Kim Woo, Mascot Testing time over I, too, am tickled pink to farewell the replacement bus shuffle. Commuters endured two years-plus of it while the heavy rail morphed into a modern metro, a very welcome addition to our transport network (“Twists and turns of metro challenge”, October 30). It’s been quite literally a testing time, months of watching the promised passage whizzing past without access as the systems were bedded down. That excitement was tempered when the station announcements commenced some weeks ago; a strange penetrating chime that can be heard up to one kilometre from the platform. It is an alert that is very alarming for residents of Hurlstone Park – the unique topography of the station acts as an echo chamber. Vegetation along the line, removed for the build, would have helped to buffer the noise, but for those in close proximity life has become unbearable. It’s a relatively easy fix. I just hope the hype around the retro metro doesn’t distract from mitigation for those who embrace the change but need the issue of audio addressed. Janet Argall, Hurlstone Park Federate ATAR It is claimed by NSW Universities Admissions Centre that an ATAR from NSW is presently equivalent to an ATAR in any other state. Other states use different methods to construct their ATARs (“National exams for years 6, 10, 12 proposed”, October 28). For example, Victoria UAC scales advanced maths differently, and Queensland uses a different proportion based on external exams. A national ATAR is required. Brad Elliott, North Rocks (Former Subject Chief Examiner, NESA)

World.title: Mushroom killer Erin Patterson to die in prison after appeal spectacularly backfires
World.content:
Graphic content NationalVictoriaMushroom trial Mushroom killer Erin Patterson to die in prison after appeal spectacularly backfires Erin Pearson and Isabel McMillan Updated October 30, 2026 — 6:23pm ,first published October 30, 2026 — 10:28am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Mushroom cook killer Erin Patterson’s only chance at freedom will lie in a last-ditch plea to Australia’s highest court after three judges found her cold and calculated crimes were so shocking she should die in jail. Patterson, 52, sat unflinching on videolink from behind bars as Court of Appeal justices Stephen McLeish, Lesley Taylor and Peter Kidd on Friday threw out her appeal against her conviction and instead increased her sentence, describing it as manifestly inadequate. Patterson is now the first Victorian woman, and only the second in the country’s history, to receive a sentence of life without parole. The first was NSW abattoir worker Katherine Knight, who stabbed her de facto husband 37 times, skinning him and cooking his body parts as a meal designed for his children in February 2000. Erin Patterson arrives at an earlier court hearing. Jason Edwards Patterson had been serving life in prison with a non-parole period of 33 years, after being found guilty by a jury last year of the poisoning murders of her in-laws, Don and Gail Patterson, Gail’s sister, Heather Wilkinson, and of attempting to murder Heather’s husband, Ian Wilkinson.



Sentencing Justice Christopher Beale, who has now retired, resisted calls at the time to jail Patterson for life with no prospect of parole, finding her case was so infamous she was likely to find custody more onerous than others. However, the Court of Appeal found Patterson’s persistent murderous intent had protracted the suffering of her victims. The justices said Patterson had coldly planned and executed the murders over nearly three weeks, including extending the invitation to lunch and hiding the truth for nearly a week as her victims lay dying. Victims Don Patterson, Gail Patterson, Heather Wilkinson and Ian Wilkinson. “Patterson’s conduct was characterised by an elaborate series of deceptions, including the false cancer claims deployed to explain the absence of the children, the false denials of having foraged for mushrooms, the repeated false assertions as to the source of the mushrooms and the destruction of evidence,” McLeish said.



“The offending was carefully planned and deliberate. It represented a cruel breach of trust to members of her extended family.” McLeish said the court found it “necessary that the sentence vindicated unequivocally the primary value that our society places on each individual human life”. “This offending was extraordinarily cold and calculated and stood to be denounced in the strongest terms,” he said. In court to hear the judgment was Erin’s brother-in-law, Nathan Patterson. Surviving lunch guest Ian Wilkinson was notably absent along with Erin’s estranged husband, Simon Patterson. Nathan Patterson sat with members of the homicide squad – including Nigel L’Estrange and Stephen Eppingstall – who appeared shocked as the decision was handed down. Outside court, they were all smiles, as were the prosecution, who grinned as they walked down William and Lonsdale streets to their nearby offices.



Director of Public Prosecutions Brendan Kissane, KC, and junior barrister Jeremy McWilliams on Friday. Joe Armao Patterson’s appeal barrister, Richard Edney, had earlier argued there were a number of potential irregularities in his client’s case, including during the jury’s seven-day sequestration at a Gippsland hotel while they were deciding Patterson’s fate. The court heard jurors had stayed in the same Traralgon hotel as members of the prosecution and police involved in the case, which Edney claimed amounted to a catastrophic and fundamental failure to comply with the trial rules. Edney said the “inexplicable failure” to separate the jury created a potential miscarriage of justice with the media seemingly knowing more about potential interactions between the jury and others at the Latrobe Valley hotel than the prosecution did. It followed an 11-week trial in Morwell, in Victoria’s east, in mid-2025, which heard from more than 50 witnesses.



PATTERSON APPEAL ARGUMENTS Patterson’s defence team submitted seven reasons the mushroom murderer’s convictions should be overturned: The jury was potentially contaminated by staying in the same hotel as prosecutors and police. Patterson was grilled unfairly by prosecutors during eight days in the witness box. The prosecution told the jury it did not have to prove a motive for the murders but then spent substantial time implying she was angry at the Patterson family over a child support dispute. Large tranches of evidence were wrongly shown to the jury, including mobile phone tower links to two areas in rural Gippsland where deadly mushrooms grew. Photos and videos found on Patterson’s devices that could have backed her claims of being a mushroom forager were not shown to the jury. Evidence from Facebook “friends” was not relevant, or their probative value was outweighed by unfair prejudice. Prosecutors used family text messages to imply Patterson had arranged the lethal lunch after fighting with the family when no motive was put forward as part of the case. McLeish, reading a summary on behalf of the three appeal judges, said that while the jury accommodation was “highly undesirable” and “plainly unfortunate”, there was no basis to believe the jury hadn’t reached its verdict according to law. Jury keepers reported no contact had occurred with anyone outside the jury pool, the court heard. This, McLeish said, was “significant” because it stood in the face of an argument otherwise based on “conjecture, guesswork or surmise”. Edney also argued that Patterson had been unfairly grilled by the prosecutor over eight days in the witness box, that 35 errors had occurred in their closing address to the jury, and that large amounts of evidence should not have been allowed into the trial.



Director of Public Prosecutions Brendan Kissane, KC, had dismissed the concerns as baseless and not warranting the granting of an appeal. The Court of Appeal found five of Patterson’s seven appeal grounds were either without merit or doomed to fail. After dismissing concerns about the jury’s sequestration, the only remaining appeal ground concerned expert evidence on mobile phone data about Patterson’s visits to two locations where death cap mushroom had been spotted. But McLeish said the evidence was admissible, and Patterson’s appeal should fail.



“The court has decided that this evidence was admissible as part of the wider circumstantial case advanced by the prosecution, which included the purchase by the applicant of a food dehydrator on the same day as one of the possible visits.” The trial was told Patterson had fed her four guests beef Wellington laced with death cap mushrooms during lunch at the mother of two’s Leongatha home in July 2023. Patterson’s Leongatha home, the scene of the fatal lunch. Joe Armao Simon Patterson, the killer’s estranged husband, had also been invited to lunch but cancelled the evening before. Heather Wilkinson and Gail Patterson died on August 4, 2023, from multiple organ failure, with a diagnosis of amanita mushroom poisoning. Don Patterson died the following night.

World.title: Tricky, playful, intriguing: Students react to HSC art exam paintings
World.content:
NationalNSWHSC Tricky, playful, intriguing: Students react to HSC art exam paintings Christopher Harris October 30, 2026 — 6:11pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Cerebral conceptual art in Amsterdam, a Greek marble sculpture from the first century – and then there was the photo of human limbs made of foam, metallic lycra and velvet. Welcome to the Higher School Certificate art exam. “I feel like it was a pretty good, chill exam overall,” Cammeraygal High School student Lily Jennings said after walking out of the exam hall on Friday afternoon. Student Lily Jennings liked the paintings the examiners chose for the HSC art exam. George Chan The 18-year-old particularly enjoyed answering questions about Indigenous artist Kaylene Whiskey’s 2019 artwork Coober Party. The piece is currently listed with Paddington’s Roslyn Oxley9 Gallery, where Whiskey’s body of work is described as “both playful and an intriguing comment on contemporary Indigenous life”.



In the exam, students were asked how Whiskey used symbolism to communicate ideas. “That was really tricky,” Lily said. Her answer focused on how pop culture was intersected with the artist’s Indigenous heritage. Zac Oppen said he learned how to create clay vases last year. George Chan The exam is 90 minutes long and includes a shorter answer section followed by an essay. Compared to other HSC exams, students get five different essay questions to choose from. “I think everyone just picks one which relates to an essay that they’ve done at home,” Lily said.



Related Article HSC Why the HSC biology exam about koala sperm, dead lizards and super salmon had students cheering For Zac Oppen, 18, he chose art because he enjoyed creating work, not necessarily sitting the exam. For his major work, he used a clay wheel to create vases after teaching himself how to do it last year. “I probably prefer the practical side a bit more, but the theory is still really interesting,” the Cammeraygal High student said. He made vases for his major work which he said was a reflection on “the beauty and the cycles of nature; kind of life and death and regeneration”. When it came to choosing an essay question, he opted for one asking about how artists communicate with their cultural historical context when conveying personal ideas.



To answer that, he referenced Titian and Francisco Goya, as well as Picasso and Fiona Foley. For Violet Buchanan, 18, her major work took women featured in major canonical artworks, including Botticelli’s The Birth of Venus, and utilised AI to transfigure her face onto the artworks. Violet Buchanan used AI, oil paint and some inspiration from women featured in art history for her major project. George Chan “It was about women in art history,” she said. The final result is not a self-portrait referencing the finest works of western art. Instead, the new versions, which she then recreated with her own oil paint, look entirely different.



“You had to wait for it to dry, and then you did the next one, and it just took forever,” she said. For year 12 students, the HSC is almost over, with next week’s physics exam on Thursday the final one. World.title: This Test series has been a classic. Sadly, cricket bosses want to strangle the game
World.content:
SportTest cricket Opinion This Test series has been a classic. Sadly, cricket bosses want to strangle the game Malcolm Knox Journalist, author and columnist October 30, 2026 — 6:00pm

October 30, 2026 — 6:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The South Africa-Australia series has been, by any reckoning, a classic of the reduced three-Test genre. It has offered everything Test cricket lovers cherish: savage momentum switches, memorable individual feats, and the sense, every session, of unpredictable possibilities branching out. Loading Each side has been down, up, down, up again. It has taken place in a mostly agreeable time slot for Australian viewers, and sleep is followed by eagerness to hear about the overnight surprises. Although the teams may not have the class of their forebears – only Kagiso Rabada of these Proteas would have made the teams of 2008-2013, and Australia’s batting is literally hit-and-miss. But this hasn’t diminished the entertainment.



It’s hard to think of a more compelling three-match Test cricket contest. How good if it went for five? Australia’s captain Pat Cummins, and teammate Travis Head, claim the wicket of South Africa’s captain Temba Bavuma, right, on day three of the third Test match between South Africa and Australia, in Cape Town. AP Oddly, however – because sports are meant to be about entertainment – attractive Test cricket is mere surface ruffle over the tidal forces beneath. Crowds have been so poor that 11,000 attending a day at Cape Town is seen as a triumph.



South Africa plays little Test cricket: since they became world champions by beating Australia in London in 2025, they had played six games. In that period, Australia, India and England played a

combined 40. For the next year, the Proteas have two Tests against Bangladesh and a three-Test rubber with England, a shrinkage from the usual five-Test tours. Like the West Indies, South Africa has a popular domestic Twenty20 competition that finances its struggling red-ball calendar. Josh Inglis celebrates his Test ton against South Africa. The match has been played in front of low crowds. Getty Images The real direction of Test cricket will be set next month when the International Cricket Council dictates its Future Tours Program (FTP). The excitement of this series in South Africa, which should be a fillip for the Test format, has no bearing on the ICC’s decisions. The strength in breadth of Test cricket, already withering, will wither more. Instead of making a case to revive and rebuild it, this series will stand as an elegy to what we will miss.



A draft of the ICC’s plans, drawn up in Dubai in September, has been circulated. Its priorities are expanding Twenty20 and locking down bilateral Test series among the club of India, Australia and England, the self-anointed “Big Three”. Another perspective Opinion

Test cricket Test cricket isn’t going anywhere. But it does need some help Greg Chappell Former Australian Test captain Five-match series, the true test of cricket, will be limited to these “marquee” events. The rest will fight for the scraps. South Africa, New Zealand, Pakistan and the West Indies, all of whom have been the best for periods of Test cricket’s history, will form a de facto second tier. The draft FTP has an element of bait-and-switch. Its downgrading of bilateral 50-over series, which will be mourned by few, will obscure its real agenda, which is to promote Twenty20 as the main format at the expense of Test cricket.



The Ashes, Border-Gavaskar and Anderson-Tendulkar trophies will be elevated and preserved, but the breadth of Test cricket, which peaked in the early 1990s, will be thinned out. It will be technically unachievable for Pakistan to return to the top, or for Bangladesh to make sustained advances, while India snub them. The West Indies were once the kings of cricket until Steve Waugh (left) and the Australians took the fight to them, including quick Curtly Ambrose (centre). Skipper Richie Richardson had to pull his paceman away from an altercation with Waugh at the Queen’s Park Oval in Port of Spain, Trinidad. AP South Africa, Sri Lanka, New Zealand and the West Indies will cross their fingers and hope to produce outstanding individuals who cover over the structural decline in red-ball cricket. Ireland and Afghanistan will get a lot of Twenty20 and a few token Tests. Notably, in the early 1990s, when Test cricket’s strength was growing, Australia, England and India were in the middle of the pack. This won’t be allowed to happen again.



It’s well acknowledged that India’s cricket economy, powered by the IPL, underwrites the rest of the game. It ramifies to Australia not just in programming: the ongoing brawl over privatising BBL clubs is just Australia being caught between the rock of IPL financial power and the hard place of impoverished independence. This is replicated around the cricket world. Travis Head celebrates the wicket of Marques Ackerman in Cape Town. AP Photo/Halden Krog The IPL and its audiences are the game’s engine room, and Test cricket is at its mercy, allowed to persist as a quid pro quo to keep England and Australia onside and to give elite Indian players a chance at establishing a nationalistic legacy more substantial than a 50 off 19 balls. This is not to paint India as the bad guys. Their audiences have made cricket the second-most popular team sport in the world after football, recognised with its inclusion in the next Olympics. This popularity comes with qualifications: the surging world game is Twenty20, followed a long way back by Test cricket involving India.



As the FTP will make clear, the “marquee” series are nothing more than Test cricket’s rearguard action. No such energy will be expended to preserve five-Test series or regular Test cricket involving the second tier. Only if India wants to subsidise it at the expense of Twenty20, can Test cricket regain the depth and diversity it once had. India has shown little such intention. Over its 150 years, there have always been multiple tiers in Test cricket. The beauty of the game, as it spread, was that the members of those tiers were changeable. For decades, the West Indies were unquestionably in the top echelon and India were not. Pakistan had a far better Test record than India. Sri Lanka started their Test era with more success than either India or Pakistan. Zimbabwe rose and fell. England and Australia sometimes dropped into the second tier. Test cricket was vibrant. The future, by contrast, is fixed. The top tier will be immovable.



Even if they win a World Test Championship, second-tier nations will still be stuck. Money talks. But genuine, diverse, unpredictable competition is not just a romance; it means money too, if only the game’s governors could envision a future of 100 or 150 years. Editor's pick Opinion

Test cricket Selectors’ disdain for Sheffield Shield is sabotaging the Test team Geoff Lawson Cricket columnist Instead, ICC members will talk about where they want cricket to be in five years. The way they are going, five years may be all that a broad, competitive Test cricket community has. South Africa and Australia have given us a treat of a three-Test series. If only there were two more games to settle it. But this marquee is a small tent, and its future is smaller. Even while we’re celebrating its virtues, the longest game will be strangled by bosses who think of the short term. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Friday.

When Isaac Quaynor attended his first spring racing carnival back in 2023, what he wore was of little consequence. “I was a bit of a deer in the headlights,” the Collingwood player and G.H. Mumm ambassador admits. “I was just happy to be here, so I didn’t really pay attention to what people were wearing.” It’s a far cry from his approach to Derby Day 2026, for which Quaynor worked with his stylist Simon Finnegan and Australian tailor Oscar Hunt to design a custom-made pinstripe suit that suggests more spritzer than simpleton. Hannah Dal Sasso and Isaac Quaynor at the G.H. Mumm marquee in the Birdcage at Flemington Racecourse. Eddie Jim “When I started working with him he wore a lot of streetwear and colour. We still do that now but we lean a lot more towards men’s tailoring and focus on the silhouette,” Finnegan explains.



Quaynor is leading the new wave of young men approaching their race-day outfits with careful intent and experimental enthusiasm. Related Article Good Weekend Red-carpet looks influencing this year’s spring racing fashions “It’s a reflection on men taking more risks now but also brands are giving men more options,” says stylist Donny Galella. “Suiting used to be very black, white, grey, beige – you know, the same colours – so it’s great to see now a plethora of all these fun colours that guys can wear, and fun suit styles: the oversized ’90s jackets, wide-leg pants, double-breasted jackets. Guys have more options and have more fun.” Frankie Foster says he’s lost count of how many ties he has. The 30-year-old former Love Island UK contestant-turned-racing commentator and presenter found himself accumulating the accessory at a rapid pace once he became a race-day regular, leaning on the tie as a cost-effective way to update his look without needing a new suit.



Frankie Foster launched his own label, Franc James, specialising in 100 per cent silk ties. Eddie Jim “I was going racing all the time and I don’t have 20 suits in my wardrobe – but I can have 20 ties,” Foster says. “And with a different shirt, tie, pocket square, hat – whatever it is – you can wear the same suit as many ways as you want.” Loading Foster became such an aficionado that in 2022 he launched his own label, Franc James, specialising in 100 per cent silk ties, hand-stitched and printed in England.



“I once calculated the value of all of them, and that’s probably when I decided: let’s stop buying them and let’s start making them.” Related Article Caulfield Cup A lesson in elegance: The Caulfield Cup fashion winners Asked what advice they’d give men keen to make their mark this Derby Day, Quaynor and Foster echo similar sentiments: get a suit that fits properly, and stay sharp. “If you want to get with the times, go for a baggier pant and stay away from anything tight,” advises Quaynor, who says he’s taken to trawling Pinterest when he needs a spark of style genius. Foster offers dually sage wisdom: “The most frequent mistake happens after you’ve had a few drinks and your tie starts to loosen,” he says.



“It looks a bit scruffy. Readjust it, make sure it’s fastened tight to the collar of your shirt, give a little pinch to make a dimple and you’re good to go.” Make the most of your health, relationships, fitness and nutrition with our Live Well newsletter. Get it in your inbox every Monday.

World.title: Ignoring homelessness hurts everyone
World.content:
NationalVictoriaEditorial Editorial Ignoring homelessness hurts everyone The Age's View Editorial October 30, 2026 — 7:00pm

October 30, 2026 — 7:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

When former New York City mayor Bill de Blasio walked Melbourne’s streets for the first time, he was overcome with envy. He marvelled at the Birrarung, the tram network and the cafe culture. This foreign place felt so far from home – so beautiful and safe, compared with the challenges of New York, he told The Age’s Melbourne Assembly last week. Loading But, beneath the gleam, he knew the city harboured something insidious. “Let’s be honest: if you don’t address homelessness, it is not just a moral thing,” de Blasio told the civic forum. “It will hurt your business climate. It will hurt people’s sense of security. There are so many painful realities.



“When you see a homeless person, it feels like a defeat. It feels like something went wrong for all of us.” The Age reported this week that Australia’s housing crisis is pushing frontline homelessness services towards collapse, with workers handing out tents instead of accommodation, and asking women fleeing domestic violence whether they can sleep in their cars. It’s time for a bold approach to drive down homelessness in Victoria. Eddie Jim Almost two-thirds of homelessness providers are turning away desperate Australians they would once have helped, with some rejecting as many people as they take in, according to a Homelessness Australia briefing prepared for the Albanese government (using University of NSW research). The findings expose a system so overwhelmed by soaring rents, chronic housing shortages and inadequate funding that it is increasingly unable to offer even emergency accommodation to people facing life on the streets.



And they put in sobering terms what all leaders, including those of Victoria’s major parties, must accept: the system is broken. Another report from the Council to Homeless Persons this week found the number of working homeless people in Victoria had surged by more than 40 per cent in four years, and 4400 full-time workers had received homelessness support in the past year alone. Related Article Homelessness Homelessness crisis hits breaking point as services turn away desperate Australians In some acknowledgment of the crisis, the parties have signalled a new willingness to act before the November state election (perhaps for the first time since COVID-19, when homeless people were housed to stop the disease spreading). The opposition has pledged to roll out a statewide homelessness strategy, pausing and reviewing the contentious high-rise public housing tower redevelopment program, and auditing vacant social housing properties under a Liberal and Nationals government.



Under Victorian Labor’s statewide expansion of a program pioneered in inner Melbourne, teams of homelessness workers will be sent onto streets to profile homeless people, build trust and connect them with housing and support. However, homelessness services warn crisis accommodation centres are regularly full before lunchtime, and that homeless people end up being placed in unsafe accommodation. A “by-name” list – or directory of every person sleeping rough – is part of the assertive outreach program, which is under way. The City of Melbourne has been operating a by-name homelessness list since 2019, rather than waiting for people to access services, but homelessness continues to grow in the CBD, with at least 140 people on the list (almost double the number in 2024). Nick Staikos, Victoria’s first homelessness minister (as of August), was spruiking the by-name list on ABC Radio Melbourne this week, as well as Labor’s investment in social housing.



Mornings host Raf Epstein was quick to point out that Victoria had the lowest proportion of social housing of any Australian state or territory. “One of Ben Carroll’s first decisions was to appoint a homelessness minister, but we have been serious about it,” Staikos told Epstein on ABC Melbourne’s Mornings program this week. “I mean, we have built more social homes and affordable homes than any government in the past. We are building 17,000 social homes. We’ve completed 12,000 of them. “We are serious, but tackling rough sleeping and homelessness is not just about the house. It is about the wraparound services. It is about the complex needs of a human being – that’s what it is.” Staikos said Labor’s $28 million assertive outreach program was about bringing the front door of services to rough sleepers, so they didn’t have to go searching for them.



De Blasio is an enthusiastic supporter of this approach, crediting New York’s similar model (and a legal “right to shelter”) as crucial to tackling homelessness in his home city. But the question remains: if services have little to offer beyond their front doors, how much hope is there to radically drive down homelessness in Victoria? At the Melbourne Assembly, de Blasio used an Americanism borrowed from the country’s national sport, baseball, to warn against the alternative to an aggressive approach. “Play the ball, or the ball will play you,” he said. “When it comes to homelessness, you must assertively address it, or I guarantee it gets worse.” Within the next term of government, both Victorian Labor and the Coalition must commit to numerical targets to drastically reduce homelessness in this state.



And they must invest further in tangible solutions to the crisis, beyond getting people to services’ front door. This means safe and secure accommodation, and social housing. Solving this calamity is a tough ask, and there are complex and varied reasons why some people become, or remain, homeless. As Staikos said, though, there is an ideal Victoria should aspire to: when homelessness happens, it should be “rare, brief and non-recurring”. World.title: Jess Wilson knows the SRL can’t be stopped. Pretending otherwise is political shenanigans
World.content:
Analysis PoliticsVictoriaVictorian election Jess Wilson knows the SRL can’t be stopped. Pretending otherwise is political shenanigans Kieran Rooney October 30, 2026 — 7:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The Coalition’s explanation of what a “pause and review” of the Suburban Rail Loop would actually entail is now as murky as the subterranean mud that tunnel boring machines are digging through. Both major parties are ensnared in an SRL conundrum wrapped in a political riddle – what to do with a major project that is too big to fail and increasingly expensive to build. Once tunnel boring machines like this one begin their work, it is extremely costly to stop them. The first stage of the under-construction rail line, running underground from Cheltenham to Box Hill, is too far gone to cancel or drastically alter without significant costs. This is not a comfortable reality for Opposition Leader Jess Wilson, who has made economic management her biggest virtue to voters. She has appointed herself shadow treasurer for this exact reason.



By repeating the mantra that they will pause and review the project with just a morsel of detail, the Coalition has, deliberately or not, allowed some wiggle room in the minds of voters. Related Article Exclusive

Victorian election Coalition says it will keep drilling Suburban Rail Loop tunnels as the massive cost of stopping is revealed Like a political Rorschach test, different groups have found their own meaning. Haters have clung to the hope that this process will find the underground line is too expensive and must be cancelled immediately. Others have rationalised that an incoming government will get their feet under the desk and accept that it has to be completed.



In this sweet spot, Wilson’s pause and review policy has allowed her to appear as a hard-nosed budget manager without being tied to any specific changes that could be criticised. Related Article Exclusive

Victorian election Victoria has ‘no choice’ but to confront growing debt problem Until this week, the word “pause” was never assumed to be the subjective part of the plan. Most people had a mental picture of tools being put down, tunnel boring machines unplugged and sites being padlocked while a Coalition government crunched the numbers. This was not quite right, the Coalition now says. Their strategy, clarified in a statement to The Age, actually does not involve sending workers home or halting digging while the review is under way.



Instead, it is a pause on signing further contracts similar to Premier Ben Carroll’s promise not to sign station-building contracts until a technical review of the project tries to find $1 billion in savings. Loading The Coalition’s statement says its policy has no technical or budgetary differences to the government’s own review decision. It would be disingenuous to now blame the media, the public or the Coalition’s political opponents for this supposed misconception. Speaking at parliament in May, when Wilson was asked on camera if pausing meant stopping work, she nodded and said yes.



When asked for how long, she said, “as long as it takes”. She has not been as unequivocal at other media appearances, but the conversation remains a matter of public record and is partly why the issue hasn’t been pressed further. Loading On Friday, shadow attorney-general James Newbury was sent out to clarify the issue and said: “Any works that can be paused will immediately be paused. “We’ve never said we’re going to breach any contract. What we have said is, tools will be down while we review the project,” he added. Later on Friday, a Liberal spokesperson sought to clarify again that “pausing the project means not committing to further contracts whilst the review about the project’s future is undertaken. Workers will continue to be paid”.



None of this makes a lot of sense when put together. It makes their position even murkier. Related Article Victorian election Deal or no deal? How the major parties are tackling the minority government risk When information is incomplete, imagination will fill the gaps. If the Coalition’s position was altered after May, they should have said so. They were given plenty of opportunities to explain the nitty-gritty of their policy and must wear the blame if it was misunderstood.



It may well be there was never an incentive to clarify the position until now. The shades of grey were better than the political realities, which are as follows: There are three tunnel boring machines digging their way under Melbourne’s east and south-eastern suburbs, and a fourth is being assembled to launch shortly;

Stopping them or terminating their work before they reach their next destination will be a logistical challenge rivalled only by the time I learned how to reverse the swing of my laundry door;

Across launch sites and the sites of six future underground stations, there are gigantic holes in the ground that have been excavated by workers believing that, at some point in the next two years, builders will come in and start building concrete platforms and walls. The opposition’s public transport spokesman, Matthew Guy, acknowledged this challenge on ABC Radio in August 2025. “If we’ve got tunnel boring machines which have gone six kilometres underground, then we can hardly fill it back in,” he said.



“The project will then proceed, there’s no doubt about it ... No government would have any choice.” Related Article Victorian election Opposition goes loco with $1.7 billion transport pitch This is an uncomfortable truth for both Wilson and Carroll, who is known to be sceptical about the project but, after becoming leader, ultimately decided to plough on with it and search for $2 billion in savings. Of these savings, $1 billion has been contested and the other $1 billion is yet to materialise. There are plenty of counterfactuals to be had about the Suburban Rail Loop, its merits and timing.



The Coalition can argue that proceeding with tunnel boring machines before the election has tied their hands, severely limited their options to manage the budget, and should have been reconsidered after the debt incurred during the pandemic. Related Article Exclusive

Suburban Rail Loop ‘Building the plane while it’s flying’: How the government rewrote the story of the Suburban Rail Loop Labor can argue that the project was already on the ballot of two elections, including one where the Coalition said they would scrap it, and it will only grow in cost the longer it is delayed. What cannot be disputed is that machines are digging underground, workers are on site, and any suspension or cancellation will not be easy. Alongside economic management, another huge part of Wilson’s pitch to voters has been restoring trust in government and being transparent.

South Africa are 40 runs in front, but they’re four wickets down. Who’s on top? Australia, according to Kerry O’Keeffe, Mark Waugh and David Warner. Here’s what they just said on Fox Cricket.

World.title: Mushroom killer Erin Patterson to die in prison after appeal spectacularly backfires
World.content:
Graphic content NationalVictoriaMushroom trial Mushroom killer Erin Patterson to die in prison after appeal spectacularly backfires Erin Pearson and Isabel McMillan Updated October 30, 2026 — 6:23pm ,first published October 30, 2026 — 10:28am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Mushroom cook killer Erin Patterson’s only chance at freedom will lie in a last-ditch plea to Australia’s highest court after three judges found her cold and calculated crimes were so shocking she should die in jail. Patterson, 52, sat unflinching on videolink from behind bars as Court of Appeal justices Stephen McLeish, Lesley Taylor and Peter Kidd on Friday threw out her appeal against her conviction and instead increased her sentence, describing it as manifestly inadequate. Patterson is now the first Victorian woman, and only the second in the country’s history, to receive a sentence of life without parole. The first was NSW abattoir worker Katherine Knight, who stabbed her de facto husband 37 times, skinning him and cooking his body parts as a meal designed for his children in February 2000. Erin Patterson arrives at an earlier court hearing. Jason Edwards Patterson had been serving life in prison with a non-parole period of 33 years, after being found guilty by a jury last year of the poisoning murders of her in-laws, Don and Gail Patterson, Gail’s sister, Heather Wilkinson, and of attempting to murder Heather’s husband, Ian Wilkinson.



Sentencing Justice Christopher Beale, who has now retired, resisted calls at the time to jail Patterson for life with no prospect of parole, finding her case was so infamous she was likely to find custody more onerous than others. However, the Court of Appeal found Patterson’s persistent murderous intent had protracted the suffering of her victims. The justices said Patterson had coldly planned and executed the murders over nearly three weeks, including extending the invitation to lunch and hiding the truth for nearly a week as her victims lay dying. Victims Don Patterson, Gail Patterson, Heather Wilkinson and Ian Wilkinson. “Patterson’s conduct was characterised by an elaborate series of deceptions, including the false cancer claims deployed to explain the absence of the children, the false denials of having foraged for mushrooms, the repeated false assertions as to the source of the mushrooms and the destruction of evidence,” McLeish said.



“The offending was carefully planned and deliberate. It represented a cruel breach of trust to members of her extended family.” McLeish said the court found it “necessary that the sentence vindicated unequivocally the primary value that our society places on each individual human life”. “This offending was extraordinarily cold and calculated and stood to be denounced in the strongest terms,” he said. In court to hear the judgment was Erin’s brother-in-law, Nathan Patterson. Surviving lunch guest Ian Wilkinson was notably absent along with Erin’s estranged husband, Simon Patterson. Nathan Patterson sat with members of the homicide squad – including Nigel L’Estrange and Stephen Eppingstall – who appeared shocked as the decision was handed down. Outside court, they were all smiles, as were the prosecution, who grinned as they walked down William and Lonsdale streets to their nearby offices.



Director of Public Prosecutions Brendan Kissane, KC, and junior barrister Jeremy McWilliams on Friday. Joe Armao Patterson’s appeal barrister, Richard Edney, had earlier argued there were a number of potential irregularities in his client’s case, including during the jury’s seven-day sequestration at a Gippsland hotel while they were deciding Patterson’s fate. The court heard jurors had stayed in the same Traralgon hotel as members of the prosecution and police involved in the case, which Edney claimed amounted to a catastrophic and fundamental failure to comply with the trial rules. Edney said the “inexplicable failure” to separate the jury created a potential miscarriage of justice with the media seemingly knowing more about potential interactions between the jury and others at the Latrobe Valley hotel than the prosecution did. It followed an 11-week trial in Morwell, in Victoria’s east, in mid-2025, which heard from more than 50 witnesses.



PATTERSON APPEAL ARGUMENTS Patterson’s defence team submitted seven reasons the mushroom murderer’s convictions should be overturned: The jury was potentially contaminated by staying in the same hotel as prosecutors and police. Patterson was grilled unfairly by prosecutors during eight days in the witness box. The prosecution told the jury it did not have to prove a motive for the murders but then spent substantial time implying she was angry at the Patterson family over a child support dispute. Large tranches of evidence were wrongly shown to the jury, including mobile phone tower links to two areas in rural Gippsland where deadly mushrooms grew. Photos and videos found on Patterson’s devices that could have backed her claims of being a mushroom forager were not shown to the jury. Evidence from Facebook “friends” was not relevant, or their probative value was outweighed by unfair prejudice. Prosecutors used family text messages to imply Patterson had arranged the lethal lunch after fighting with the family when no motive was put forward as part of the case. McLeish, reading a summary on behalf of the three appeal judges, said that while the jury accommodation was “highly undesirable” and “plainly unfortunate”, there was no basis to believe the jury hadn’t reached its verdict according to law. Jury keepers reported no contact had occurred with anyone outside the jury pool, the court heard. This, McLeish said, was “significant” because it stood in the face of an argument otherwise based on “conjecture, guesswork or surmise”. Edney also argued that Patterson had been unfairly grilled by the prosecutor over eight days in the witness box, that 35 errors had occurred in their closing address to the jury, and that large amounts of evidence should not have been allowed into the trial.



Director of Public Prosecutions Brendan Kissane, KC, had dismissed the concerns as baseless and not warranting the granting of an appeal. The Court of Appeal found five of Patterson’s seven appeal grounds were either without merit or doomed to fail. After dismissing concerns about the jury’s sequestration, the only remaining appeal ground concerned expert evidence on mobile phone data about Patterson’s visits to two locations where death cap mushroom had been spotted. But McLeish said the evidence was admissible, and Patterson’s appeal should fail.



“The court has decided that this evidence was admissible as part of the wider circumstantial case advanced by the prosecution, which included the purchase by the applicant of a food dehydrator on the same day as one of the possible visits.” The trial was told Patterson had fed her four guests beef Wellington laced with death cap mushrooms during lunch at the mother of two’s Leongatha home in July 2023. Patterson’s Leongatha home, the scene of the fatal lunch. Joe Armao Simon Patterson, the killer’s estranged husband, had also been invited to lunch but cancelled the evening before. Heather Wilkinson and Gail Patterson died on August 4, 2023, from multiple organ failure, with a diagnosis of amanita mushroom poisoning. Don Patterson died the following night.

World.title: Tricky, playful, intriguing: Students react to HSC art exam paintings
World.content:
NationalNSWHSC Tricky, playful, intriguing: Students react to HSC art exam paintings Christopher Harris October 30, 2026 — 6:11pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Cerebral conceptual art in Amsterdam, a Greek marble sculpture from the first century – and then there was the photo of human limbs made of foam, metallic lycra and velvet. Welcome to the Higher School Certificate art exam. “I feel like it was a pretty good, chill exam overall,” Cammeraygal High School student Lily Jennings said after walking out of the exam hall on Friday afternoon. Student Lily Jennings liked the paintings the examiners chose for the HSC art exam. George Chan The 18-year-old particularly enjoyed answering questions about Indigenous artist Kaylene Whiskey’s 2019 artwork Coober Party. The piece is currently listed with Paddington’s Roslyn Oxley9 Gallery, where Whiskey’s body of work is described as “both playful and an intriguing comment on contemporary Indigenous life”.



In the exam, students were asked how Whiskey used symbolism to communicate ideas. “That was really tricky,” Lily said. Her answer focused on how pop culture was intersected with the artist’s Indigenous heritage. Zac Oppen said he learned how to create clay vases last year. George Chan The exam is 90 minutes long and includes a shorter answer section followed by an essay. Compared to other HSC exams, students get five different essay questions to choose from. “I think everyone just picks one which relates to an essay that they’ve done at home,” Lily said.



Related Article HSC Why the HSC biology exam about koala sperm, dead lizards and super salmon had students cheering For Zac Oppen, 18, he chose art because he enjoyed creating work, not necessarily sitting the exam. For his major work, he used a clay wheel to create vases after teaching himself how to do it last year. “I probably prefer the practical side a bit more, but the theory is still really interesting,” the Cammeraygal High student said. He made vases for his major work which he said was a reflection on “the beauty and the cycles of nature; kind of life and death and regeneration”. When it came to choosing an essay question, he opted for one asking about how artists communicate with their cultural historical context when conveying personal ideas.



To answer that, he referenced Titian and Francisco Goya, as well as Picasso and Fiona Foley. For Violet Buchanan, 18, her major work took women featured in major canonical artworks, including Botticelli’s The Birth of Venus, and utilised AI to transfigure her face onto the artworks. Violet Buchanan used AI, oil paint and some inspiration from women featured in art history for her major project. George Chan “It was about women in art history,” she said. The final result is not a self-portrait referencing the finest works of western art. Instead, the new versions, which she then recreated with her own oil paint, look entirely different.



“You had to wait for it to dry, and then you did the next one, and it just took forever,” she said. For year 12 students, the HSC is almost over, with next week’s physics exam on Thursday the final one. World.title: This Test series has been a classic. Sadly, cricket bosses want to strangle the game
World.content:
SportTest cricket Opinion This Test series has been a classic. Sadly, cricket bosses want to strangle the game Malcolm Knox Journalist, author and columnist October 30, 2026 — 6:00pm

October 30, 2026 — 6:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The South Africa-Australia series has been, by any reckoning, a classic of the reduced three-Test genre. It has offered everything Test cricket lovers cherish: savage momentum switches, memorable individual feats, and the sense, every session, of unpredictable possibilities branching out. Loading Each side has been down, up, down, up again. It has taken place in a mostly agreeable time slot for Australian viewers, and sleep is followed by eagerness to hear about the overnight surprises. Although the teams may not have the class of their forebears – only Kagiso Rabada of these Proteas would have made the teams of 2008-2013, and Australia’s batting is literally hit-and-miss. But this hasn’t diminished the entertainment.



It’s hard to think of a more compelling three-match Test cricket contest. How good if it went for five? Australia’s captain Pat Cummins, and teammate Travis Head, claim the wicket of South Africa’s captain Temba Bavuma, right, on day three of the third Test match between South Africa and Australia, in Cape Town. AP Oddly, however – because sports are meant to be about entertainment – attractive Test cricket is mere surface ruffle over the tidal forces beneath. Crowds have been so poor that 11,000 attending a day at Cape Town is seen as a triumph.



South Africa plays little Test cricket: since they became world champions by beating Australia in London in 2025, they had played six games. In that period, Australia, India and England played a

combined 40. For the next year, the Proteas have two Tests against Bangladesh and a three-Test rubber with England, a shrinkage from the usual five-Test tours. Like the West Indies, South Africa has a popular domestic Twenty20 competition that finances its struggling red-ball calendar. Josh Inglis celebrates his Test ton against South Africa. The match has been played in front of low crowds. Getty Images The real direction of Test cricket will be set next month when the International Cricket Council dictates its Future Tours Program (FTP). The excitement of this series in South Africa, which should be a fillip for the Test format, has no bearing on the ICC’s decisions. The strength in breadth of Test cricket, already withering, will wither more. Instead of making a case to revive and rebuild it, this series will stand as an elegy to what we will miss.



A draft of the ICC’s plans, drawn up in Dubai in September, has been circulated. Its priorities are expanding Twenty20 and locking down bilateral Test series among the club of India, Australia and England, the self-anointed “Big Three”. Another perspective Opinion

Test cricket Test cricket isn’t going anywhere. But it does need some help Greg Chappell Former Australian Test captain Five-match series, the true test of cricket, will be limited to these “marquee” events. The rest will fight for the scraps. South Africa, New Zealand, Pakistan and the West Indies, all of whom have been the best for periods of Test cricket’s history, will form a de facto second tier. The draft FTP has an element of bait-and-switch. Its downgrading of bilateral 50-over series, which will be mourned by few, will obscure its real agenda, which is to promote Twenty20 as the main format at the expense of Test cricket.



The Ashes, Border-Gavaskar and Anderson-Tendulkar trophies will be elevated and preserved, but the breadth of Test cricket, which peaked in the early 1990s, will be thinned out. It will be technically unachievable for Pakistan to return to the top, or for Bangladesh to make sustained advances, while India snub them. The West Indies were once the kings of cricket until Steve Waugh (left) and the Australians took the fight to them, including quick Curtly Ambrose (centre). Skipper Richie Richardson had to pull his paceman away from an altercation with Waugh at the Queen’s Park Oval in Port of Spain, Trinidad. AP South Africa, Sri Lanka, New Zealand and the West Indies will cross their fingers and hope to produce outstanding individuals who cover over the structural decline in red-ball cricket. Ireland and Afghanistan will get a lot of Twenty20 and a few token Tests. Notably, in the early 1990s, when Test cricket’s strength was growing, Australia, England and India were in the middle of the pack. This won’t be allowed to happen again.



It’s well acknowledged that India’s cricket economy, powered by the IPL, underwrites the rest of the game. It ramifies to Australia not just in programming: the ongoing brawl over privatising BBL clubs is just Australia being caught between the rock of IPL financial power and the hard place of impoverished independence. This is replicated around the cricket world. Travis Head celebrates the wicket of Marques Ackerman in Cape Town. AP Photo/Halden Krog The IPL and its audiences are the game’s engine room, and Test cricket is at its mercy, allowed to persist as a quid pro quo to keep England and Australia onside and to give elite Indian players a chance at establishing a nationalistic legacy more substantial than a 50 off 19 balls. This is not to paint India as the bad guys. Their audiences have made cricket the second-most popular team sport in the world after football, recognised with its inclusion in the next Olympics. This popularity comes with qualifications: the surging world game is Twenty20, followed a long way back by Test cricket involving India.



As the FTP will make clear, the “marquee” series are nothing more than Test cricket’s rearguard action. No such energy will be expended to preserve five-Test series or regular Test cricket involving the second tier. Only if India wants to subsidise it at the expense of Twenty20, can Test cricket regain the depth and diversity it once had. India has shown little such intention. Over its 150 years, there have always been multiple tiers in Test cricket. The beauty of the game, as it spread, was that the members of those tiers were changeable.
