For decades, the West Indies were unquestionably in the top echelon and India were not. Pakistan had a far better Test record than India. Sri Lanka started their Test era with more success than either India or Pakistan. Zimbabwe rose and fell. England and Australia sometimes dropped into the second tier. Test cricket was vibrant. The future, by contrast, is fixed. The top tier will be immovable.



Even if they win a World Test Championship, second-tier nations will still be stuck. Money talks. But genuine, diverse, unpredictable competition is not just a romance; it means money too, if only the game’s governors could envision a future of 100 or 150 years. Editor's pick Opinion

Test cricket Selectors’ disdain for Sheffield Shield is sabotaging the Test team Geoff Lawson Cricket columnist Instead, ICC members will talk about where they want cricket to be in five years. The way they are going, five years may be all that a broad, competitive Test cricket community has. South Africa and Australia have given us a treat of a three-Test series. If only there were two more games to settle it. But this marquee is a small tent, and its future is smaller. Even while we’re celebrating its virtues, the longest game will be strangled by bosses who think of the short term. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Friday.

World.title: Youth Homeless Summit appeals for greater attention to plight of young people
World.content:
"When was the last time you had to think about whether you were allowed to feel safe? Not whether you were safe, but whether you could allow yourself to believe that you were safe?"

Those were the opening words of 19-year-old Anaru Mihaere (Ngāti Kahungunu ki Wairoa), who challenged a room of more than 100 housing and youth advocates to consider the realities faced by young people experiencing homelessness.

"When was the last time you sat down to eat and had to worry about whether there was enough food?

"When was the last time you wanted desperately, just one moment, one single moment, where you didn't have to worry about anything and could just simply breathe?

"For me, as a young person who grew up in the care of Oranga Tamariki and experienced homelessness, these were some of the hardest questions I had to live with."

The Youth Homeless Summit brought together housing and youth advocates from across the motu. Layla Bailey-McDowell

Anaru's kōrero set the tone for the country's first Youth Homelessness Summit, organised by youth homeless collective Manaaki Rangatahi and held in Auckland on Friday.

New research estimates about 12,200 rangatahi aged 16-24 experienced homelessness or severe housing instability in March 2023 - almost four times the number captured through direct housing evidence.

About two-thirds - or 8121 young people - experienced hidden homelessness, with their circumstances not reflected in conventional homelessness data.

Rangatahi and frontline workers came together to turn lived experience into action, and find solutions to youth homelessness. Layla Bailey-McDowell

Commissioned by Manaaki Rangatahi and conducted using Stats NZ's Integrated Data Infrastructure (IDI), the research also found rangatahi Māori were over-represented at about 2.3 times their share of the population.

Rangatahi Māori are more than five times as likely to experience hidden homelessness or housing deprivation, according to research lead Oliver Vovchenko.

Mihaere told RNZ the figures reflected a reality that many young people navigated without adequate support.

"In neglecting youth, you're neglecting Aotearoa's future," he said.

Anaru Mihaere grew up in Oranga Tamariki and wants a future where young people no longer need to advocate for basic support. Layla Bailey-McDowell

Mihaere was one of seven rangatahi who shared their experiences during a youth panel discussion, where the kōrero quickly turned from the scale of the problem to what needed to change.

Rangatahi and youth advocate Platinum questioned why youth homelessness did not receive greater attention.

"The biggest question that us rangatahi are really asking is why doesn't it matter enough?

"Homelessness is the consequence of the government's disservice and failure to look after us rangatahi, and look after our people in general."

Frontline workers from across Aotearoa say youth homelessness is the worst they've ever seen. Layla Bailey-McDowell

Mihaere said services needed to be designed around what young people actually wanted, rather than being labelled as youth-focused.

"We have a lot of organisations in general that are very rangatahi-based, but they're not focused on rangatahi.

"They offer a lot of rangatahi services, but they don't actually talk to the rangatahi about what they want."

He said youth housing providers also struggled with limited funding and capacity, leaving many young people without anywhere to turn.

"Age shouldn't matter, when it comes to experience. Everyone has experience, all of us have experience.

"We are all experts in our own lives."

His hope was for a country "where homelessness isn't a problem because it isn't existing", and where young people and their whānau can live without constantly worrying about the safety of their futures.

Zebion (front), pictured alongside other tāne from Grace Foundation, encourages other rangatahi to not be afraid to seek help. Layla Bailey-McDowell

Another rangatahi panelist, Zebion from Grace Foundation, spoke about being kicked out of home at a young age, and spending years moving between houses and sleeping on the streets.

By the time he was 16-17, he had turned to drugs and alcohol, and eventually lost contact with his whānau.

He later went to prison, where he became sober, and said finding support through Grace Foundation helped him rebuild his life.

"Once I got here, I realised that I was missing a lot of routine, structure, stability in my life that was accessible, if I had just asked for help," he told RNZ.

Zebion said young people needed more places to turn to, like services where they could connect with people who had experienced similar circumstances.

His message to other rangatahi struggling with homelessness was that "you're not alone, you don't have to do it alone".

The kaupapa included a rangatahi panel, where young people shared their lived experiences of youth homelessness. Layla Bailey-McDowell

Another Grace Foundation panelist said youth homelessness should matter to everyone, because without a stable home or support, young people could become more vulnerable to influences that led them into crime.

"There's a lot of us that come from homelessness that may lead to a lot of youth crimes, because we have no home environment or someone there for us, so we're out and about in the streets," he said.

"Mixed with the wrong people, start doing bad choices, because you know it's uncomfortable, because you have no-one to guide you, because there's a lot of bad people being out in the streets."

He said if rangatahi had that opportunity to get off the streets at a young age, it could prevent them from going down the wrong path.

Children's Commissioner Jane Searle says homelessness affects far more than a young person's ability to access somewhere to sleep. Layla Bailey-McDowell

Children's Commissioner Jane Searle attended the kaupapa, and said the gap between what was happening on the frontline and what was reaching decision-makers in Wellington was too wide.

"I often see the irony in the issue of youth homelessness, and that is often not seen, not spoken about and very misunderstood, yet it is casting a long shadow over the lives of the future of this country."

She said homelessness affected far more than a young person's ability to access somewhere to sleep - it also affected their dignity, identity, connection to whānau and ability to participate in society.

An art installation made by rangatahi from Kākano Youth Arts Collective depicts 'from a trap house to a home'. Layla Bailey-McDowell

Manaaki Rangatahi is calling for a legally recognised right to adequate housing, legislation preventing government agencies from discharging young people into homelessness and sustained investment in youth housing services.

World.title: Surprise discovery at Walton School captures imaginations across the world
World.content:
Walton School principal Jeremy Kurth has been sitting on a quarter-century-old riddle that is close to unravelling.

In 1999, students from the Waikato country school - located between Morrinsville and Matamata - planted a time capsule, with messages to their future selves about the time they grew up in.

The capsule took the form of a simple envelope that contained other smaller envelopes from each child in the year 5/6 class. It came with instructions that they were not to be opened by anyone except the original authors.

Kurth has tried hard to follow those wishes.

Audio player for " Waikato uncovers 26 year old time capsule " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/education/2243683%2Fsurprise-discovery-at-walton-school-captures-imaginations-across-the-world

Waikato uncovers 26 year old time capsule Checkpoint Download MP3 6m

"We're trying to contact as many as we can," he told RNZ Checkpoint. "We're hoping we can get them to come in and read them, and we can record them and put them on Facebook.

"There are a couple we've had to scan to Australia or down south to let them read it first, and we might get some of our current students to read them out."

As per instructions, former Walton principal Bob Marlow, now 78, was invited back to open the time capsule, which was hidden away in a fireproof container in the school's photocopy room.

"He was the former principal of our school from 1988-2012 and I took over in 2013," Kurth said. 'He's a bit of a legend in our area of the Walton community.

"He's a great guy and he was pretty stoked to be able to open this envelope. He could recollect all the kids' names - he was reading them out and knew exactly where they were now.

"It was quite remarkable seeing the attachment he still had with these former students. It was a beautiful thing."

While Kurth has mainly resisted the temptation to open the individual envelopes, he has had to send the contents of some further afield, gaining an insight into what was written 26 years ago.

"They had a template with a few questions and the kids each wrote their answers to that," he said. "I've had a peek into what they are - a bit of a prediction of what they might do in the future, what they might do or what they hoped to do.

"Some of the handwriting is a bit interesting and the spelling is a bit wayward, but you know, they're 10-year-old kids.

"There was typical stuff at the start - favourite TV shows, actresses and food, and things like that - which led into what you'd like to do in the next 25 years, what hopes you might have, jobs you wanted to do and places you'd like to visit. It gave them the opportunity to be pretty broad with their answers, if they wanted to."

Of the 24 envelopes uncovered, only five authors have been tracked down.

"We know some of them are still in the local community, and we hope word of mouth will reach them and they'll pop in next week," Gurth said.

The discovery has captured the imagination of social media across the globe.

Faced with a similar exercise today, Gurth hoped his students would reflect the non-curriculum lessons taught at Walton School.

"Probably just show kindness and be good," he offered. "That's the key message we're trying to tell our kids.

World.title: Controversial consent to dump Wānaka human waste on farmland reviewed after 'inaccuracies' found
World.content:
Otago Regional Council will review a controversial consent to dump treated human waste from Wānaka on farmland near Lauder after discovering inaccuracies in the original application.

The non-notified consent was granted in January for Queenstown Lakes District Council contractor SJ Allen Holdings.

The decision led to outcry from locals who were worried about the potential impact on their water and health as well as frustration about a lack of consultation.

The council said the review would consider whether the consent conditions were adequate, after finding inaccuracies relating to the site.

"Council has reached the view that there are inaccuracies in the consent-holder's application and as a result, the actual or potential adverse effects on the environment arising from the activity were not adequately identified and assessed in the application," a council report said.

"These inaccuracies materially influenced the council's decision on the application."

The review would include considering the scope of the consent, the discharge limits, soil contamination limits, restrictions to the land disposal area, reporting and groundwater monitoring.

The review was expected to cost the contractor approximately $80,000 but the council said the company did not need to stop work while it was carried out.

Council chief executive Richard Saunders said staff had notified the contractor, including which consent conditions would be examined and the reasons for the review.

He said the decision had been made after "careful consideration", including examining information that was available at the time the original consent decision was made.

The council would continue to monitor the site and assess compliance, Saunders said.

Federated Farmers Otago president Anna Gillespie welcomed the decision, saying it was a major win for rural New Zealand.

"(Otago Regional Council) should never have issued this consent but I do thank them for now recognising the widespread concerns and environmental risk by initiating a review," she said.

"Just one of the reasons farmers and others have been so angered by what's happened is that the original consent application was discussed and decided in-house by (Otago Regional Council), with no hearing or invitation for submissions.

"When news broke that trucks were rolling into Lauder to begin dumping up to 2000 tonnes of wastewater sludge a year in their neighbourhood, it was a complete surprise and a very unwelcome one."

Gillespie called for the consent to be cancelled and for Otago councillors to investigate how to deal with urban human effluent within their own boundaries.

Earlier in the week Central Otago mayors and councillors wrote to their Queenstown Lakes counterparts about their significant concerns and urged them to halt the operation.

At the time, Central Otago mayor Tamah Alley said locals were frustrated they had been denied a say and felt the decision was inherently unfair.

"They understand that sludge needs to go somewhere - they are farmers - but they are concerned that particular piece of land is not necessarily the right piece of land for that activity to take place," she said.

"They're worried about the odour. They're worried about the dust coming off the site. They're worried about the impact on local waterways, which includes the places where people get their drinking water."

Alley asked councils to work together to find a mutually agreeable long-term solution.

In response, Queenstown Lakes mayor John Glover said he understood locals' concerns and was open to discussing alternatives.

He said his council had relied on the consent in good faith, which was saving more than $1 million compared to carting the waste to Winton landfill.

Central Otago District Council last month voted to send its growing volume of sludge to Winton following community pushback and the discovery that the Lauder site was not going to meet its needs or save money.

Otago Regional Council has indicated that if the review was notified there would be a 20 working-day timeframe for submissions and a hearing could potentially be held.

The council invited the contractor to propose new consent conditions to address its concerns.

World.title: Teen accused of murdering schoolboy snatched phone to film bloody video, court hears
World.content:
Content warning: This story describes the scene of a homicide

Witness says teen murder-accused snatched her phone and recorded bloody video

She says she tried to stop him getting involved in a fight

Forensic scientist describes blood-covered scene.

A teenage girl who witnessed a fatal attack outside a party says a teen accused of murdering a schoolboy snatched her phone from her to record a bloody video.

The murder-accused was among a group of people who were laughing after the attack happened, the teenage girl told the High Court at Palmerston North on Friday.

The accused, who was 15 at the time, is facing trial for murdering 15-year-old Kaea Karauria in the early hours of 11 May last year in Napier.

The murder-accused admits he stabbed Kaea, but the defence has told the jury it should find him guilty of manslaughter, not murder.

The Crown says the murder-accused - who has Mongrel Mob tattoos across his face - was part of a group that attacked Kaea because of a minor incident at a party a few weeks earlier, and because of the mistaken belief he was associated with Black Power.

The accused has significant intellectual impairments and the defence says he wouldn't have known his reckless actions could have caused a death.

Crown prosecutor Stephen Manning says the teen is guilty of murder. JIMMY ELLINGHAM / RNZ

Witness says murder-accused ran towards fight

The witness, whose name is also suppressed, said she was drinking vodka pre-mix RTDs with a friend at a house in the Hastings suburb of Flaxmere when the murder-accused messaged on Instagram and asked if she wanted to be picked up.

She thought they'd head up Te Mata peak, near Havelock North, but they instead headed to Napier, where the group, including the accused's friends, drove around between parties.

Around the time they arrived at one on Dinwiddie Avenue, in the suburb of Onekawa, one of the murder-accused's friends was told that Kaea had touched his girlfriend at a party a few weeks earlier. That friend reacted badly.

On the street outside the party, a circle of people formed around Kaea, who the witness didn't know at the time, punching and kicking him.

The witness was sitting on the lap of the murder-accused in a car. When he saw what was happening she said he pushed her off him, jumped out and joined in. She tried to stop the accused, as she didn't want him getting involved.

"I knew it was a fight. I just didn't know who was fighting," she said.

She didn't see a knife, but at one stage saw Kaea on the ground, surrounded. She then saw him get up and sprint around the corner, to Alexander Ave, where he subsequently collapsed and died.

Defence lawyer Tim Braithwaite acknowledges Kaea Karauria's death is devastating. JIMMY ELLINGHAM / RNZ

The witness said some of the group, including the murder-accused, followed. They returned minutes later. At the time the witness was taking a "boomerang" with her mates - a selfie for Instagram.

"All I heard was laughing. And when he [the accused] saw me, he grabbed my phone off me," the witness said. "There was blood on him, but I didn't see that until after he grabbed my phone."

The murder-accused recorded a video of his bloodied right hand, in which he was holding a knife.

"After he took the video. I snatched my phone back. They just all hopped back in the car."

The video has been played to the court several times. In it someone yells "sieg f...... heil" - a common phrase among the Mongrel Mob. The witness said it sounded like one of the murder-accused's friends.

The witness said a group, including the murder-accused, sped back to Flaxmere, spending the night at her house. She said they didn't talk about what happened, but the murder-accused had blood on his hands, and one of his friends had a deep cut to his hand.

They left the following morning and shortly after the murder-accused messaged and asked the witness to send him the video, which she did.

Glenys Knight has described what she found when she examined the scene of Kaea Karauria's death. RNZ/Jimmy Ellingham

Grisly scene examined

Forensic scientist Glenys Knight said she examined the scene in the aftermath of Kaea's death, and traced blood along Dinwiddie Avenue, into the Alexander Avenue property where he collapsed.

Some blood samples were taken for DNA analysis, to identify who they belonged to.

"I would love to get a lot more done, but it's a very expensive process so we have to be selective."

Knight told the jury the "initial blood-letting incident" happened on Dinwiddie Avenue, before drops of blood headed up the road and around the corner. She said it was possible to see the direction someone was headed by looking at how blood had hit a surface.

About Dinwiddie Avenue, she described several photographs shown to the jury: "On the concrete in front of the gate we can see numerous blood stains, some of which are quite large. These are indications that large blood stains are being released from the body under hydraulic pressure, so the pressure of the heart, in this instance, is pumping out blood.

"In this case it means that Kaea received an arterial breach in this area and his artery was bleeding - shooting out a lot of blood."

Following the spatter on Alexander Avenue, she said it appeared Kaea had tried to clear a large gate into a property, but had instead jumped over a smaller fence.

"There was a lot of what we call 'transfer blood staining' on the top of that fence, which shows that a blood-stained surface has directly contacted the top of that fence and transferred some blood on to that area."

World.title: Nitrate levels still rising in most Canterbury wells
World.content:
Almost 60 per cent of Canterbury wells are still recording increasing nitrate concentrations, a new groundwater survey shows.

The [www.ecan.govt.nz/get-involved/news-and-events/2026/groundwater-survey-highlights-ongoing-nitrate-challenge-despite-fewer-e-coli-detections Canterbury regional council survey], carried out in 2025, found nitrate levels exceeded the drinking water limit of 11.3mg/L in about 10 percent of the 358 wells tested.

In the Ashburton zone, almost 30 percent of wells exceeded the limit.

Regional council water and land science manager Elaine Moriarty said the results showed nitrate levels remained a long-term challenge in Canterbury.

"Groundwater is hugely important to Canterbury. It's the source of drinking water for many communities and it also feeds a lot of our lowland springs and streams," she said.

"There isn't any major change from last year that we can see in the numbers but change in groundwater is a long game and the actions on land often take between three to five years in some areas of Canterbury. In other areas with deeper groundwater the change is a lot longer."

On Friday, during a visit to Christchurch ahead of the election, the Green Party pledged to make it easier for people to check the safety of public drinking water supplies.

The Greens want to introduce a bill requiring the Water Services Authority to regularly publish drinking water quality data online.

Greens environment spokesperson Lan Pham said nitrate pollution came at a cost.

"Schools and communities are actually facing the costs of finding drinking water that isn't polluted by nitrates," she said.

"This is unacceptable. We want people to be empowered to know these things so they can put pressure on the right authorities, on government to actually turn the tide and protect our water at its source."

The Green Party pledged to make it easier for people to check public drinking water safety during a campaign visit to Christchurch on Friday. Nathan Mckinnon/RNZ

Greens co-leader Marama Davidson said up to 100,000 people fell ill each year from polluted drinking water.

"Nitrate pollution in our rivers is getting worse and it's costing ratepayers in Ashburton, Selwyn, Waimate, and Gore at least $17 million combined. Five schools in Otago, Canterbury, and Waikato have had to upgrade their water systems just so their children can have a safe drink of water at playtime," she said.

More than 20 schools have had drinking water with elevated nitrate levels above half the legal limit, which has been linked to serious health outcomes.

Of the wells tested in Canterbury, 59 percent showed increasing nitrate concentrations, while 24 percent showed decreasing trends, with the remaining 17 per cent showing no clear trend.

The 2024 survey showed nitrate levels increasing in 62 percent of wells and about 10 percent of wells tested had nitrates above the drinking water limit.

Moriarty said they were a mix of public and privately-owned wells and not all were used for drinking water.

Nitrate levels could worsen before improving, she said.

"Environment Canterbury fully acknowledges it is a challenge for us and one that we are actively working with our community to support them with," she said.

The council said fewer wells showed evidence of E coli, with the number dropping from 49 in 2024 to 23 in 2025.

The survey also found more than half of the shallow groundwater tested near Canterbury waterways had nitrate levels above the environmental bottom line, posing a potential risk to rivers and streams.

Higher nitrate concentrations were found in areas around and downstream of intensive farming.

Colin Hurst. Supplied / Federated Farmers

Federated Farmers president Colin Hurst said farmers were working hard to reduce nitrogen loss.

"The dairy farmers are reducing their stocking rates, planting the likes of plantain that has the ability to mop up some of the nitrogen, farmers are undertaking precision farming, so only applying the fertiliser where it's needed," he said.

"Farmers are fencing off their waterways and there are a lot of plants being planted in the waterways to reduce nitrates. It's going to take a little bit of time to sort these things out but we're on the journey."

DairyNZ general manager policy and government relations Roger Lincoln said Canterbury dairy farms had reduced nitrogen loss per hectare by 30 percent over the past decade.

Nationally, 97 percent of dairy farms had a farm environment plan, he said.

"DairyNZ, together with government and other partners, has invested $35 million over the past five years developing lower-nitrogen farming systems and this work continues," Lincoln said.

"A four-year Lincoln University farmlet trial found pastures containing an average of 17 percent plantain reduced annual nitrate leaching by around 33 percent, while maintaining milk production. We're working with farmers to translate that research into practical adoption on farm."

In June, RNZ revealed the Ministry of Health had quietly launched a review into the health effects of nitrate in drinking water after the Danish government reduced its drinking water limit by almost 90 percent.

World.title: 'Our system may entirely collapse': Nelson doctor fears no one listening over dire impact of shortstaffing
World.content:
Audio player for " Urologist says staffing levels at Nelson Hospital are 'dire' " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/health/2242415%2Four-system-may-entirely-collapse-nelson-doctor-fears-no-one-listening-over-dire-impact-of-shortstaffing

Urologist says staffing levels at Nelson Hospital are 'dire' Checkpoint Download MP3 9m

A doctor struggling to cope with staffing levels at Nelson Hospital says he and his colleagues fear no one is listening to them.

Dr Patrick Meffan has been a urologist in Nelson for more than three decades. He is now the sole doctor in the region doing complicated surgery for a number of cancers.

He said the current problems with healthcare were decades in the making.

"It really was magnified when two colleagues left a year ago and neither of those have been replaced. I have tried by every method I can to try and get this problem resolved and I don't think I'm being heard," he told Checkpoint.

"I've been worried that our system may entirely collapse and leave everyone stranded."

The current staffing levels meant some people would miss out on being seen, he said.

Operations involving the prostate, bladder and kidneys were difficult, he said, and he was having to do far more to keep up.

"In most of my career, I have done one of those a fortnight, roughly.

"In the last little while I've been doing two a week - so that's approximately four times as much.

"I'm not getting any younger, and the physical demands of that are pretty hard. I think even outside of that that's a lot of work to do," he said.

Te Whatu Ora said it shared doctors' concerns over staffing at the Nelson-Marlborough urology service. RNZ / Peter de Graaf

"They are an operation that takes, generally, three or four hours. But sometimes up to six hours," he told Checkpoint.

Staffing levels meant smaller cases were taking a back seat too.

"The smaller cases are the ones that are waiting a long period of time, maybe even up to a year sometimes."

Invercargill was a good example of what happens with healthcare when you "get to the point of implosion", he said, and Nelson was not far behind.

"I find it enormously frustrating and I've had a lot of sleepless nights trying to work this all out.

"Everyone struggles with this fact that we have a system that the clinicians all think is failing, and then all of the bureaucratic side is saying 'oh, no, we've got this'.

"That's fundamentally where I can't see a way forward from this, unless there is an understanding that the health management system is, in my view, broken.

"Everyone talks about a broken health service. I think we've got a broken management service."

Te Whatu Ora said it shared doctors' concerns over staffing at the Nelson-Marlborough urology service, which had been impacted by a global shortage of specialists.

It anticipated having two more urologists on board halfway through 2027.

Nelson Hospital's interim chief medical officer Dr Derek Sherwood said wait lists for initial specialist urology appointments had almost halved since last year.

World.title: Harry Mowbray's 'Split Your Vote' website probed by Electoral Commission
World.content:
Audio player for " Harry Mowbray discusses his 'Split Your Vote' campaign " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/politics_election-2026/2235548%2Fharry-mowbray-s-split-your-vote-website-probed-by-electoral-commission

Harry Mowbray discusses his 'Split Your Vote' campaign Midday Report Download MP3 11m

Businessman Harry Mowbray, who created a website encouraging vote-splitting, says the MMP electoral system is a "complete dog".

He confirmed part of his strategy was to discredit MMP and "show people how bad it is".

Mowbray was speaking to Midday Report about the Electoral Commission looking into his website, which he says he's taken offline.

A complaint was made about it, and Mowbray has made "an assumption" that it was the National Party, which has been publicly critical of vote-splitting, responsible.

National confirmed it was behind the complaint on Friday afternoon.

"This and similar campaigns are deliberate attempts to confuse voters in what is already a very close election, and we do not support them," a National Party spokesperson said.

"The reality is very simple. If you want a National government you need to make sure National is bigger than Labour. The only way to do that is to party vote National.

"This particular campaign did not comply with the election rules everyone has to operate under. We referred it to the Electoral Commission, but we doubt we were the only ones."

Mowbray said the letter he received from the Electoral Commission asked if he had got permission for the website content from the party secretaries of ACT and New Zealand First.

"They didn't ask if I had it from National so they obviously know the answer to that," he said.

The website is designed to give the centre-right a disproportionate number of seats to its party vote through the overhang, by telling people to give their candidate vote to National and their party vote to ACT or New Zealand First.

"It's working unbelievably. The number of people that I don't know and end up talking to and they say, 'we've heard about it and we're going to split our vote', or say they don't know what it means and then I spend five minutes explaining it, and they say 'oh we get it now'."

Mowbray says Te Pāti Māori "started it" when it comes to tinkering with MMP, "and I'm showing you how we can finish it".

He believes the current system is "completely undemocratic" in that the minor parties have a much stronger voice in Parliament than their party vote should allow.

Mowbray explained the process for setting up the website and what he believed to be allowed.

The Electoral Commission "told me I haven't had secretaries for ACT or New Zealand First give permission to promote", he said.

"I didn't realise having the website was going to get classified as a promotion, because it's in my name. You're allowed to say pretty much anything you like as an individual ... that's what I was doing."

Mowbray said he was asked by the Electoral Commission whether he paid for a domain name to set-up the website, which he did for the cost of $35.

"As soon as I pay for a domain name it becomes an . I'm allowed to spend $17,000 and I haven't done that yet."

He wasn't asked to take down the website but "if it's a problem then it's down".

Asked by RNZ to confirm or deny the allegation it was behind the complaint, a spokesperson for the National Party said it wouldn't be "commenting on this story".

The Electoral Commission told RNZ it was investigating the "advertising" and whether it was "authorised", and it wouldn't be appropriate to comment further at this stage.

Party messaging must come with an authentication statement, for transparency reasons.

Earlier this week, Mowbray said he'd been pushing the message that a centre-right government could "best be achieved" by vote splitting, "supporting the local National MP or candidate with their electorate vote but giving their party vote to NZ First or ACT as coalition partners".

"That gives their party vote some effect while giving the centre-right coalition a better chance of winning."

The complaint comes as the overhang strategy gains momentum, and National has responded in turn, with a video from former prime minister Sir John Key saying not to put the election to chance.

"It's a really close election," National leader Christopher Luxon said on Friday.

"It's going to come down to the wire. As I said yesterday, there'll be one or two points in it all."

He said if voters want National, they have to vote for it.

"In an MMP system, you party vote for it."

This is not the first time National has called on Sir John Key's services to deliver a message to voters during an election campaign.

In 2023, Key released a video 10 days before the election, urging Kiwis to give their party vote to National to avoid waking up in "limbo land" without a clear result.

He argued then that National needed enough votes to govern without "lots of moving parts", but conspicuously avoided mentioning NZ First or its leader Winston Peters by name.

Key also warned prolonged negotiations would delay action on the cost of living.

The intervention was ultimately unsuccessful in its bid to prevent National being reliant on NZ First to form a government.

The country's first three-way coalition was formed about 40 days after the 2023 election, following lengthy talks.

ACT candidate Paul Henry was asked about the Electoral Commission complaint and the implication from Mowbray it had come from the National Party.

"I would be surprised if he hadn't expected that something like this would happen," Henry responded.

Asked what he made of the vote splitting strategy gaining momentum, Henry said, "it's maths isn't it?"

"Anyone that really understands mathematics will know that most of what they're saying is correct based on assumptions.

World.title: Governor-General pays tribute to Sir David Gascoigne, respected lawyer and arts advocate
World.content:
Governor-General Dame Cindy Kiro has paid tribute to Sir David Gascoigne, who died at the beginning of the week.

Sir David, a respected lawyer and former judicial conduct commissioner, died at his home on Monday, aged 86 years old.

He was the husband of former Governor-General Dame Patsy Reddy, who preceded Dame Cindy in the role.

"During Dame Patsy's five years as Governor-General, Sir David was a constant presence at her side, supporting her in her service to New Zealand. I will always be grateful for the generosity and graciousness Sir David and Dame Patsy showed Dr Davies and me as we prepared to take up our roles at Government House," Dame Cindy wrote on social media.

Sir David was recognised as a passionate advocate for the arts.

The Arts Foundation - Te Tumu Toi said Sir David's support helped shape "some of our country's most important cultural organisations", including the New Zealand Opera and the New Zealand International Festival of the Arts.

"His belief in the value of creativity and the people behind it leaves a lasting legacy," a spokesperson wrote.

The New Zealand Film Commission highlighted his work on the legislation which established the Commission and his 15 years on the Commission, including eight years as chair.

"His contribution continued well beyond NZFC. He later chaired the New Zealand Film Production Fund and led its transformation into the New Zealand Film Heritage Trust - Te Puna Ataata, helping safeguard the rights, materials and legacy of New Zealand films for future generations."

The Aotearoa Festival of the Arts said Sir David was a founding trustee of the Festival Board in 1986 and, as chair during the 1994, 1996 and 1998 festivals, provided "invaluable strategic oversight and financial leadership" for the early decades of the festival.

World.title: Retiring Swan Rampe 'hurt' over Pullman Hotel saga
World.content:
Sydney stalwart Dane Rampe "selfishly" grappled with putting off retirement, feeling hurt and upset that the Pullman Hotel saga had derailed his final AFL season.

The 36-year-old defender, who has confirmed his playing career is over, had quietly settled on making this season his last and seemed on track to have one last crack at an elusive premiership after the Swans finished second on the ladder ahead of the finals.

But Sydney's premiership bid — as Swans chairman Andrew Pridham put it — was "torpedoed" after vice-captain Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, James Jordon and Riley Bice were stood down.

The five were suspended from round 24 and the club's two finals for what the Swans termed a "serious breach of expected club behaviour and standards".

Those AFL-endorsed club bans were separate from a police investigation into an alleged sexual assault at the Pullman Hotel, which is ongoing. No charges have been laid and there is no suggestion of wrongdoing on the part of the suspended players.

Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner and Riley Bice were among the Swans players suspended by the club. (AAP: Dan Himbrechts)

Rampe, who played in four losing grand finals (2014, '16, '22 and '24) across 289 games, confessed to his personal hurt at what happened.

The former Swans co-captain was emotional and held back tears as he announced his retirement on Friday in front of family, teammates and media.

"Deep down, I probably knew at this time last year, this was going to be my last year," Rampe said on Friday.

"Everything was going swimmingly … and then, I'm not going to lie, the events that happened at the back end of the season really muddied those waters.

"It really threw into disarray what I was thinking, what I hadn't probably admitted to myself yet.

"Selfishly, there was part of me that felt a little bit upset and hurt by what had happened.

"I was struggling to accept whether this was the way I was going to bow out.

"And then, coupled with that, was the place in which the club found itself. It didn't feel right. It didn't feel right leaving with where things are at."

Rampe said conversations with coach Dean Cox and football Leon Cameron had helped him achieve "clarity" surrounding his retirement.

He was re-drafted as a rookie this season alongside fellow defender Jake Lloyd, who has signed on for a 15th season.

Dane Rampe captained the Swans in a Grand Final defeat to Brisbane in 2024. (AAP: James Ross)

Cox "delicately" suggested that Rampe was struggling to meet the physical demands after 14 seasons in the system.

"I couldn't quite give the 100 per cent that made me Dane Rampe, the Swans player," Rampe said.

"I'm grateful for the way he [Cox] delicately posed that to me, because it was something I needed to hear.

"Given the emotions of the back end of the season, it was hard for me to see the forest for the trees."

A Swans fan who sprinted onto the SCG in 1999 after Tony Lockett broke the league's goal-kicking record, Rampe has been a heart-and-soul player since he was drafted as a rookie in 2012, aged 22.

He made his debut in 2013 and went on to co-captain the Swans with Josh Kennedy and Luke Parker from 2019 to 2023.

Rampe is a Bob Skilton Medallist (2019) as the club best and fairest and an All-Australian ('16), making him one of the club's greatest rookie-list success stories alongside childhood idol Brett Kirk.

When captain Callum Mills suffered an ACL injury last month in their semi-final win over Brisbane, it was only natural for the Swans to turn to Rampe.

Rampe would captain the Swans in what would be his final match, the club's preliminary final loss to Fremantle.

Dane Rampe reacts emotionally on the final siren of Sydney's first game following the Pullman Hotel incident. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Matt King)

With nothing confirmed for his future besides a break from the AFL, Rampe said he leaves the club with confidence.

"I'm completely at peace with where the club sits," Rampe said.

"Does that mean that we're not going to be having robust conversations? Absolutely not.

"In fact, I hope to hear that they are having challenging conversations going forward, and that the media is reporting difficult conversations.

"That's a sign of a healthy club, a healthy culture, and I urge and implore the boys and the rest of the club to lean into that."

AAP

World.title: Player prepares for World Cup after career reshaped by injury
World.content:
There are many things to prepare for when playing a game of rugby league. How to break a line, gain an edge or pick a way through a defence.

You don't prepare for one unfortunate tackle to alter the course of your life forever.

In 2020, at the age of 18, while playing for the Narellan Jets in south-west Sydney, Bryce Crane was on the wrong end of a tackle and suffered permanent nerve damage and paralysis of his right arm.

Yet, there was only one thing on his mind.

"You don't really quite understand how much something means to you until it is ripped away," Crane said.

"It's weird to think about but I didn't think about my life, I just thought that I lost the game that I loved growing up playing."

For the love of the game

Crane was told not to worry about the sport. Now, he is preparing for a home World Cup as Australia's Physical Disability Rugby League (PDRL) star fullback.

Australia will host New Zealand and England in the three-team round-robin tournament which runs from October 30 to November 8 in Sydney.

Crane (left) says it will mean a lot to once again represent Australia at the tournament. (Getty Images: Ashley Allen)

"It's really exciting to get into the World Cup; we have had a few camps with the squad, so we are getting around knowing each other," Crane said.

It will be his second PDRL World Cup after he starred for Australia in the inaugural edition in 2022.

Despite Australia failing to win a game, Crane's performances earned him a spot in the Rugby League World Cup Dream Team, which also contained players from the men's, women's and wheelchair tournaments.

He was the only PDRL player in the team, and was named alongside fellow Australian internationals Josh Addo-Carr, Cameron Murray and Tarryn Aiken.

Bryce Crane was a stand-out for Australia at the 2022 World Cup. (Getty Images: Ashley Allen)

In the eyes of his teammates though, he does not just contribute to the team through his talismanic play.

Luke Vella, who is also an NRL assistant coach at the Canterbury-Bankstown Bulldogs, knows the hallmarks of a top-quality player.

"He is obviously very skilful and has a great ability to play the game, but he is very humble," Vella said.

"He is also very encouraging, there is times I know Bryce can make a break or make a tackle, but he puts others before himself quite often and encourages them and supports them along with their game."

Full circle moment

The final of the tournament will be held at the Sydney Football Stadium before one of the men's semifinals, the biggest stage the game has been played on so far.

Vella was injured at the ground while playing for the Bulldogs' under-20 side in 2014, and should Australia qualify for the decider, he will step onto that field for the first time in a playing role since then.

Luke Vella is part of the Australian PDRL team. (Supplied: Lainey Gaudron)

"It's funny, I haven't really thought about it too much to be honest," Vella said.

"Obviously the stadium got knocked down and rebuilt, it is a little bit different.

"I can't really describe what the emotions would be if we get there and I get the opportunity to play on the field again."

Vella's passion for the game quickly returned after his career-ending injury, and in 2019, he was named head coach of the Bulldogs' under-20s team, giving him a chance to push players to achieve dreams of making the NRL.

After coaching the team to the Jersey Flegg Cup in 2023, he earned his promotion to the first grade coaching ranks for the 2024 season, while balancing his return to playing.

He made his international debut for Australia against New Zealand in November 2024 in Auckland.

"When I got injured at 20, I fell back in love with it because it got taken away from me," Vella said.

"I love it because my thing for coaching is to develop players and help them achieve their goals, but then the competitive side, running around, throwing the ball around, a bit of contact too.

"All things rugby league, all come back to love."

For Crane and Vella, the pride in representing their country is palpable.

"At the end of the day, I'm not just representing myself, my family, my country, but I'm also representing people with all different types of disabilities," Crane said.

"I feel like that is a pretty cool thing to do."

This content was produced for the ABC's International Day of People with Disability coverage, which runs from November 19 to December 25, 2026.

The ABC is partnering with International Day of People with Disability to recognise the contributions and achievements of the 5.5 million Australians with disability.

World.title: Dream shakes off scheduling controversy to force WNBA Finals decider
World.content:
Izzy Borlase's dream of winning a WNBA championship ring with Atlanta remains alive and kicking after the Australian rookie helped the Dream drag the finals series into a winner-takes-all decider against the Golden State Valkyries in San Francisco.

Game seven in San Francisco on Sunday (AEDT) should be a Halloween spine-tingler, with 22-year-old Borlase dreaming of joining 11 previous Australian winners of WNBA championships.

Opals ace Borlase was one of only seven players picked by Atlanta coach Karl Smesko as the Dream powered its way to an emphatic series-levelling 80-69 victory in front of a noisy near sellout crowd.

The Dream brushed aside the irritation and indignity of having to play the pivotal game six at lunchtime, rescheduled to accommodate a regular season home game for men's counterparts the Atlanta Hawks.

Izzy Borlase was used sparingly as the Dream leaned on the starting five. (Getty Images: Kevin C. Cox)

Increased interest in the Dream's finals run saw a number of games shifted to the home of the NBA's Hawks, which can accommodate 17,000 people, but game six was initially scheduled to be played at the Dream's regular-season home arena, with a 3,500-seat capacity.

After an outcry about the sixth game of the Hawks' 82-game regular season taking precedence over the Dream's push for their first title, the contest was moved to the bigger venue but forced into a 12:30pm (local time) slot to allow the Hawks to face the Cavaliers in prime time.

Borlase played very much a support role in her 12 minutes of court action as Atlanta's powerful starting line-up took control in an opening blitz and never looked back after holding a 17--point advantage at the end of the first quarter.

The Dream was sparked by Allisha Gray (23 points), Rhyne Howard (21) and another double-double from star Angel Reese, who had 14 rebounds and six assists to go with her 15 points.

Atlanta, shooting hot, only ever looked remotely rattled in the final quarter as the visitors, seeking to seal the win that would have brought them the title for the first time in just their second season, got to within eight points going into the final minute.

But there was no cause for alarm as Gray sank a three-pointer under pressure to get the home crowd roaring.

This marks the first time the WNBA Finals has gone to a decider since 2019, when the Washington Mystics beat the Connecticut Sun 3-2 in a best-of-five series.

This season marks the second time the championship has been decided in a best-of-seven format, with last year's victory by the Las Vegas Aces over the Phoenix Mercury coming via a 4-0 sweep.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

AAP/ABC

World.title: For the fans who became heroes, Samoa vs Tonga is bigger than a grand final
World.content:
Ahead of their sold-out Rugby League World Cup match on Sunday, the new faces of the eternal rivalry between Tonga and Samoa didn't quite go straight from the stands onto the field, but they went pretty close.

Four years ago, when the two met in the last World Cup, Francis Manuleleua was hunched over in his bedroom in South Auckland, watching the game on his phone.

He was 18, with the rugby league world at his feet, and after Samoa held on for a pulsating 20-18 victory, he snatched up a flag and marched into the street because his life had changed forever.

Loading...

"Growing up I was always picked in the Kiwi teams, Under 16s and Under 18s and that, so there was a feeling of wanting to pull on that black jersey in either league or union," Manuleleua said.

"But after that 2022 World Cup, seeing all the boys play, how much it meant to them, that's when it changed for me and I thought to myself 'this is the jersey I'd want to put on if I ever get the opportunity'."

Across the Tasman, Sua Fa'alogo was part of the same celebratory throng, wherever the four winds could take Samoans from their islands.

The parades of the Samoan and Tongan fans have become legendary. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor )

The 23-year-old was born and raised in Samoa, in the village of Si'umu, and lived there until he was nine, when his parents moved to Melbourne to find a better life for him and his eight siblings.

Leka Halasima's story was similar: he was born in Tofoa, Tonga, before moving to New Zealand as a boy.

In 2024, a few months after his NRL debut and well before every league fan knew his name, he watched his two nations go head-to-head in the Pacific Championship, cheering on the Mate Ma'a in a 25-24 victory.

Halasima has gone from admiring his heroes to playing alongside them. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer )

"Then the next year I was playing with them," Halasima said.

Now the 21-year-old Warriors tyro is doing more than just playing, he is starring alongside the heroes of his childhood and taking forward what they started.

"For a young person like me, I've been a fan since that 2017 World Cup and to go from being in the stands cheering to playing alongside people like Jase (Jason Taumalolo), who I look up to, it's an honour. It's a privilege," Halasima said.

Fa'alogo, Manuleleua and Halasima are not just three of rugby league's brightest young stars; they are part of a new generation inheriting a relationship thousands of years in the making.

Samoa creates rugby league magic The passion of the Pacific shines through in Samoa's rugby league team, and the pride the people have is evident on the island.

The history and culture of Tonga and Samoa are proudly separate and distinct but also irrevocably intertwined by centuries of love and blood and faith, first back in the islands and now within the great Pasifika diaspora.

Today, that relationship plays out in all its colour and splendour on the rugby league field, in grand occasions that prove Tonga and Samoa are a people as much as they're a place.

That place can be wherever either nation plays on their own, but it happens the most when they face one another.

Tonga and Samoa can meet anywhere in the world and their people will find them. (Getty Images: Michael Steele )

It's been this way long enough that players like Manuleleua, Fa'alogo, and Halasima grew up on occasions like this and dreamed of being part of it.

"Since the draw came out, I've been thinking of this day. I'm pretty sure every islander around the world can't wait for it," Halasima said.

"This is pretty much finals footy, this is what it's all about."

Manuleleua played in the NRL grand final for Newcastle earlier this month in what was the most important night of his young life — until Sunday.

Tonga and Samoa renew rugby league's greatest international rivalry Between them they have a population smaller than Canberra, but when they meet on Monday morning for a shot at the semi-finals, Tonga and Samoa will be the talk of the rugby league world.

"This will probably be the biggest game I've ever been a part of it. A grand final is pretty big too, but the rivalry between Samoa and Tonga runs deeper than footy," Manuleleua said.

"A few of my mates are Tongan, and we know deep down we have that hatred for each other when it comes to coming up against them.

"As soon as we cross that white line there's no friends, but after those 80 minutes we'll get together, have a beer and everything will be all sweet."

These games can happen anywhere, because while the islands are always home, the Pasifika diaspora has taken them to the world, and another home can happen wherever Samoans or Tongans come together.

Last year's Samoa-Tonga game attracted more than 45,000 people. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

Four years ago it happened in Warrington, 12 months ago it happened in Brisbane in front of 45,000 people in a game that felt like the State of Origin of the new century, and on Sunday it will happen in Parramatta.

Manuleleua's parents are coming over from Auckland but his siblings, he jokes, will have to make their own way.

Halasima will have his partner and newborn son there, as well as his parents, sisters, aunts, and uncles coming from New Zealand and up from Melbourne.

For Fa'alogo it will be an even more special day because his father, Eti, has never seen him play for Melbourne or Samoa in the flesh but he will be there on Sunday to watch his youngest become a part of history.

Sunday will mark a special occasion for Fa'alogo. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor )

"I can't wait. He's done so much for me," Fa'alogo said.

"I just want to give back to him for everything he did, for bringing me over and trying to give me the opportunity for a better life."

The game itself is a coin flip. Tonga is bigger, stronger and more battle-hardened; Samoa is faster and has more strike as proven by their big win last year.

The former is already locked into a semifinal spot, and the latter may well be by kick-off depending on the scoreline between England and Papua New Guinea, but this is a game that is bigger than a World Cup and larger than life.

The fresh faces feel the legacy of the history between the two nations even as they write its latest chapter, and they want to pass it down just as it was passed to them.

Earlier this year, Fa'alogo went back to Si'umu as part of a trip with the Storm.

He went to his old house and his old school and caught up with family.

Wherever he went, children followed. It has been that way ever since he made his NRL debut in 2023 and his Samoan debut a few months later, but Fa'alogo might not ever get used to it.

"I was shocked," Fa'alogo said.

"Back then I was one of them."

World.title: Australia's Cape Town desperation evident on another pulsating Test day
World.content:
If there was any doubt how much the Cape Town Test matters to Pat Cummins's Australian team, one only needed to clock the cooing pack of them careening towards Cameron Green and Mitchell Starc an hour into the evening session of day three at Newlands.

The catch Green claimed to send his teammates into raptures was straightforward enough, its genesis and aftermath a little more dramatic.

Proteas opener Marques Ackerman, set fair on 62 and attacking everything Australia threw at him, had tried to limbo away from a Starc bouncer that followed him like a heat-seeking missile. Not quite agile enough with his Matrix manoeuvre, Ackerman faintly edged the ball flush into his faceguard, from which it ballooned into the cordon.

Unsure of the deflection and with his ears still ringing from the ding on his grill, Ackerman walked over to his skipper Temba Bavuma to discuss a review of the umpire's call, perhaps as surprised as the Australians when Travis Head arrived on the scene to inquire after his health.

But, in all the chaos and confusion, the crucial 15 seconds had passed before Ackerman could signal for a review. He had to depart.

It has been that sort of series, really; so many periods of ascendancy abruptly terminated by moments of genius, madness and confusion, and so many subversions of the pattern recognition Test cricket followers can normally rely on to impose a sense of order on what they're looking at.

South Africa finished the so-called moving day at 4-140 and 40 runs ahead. It would have wanted to be further in front. It could easily have been far worse off.

Earlier, in the latter stages of its first innings of 429, Australia probably let an extra 100 runs go begging. It sets up a perfect scenario even for those Australian fans who are not normally night owls: a thrilling finish on Friday night into Saturday morning.

On a pulsating day that produced 243 runs and 10 wickets, there was a second Test century for the recalled Josh Inglis and 80 for Alex Carey, both of whom fell to the off-spin of Simon Harmer.

In a Test featuring plenty of runs, only Josh Inglis has reached triple figures. (Getty Images: Grant Pitcher/Gallo Images)

An obscurity to most Australians before this series, and tipped to be dropped after the first Test, Harmer was in the thick of everything again with four wickets, two catches, a busted finger and plenty of chatter.

Youngster Cooper Connolly, looking entirely at home at Test level, made a patient 29 from 83 deliveries and might have kicked on further with better support from Australia's tail; the loss of 6-59 to finish off Australia's first innings was, as Pat Cummins often phrases such things, not ideal.

Yet it was still a 100-run lead, and early in South Africa's second innings you got the sense the game was about to break right open for an early finish.

In quick succession, Aiden Markram, who has been a thorn in Australia's side, lazily slapped a loose one from Starc into the clutches of Head at mid-off, and David Bedingham, seemingly rattled by a Starc bouncer that cannoned into his chest, holed out with another inexplicable hook.

The Proteas were 2-31, still 69 runs behind, and the hyenas were circling.

Via the counter-attack of Ackerman, then in a slow and steady partnership between Temba Bavuma and Matthew Breetzke, South Africa began its rally. Yet there was one last twist in store with barely 15 minutes left in the day's play.

Having tortured Bavuma for a few hours with his sharp turn out of the footmarks, Nathan Lyon removed the Proteas skipper again, this time a dipping off break that snuck between bat and pad to castle the lunging batsman. Bavuma is not quite to Lyon what Daryll Cullinan once was to Shane Warne, but he is not far off.

Proteas captain Temba Bavuma posed a major threat to Australia. (Getty Images: Grant Pitcher/Gallo Images)

On the matter of hoodoos, much has been made in recent days of Cummins's record-breaking streak without a wicket.

It continued today, despite periods in which the Aussie skipper bowled with genuine pace and guile, although his desperation to break his drought was made clear by one ill-advised review. Even when it is 1.6 metre Bavuma in the firing line, it is always difficult to get an LBW call when it hits above the batsman's knee roll.

In truth, the odd brain fade was perfectly excusable due to the ratcheting up of the atmosphere as this game progressed.

Some testiness and conflict in this series was inevitable, but it has manifested in curious ways. Each team's most vocal player — Marnus Labuschagne for Australia, Matthew Breetzke for the Proteas — has been its worst performed.

Breetzke, in fact, finally started to come good late on day three, and will resume tomorrow believing he is the man to turn the game for his country.

Given the way these two teams have echoed each other's efforts in the past few weeks, perhaps that suggests one last tantalising and slightly mad prospect in the Australian chase: how about Marnus Labuschagne as the last-minute hero?

World.title: Quick hits: Marnus caught in ugly exchange after all-time send off
World.content:
Marnus Labuschagne was involved in an ugly moment of DRS drama after giving a retaliatory send-off, as Temba Bavuma threw his wicket away in the shadows of stumps.

Here are the quick hits from day three of the third Test between Australia and South Africa.

1. DRS drama and Labuschagne's ugly exchange

It was one of the most contentious moments of the series when, midway through the evening session, with South Africa 2-95 and still five runs behind, Mitchell Starc collected Marques Ackerman with a steepling, searing bouncer.

The South African lost his balance as the ball thudded into what looked to be a mixture of helmet and bat before flying to Cam Green behind the wicket.

The Australians went up and so did the umpire's finger.

Undoubtedly dazed from the contact, the batter regained his composure and met with partner Temba Bavuma.

Eventually, a referral was called for, but only as the DRS timer ticked to zero.

Ackerman called for the review as the timer hit zero. (Fox Cricket)

It was touch and go, but the officials deemed Ackerman had taken too long, despite the severity of the hit.

With the South Africans pleading their case to the umpires, the ever-vocal Marnus Labuschagne could be heard giving his own opinion over the stump mic.

"The timer's up, oh no, see you buddy!" Labuschagne said from his position at the other end of the wicket.

Meanwhile, Travis Head had made his way over to the South African camp.

"Heady, what are you doing mate? He's off!" Labuschagne could be heard saying.

Head, hands outstretched towards batter and umpire in what appeared to be a peace offering, turned back towards his team and replied.

"I'm just checking if he's alright," Head said.

Head made his way over to check on Ackerman. (Fox Cricket)

Reluctantly, Ackerman made his from the middle, but spent some time at the boundary in the futile hope of being called back.

Thankfully, the replays showed the ball had collected a thick edge before crashing into visor, meaning Ackerman was doomed to be out for 62 even if the review had been permitted.

The technology showed Ackerman was rightly given out. (Fox Cricket)

2. Bloodied Harmer keeps South Africa in the game

Simon Harmer, left, made the breakthrough in the first hour of day three. (AP Photo: Halden Krog)

With an advantage to press home at the beginning of day three, the set Australian pair of Alex Carey and Josh Inglis would have been hoping for at least another full session of batting.

The conditions were perfect, the pitch was flat, and things looked very promising as Inglis reverse-swept his way to a hugely impressive second Test century.

However, neither wicketkeeper-batter would see the other side of the first drinks break, with off spinner Simon Harmer once again doing the damage.

Only moments after ripping a nail and bloodying his fingers while attempting a low catch with his non-bowling hand, Harmer had Inglis caught behind for 102.

Harmer received some treatment on a torn nail before dislodging the two set batters. (Fox Cricket)

It was a brilliant delivery; drifting away, spinning in and kissing the outside edge of the Western Australian's blade.

Four overs later, a similarly exquisite off break had Carey (80) nudging to Aiden Markram at slip, and Harmer, a fingernail down, had dragged his side back into the game.

Australia's tail proceeded to eke out a 100-run first-innings lead, eventually dismissed for 429.

3. Marnus gives it to Bedingham

Labuschagne was in quite a mood on day three.

Before the DRS drama in the evening session, the Queenslander took quite some pleasure in giving it back to Proteas batter David Bedingham.

On day two, Matthew Breetzke had joyously celebrated Labuschagne's five-ball duck by leaping over the pitch and shouting directly at the Australian.

And when Bedingham holed out to Josh Hazlewood during the middle session on day three, Labuschagne responded in similar fashion.

The Queenslander had his chest puffed out as he ran towards the South African, face red and fist pumping, screaming what you can only imagine was something entirely considered and reasonable.

Bedingham was out for 11 and South Africa's second innings was already beginning to teeter at 2-31.

4. A strange moment on the hill

It was an unlikely proposal. (Fox Cricket)

It was a strange morning on the hill.

During the first session, the broadcast cameras found a man holding a sign that read: "Ryan Rickelton, is your mum single?"

The middle-aged gentleman received a good amount of screen time, which he used to blow kisses and adjust his sunglasses in a performance that probably wouldn't have endeared him to anyone in the Rickelton family.

Rickelton, South Africa's wicketkeeper-batter, was stony-faced in response, before pursing his lips and shaking his head solemnly.

The commentators were lost for words at what was an uncomfortable moment for everyone involved — and especially, you'd imagine, for Ryan Rickelton's mother.

5. Bavuma throws it away in the shadows of stumps

Stumps were in sight for Bavuma and Breetzke.

The South African pair had so diligently rebuilt South Africa's innings after Ackerman's dismissal, and had just eight more balls to survive.

But with shadows lengthening at Newlands and with the pitch offering more and more for the slower bowlers, Nathan Lyon conjured a little bit of magic.

It was the perfect off spinner's delivery; drifting, turning sharply and bowling a swinging Bavuma clean through the gate.

However, it was a wildly inappropriate shot from the usually so-considered Bavuma, and the South African captain couldn't quite believe what had happened.

Bavuma was a picture of regret on his way from the middle. (Fox Cricket)

He grimaced and shook his head as he made is way from the middle for 35, with South Africa finishing the day on 4-140 and just 40 runs in front.

World.title: Wallaby 'incredibly proud' as brother represents Australian Deaf Rugby
World.content:
For as long as he can remember, Wallabies back-rower Charlie Cale has always been able to rely on his older brother Jack.

Growing up in Sydney's northern suburbs, they would often team up together against the eldest of the Cale boys, Sam, in fierce backyard rugby battles.

Even when it came to studying during their school years, Charlie knew Jack was in his corner.

"He helped me with a lot of my schoolwork," Charlie fondly tells ABC Sport.

"There's been a few exams … he's helped me in a lot of ways, actually.

"That's the best thing about Jack. He's always been there for me and anyone else that has needed him.

"He's one of a kind."

Jack's encouragement is repaid by the support he receives from Charlie and Sam, who both keenly follow his career with the Australian Deaf Rugby (ADR) men's squad.

Last Tuesday night in Sydney, Charlie proudly presented Jack, Australia's vice-captain, with his official team tie ahead of the World Deaf Rugby Sevens Championship, which begin in Tokyo this weekend.

Australia's men's and women's squads are among the favourites to emerge triumphant once the tournament concludes on November 3.

Jack Cale (right) pictured with brothers Charlie (centre) and Sam. (Instagram: Tim Cale)

Jack is grateful to have Charlie and Sam's backing as he juggles rugby commitments with his job as a lawyer.

"It's always been really helpful having two brothers to go through a rugby career with," says Jack, who has played for Eastwood (Shute Shield) and Mosman (Subbies) at club level.

"We're always checking in with each other, trying to watch each other's games.

"Charlie, even with the limited time he gets outside of training with Brumbies and Wallabies squads, is always trying to watch our games as well."

Charlie Cale has played six Tests for the Wallabies. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde)

On the international stage

Jack's introduction to deaf rugby came out of the blue.

"In late 2022, I got a phone call from an old coach of mine on a Saturday morning," says Jack, who had played colts and grade rugby in Sydney by this stage.

"He gave me a call and said, 'Mate, there's this deaf rugby trial happening down at Hunters Hill.'

"Of course, I didn't know what he was talking about as I hadn't really heard anything before.

"I went down there and ran around in a bit of a sevens trial, for maybe 20 or 25 minutes.

"I didn't think I'd actually played that well. I didn't touch the ball that much.

"I came off the field and I wasn't sure what to expect."

Jack Cale during his Eastwood playing days. (Instagram: Tim Cale)

A letter arrived in the mail a few months later in early 2023, informing Jack he was selected in the ADR men's squad for the World Deaf Rugby Sevens Championship, which were being held in Córdoba, Argentina in April of that year.

There was one small problem, though.

Jack found out about his selection during the club rugby off-season, meaning he was not exactly at peak fitness.

"I had to get myself fit pretty quickly without any rugby training, which was a bit of a struggle," Jack laughs.

Australia finished runner-up in the men's competition at the 2023 world titles. (Instagram: Australian Deaf Rugby)

Jack worked his way back into shape and seamlessly joined the Australian line-up, which he helped lead in his vice-captaincy role.

They made the final, gallantly losing 20-5 to Wales, while Australia finished third overall in the women's competition.

In Tokyo, the men's squad faces England, Japan, Hong Kong China and Italy in the pool stage, with the top three advancing to the knockout rounds of the tournament.

The Australian women's team were presented with their ties in Sydney on Tuesday night. (Supplied: Alfred Naputo)

Australia is one of six teams in the women's draw, where it plays Fiji, England, Wales, New Zealand and a combined Barbarians team in a single pool.

Australian squads: Men: Tim Anstey (c), Jack Cale (vc), Anau Takiari, Ben Rogers, Charlie Jeffries, Cruz Lemming, Geofrey Reynolds, Kyle Howlett, Josh Chapman, Josh Doe, Royden Chatfield, Tom Witts, Dave Kearsey (coach) Women: Sydnee Cooke (c), Amy Reid, Ashanti Pennell, Bridie Searle, Bianca Roberts, Cathy Ross, Kari Massey, Khiara McCormick, Olivia Hall, Peta Stephens, Sally Faehrmann, Robbie Pirika (coach)

Each will progress, with the two top-ranked teams moving directly to the semifinals.

Having avoided Wales in the men's round-robin matches, Jack considers England to be Australia's main threat in the preliminary phase.

"You've obviously got to go match by match," Jack says.

"It's important to get through the pool stage as well as we can and then the mindset obviously shifts to the knockout stages.

"I'd consider us in the better pool for the opportunity to do that."

Embracing challenges

To participate in World Deaf Rugby tournaments, players must have an average bilateral hearing loss across both ears of at least 40 decibels.

The level of hearing loss varies from player to player in the Australian teams, which illustrates to Jack the importance of non-verbal communication during matches.

"I stepped into this environment where nothing was said on a rugby field," he says.

"It was a bit of a challenge to get used to that.

"But I also really enjoyed that challenge, being able to communicate with some of those guys whose hearing is a lot more affected than mine is."

The Australian men's team at Tuesday night's tie presentation. (Supplied: Alfred Naputo)

As much as Jack loves playing alongside his Australian teammates, he also gets a kick out of facing them in club rugby.

On one such occasion last year, he and Australian captain Tim Anstey opposed each other when Mosman met Newport in the NSW Subbies competition.

"It's pretty awesome playing against someone like that, who you now travel with on international tours," Jack says.

"But it's also surreal finding out that someone you might have been playing rugby against is also partially deaf and had the same struggles as you growing up, and you're now representing your country with them.

"It's pretty cool."

Tim Anstey (left) and Jack Cale after a Subbies match in 2025. (Instagram: Australian Deaf Rugby)

While Jack relishes every chance to represent Australia, spreading the message of inclusivity is just as important to him and everyone involved in deaf rugby.

ADR states its goal is to give every deaf and hard-of-hearing athlete the opportunity to play the game, regardless of their experience level.

"We want to find as many deaf or hard-of-hearing rugby players as we can," Jack says.

"It's really just word of mouth within deaf and hard-of-hearing communities."

Jack's family is also firmly behind the cause.

"I've got a lot of respect for this [ADR] program," says Charlie, who has played six Tests for the Wallabies.

"It gives these guys a platform and opportunity they may have lacked growing up.

"We know how much it means to Jack and therefore it means a lot to us."

Family support

Charlie got up early in the morning to watch Jack play at the world titles in Córdoba three years ago.

But a friendlier time zone will make it easier for him to follow his brother's progress in Tokyo.

"I don't think I've missed a game," Charlie says.

"I've woken up at 2am or 3am. I love watching him play."

Jack Cale (centre) with his parents Tim (left) and Sue. (Instagram: Tim Cale)

As he did in Córdoba, Jack will have his devoted mum and dad, Sue and Tim, barracking from the sidelines in Tokyo.

The Cale parents do everything possible to watch their three sons play rugby.

"I don't think our mother has missed a rugby game of ours in God knows how many years," Jack says.

"Dad is always on the phone, straight after games, checking in with us and seeing how we've gone."

Just as he helped Charlie all those years ago with his schoolwork, Jack knows he can also depend on the support of his family.

"We're incredibly proud of him," Charlie says.

World.title: WBBL season gets underway with Thunder thumping of Renegades
World.content:
Anika Learoyd has carved out a career-best innings as the Sydney Thunder began its WBBL campaign with a convincing six-wicket win over the Melbourne Renegades in the season opener.

Learoyd made 48 off 37 balls after off-spinner Georgia Voll (4-26) did most of the damage in the first match of a double-header at Junction Oval today.

The Melbourne Stars host the Hobart Hurricanes in the night game.

In at first drop, after Voll made 25 off 18, including the Thunder's only six of the match, Learoyd hit nine boundaries and put on 62 with Heather Knight in a match-winning third-wicket partnership.

The pair took 28 runs from the power surge, putting the Thunder within sight of victory.

Knight (29 not out off 22 balls) and Nadine de Klerk (12no off six) finished the job, guiding their team to 4-140 with 18 balls to spare.

Learoyd admitted feeling "really nervous" batting near the top of the order, but will take confidence from starting the season with a strong performance.

Earlier, Voll's four wickets and hand in a run-out were crucial in restricting the Renegades to 9-138 from their 20 overs.

Renegades opener Hayley Matthews gave her side a strong start, blasting 45 from 30 balls before holing out in the deep.

Matthews put on 56 for the first wicket with Courtney Webb (22 from 24), and Georgia Wareham made a handy 23 from 19, but a late-innings collapse ended their chances.

The Renegades lost 5-2 in seven balls through the 17th and 18th overs as Voll wreaked havoc.

AAP

Tech.title: The director of Obsession put a new horror short on YouTube
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Curry Barker, the director behind the hit horror film Obsession, just published a new horror short on YouTube. The short, titled “Mama Bear,” is nearly five minutes long. The video is pretty unnerving, and fair warning that it gets a little graphic, but it’s a fun one to watch if you’re looking for something scary ahead of Halloween on Saturday.

Barker wrote, directed, and edited “Mama Bear,” according to the description for the video, which was published on his that’s a bad idea YouTube channel. The description also has a note thanking Windows for “sponsoring this short film,” and Barker was featured in an Instagram video earlier this week with a Surface laptop.

Barker will follow Obsession with Anything but Ghosts, which debuts in May 2027. Horror is big business right now, with the film Backrooms, directed by YouTuber Kane Parsons, also proving to be a big box office success this year. Parsons debuted a new Backrooms YouTube episode in August.

Tech.title: Intel says it’s selling every affordable laptop chip it can make
Tech.content:
During Intel’s latest earnings call, CEO Lip-Bu Tan said that demand for its budget-focused Wildcat Lake chips “is outstripping supply.” According to CFO David Zinsner, the chips are now sold out. Zinsner said Intel has “seen significant growth in Wildcat Lake. It’s coming exactly at the right time because it’s cost-optimized and we’re seeing a lot of focus in that regard.”

As shortages of RAM and other components have driven up PC prices over recent months, Intel’s Wildcat Lake chips have been appearing in new lower-cost Windows laptops on par with the MacBook Neo, like the new Dell XPS 13 or the HP Omnibook 5 14. Wildcat Lake laptops like these have budget-friendly starting prices, but often with just 8GB of RAM, which Windows laptops can struggle to get by on.
